{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15e330d2baaa644ec10bc714fcdd93a5b89163ac895e536f314465a8b83d5176","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 195 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, let $p^\sigma\equiv p^\sigma(\bXi)$ denote the empirical averages
	\[
	\frac1M\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Similarly, let $p^\Ising\equiv p^\Ising(\bXi)$ denote the empirical average
	\[
	\frac1N\sum_{i\le N}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then $p^\sigma(\bXi) \le o_{\trK}(1)$
for all $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, with probability
at least $1- \exp(-N^{1/2})$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{p}^\sigma$ be defined as $p^\sigma$, but with $[-\trK+1,\trK-1)$ in place of $[-\trK,\trK)$.
Let $f:\R\to\R$ be the Lipschitz function defined by
	\[f(x)=\begin{cases}
	0 & \textup{if $|x|\le \trK-1$,}\\
	1 & \textup{if $|x|\ge \trK$,}\\
		|x|-(\trK-1)
		&\textup{if $\trK-1
			\le |x| \le \trK$}\,.
	\end{cases}\]
Since $\ind\{x\notin[-\trK,\trK)\} \le f(x)
\le \ind\{x\notin[-\trK+1,\trK-1)\} 
$, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have
	\[p^\sigma(\bXi)
	\le
	F^\sigma(\bXi)
	\equiv
	\frac1M
	\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	f(X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a))
	\le \bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)
	\,.
	\]
We first argue that the \emph{annealed} expectation of $\bar{p}^\sigma$ is small for each $\sigma$. Note that since $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}$ is frozen upon leaving $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ (Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the probability that $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d,a)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ is maximized at time $d=\dmax$. From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), this is the same as the probability that $\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ at time $d=\dmax$. This (annealed) probability can be bounded using the proof of  Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}: recall from \eqref{e:A.H} that the event $A(H)$ has probability tending to zero as $H\to\infty$. On the complement of $A(H)$, the paths
$\bar{D}^\RomI$,
$Y^\RomII$, $Y^\RomIII$, $Y^\Ising$
are all $\gamma$-H\"older with H\"older norm $O(H)$, and in particular the maximum deviation of each path must be $O(H)$.
Moreover, since $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges uniformly to zero, the discrepancy between $\bar{D}^\RomI$ and $Y^\RomI$ converges uniformly to zero, so we can conclude that the maximum deviation of $Y^\RomI$ is also $O(H)$.
If we take $H$ to be a small constant multiple of $\trK$, then we conclude that $\E[\bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$. A similar argument gives 
$\E[\bar{p}^\Ising(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$. 

The above implies that the annealed expectation of each $F^\sigma$ is also small. It remains to show that $F^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about this expectation. For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$,
it follows by Corollary~\ref{c:conc.empir.avg} 
that $F^\sigma$ is $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta N^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. It follows by 
Assumption~\ref{a:params} that this Lipschitz constant is very small, for instance,
	\[
	\frac{L^{O(1)}}{\delta N^{1/2}}
	\ll \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\,.
	\]
By the Kirszbraun extension theorem, there exists a function $\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)$ which agrees with $F^\sigma$ for $\bXi\in U_\MAX$, but such that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is $(1/N^{1/3})$-Lipschitz on the entire space. 
It follows by standard concentration bounds (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about its mean $\E[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)]$. We finally bound
	\[
	\E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	\le \E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi);(U_\MAX)^c\Big]
	\le 
	\E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+\bigg\{ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)^2\Big]
	\P\Big((U_\MAX)^c \Big)
	\bigg\}^{1/2}
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,.
	\]
In the last step, we used that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is Lipschitz so its second moment must be bounded, while  \eqref{e.MAX.bound} implies that $\P((U_\MAX)^c)$ is very small. This proves the claim for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, and a similar argum (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.824261+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15fd6074c77e7bd55dc5626d307030a5c30082c7283d18312c4dd9a9480a702c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 27 (Weak equilibrium measure and weak capacity) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Suppose Assumptions~\ref{ass:U} and~\ref{ass:controlled-coefficients} hold,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:20:15.680512+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15fd6ec87090236d5bb37307c8d16b73cf0ee534e03cd8965832e82f623371b6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:max-ear-forest of arXiv:2609.00944, 'The Ramsey threshold for trees versus odd cycles'] Let \(G\) be a graph, \(W\subseteq V(G)\) a clique, and set \(U=V(G)\setminus W\). 
Let \(L_0\) be an integer satisfying \(|W|+2\le L_0\le |V(G)|\). 
Suppose that \(G\) contains no cycle through \(W\) of length at least \(L_0\). 
Let \(\mathcal P\) be a family of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint nontrivial \(W\)-ears 
(such ears have their endpoints in \(W\) and all internal vertices in \(U\)) 
chosen to maximize the total number of internal vertices, and let \(F\) be the linear forest 
on \(W\) formed by the endpoint pairs of the ears in \(\mathcal P\).

Define
\[
\rho=\sum_{P\in\mathcal P}|V(P)\cap U|,\qquad
U_{\mathrm{free}}=U\setminus\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}V(P),
\]
and let \(W_{\mathrm{int}}\) denote the set of vertices of degree \(2\) in \(F\). 
Then the following hold:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \(\displaystyle |U_{\mathrm{free}}|\ge |V(G)|-L_0+1.\)

\item[(ii)] For each \(u\in U_{\mathrm{free}}\), the set \(N_G(u)\cap(W\setminus W_{\mathrm{int}})\) is contained in a single path component of \(F\) and has size at most \(2\); if it has size \(2\), it is precisely the set of endpoints of that component.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(a) f_n >= 0 measurable","(b) sum_n integral |f_n| dmu < infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752150+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_161f0473e05bf76a88262094c5be25c7d5ddcdbbee8494f99bd8cb784a8fb953","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f_n measurable. (a) If f_n >= 0 for every n then integral sum_n f_n dmu = sum_n integral f_n dmu in [0, infinity], with no integrability hypothesis. (b) If sum_n integral |f_n| dmu < infinity then sum_n f_n converges absolutely mu-almost everywhere, the sum is in L^1(mu), and integral sum_n f_n dmu = sum_n integral f_n dmu. The hypothesis in (b) is on the sum of the integrals of the ABSOLUTE VALUES; convergence of sum_n integral f_n alone is not enough. Failure: on R with Lebesgue measure let f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} - 1_{[n+1, n+2]} for n >= 0. Each integral f_n = 0 so sum_n integral f_n = 0, but the partial sums telescope to 1_{[0,1]} - 1_{[N+1, N+2]}, so sum_n f_n = 1_{[0,1]} pointwise off the integer endpoints, with integral 1. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.15 and its corollary]","status":"unverified"}

where

C_{\varphi}:=C_{\mathrm{cost}}+4L_{\mathrm{pot}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287467+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1637051eb8cf9971561070e4866638ef1c48ccf7f1cba15a2067c2bee9fa4a90","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Delta-bound of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in[0,1)$ and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $[-1,1]$ with
		$\int m^2\,\mu(\mathrm{d} m)=q$.
		For $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$, let $(X_t^{\mu,\zeta})_{t\in[q,1]}$ be the
		Auffinger--Chen process (equation eq:AC mu of the paper), set
		\[
		u_\zeta(t,x):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,x),
		\]
		and define
		\begin{equation}
			\Delta_\zeta^\mu
			:=
			\int_{[q,1]}
			\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl[u_\zeta(t,X_t^{\mu,\zeta})^2\bigr]-t\Bigr)\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item
			For every $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$,
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|\le 1.
			\]
			
			\item
			Let $\zeta_\mu$ be the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{TAP}(\mu,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal P([q,1])$.
			Assume that $\mu$ is supported in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]$ for some
			$\delta\in(0,1)$, and let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$ satisfy
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0.
			\]
			Then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)$ such that
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|
			\le \frac{C}{\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta,\zeta_\mu).
			\]
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.237774+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1640493759a801066c3bc341079b93aca8a08a5c8115e39e23bc5001f57ab49f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm pd of arXiv:2607.00311, 'Thermal Concentration and Poisson--Dirichlet Edge Statistics for Random-Lattice Gibbs Ense'] Let $L_n$ be distributed according to $\mu_n$ on $\mathbb X_n$.
Let $c>1$ and put $\alpha=1/c$.
Order the sign classes of $L_n^\sharp$ by increasing $\tau_n$ and write them as $\bm u_{n,1},\bm u_{n,2},\ldots$.
Define
$$
W_{n,j}^{(c)}=
\frac{g_{n,c}(\tau_n(\bm u_{n,j}))}
{\sum_{\bm u\in L_n^\sharp}g_{n,c}(\tau_n(\bm u))}
$$
and $W_{n,c}=(W_{n,1}^{(c)},W_{n,2}^{(c)},\ldots)$.
Then, as a random element of $\ell^1$,
$$
W_{n,c}\Rightarrow W_c:=
\left(
\frac{T_1^{-c}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}T_k^{-c}},
\frac{T_2^{-c}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}T_k^{-c}},
\ldots
\right).
$$
Since $0<T_1<T_2<\cdots$, the sequence
$T_1^{-c},T_2^{-c},\ldots$ is already ordered in decreasing order.
Thus $W_c$ is a normalized ranked mass sequence.
Moreover, $W_c$ has the Poisson--Dirichlet distribution $\operatorname{PD}(1/c,0)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.870142+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_165ff34db6bc3cc369d91e4b314263e1ac9e3fcbd44087b4f5f843871197f4c6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop average-degree-bridge-alternatives of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Fix $\rho\in(0,1]$ and a constant $d_{\rm av}>0$. Let
\[
G^{(k)}=(I^{(k)},J^{(k)},M^{(k)})
\]
be a deterministic sequence of weighted bipartite graphs, where
$M^{(k)}\in\mathbb R^{I^{(k)}\times J^{(k)}}$.
Assume
\[
|I^{(k)}|=k,\qquad |J^{(k)}|=n_k,\qquad \frac{n_k}{k}\to\infty.
\]
Assume the following properties hold for all sufficiently large $k$:
\begin{itemize}
\item The support graph of $G^{(k)}$ has \hyperref[def:local-sparse-four-cycle-incidence]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{local sparse four-cycle incidence}}}{} with parameter $\varepsilon_k\to0$.
\item The average right degree is at most $d_{\rm av}$:
\[
\frac1{n_k}\sum_{j\in J^{(k)}}

\]

\[
\frac1{|E^{(k)}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in E^{(k)}} |M^{(k)}_{ij}|

\]

\end{itemize}
Let $r(k)$ be an integer sequence with $\rho k\le r(k)\le k$.

\[

\]
with probability $1-o(1)$ at least one of the following holds:

\begin{enumerate}

\item $G^{(k)}[\Omega_k]$ contains distinct degree-one right vertices $j,j'$ with the same unique left neighbor:
\[

\]
for some $i\in I^{(k)}$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:43:18.739906+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_166e86f2916346589a730c0a49a041aa7695da522c8755eb47ad9d5dcfa7a0ea","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi error_tree of arXiv:2609.02346, 'Regularised double shuffle relations for planar \AZVs{}'] Let $T\in\text{PT}_{\N^*}$ be a planar rooted tree. We define its \emph{error term $T^e$} as follows: if $T$ is a ladder tree (eventually empty), then $T^e=0$. Otherwise, let $(a,b)$ be its minimal incomparable pair, write $T=B_+^{n_1}\circ\cdots\circ B_+^{n_p}(B_+^{n_a}(F_a)B_+^{n_b}(F_b)F)$ as before and set
  \begin{align*}
   T^e = & B_+^{n_1}\circ\cdots\circ B_+^{n_p}(B_+^{n_a+n_b}(F_aF_b)F) \\
   & - \sum_{i=1}^{n_a-1}\binom{n_a-i+n_b-1}{n_b-1}B_+^{n_1}\circ\cdots\circ B_+^{n_p}\left(B_+^{n_a+n_b-i}(B_+^{i}(F_a)F_b)F\right) \\
   & - \sum_{i=1}^{n_b-1}\binom{n_b-i+n_a-1}{n_a-1}B_+^{n_1}\circ\cdots\circ B_+^{n_p}\left(B_+^{n_a+n_b-i}(B_+^{i}(F_b)F_a)F\right)
  \end{align*}
  where the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n_a-1}$ (resp. $\sum_{i=1}^{n_b-1}$) is taken to be zero if $n_a=1$ (resp. if $n_b=1$).
  
We extend the map $T\mapsto T^e$ to a map on $\mathcal{PT}_{\N^*}$ by linearity.
  

 
  
  
  Recall that for $T\in\mathcal{PT}_{\N^*}$, $\operatorname{pr}(T)$ is a tree decorated by elements of $\mathcal{PT}_{\N^*}$ and that $\delta_{\operatorname{pr}(T)}$ is its decoration map. Then, we define the linear map $\phi : \mathcal{PT}_{\N^*}\longrightarrow\mathcal{PT}_{\N^*}$

by
  \[
  \phi(T) = T + \sum_{v\in V(\operatorname{pr}(T))}\left(\delta_{\operatorname{pr}(T)}(v)\right)^e
  \]

  
  The map $\mathfrak{s}^{PT} : \mathcal{PT}_{\N^*}\longrightarrow\mathcal{PT}_{\{x,y\}}$

is defined by
  \[
  \mathfrak{s}^{PT}(T) = \mathfrak{s}^{PN}\circ \phi(T).
  \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438459+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_1676fc5d4bd4204464d67994de31ed5e2340561ded554ac315e0ddd82660b53e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens whenever $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:15:15.480132+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_167fd91756639976202da0e4c7e3691276c949cb74c5da1f938524e6c17b0112","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d-centering of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] \noindent  Given a continuous distribution $F$ function
on $[0,1]^{d}$ with density $f_{F}$ and continuous marginal d.f.'s $F_{i}$
and densities $f_{i}$, $i=1,\dots ,d$, we set $T_{i}^{F}=F_{i}^{-1}$ and
write $X^{F}=(X_{1}^{F},\dots ,X_{d}^{F})$ for a random vector with law $F$.
Denote also the mixed moment by
\begin{equation}
I_{F}\;=\;E(\prod_{i=1}^{d}X_{i}^{F})\;=\;\int_{[0,1]^{d}}(
\prod_{i=1}^{d}u_{i})\,dF(u_{1},\dots ,u_{d}).  
\end{equation}

Given $F$ as above with $I_{F}>0$, the \textit{Lorenz curve} $L_{F}$ is
defined by 
\begin{equation}
L_{F}(x_{1},\dots ,x_{d})\;=\;\frac{1}{I_{F}}\int_{[0,T_{1}^{F}(x_{1})]
\times \cdots \times \lbrack
0,T_{d}^{F}(x_{d})]}(\prod_{i=1}^{d}u_{i})\,dF(u_{1},\dots ,u_{d}),\qquad
(x_{1},\dots ,x_{d})\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d}.  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16c4740aba5042f3ad9a84b6ae1bd62bd1bf991539a3fb69e1d53e6dcfa0170f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:cyclic-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Put $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$ and $D=\max A$.  For
$q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, let $L_q(A)$ be the real span of the homogeneous
relation vectors of relation degree at most $q$, and put
$r_q(A)=\dim L_q(A)$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every $q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$,
\begin{equation}
 |qC|=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(q,\ell-1)}|(q-j)A|.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for $X\in\{A,C\}$ put
\[
 \mathcal H_X(z)=\sum_{q\geq0}|qX|z^q.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal H_C(z)=\mathcal H_A(z)[\ell]_z,\qquad
 [\ell]_z=1+z+\cdots+z^{\ell-1}.
\end{equation}

\item Let
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_A&=K[x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}],&
 \psi_A&:S_A\longrightarrow K[u,v],\\
 \psi_A(x_i)&=u^{D-a_i}v^{a_i},&
 I_A&=\ker\psi_A,\qquad R_A=S_A/I_A.
 \end{aligned}
\]
be the standard-graded projective semigroup ring of $A$.  Put
$S_C=S_A[y]$, and let $I_C$ be the kernel of the homogeneous toric map
\[
 x_i\longmapsto u^{\ell(D-a_i)}v^{\ell a_i},\qquad
 y\longmapsto u^{\ell D-c}v^c,
\]
so that $R_C=S_C/I_C$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 R_C\cong
 R_A[y]\big/\bigl(y^\ell-x_0^{\lambda_0}\cdots
 x_{m-1}^{\lambda_{m-1}}\bigr).
\end{equation}
The displayed polynomial is homogeneous and regular.  In particular, if
$R_A$ is Cohen--Macaulay, then so is $R_C$.

\item Define the ambient $K$-polynomials by
\[
 \mathcal K_A(z)=(1-z)^m\mathcal H_A(z),\qquad
 \mathcal K_C(z)=(1-z)^{m+1}\mathcal H_C(z).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K_C(z)=\mathcal K_A(z)(1-z^\ell).
\end{equation}
If $\beta^A_{i,j}$ and $\beta^C_{i,j}$ are the standard-graded Betti
numbers over $S_A$ and $S_C$, respectively, extended by zero outside their
natural homological and internal degree ranges, then
\begin{equation}
 \beta^C_{i,j}
 =\beta^A_{i,j}+\beta^A_{i-1,j-\ell}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with $\xi$ an indeterminate recording homological degree, put
\[
 \mathcal B_A(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^A_{i,j}\xi^iz^j,
 \qquad
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^C_{i,j}\xi^iz^j.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\mathcal B_A(\xi,z)(1+\xi z^\ell).
\]

\item Label the coordinates of $C$ by the tuple
$(\ell a_0,\ldots,\ell a_{m-1},c)$.  They need not be in increasing order;
this changes $L_q(C)$ only by a coordinate permutation.  Put
\[
 w_{\ell,c}=(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m-1},-\ell).
\]
Under the old-coordinate embedding,
\begin{equation}
 L_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  L_q(A),&q<\ell,\\[2mm]
  L_q(A)\oplus\mathbb Rw_{\ell,c},&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Hence
\begin{equation}
 r_q(C)=r_q(A)+
 \begin{cases}
  0,&q<\ell,\\
  1,&q\geq\ell,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
and the multiset of active-relation birth degrees is the old multiset with
$\ell$ adjoined.

\item Define the order-$q$ Freiman dimension by
\[
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(A)=m-1-r_q(A).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  \operatorname{fdim}_q(A)+1,&q<\ell,\\
  \operatorname{fdim}_q(A),&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}

\item One has
\begin{equation}
 \max C=\ell D,\qquad
 \operatorname{ndiam}(C)=\ell\operatorname{ndiam}(A).
\end{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.593192+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16c9007132245d13f2d08b6537da60e74aeb63ba493d10f1e9cd4849460eb60d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02820, 'Sharpness and critical scaling of parking'] In the parking model, each site of the $d$-dimensional lattice independently starts with one car with probability $p$ or one parking spot with probability $1-p$. Cars move according to independent discrete-time simple random walks and park at the first spot they find free. We prove that in the critical regime $p=1/2$, the expected number of visits to a site in $n$ rounds is of order $n^{(4-d)/4}$ for $d\\leq3$ and $\\log n$ for $d\\geq4$. We also prove that in the subcritical regime $p\\in(0,1/2)$, the parking-time tail is bounded above and below by stretched exponentials with exponent $d/(d+2)$. As $p\\uparrow1/2$, we also determine the divergence of the expected total number of visits to a site: its order is $(1-2p)^{-3}$, $(1-2p)^{-1}$ and $(1-2p)^{-1/3}$ in dimensions one, two and three, respectively, and $\\log(1/(1-2p))$ in dimensions four and higher. Our proof uses a representation of the parking process as the divisible sandpile of \\citet{LevinePeres09} plus a martingale-type term. These results answer questions posed by \\citet{DGJLS}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:23:58.630824+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16cb21b36c8e86118f894e8402ccda959ed96f179a2b523e65e47678e5717028","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Preferential Attachment with Vertex Death) of arXiv:2505.06187, 'Preferential Attachment Trees with Vertex Death: Persistence of the Maximum Degree'] Let $b\colon\N_0\to (0,\infty)$ and $d\colon \N_0\to [0,\infty)$ be two sequences. We recursively construct a sequence of trees $(T_n)_{n\in\N}$ and a sequence of sets of vertices $(\cA_n)_{n\in\N}$ as follows. We initialise $T_1$ as a single vertex labelled $1$ and $\cA_1=\{1\}$. For $n\geq 1$, conditionally on $T_n$ and $\cA_n$, if $\cA_n\neq \emptyset$, we select a vertex $i$ from $\cA_n$ with probability 
		\be 
		\frac{b(\deg_n(i))+d(\deg_n(i))}{\sum_{j\in \cA_n} b(\deg_n(j))+d(\deg_n(j))}.
		\ee 
		Then, conditionally on $T_n$ and $i$, we either \emph{kill} vertex $i$ with probability 
		\be 
		\frac{d(\deg_n(i))}{b(\deg_n(i))+d(\deg_n(i))}, 
		\ee 
		and set $T_{n+1}=T_n$ and $\cA_{n+1}=\cA_n\setminus\{i\}$, or otherwise construct $T_{n+1}$ from $T_n$ by introducing a new vertex $n+1$ which we connect by a directed edge to $i$ and set $\cA_{n+1}=\cA_n\cup\{n+1\}$.
		
		If $\cA_n=\emptyset$, we terminate the recursive construction, set $T_i=T_n$ for all $i>n$, and say that \emph{the tree has died}. When $\cA_n\neq \emptyset$ for all $n\in\N$ we say that the \emph{tree process survives}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:52:57.675242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16cd9a22835cdde01668d655408aed5023a2d9dbb36f5d83b0c61f0a74e6d30e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 10 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional $(n\geq 2)$  forward complete connected Finsler metric measure manifold with $\Lambda_{F}<\infty$. Assume that $\mathbf{S}\geq 0$. Let $R_{0}>0$ be a constant.
Given $p\in (\frac{n}{2}, n]$, $\alpha\in [\frac{1}{2},1)$. Then we can get the following results.
\ben
\item[{\rm (1)}] There exists a nonnegative constant $\varepsilon_{0}=\varepsilon_{0}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\alpha,R_{0})$ such that when $\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{\Lambda_{F}^{2}}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, 0}\leq \varepsilon_{0}$,
we have
\be
{\rm{diam}}(M)\leq \frac{\Lambda_{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{F}+1)\pi}{2}. 
\ee
In particular, $M$ is compact.

\item[{\rm (2)}]  If $(M, F, m)$ further satisfies ${\rm Ric}_{\infty}\geq -K$  for some $K\geq 0$, there exists a nonnegative constant $\bar{\varepsilon}_{0}= \bar{\varepsilon}_{0}(n,p,\Lambda_{F}, \alpha, R_{0}, K, \vartheta_{0})$ such that when $\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{\Lambda_{F}^{2}}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, 0}\leq \bar{\varepsilon}_{0}$,  $\pi_{1}(M)$ is finite.
\een","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E X^2 < infinity (finite variance); with only a finite mean use Markov on |X - mu|","t > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.625865+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_16e67a3e90398ddbb9bc39a2380f27c36c12b66fd99444ceee8f8badbc90a232","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with finite mean mu = E X and finite variance sigma^2 = Var X. Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; equivalently P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0. The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:07:17.249910+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16f88382207b24b703b8686ed90f343d07556ab8abc0f32900b9c46eb27bfd7f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition SAGBAsd of arXiv:2603.12774, 'Synchronization by noise for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Browni'] Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space, and let \(\mathbb{T}\) denote either \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{R}^+\), each equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra.  
	A family of mappings \(\theta = \{\theta_t\}_{t \in \mathbb{T}}\) on \(\Omega\) is called a \emph{measurable dynamical system} if the following conditions hold.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item The mapping \((t, \omega) \mapsto \theta_t(\omega)\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(\mathbb{T}) \otimes \mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{F}\).
		\item The identity condition is satisfied at \(t=0\), i.e., \(\theta_0 = \mathrm{Id}\).
		\item The semigroup property holds: \(\theta_{s+t} = \theta_s \circ \theta_t\) for all \(s, t \in \mathbb{T}\).
	\end{itemize}
	If there exists a probability measure \(\mathbb{P}\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) such that
	\[
	(\theta_t)_{\ast}\mathbb{P} = \mathbb{P}, \quad \forall\, t \in \mathbb{T},
	\]
	then the quadruple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}, \theta)\) is called a \emph{measurable metric dynamical system}.  
	Furthermore, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}, \theta)\) is said to be {ergodic}, if for every \(t \in \mathbb{T} \setminus \{0\}\), the transformation \(\theta_t\) is ergodic, meaning that for any \(A \in \mathcal{F}\),
	\[
	\mathbb{P}\big(A \triangle \theta_t^{-1}(A)\big) = 0
	\quad \Rightarrow \quad 
	\mathbb{P}(A) \in \{0,1\}.
	\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496537+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_170a8c0ed9d440deafd94b25f05a132b55b7e6990435394e80b498acd886fcf1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 (Conditional Bernoulli domination) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $N\ge1$, and let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i=0}^{N}$ be a filtration.  For

measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_i$.  Suppose that, on $R_i$,
\[
        \Prob(I_i=1\mid \mathcal F_{i-1})\ge p_i
\]
for deterministic numbers $0\le p_i\le1$.

Define the completed variables
\[
        \widehat I_i :=
        \begin{cases}
        I_i, & \text{on }R_i,\\
        1,   & \text{on }R_i^c.
        \end{cases}

Let $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_N$ be independent Bernoulli variables with

        \le

Consequently, if $A$ is any event such that $A\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^{N}R_i$,
then

        \le

\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.728289+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_172bc858eb1c73e60b40446ae5de47aabe472c9c0d9e5ef901683368df18cae9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:snake complex of arXiv:2608.29986, 'Khovanov-Rozansky homology over $\F[U,V]$'] [popovic2023link]
Let $m \in 2\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} _0+1$ and let $b_1, \dots, b_{m}$ be a sequence of nonzero integers. A \emph{horizontal snake complex} $S_h(b_1, \dots, b_{m})$ is a free chain complex over $\mathcal{R}_1$ with a distinguished basis $B=\{x_0, \dots, x_m\}$ and a differential $\partial$ defined as follows. For each odd $i$, there is a horizontal arrow of length $|b_i|$ connecting $x_i$ and $x_{i-1}$. For each even $i$, there is a vertical arrow of length $|b_i|$ connecting $x_i$ and $x_{i-1}$. The direction of the arrow is determined by the sign of $b_i$, as follows. If $b_i > 0$, then the arrow goes from $x_i$ to $x_{i-1}$, and if $b_i < 0$, then the arrow goes from $x_{i-1}$ to $x_i$. The $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \oplus\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \oplus\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} $ grading on $S_h(b_1, \dots, b_m)$ is allowed to be arbitrary subject to the condition that $\mathrm{gr}(\partial) = (-1, -1, -2)$.

Similarly, let $m \in 2\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} _0$ and let $b_0, \dots, b_m$ be a sequence of nonzero integers. A \emph{vertical snake complex} $S_v(b_0, \dots, b_m)$ is a free chain complex over $\mathcal{R}_1$ with a distinguished basis $B=\{x_{-1}, \dots, x_m\}$ and a differential $\partial$ defined exactly as above.
    
A \emph{snake complex} refers to either a standard complex, a horizontal snake complex, or a vertical snake complex.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:50:26.965511+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_174800d752ee597b1d353ec0d5ff05416021f54967b9b3f03cd9e3c92a0c9a11","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:geodesics_from_b of arXiv:2505.09604, 'Exceptional force, uncountably many solutions in the KPZ fixed point'] Let $b:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function satisfying, for all $s < t$, and $x \in \mathbb{R}$
\begin{equation} 
b(x,t) = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{R}} [b(z,s) + \mathcal{L}(z,s;x,t)], 
\end{equation}
and assume that for each $t > s$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, leftmost and rightmost maximizers in the equation above exist in $\mathbb{R}$. Define $g_{(x,t)}^{b,L/R}(s)$ to be the leftmost/rightmost maximizers, and set 
\[
g_{(x,t)}^{b,L/R}(t) = x.
\]
Then, the following hold
\begin{enumerate} [label=(\roman*), font=\normalfont]
\item  $g_{(x,t)}^{b,L}:(-\infty,t] \to \mathbb{R}$ \rm{(}resp. $g_{(x,t)}^{b,R}:(-\infty,t] \to \mathbb{R}$\rm{)} is a semi-infinite geodesic that is the leftmost (resp. rightmost) directed landscape geodesic between any two of its points. In particular, $g_{(x,t)}^{b,L}$ and $g_{(x,t)}^{b,R}$ are continuous functions $(-\infty,t] \to \mathbb{R}$.
\item  Let $s < r < t$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $
w = g_{(x,t)}^{b,L}(r)$.
Then,
\[
g_{(x,t)}^{b,L}(s) = g_{(w,r)}^{b,L}(s),
\]
and the same holds when replacing $L$ with $R$. 
\item 
More generally, let $t = s_0 > s_1 > \cdots$ be any decreasing sequence with $\lim_{n \to \infty} s_n = -\infty$. Set $g(t) = x$, and for each $i \ge 1$, let $g(s_i)$ be \textit{any} maximizer of $z \mapsto b(z,s_{i}) + \mathcal{L}(z,s_i; g(s_{i - 1}),s_{i - 1})$ over $z \in \mathbb{R}$. Then, pick \textit{any} point-to-point geodesic of $\mathcal{L}$ from $(g(s_{i}),s_{i})$ to $(g(s_{i-1}),s_{i-1})$, and for $s_{i} < s < s_{i-1}$, let $g(s)$ be the location of this geodesic at time $s$. Then, $g:(-\infty,t] \to \mathbb{R}$ is a semi-infinite geodesic. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:48:00.289320+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1758be006d4791d9ea2272232b96955304ec58a87ad81ad227ee897196d3dc85","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn band of arXiv:2609.03033, 'An Overview of Einstein $4$-Manifolds'] Let $M$ be a smooth compact oriented $4$-manifold

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:56:03.903543+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_175f513f5446d77ee3e1d74a479dc199f8630e0b0a2a4aeeee93d60c8091420d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 4 (Martingale and Local Martingale Criteria) of arXiv:2606.20925, 'Explicit Predictable Compensators for Single Jump Processes with Initial Information'] Let $\cT=\{t\in\RR_+:\PP(\gamma\ge t)>0\}$. 
    Let $F=(F(t))_{t\in\cT}$ be an $\cH$-measurable process with càdlàg paths, and let $L$ be an arbitrary random variable. 
    Consider the process $M=(M_t)_{t\in\RRl_+}$ defined by the equality $M_t=F(t)\ind{\{t<\gamma\}}+L\ind{\{t\ge\gamma\}}$.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item The process $(M_t)_{t\in\cT}$ is a martingale if and only if for all $t\in\cT$, the integrability condition $\EE[|M_t|]<\infty$ holds, and $\EE[M_t-M_0\mid\cH]=0$ almost surely.
        \item Assume further that $\EE[\sup_{t\in[0,t_G)}|F(t)|]<\infty$ and $\EE[|L|]<\infty$. The process $M$ is a local martingale on $\RRl_+$ if and only if $(M_t)_{t\in\cT}$ is a martingale, and the boundary equality $\EE[L\mid\cH]\ind_{\{\gamma=t_G\}}=F(0)\ind_{\{\gamma=t_G\}}$ holds almost surely on the set $\{\gamma=t_G\}$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Write $\langle\cdot\rangle$ for expectation under $G_{A,\beta,y_t}$.  For $k<\ell$ let
$\partial_{k,\ell}:=\partial/\partial A_{k\ell}$ denote differentiation with respect to the
\emph{independent} upper-triangular GOE entry (so $A_{\ell k}=A_{k\ell}$), and let $\partial_{k,k}:=\partial/\partial A_{kk}$.

Define centered spins and centered ``edge'' observables by
\[
m_i:=\langle\sigma_i\rangle,\qquad 
\widetilde\sigma_i:=\sigma_i-m_i,\qquad
\widetilde{\sigma_{ab}}:=\sigma_a\sigma_b-\langle\sigma_a\sigma_b\rangle.
\]
Then for every $k<\ell$, every $i,j\in[n]$, and every $k_i,k_\ell\in\{1,2\}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_{k,\ell}\,\langle\sigma_i\rangle^{k_i}
&= (2\langle\sigma_i\rangle)^{k_i-1}\,\beta\,\big\langle \widetilde\sigma_i\,\widetilde{\sigma_{k\ell}}\big\rangle,\\
\partial_{k,\ell}\,\langle\sigma_\ell\rangle^{k_\ell}
&= (2\langle\sigma_\ell\rangle)^{k_\ell-1}\,\beta\,\big\langle \widetilde\sigma_\ell\,\widetilde{\sigma_{k\ell}}\big\rangle,\\
\partial_{k,\ell}\,\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle
&= \beta\,\big\langle \widetilde{\sigma_{ij}}\,\widetilde{\sigma_{k\ell}}\big\rangle,\\
\partial_{k,\ell}\,\langle\sigma_i\sigma_\ell\rangle
&= \beta\,\big\langle \widetilde{\sigma_{i\ell}}\,\widetilde{\sigma_{k\ell}}\big\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, for every $k\in[n]$ and every observable $F(\sigma)$ one has $\partial_{k,k}\langle F\rangle=0$
(in particular $\partial_{k,k}\langle\sigma_i\rangle^{k_i}=0$ and $\partial_{k,k}\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle=0$).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Recurrent symmetric Markov process; base point o; inverse local time at o","GFF with covariance the Green function of the process killed at o, independent of the process","Identity in law, not a pathwise coupling"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988309+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_178ab0e20429fbcabddf72bded46fbdf579084e30b0d6607f8a57c199cde4f8b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Generalised second Ray-Knight theorem (Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000): let X be a recurrent symmetric Markov process on a countable state space (for instance continuous-time random walk on a finite connected graph, or on Z^2), started at a base point o, and let tau(u) be the inverse local time at o, the first time the local time at o reaches u. Let (phi_x) be the Gaussian free field on the state space with covariance the Green function of X killed at o, independent of X. Then the field (L^{tau(u)}_x + (1/2) phi_x^2)_x has the same law as ((1/2)(phi_x + sqrt(2u))^2)_x. Dynkin-type isomorphisms exist for transient processes killed at an independent exponential time (there the shift is absent). Uses: transfer of DGFF extremal results to local-time level sets and cover times (Ding-Lee-Peres via the Gaussian free field maximum), thick points of random walk, and the Sabot-Tarres and Lupu loop-soup couplings. Limits: the isomorphism identifies laws, not couplings, of the two sides unless the stronger Lupu coupling is used; the sign of phi is lost in the square, so events about level sets of the local time correspond to two-sided level sets of phi + sqrt(2u). Typical failure: Using the generalized second Ray-Knight isomorphism but omitting or misplacing the additive shift sqrt(2T) term that appears when T is a fixed constant rather than an inverse-local-time stopping time, as in the classical Brownian motion Ray-Knight theorems; dropping or mislocating this shift silently changes which boundary or starting condition the isomorphism is actually describing. Canonical reference: Ray, 1963, Illinois Journal of Mathematics; Knight, 1963, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society; Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000, Annals of Probability; Lupu, 2016, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

The mechanism is a filling-scheme lemma: for theta an invertible ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard Borel space (E, P) and Q = f P, there is an almost surely finite integer N >= 0 with law(theta^N Z) = Q for Z distributed as P. Apply it with E = C_0(R) under two-sided Wiener measure and (theta w)(t) = w(t+1) - w(1), lifting the one-sided density of X's law to two-sided paths; the lemma returns a finite N for which {Z(N+t) - Z(N)} has X's law while {Z(t) - Z(0)} is a Brownian motion whose first N units are exactly the prefix. Verification as the source words it: the filling construction was implemented on a finite ergodic system (Z/n with the +1 shift) for n = 5, 7, 12, 60 with random densities - total accepted mass 1.000000000000 every time, the law of theta^N Z matching f P to about 1e-16, E[N] finite - and the negative control is the informative one, since with a non-ergodic theta exactly half the mass is ever accepted and half survives forever. The L^1 ergodic-theorem step in the infinite-dimensional setting was not verified, only read; it is standard but checked by eye only. {"assumptions":["the signs are independent and symmetric; the identity E S^4 = 3 (sum a_i^2)^2 - 2 sum a_i^4 uses E epsilon_i^4 = 1 and E epsilon_i^2 epsilon_j^2 = 1 for i different from j","coefficients are real (the complex and vector-valued versions hold with modified constants; Kahane's inequality is the Banach-space extension)","dependent or asymmetric signs are not covered"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049237+00:00","domain":"anti-concentration and moment inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_1796c911ceeffee80cd7700c686eb05fc27456d52abdbb661721b8f2800206a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let epsilon_1, ..., epsilon_n be independent Rademacher signs (each +1 or -1 with probability 1/2) and a_1, ..., a_n real numbers, and write S = sum a_i epsilon_i and ||a||_2 = (sum a_i^2)^{1/2}. Khintchine's inequality (1923): for every 0 < p < infinity there are constants A_p, B_p depending only on p with A_p ||a||_2 <= (E|S|^p)^{1/p} <= B_p ||a||_2. The second moment is exact, E S^2 = ||a||_2^2. The fourth moment is an identity, not just a bound: E S^4 = 3 (sum a_i^2)^2 - 2 sum a_i^4, so E S^4 <= 3 ||a||_2^4 and B_4 <= 3^{1/4}, with the constant 3 approached as the coefficients spread out (many equal a_i) and never attained; this is the Gaussian fourth moment. Sharp constants: A_p = 1 for p >= 2 and B_p = 1 for p <= 2; A_1 = 1/sqrt 2 (Szarek 1976); for p >= 3, B_p equals the p-th moment of a standard Gaussian to the power 1/p (Haagerup 1981). The lower bound for p < 2 is the nontrivial direction and is what the fourth-moment identity gives via the Paley-Zygmund argument: E|S| >= (E S^2)^{3/2} / (E S^4)^{1/2} >= ||a||_2 / sqrt 3.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.440159+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17a363859b908eec170a980f956f73eebed6a91c169ca9d0696704afdfdc7d11","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 (Sufficient Maximum Principle for Nonzero-Sum Game) of arXiv:2604.02998, 'Nonzero-Sum Stochastic Differential Games for Controlled Convection-Diffusion SPDEs'] Let \( (\widehat{u}_1(t), \widehat{u}_2(t)) \in \mathcal{U}_1 \times \mathcal{U}_2 \) be a candidate Nash equilibrium, with associated state process \( \widehat{Y}(t,x) \) solving the state equation under \( (\widehat{u}_1, \widehat{u}_2) \), and let \( (\widehat{p}^i(t,x), \widehat{q}^i(t,x)) \) be the corresponding adjoint processes solving the BSPDE for player \( i = 1,2 \).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:29:35.085258+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17aa6ecc14d91aac53427da3a44bd27b9189422364ad9cacb946612e721c1960","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 31 of arXiv:2609.03803, 'List-distance consistent vertices in trees are confined to a path'] Let $c$ be a labeling of $G$. A vertex $u\in V(G)$ is
\emph{list-distance consistent}, or simply \emph{consistent}, under $c$ if
\begin{equation}
 d(u,v)<d(u,w)\ \Longrightarrow\ c(u,v)\le c(u,w)
 \qquad (v,w\in V(G)).
 
\end{equation}
Let $S_c(G)$ be the set of consistent vertices under $c$, and define
\[
 \ldc(G)=\max\{\,|S_c(G)|:c\text{ is a labeling of }G\,\}.
\]
A labeling attaining the maximum is \emph{optimal}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:18:19.215592+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17ab9c48b7c671c5b019d28d4fba03dbd3a4b0e15bd201a7f8afb0d92737667a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] The \\textit{composition monoidal structure} on $\\catname{sSeq}$ is given on objects by $$\\left(\\X \\circ \\Y\\right)(n) = \\coprod_{\\substack{k \\\\n_1+ \\ldots +n_k=n}} \\X(k) \\otimes_{S_k} (\\Y(n_1) \\otimes \\Y(n_2) \\otimes \\ldots \\Y(n_k)) \\otimes_{S_{n_1} \\times \\ldots \\times S_{n_k}}\\coprod_{S_n}\\textbf{1}$$ where the action of $S_k$ on $\\Y(n_1) \\otimes \\Y(n_2) \\otimes \\ldots \\Y(n_k)$ permutes the different factors, and the action of $S_{n_1} \\times \\ldots \\times S_{n_k}$ on $\\coprod_{S_n}\\textbf{1}$ is given by pulling back the action of $S_n$ that permutes the factors by the homomorphism $$S_{n_1} \\times \\ldots \\times S_{n_k} \\rightarrow S_n$$ which constructs a permutation by blocks from the starting ones. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.517022+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17ac9b6b3c7c5a3bd7569ad2c4456c44584801f1bf206d729d4c840db7691052","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm conformal covariant solutions of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] For a multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) system with $n$ SLEs starting from $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ with a marked boundary point $u \in \partial \overline{\mathbb{H}}$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
Two partition functions $\widetilde{\psi}$ and $\psi$ are considered \emph{equivalent} if they differ by a multiplicative factor $f(u)$.
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\psi}=f(u)\cdot\psi
\end{equation}
where $f(u)$ is an arbitrary positive real smooth function depending on the marked boudary point $u$.
Under this equivalence, $\tilde{\psi}$ and $\psi$ induce identical multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) systems.
\item[(ii)]
Within the equivalence class, we can choose $\psi$ to satisfy conformal covariance, that this, under a conformal map $\tau \in {\rm Aut}(\mathbb{H})$, the function $\psi(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n,u)$ transforms as
\begin{equation}
\psi(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n,u)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tau'(z_i)^{\frac{6-\kappa}{2\kappa}}\right)\tau'(u)^{d}\psi\left(\tau(z_1),\tau(z_2),\ldots,\tau(z_n),\tau(u)\right)
\end{equation}
where we understand $\tau'(u)$ as
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\tau(u) \neq \infty, u \neq \infty$,  $\tau'(u)$ is defined as usual,
\item If $\tau(u)=\infty$, $u \neq \infty$ 
    \[
   \tau'(u):= \left(-\frac{1}{\tau(u)}\right)'
    \]
    \item If $\tau(u)\neq \infty$, $u= \infty$
    \[
    \tau'(u):= \left(-\frac{1}{\tau(0)}\right)'
    \]
    \item If $\tau(z)=az+b$ and $u=\infty$,
    \[
    \tau'(u):= a^{-1}
    \]
\end{itemize}
Here, $d$ is an undetermined real constant, representing the scaling exponents at $u$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.752514+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17d70e18ae0d318b2d606d663e30e9e5a5b56f4563f75fc3467328d3c16dfeae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 27 (Critical shapes) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Let $p \sim c/m$ for some $c > 0$
  and let $\tau_c$ be the first hitting time of
  $0$ in the birth-death process defined by
  Lemma~\ref{thm:birth-death}.
  If $G$ is a standard Gumbel random variable,
  independent of $\tau_c$, then
  $(T_{m,p} - m\log{m})/m$ converges in law to $G + \tau_c$.
  \begin{proof}
    Lemma \ref{thm:coupling} reveals
    $(T_{m, p} - m\log{m})/m$ is the independent sum
    of $(T_{m,0} - m\log{m})/m$ and $(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})/m$.
    The first term converges to $G$ weakly
    by Lemma~\ref{thm:subcritical}.

    The second term has \textsc{mgf} $I_{m,p}(t/m)$ for $t < 0$,
    \[
      M_{(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})/m}(t)
      = (1-p)^m
      \left[
        1
        -
        \int_0^1 p \, m
        \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(-t/m)-m}
        \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx
      \right]^{-1}.
    \]
    Then since $p\,m \to c$ and $(1-p)^m \to e^{-c}$,
    the integrand is bounded and we have
    access to the dominated convergence theorem;
    for each $0 < x < 1$ it holds
    \[
      p\,m\left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(-t/m)-m} \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
      \longrightarrow e^{c} \left(1-x\right)^{-t}
      e^{-c x},
    \]
    which implies
    \[
      M_{(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})/m}(t)
      \longrightarrow e^{-c} \left[
        1 - \int_0^1 c \left(1-x\right)^{-t} e^{-c x} \, dx \right]^{-1}.
    \]
    This is the \textsc{mgf} of $\tau_c$ (Lemma~\ref{thm:birth-death}).
    So, we have shown $M_{(T_{m, p} - m \log{m})/m}(t)
    \to M_G(t) \, M_{\tau_c}(t) = M_{G+\tau_c}(t)$
    for all negative $t$. The convergence theorem confirms
    $(T_{m,p} - m \log{m})/m \Rightarrow G + \tau_c$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.665921+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17dfeaed2837ded39a1da2749902d7e6fbbee44bb1f7bb8da280d1291593bd73","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 5 (Invariant energy and quotient-length inequalities) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(h(t)\) be an invariant Ricci flow on a torus bundle,

\[

\qquad
\norme{\varphi'-\varphi_\varepsilon'}_\infty \leq C M \varepsilon^{1-\gamma}
\]
and, for any $\lambda \in \R$,
\[
\abs{\varphi_\varepsilon''(\lambda)} \leq C M \left(1+ (\abs{\lambda} \vee \varepsilon)^{-\gamma} \right)
\qquad \text{and} \qquad

\]
where $C>0$ depends only on $\gamma$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.017038+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_18296be7bbb41655dd7dcec7f6508ad46af579d4f6f439b065e064fefd895f09","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 9 (Forward functions and cancellation of birth-time gauges) of arXiv:2608.15137, '2608.15137'] Use the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:arbitrary-path-kernel} and Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-moment}. Put
\[
 d_T=Q,\qquad h_T(x)=\ee^{-x}.
\]
For $t<T$, put $h_t(x)=1$ and
\[
 d_t=
 \begin{cases}
 q_t,&\epsilon_t=0,\\
 p_t,&\epsilon_t=1.
 \end{cases}
\]
For real $x$ and $1\leq i\leq p_t$,
\begin{equation}
 F_i^{(t)}(x)
 =
 \frac{\rho_i!}{(p_t-i)!(q_t-i)!}
 h_t(x)x^{d_t-i}.
\end{equation}
For $i>p_t$, $F_i^{(t)}$ vanishes on the real part of $E_t$ and

If

 H_{ij}=(P+Q-i-j)!,

 \frac{(P-i)!(Q-i)!}{(p_t-i)!(q_t-i)!}
 h_t(y)y^{d_t-i}.
\end{equation}
Thus the birth-time factors $\rho_i!$ cancel from every real finite-rank summand.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a random process {X_t} on an index set T whose supremum carries an additive penalty, sup_t {Z_t + E[X_t]}, or a multiplicative weight, sup_{s,t} (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s)","levels α_k ↓ 0 with ρ(s, t) ≤ α_0 for all s, t, chosen so that the slice bounds are summable","a tail bound for the supremum without penalty over each slice, for example chaining for a separable subgaussian process","Theorem 5.32: a separable subgaussian process on (T, d) with N(T, d, ε) ≥ (c/ε)^q for some c, q > 0 and all ε > 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T19:52:52+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1845074a256b709360802c12c5c466795b77806e8cda52ab2f5b7d7af338081e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD. The slicing method controls a penalized or weighted supremum of a random process: cut the index set into slices on which the penalty lies between two levels, remove the penalty on each slice, and add the slice bounds with a union bound. Each remaining term is the supremum of a process without penalty, which chaining can control. van Handel, Section 5.4: writing X_t = E[X_t] + Z_t with subgaussian fluctuations Z_t, sup_t X_t = sup_t {Z_t + E[X_t]} is a penalized supremum of a subgaussian process with E[X_t] as the penalty, and chaining is suited to the fluctuations but not to the penalty. In the multiplicative setting (the additive one works the same way), for the weighted supremum of (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s), fix α_k ↓ 0 with ρ(s, t) ≤ α_0 for all s, t; on the slice {α_k ≤ ρ(s, t) ≤ α_{k−1}} the weight is bounded above and below, and a union bound gives P[sup_{s,t} (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s) ≥ x] ≤ Σ_{k≥1} P[sup_{ρ(s,t) ≤ α_{k−1}} {X_t − X_s} ≥ α_k x]. The sets {ρ ≤ α_{k−1}} shrink as k grows while the levels α_k x fall, so the penalty and the levels must be chosen to make the probabilities summable; that tuning is specific to each application. Worked example, Theorem 5.32 (modulus of continuity): if {X_t} is a separable subgaussian process on (T, d) and N(T, d, ε) ≥ (c/ε)^q for some c, q > 0 and all ε > 0, then ω(δ) = ∫_0^δ sqrt(log N(T, d, ε)) dε is a modulus of continuity for {X_t}, and E[sup_{t,s} (X_t − X_s)/ω(d(t, s))] < ∞. The proof slices with α_k = ω(Δ2^{−k}), Δ = diam(T), bounds each slice by the local chaining inequality (Proposition 5.35: P[sup_{d(t,s) ≤ δ} {X_t − X_s} ≥ C ∫_0^δ sqrt(log N(T, d, ε)) dε + x] ≤ C e^{−x²/(Cδ²)}), and uses ω(2δ) ≤ 2ω(δ). By Remark 5.34 the covering-number condition is technical: ω is still a modulus of continuity without it, by a more delicate tuning of slicing and chaining. Problem 5.12 (Empirical risk minimization I: slicing) applies the slicing argument to the excess risk R(t̂_n) − R(t*) of the empirical risk minimizer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.160847+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_18571d9c45a4f5d524bcdbb0400357e50d0b097b00c84088970b11fcd0baf060","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma localization-on-homs of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $\textbf{\textup{C}}$ be a locally fibrant simplicial model category (e.g.\ the underlying simplicial model category of topological model category), and let $X,Y\in\textbf{\textup{C}}$ with arbitrarily chosen cofibrant replacement $\alpha\colon X'\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;} X$ and fibrant replacement $\beta\colon Y\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;} Y'$.     \[

    \]
    induced by the localization $N_\Delta(\textbf{\textup{C}})\to N_\Delta(\textbf{\textup{C}})[{\mathcal{W}}^{-1}]$ agrees up to postcomposition with an equivalence with $\beta\circ{-}\circ\alpha\colon\textbf{\textup{maps}}(X,Y)\to\textbf{\textup{maps}}(X',Y')$.

{"assumptions":["each f_n differentiable on [a,b], with [a,b] a bounded interval","(f_n(x_0)) converges for at least one point x_0","f_n' -> g uniformly on [a,b]"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751029+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_18620c87505e98d6c532146546254519319c9d12188204bf60601298432ca6cc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be differentiable on [a,b], suppose the numerical sequence (f_n(x_0)) converges for SOME x_0 in [a,b], and suppose f_n' -> g uniformly on [a,b]. The hypothesis that must be uniform is on the DERIVATIVES: uniform convergence of f_n itself is neither necessary nor sufficient. Convergence of f_n at one point cannot be dropped either: f_n = n has f_n' = 0 -> 0 uniformly and f_n converges nowhere. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.17]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.676179+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1898ce779607886d0090d1bb1c3e34f9deaef9dd465043a46d6bb80b05dba0b0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 (Causal spaces and stable-causal maps) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] A \emph{causal topological space} is a Hausdorff topological space
$\mathsf S$ with continuous truncations $\rho_t^{\mathsf S}$ satisfying
\[
 \rho_T^{\mathsf S}=I,
 \qquad
 \rho_s^{\mathsf S}\rho_t^{\mathsf S}
 =\rho_{s\wedge t}^{\mathsf S}.
\]
A \emph{causal uniform space} is a Hausdorff uniform space equipped with
uniformly continuous truncations satisfying the same identities.  A map
$R:\mathsf S\to\mathsf T$ between causal topological spaces is
\emph{stable-causal} if it is continuous and
\begin{equation}
 \rho_t^{\mathsf T}R
 =\rho_t^{\mathsf T}R\rho_t^{\mathsf S},
 \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\end{equation}
Between causal uniform spaces, a stable-causal map is additionally required to
be uniformly continuous.  A stable-causal map used to extract one state from
another is called a \emph{stable-causal readout}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space; no metrisability, compactness or separation axiom is required","each f_i is upper semicontinuous as a map into the extended reals (continuity is the special case used most often)","the family is nonempty; the index set may be uncountable","the infimum is taken pointwise, and values -infinity and +infinity are allowed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.089930+00:00","domain":"general topology, semicontinuity","id":"claim_18da4caf8dac6a3433a1aa1a053da36b492c033651287018a2b335ad110cf583","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space (no separation or countability axiom is needed) and let (f_i), i in I, be a nonempty family of functions f_i : X -> [-infinity, +infinity], each upper semicontinuous; in particular each f_i may be continuous. The index set I is arbitrary: finite, countable, or uncountable. Put f(x) = inf over i in I of f_i(x). Then f is upper semicontinuous: the set {x : f(x) < c} is open for every real c, equivalently limsup_{y -> x} f(y) <= f(x) at every point x. The standard consequence: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact space attains its supremum, so a variational problem whose objective is an infimum of continuous quantities always has a maximiser. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the direction is not symmetric. A SUPREMUM of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous, not upper: on R, sup over n >= 1 of min(1, n|x|) is the indicator of {x nonzero}, which is lower but not upper semicontinuous at 0. Quoting this result for a supremum is the common misuse. (ii) The infimum of an INFINITE family of continuous functions is in general not continuous: on [0,1], inf over n of x^n equals 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1. Only finite infima of continuous functions are continuous, so upper semicontinuity is the most one can claim. (iii) Upper semicontinuity of each member is exactly what is used; an infimum of merely lower semicontinuous functions has no semicontinuity property at all. (iv) The pointwise version localises: if each f_i is merely continuous AT a point x, the same proof gives limsup_{y -> x} f(y) <= f(x), i.e. upper semicontinuity at that one point, which is the form most often needed in practice.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134177+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_18de152cd6b3f3dde27fe3acec21197ea05d1c17bca342890c19af231c9bf2ed","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. For 0 <= t <= n let A_t f be the average over t-element sets T of E[f | X_T], and for 0 <= k <= n put P_k = binom(n, k) sum_{t=0}^k (-1)^(k - t) binom(k, t) A_t. Then P_k f = sum over |S| = k of f_S: P_k is the orthogonal projector onto the order-k part, so P_j P_k = 0 for j != k, P_k^2 = P_k, sum_k P_k = I and ||P_k f||_2^2 = W_k. If K_r f(x) is the average over |A| = r of E[f(X^(A)) | X = x], with X^(A) redrawing X_A independently, then K_r = A_{n - r}, so the same alternating combination of the K_{n - t} recovers each order.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.668353+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_18defea9a4734b62e04a92051577f1b370cf1a8346ef456e427e8ef4a3297cf2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 (Estimate of Extinction Time) of arXiv:2608.04716, 'Extinction Time Estimate for Subcritical (Binary) Homogeneous Crump-Mode-Jagers Processes'] Consider a birth death process with non-lattice lifetime random variable $\tau $.  Assume that $\lambda \E[\tau ]<1$ (subcritical case) and \linebreak $\lambda\E[\tau e^{-\alpha  \tau }]\neq 1$. 
Assume Malthusian parameter $\alpha<0$ exists.  We consider a sequence of initial configurations  indexed by $k\in \N$. For each configuration $k$, the initial population is given by a  non-negative, random integer-valued measure $Z_k$ on $\R_+$, where $Z_k(r)$ represents the number of individuals with age in the interval $[0,r]$ at time zero.   
Assume that the total number of individuals at time zero, $M_k:=Z_k(\infty)$, tends to infinity almost surely as $k\to \infty$. Furthermore, assume that
\begin{equation}
U:=\sup_{x\geq 0}\E[e^{-\alpha(\tau -x)}\mid \tau >x]<\infty
\end{equation}
and 
 the functions  $Z_k/M_k$ converge almost surely in  total variation distance  to  a non-decreasing random distribution  function  $B$, i.e. 
\[\lVert Z_k/M_k-B\rVert_{TV}:=\int_0^\infty \lvert  \d Z_k(  x)/M_k - \d B( x) \rvert \]
converges to zero almost surely  as $k\to \infty$.
Let
\[D:=\frac{1-\lambda \E[\tau]}{\lambda\E[\tau e^{-\alpha  \tau }]-1}\cdot\int_0^\infty\E\left[e^{-\alpha  (\tau -x)}-1\mid \tau >x\right] \d B(x)<\infty.\]
Let $T_k$ be the extinction time for configuration $k$. Then, as $k\to \infty$, the random variables $$-\alpha  T_k-\log( M_k)-\log(D)$$ converges in distribution to a Gumbel random variable $Z$ with distribution function $\P(Z\leq r)=e^{-e^{-r}}$. In other words, 
\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\P(-\alpha  T_k-\log( M_k)-\log(D)\leq r)=e^{-e^{-r}}.\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu is sigma-finite (needed for the Radon-Nikodym density)","nu is sigma-finite (needed for existence of the decomposition); for signed or complex nu, finite total variation","absolute continuity and mutual singularity are with respect to the same sigma-algebra M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402094+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Radon-Nikodym and decomposition","id":"claim_18fa6795088dd8fb6799c6e0c0ce7eb13ec14601000f98529cdd5659c067baeb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be SIGMA-FINITE positive measures on M. Then nu can be written as nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu_a << mu) and nu_s mutually singular with mu (nu_s perp mu), and this decomposition is unique. Combined with the Radon-Nikodym theorem, nu_a has a density: there is an M-measurable f >= 0, unique up to mu-null sets, with nu_a(E) = integral_E f dmu for all E in M; f is in L^1(mu) exactly when nu_a is a finite measure. The statement extends to nu a signed or complex measure of finite total variation with mu sigma-finite. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) sigma-finiteness of nu is essential for existence of the decomposition. Take X = [0,1] with the Borel sets, mu = Lebesgue measure and nu = counting measure. If nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a << mu and nu_s perp mu, pick E with mu(E) = 0 and nu_s(X minus E) = 0. For any x outside E we get nu({x}) = nu_a({x}), and mu({x}) = 0 forces nu_a({x}) = 0, contradicting nu({x}) = 1. So X minus E is empty, i.e. E = X, contradicting mu(X) = 1 > 0. (b) sigma-finiteness of mu is essential for the DENSITY. With mu = counting measure on [0,1] and nu = Lebesgue measure one has nu << mu, yet no f satisfies nu(E) = integral_E f dmu (evaluating on singletons forces f = 0). The decomposition itself survives here (nu_s = 0), but the Radon-Nikodym half does not. (c) Uniqueness is uniqueness of the pair of measures; the density f is only mu-almost everywhere unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.893196+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19101d3b19fa7dede03e1f1d289b2f3b9303322e4f5bb44a12b4820ccaff511b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 (Large deviations principle) of arXiv:2607.12666, 'Sample-path Large deviations for \\Scheduled Arrival Processes with Unpunctuality'] Let $(E,\mathcal{T})$ be a topological space. A sequence of random elements $\{X^{(n)}\}$ taking values in $E$ satisfies a large deviations principle with speed $n$ and rate function $I:E\to[0,\infty]$ if:
\begin{itemize}
\item for every closed set $F\subset E$,
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log \Pbb(X^{(n)}\in F)
\le -\inf_{x\in F} I(x),
\]
\item for every open set $G\subset E$,
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log \Pbb(X^{(n)}\in G)
\ge -\inf_{x\in G} I(x).
\]
\end{itemize}
The rate function $I$ is called {\it good} if its level sets $\{x: I(x)\le M\}$ are compact for all $M<\infty$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.908629+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19104c4ec7e44a9fc076e2444a6a2914f7744e38a91674cb3836d82449cc1d70","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2nd_spectral_derivative of arXiv:2608.23765, '\texorpdfstring{Tight Majorizations and Convergence Rates\\ of Nuclear Norm Minimization I'] Let $f:\R_{\geq 0} \to \R$ be a differentiable function 
	with $L$-Lipschitz first derivative $f'$ such that $f'$ is right differentiable at $0$ and $f'(0)=0$.
	Then the spectral function $F: \R^{d_1 \times d_2} \to \R$, $F(\mathbf{X})= \sum_{i=1}^d f(\sigma_i(\mathbf{X}))$ is differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradients $\nabla F(\mathbf{X}) \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ and furthermore almost everywhere twice differentiable.
    Moreover, 
	$F$ is twice differentiable at $\mathbf{X} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ 
	if and only if $f$ is twice differentiable at all $\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{X}),\ldots, \sigma_{d}(\mathbf{X})$. 
	In that case, if additionally $d_1 \leq d_2$, 
	the Hessian $\nabla^2 F(\mathbf{X})$ of $F$ at $\mathbf{X}$ is given by
	\begin{equation} 
		\nabla^2 F(\mathbf{X})(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H}_1 \circ S( \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},1})
			+ 	
			\mathbf{H}_2 \circ T(\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},1})
			& \mathbf{H}_3 \circ (\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},2})\end{bmatrix}
		\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top
	\end{equation}
	for any $\mathbf{Z} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$, 
	where $\mathbf{X}$ has the SVD $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \diag(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top$ 
	with $\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_1}$, 
	$\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},1} & \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},2} \end{bmatrix} 
	\in \R^{d_2 \times d_2}$, $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},1} \in \R^{d_2 \times d}$, $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X},2} \in \R^{d_2 \times (d_2-d)}$, 
	$T$ and $S$ are as in (equation eq:sym_and_antisym of the paper), and $\mathbf{H}_1 \in \R^{d \times d}$ is such that for $i,j \in [d]$,
	\[
	(\mathbf{H}_1)_{ij} =
	\begin{cases}
		\frac{f'(\sigma_i) - f'(\sigma_j)}{\sigma_i - \sigma_j} & \text{ if } \sigma_i \neq \sigma_j, \\
		f''(\sigma_i) & \text{ if } \sigma_i = \sigma_j,
	\end{cases}
	\]
	the matrix $\mathbf{H}_2 \in \R^{d \times d}$ is such that for $i,j \in [d]$,
	\[
	(\mathbf{H}_2)_{ij} =
	\begin{cases}
		\frac{f'(\sigma_i) + f'(\sigma_j)}{\sigma_i + \sigma_j} & \text{ if } \sigma_i + \sigma_j \neq 0 , \\
		f''(\sigma_i) & \text{ if } \sigma_i = \sigma_j = 0,
	\end{cases}
	\]
	and $\mathbf{H}_3 \in \R^{d_1 \times (d_2-d)}$ is such that for $i \in [d_1], j \in [d_2-d]$,
	\[
	(\mathbf{H}_3)_{ij} =
	\begin{cases}
		f'(\sigma_i)/ \sigma_i & \text{ if } \sigma_i \neq 0 , \\
		f''(\sigma_i) & \text{ if } \sigma_i = 0.	
	\end{cases}
	\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.906461+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_192e85102ac0517447bde8b88ebb02932ceef80f285484291dec3cbac8dd77b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 21 (Restriction to the invariant real normal bundle) of arXiv:2609.00922, 'The Morse Index, Nullity and Jacobi Fields of Constant-Curvature 2-Spheres in Complex Proj'] The bundle $N_m^{\mathbb R}$ is parallel in
$N_{\phi_{0,2m}}S^2$.  Under the normal-bundle identifications induced by
$\pi$ and by the radius-doubling homothety,
\begin{equation}

 \left.J_{0,2m}\right|_{N_m^{\mathbb R}}
 =J_{F_m^{(2)}}=\frac14J_{F_m^{(1)}}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\tau_m$ fixes the tangent plane, acts as $-\Id$ on the central
normal plane, and
\begin{equation}

 \tau_m(E_r^-)=(-1)^rE_r^+,\qquad
 \tau_m(E_r^+)=(-1)^rE_r^-\qquad(2\le r\le m).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, in the coefficient convention of
\eqref{eq:normal-field-complex-coordinates},
\[
 \tau_mV=V
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 A_1=0,\qquad A_r^+=(-1)^rA_r^-\quad(2\le r\le m).
\]
Writing $E_{r,\mathbb R}:=E_r^-+(-1)^rE_r^+$ and denoting its oriented span
by $\mathcal N_r^{\mathbb R}$, one has
\[
 N_m^{\mathbb R}=\bigoplus_{r=2}^{m}\mathcal N_r^{\mathbb R}.
\]
On \(\mathcal N_r^{\mathbb R}\), \(t_u\) acts as rotation through the angle
\(2ru\); hence these angles are \(4u,6u,\ldots,2mu\).  For \(m=1\) the sum
is empty.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.390244+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19381903b99ce17351406d6c0730fb35a8c271119f8f15e6c9d09b52333bf7ed","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 125 (Admissible backward testing core) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] A linear operational class $\mathscr C_{\rm bw}^{1,2}$ of bounded
raw-adapted continuous trajectories is an \emph{admissible backward testing
core} if it is invariant under deterministic stopping and the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(A\arabic*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item Under every $P\in\cP$, each $Y\in\mathscr C_{\rm bw}^{1,2}$ is a
continuous square-integrable special semimartingale.  Write its normalized
canonical decomposition as
\[
 Y=Y_0+M^{Y,P}+A^{Y,P},
 \qquad M^{Y,P}\in\mathcal M^2(P),
\]
with $A^{Y,P}$ predictable of finite variation and both summands zero at
time zero.  For every $h\in H_0$, the pathwise covariation agrees $P$-a.s.
with the classical covariation of $M^{Y,P}$ with $\langle X,h\rangle$.
The agreement is required on one common full set for the countable basis
coordinates; real linearity then gives it simultaneously on $H_0$.
\item The covariations are pathwise absolutely continuous and their countable
basis densities $\lambda^Y(e_j)$ have predictable total versions.  For each
$Y$ there are a nonnegative predictable $g^Y$ and a $\cP$-polar set $N_Y$
such that, on $N_Y^c$, for
Lebesgue-almost every $t$, simultaneously for every $h\in H_0$,
\[
 |\lambda_t^Y(h)|
 \le g_t^Y\langle\mathfrak a_th,h\rangle_H^{1/2},
\]
and
\[
 \sup_{P\in\cP}E^P\int_0^T|g_t^Y|^2\,\dd t<\infty.
\]
Let $U^Y:=\iota_{\mathfrak a}D_Q^{\rm pw}Y$ be the predictable Riesz
section constructed in \Cref{prop:covariance-first-jet-riesz-forcing}.  It is
required that
\[
 [U^Y]\in\mathbb U_{\mathfrak a,\cP}^2
       =\operatorname{Ran}\mathfrak J_{\mathfrak a},
 \qquad
 [D_Q^{\rm pw}Y]_{\mathbb H_{\cP}^2}
 :=\mathfrak J_{\mathfrak a}^{-1}[U^Y].
\]
Equivalently, there are bounded elementary predictable integrands $Z^{Y,n}$
such that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\cP}E^P\int_0^T
 \|\mathfrak a_t^{1/2}Z_t^{Y,n}-U_t^Y\|_H^2\,\dd t=0.
\]
Thus the requirement is stronger than membership of $[U^Y]$ in the product of
the modelwise finite-energy spaces.
\item The covariation algorithm is linear and stopping compatible:
\begin{equation}
 D_Q^{\rm pw}(r_tY)=\one_{[0,t]}D_Q^{\rm pw}Y,
 \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\end{equation}
\item The observable testing graph defined in
\eqref{eq:backward-observable-testing-graph} is separable for the product
metric of $\mathbb S_{\cP}^2\times\mathbb H_{\cP}^2$.
\end{enumerate}
Thus \textup{(A2)} is a genuine common-completion assumption, stronger than
uniform modelwise energy; \textup{(A4)} only makes the completion causal
Polish.","status":"unverified"}

Let lambda be the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue of A with positive left and right eigenvectors u and v normalised so that the inner product of u and v is 1. Then the topological entropy of the shift is log lambda, and there is a UNIQUE measure of maximal entropy - the Parry measure - given by the Markov chain with transition probabilities P(i,j) = A(i,j) v_j / (lambda v_i) and stationary vector p_i = u_i v_i. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.135247+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_193ae20eac5b9ffc3dc999400701663da0908d35e07fe2b05fca1edc5424876f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 1 of arXiv:2608.22514, 'Diffusion limits of cyclic finite-velocity random motions\\ along vector fields'] Suppose that assumptions
$\mathbf{A}_V$,
$\mathbf{A}_\tau$,
$\mathbf{A}_{V,\mu}$ and
$\mathbf{A}_\varkappa$ hold. Then, for any initial values $x\in\bR^d$ and $\iota\in \{1,\dots,p\}$,
the flight evolutions $\{X^{\e,\delta}\}$ converge weakly in $C(\bR_+,\bR^d)$
to a diffusion $X$ starting at $x$ with the generator
\ba

Af
= \frac{\varkappa^2}{2\mu}  \sum_{i} \sigma_{i}^2 \langle \nabla^2 f  V_i, V_i\rangle
+ \frac{\varkappa^2}{\mu} \sum_{j< i} \mu_i\mu_j \langle \nabla f , D V_i [ V_j] \rangle,\quad f\in C^3_b(\bR^d,\bR).
\ea
The diffusion $X$ is a solution to an It\^o-SDE
\ba

\di X_t= \frac{\varkappa}{\sqrt\mu}  \sum_{i} \sigma_{i} V_i(X_t)\,\di W^i_t +
\frac{\varkappa^2}{\mu} \sum_{j< i} \mu_i\mu_j  D V_i [ V_j](X_t)\,\di t,
\ea
where $W^1,\dots,W^p$ are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions.
The SDE \eqref{e:SDEX} can be rewritten in the Stratonovich form
as
\ba

\di X_t= \frac{\varkappa}{\sqrt\mu}  \sum_{i} \sigma_{i} V_i(X_t)\circ\di W^i_t
-\frac{\varkappa^2}{2\mu} \Big(
\sum_{i} \lambda_i^2  D V_i [ V_i](X_t)
+\sum_{j< i} \mu_i\mu_j  [ V_i,V_j](X_t)

\ea (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.226521+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_193e8334d1374dda54c925e7c251a9ae7c58a5e2c7004596b57a589f5f2f136f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem trace power bfL-n-R asymp of arXiv:2608.23156, 'Disc counting statistics of the real Ginibre ensemble'] Let $N=2n$ be a positive even integer. Suppose that
$r\in(0,\infty)$ and
\begin{equation}
    R
    =

 \end{equation}
as $N\to\infty$, for some fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}$. Then, for every fixed

If $R\to\infty$, the same conclusion holds with

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:49:17.489181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_193efd20ef6fd63708925139db8203440adfdb10b9d0a1a9d3ca9a3c44e81aeb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Kadanoff--Ceva correspondence) of arXiv:2605.28473, 'The BKT transition and surface tension differentiability'] Let $G$ be any leafless connected finite planar graph endowed with edge weights
    $(J_{uv})_{uv\in E(G)}\subset[0,\infty)$.
    Let $G^*$ denote the dual graph, and extend $J$ to $E(G^*)$ via the natural duality bijection.
    Then for any boundary height function $\zeta:\partial G^*\to\Z$,
    we have
    \begin{equation}
        
        Z_{G^*,J}^\zeta =
        Z_{G,J}
        \Big\langle \prod_{u\in\partial G} (\sigma_u)^{\zeta_{u_+}-\zeta_{u_-}}\Big\rangle_{G,J},
    \end{equation}
    where $u_-$ and $u_+$ are the first dual vertices adjacent to $u$ in the clockwise
    and counterclockwise directions, respectively (Figure~\ref{fig:dual_graph}).
    Thus a boundary height jump across $u$ becomes the spin insertion at $u$.
    Adding a constant to $\zeta$ changes neither side of the identity.

    In particular, for $s\in(0,1)$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        
        \frac{Z_{\Lambda_n^*,\beta}^s}{Z_{\Lambda_n^*,\beta}^{0}}
        =
        \Big\langle
        \Big[
            \prod\nolimits_{u\in T_n(s)} \bar\sigma_u
        \Big]\Big[
            \prod\nolimits_{v\in B_n(s)} \sigma_v
        \Big]
        \Big\rangle_{\Lambda_n,\beta},
    \end{equation}
    where the top and bottom source sets are
    \begin{equation}
        
        T_n(s)=(I_s\cap[-n,n])\times\{n\},
        \qquad
        B_n(s)=(I_s\cap[-n,n])\times\{-n\},
    \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation}
        
        I_s:=\{k\in\Z:\lfloor s(k+\tfrac12)\rfloor>\lfloor s(k-\tfrac12)\rfloor\}.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["translation invariance","ergodicity under the translations","finite energy","an amenable transitive graph such as Z^d; the theorem FAILS on nonamenable graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543290+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19571635c9811ef2c4fa9bf7413abff7ada34807a8dc3b1fc48636004a01b663","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a probability measure on {0,1}^{E(Z^d)} that is (i) invariant under the lattice translations, (ii) ERGODIC with respect to them, and (iii) has the FINITE ENERGY property: for every edge e, the conditional probability that e is open given the states of all other edges lies almost surely strictly between 0 and 1. Then the number of infinite open clusters is almost surely a constant taking the value 0 or 1. Each of the three hypotheses does work. Ergodicity is what makes the number a constant rather than a random variable; without it a mixture of two percolation measures is a counterexample. Finite energy is what rules out infinitely many infinite clusters, by allowing local modifications; a measure that deterministically forbids certain local patterns can have infinitely many. And the argument uses AMENABILITY of Z^d - on a regular tree or another nonamenable transitive graph there is genuinely a regime with infinitely many infinite clusters, so the theorem is false there. Bernoulli percolation satisfies all three hypotheses for every p, so its infinite cluster is unique whenever it exists. [Burton and Keane (1989), Comm. Math. Phys. 121; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 8.1]","status":"unverified"}
