{"assumptions":["a Markov chain, here a Galton-Watson branching process, with an identified P-harmonic function h appropriate to the conditioning event","for Kesten's tree specifically: finite-mean offspring distribution with criticality or subcriticality correctly identified, and a precisely specified conditioning event","existence of the relevant weak-convergence limit of the conditioned law to the h-transformed law, which must be checked rather than assumed","correct identification of the size-biased offspring law along the spine, which differs from the original offspring law"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994756+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_195cce09417950c349c4fdda5edd9f33edbe4cce03fe18f997181d11d952556c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Given a Markov chain with kernel P and a nonnegative P-harmonic function h, the Doob h-transform defines a new Markov chain with kernel P^h(x,y) = P(x,y) h(y)/h(x), representing the law of the original chain conditioned, in an appropriate limiting sense such as conditioning to survive forever or on an asymptotic event, to respect the weighting given by h. Applied to a critical or subcritical Galton-Watson branching process conditioned to survive forever, or, for critical trees, conditioned to have total size n with n -> infinity, the Kesten tree construction realizes the limiting law as an explicit infinite random tree: a single infinite spine, with each spine vertex additionally carrying an independent number of extra children distributed according to the size-biased-minus-one offspring law, each extra child then supporting an ordinary, unconditioned Galton-Watson subtree. This gives the exact local weak limit of large conditioned critical or subcritical branching trees and underlies scaling-limit results, such as convergence to the continuum random tree, that first pass through this explicit infinite-tree description. It does not directly give scaling limits of the whole tree's metric structure, which requires an additional contour or height-function argument, and the exact form of the spine's offspring law is specific to the conditioning event used, since conditioning on survival forever and conditioning on total size n give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees. Typical failure: Confusing the different conditioning regimes for the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, such as conditioning on survival to infinity versus conditioning on total progeny exactly n as n -> infinity versus conditioning on height n, as if they all give the identical Kesten tree limit; they give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees, differing in the spine's offspring bias and finer distributional details, and using one variant's known properties for a computation set up under a different conditioning is a frequent, easy-to-miss error. Canonical reference: Doob, 1957, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Lyons, Pemantle and Peres, 1995, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.873192+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_196dc52f07f00d6043b3137b21fc6c200d1241e94baf64b25a1082e146b614ec","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:hill of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] The vertices of $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ are the non-terminal vertices of $G$, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{H}_u[G]) = \overline{Z}$. The edges and labels of $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ are acquired from those of $G$ through the following rules.
\begin{enumerate}[topsep=1em]
    \item If $j, k \in \overline{Z}$ are non-terminal vertices with $k \neq u$ ($j = u$ is allowed) and there is an edge $j \to_G k$, then there is an edge $j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} k$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} k) = \ell(j \to_G k) \,.
    \]
    \item If $j \in \overline{Z}$ is a non-terminal vertex and there is an edge $j \rightarrow_G u$, then there is an edge $j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u) = \ell(j \to_G u) + \sum_{j \rightarrow_G z ,\, z \in Z} \ell(j \rightarrow_G z) \,.
    \]
    \item If $j \in \overline{Z}$ is a non-terminal vertex other than $u$ ($j \neq u$) without an edge to $u$ ($j \not\to_G u$) but with at least one edge, $j \to_G z$, to some $z \in Z$, then there is an edge $j \rightarrow_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \rightarrow_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u) = \sum_{j \rightarrow_G z ,\, z \in Z} \ell(j \rightarrow_G z) \,.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
There are no other edges in $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the cleaners compared are consistent for the population covariance (sample, eta-RIE without floor, LW2020, NERCOME)","the ensemble error covariance is rank-deficient in practice (members near-collinear), so the unconstrained plug-in has near-null sample directions"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:18:07.916034+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_1979e55efac080980a9b8016771f4431a63d793eddbb97023ada620cc4079e30","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Read the ladder result (every consistent cleaner ties inside the long-only stack; floors and linear shrinkage lose) through the entrywise bound. The long-only plug-in's excess risk is bounded by twice the ENTRYWISE error $\\varepsilon = \\max_{ij}|\\hat\\Sigma_{ij} - \\Sigma_{ij}|$, which is $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ for the sample covariance and of the same order for every consistent estimator (a consistent nonlinear shrinkage moves the eigenvalues by $O(n^{-1/2})$ relative, hence the entries by the same order) - so all of them obey the same bound and, on the well-conditioned active submatrix, produce the same weights. A fixed floor $f\\sigma^2$ on the small eigenvalues, or a linear shrinkage $\\rho(\\mu I - \\hat\\Sigma)$, is a BIAS of size $f\\sigma^2$ (or $\\rho|\\mu - \\Sigma_{ii}|$) in the entries spanned by those directions that does not vanish with $n$; it cannot tighten the bound and it displaces the plug-in wherever an active member has weight in a floored direction. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351333+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_197fd81c61a387ed4f4ffa33aae87e6ff61a3b1bfc51e95f015c5e93be32b7ab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 186 (discrete quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\vY$ and $\vY^\frozen$ be the spatial rerandomization processes from Definitions~\ref{d:rerand} and \ref{d:rerand.Ising}. Let $\vD$ and $\vD^\frozen$ be the associated drift processes from Definition~\ref{d:D}.
We now let 
	\begin{align*}
	\vZ &\equiv \vY-\vD\,,\\
	\vZ^\frozen 
		&\equiv \vY^\frozen-\vD^\frozen\,,
	\end{align*}
so these are martingales with respect to the filtration $\cG(q_d)$ from \eqref{e:gaus.filt}. In this subsection we consider the ``quadratic variations'' (and ``covariations'') for the $Z$ processes. To this end, for $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, define 
$Q^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d) 
	=  \bE \bigg[
		\Big( \Delta Z^\sigma(q_d)\Big)
		\Big(\Delta Z^\tau(q_d)\Big)
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\,,\eeq
started from $Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_0)=0$. Clearly $Q^{\sigma,\tau}=Q^{\tau,\sigma}$; and we will also abbreviate $Q^{\sigma}\equiv Q^{\sigma,\sigma}$. We define likewise $Q^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A is normal"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T07:35:54.838059+00:00","domain":"matrix perturbation theory, pseudospectra and the Sylvester equation","id":"claim_1981cd0345bdb830c76a6ec391b8dab5cddfc4b539a21d002dd9da030a75238a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a normal n by n matrix A, sigma_min(zI - A) = dist(z, spec A) for every z, so Lambda_epsilon(A) is the union of the closed disks of radius epsilon about the eigenvalues. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.971484+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1981e897d5377aaadf9eacaaefa7656c08143c63a70f8bd35569330a86f0f4e1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 26 (Uniform logarithmic envelopes) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let \(r\ge1\), let \(T\) be compact, and suppose
\begin{equation}
 \|T\|_{\mathfrak W^{[r]}}\le b.
 
\end{equation}
Then \(T\in\mathcal S_2\), and there is a constant \(C_r\), depending

\begin{align}
 \mathfrak F_T(a)
 &\le C_r(ab)\bigl(\log(e+ab)\bigr)^{r-1},
 \\
 \zeta_T(1+\varepsilon)
 &\le C_r b^{1+\varepsilon}\varepsilon^{-r}.
 
\end{align}
The same bounds hold for every flattening of a tensor whose

Rees coefficient has been placed in grade \(r\), all upper Mellin and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.302412+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19a5425d5320073dffe4e7e97162d0002e041499308edf2a775c6e7dbda71421","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:band-limited-orbit-coding of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Fix

uniformly in $z\in Z$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Finally,

	-\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg|
	&\le2\eta\,.
	\end{align*}
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same holds with $(\vY^\frozen,\vX^\frozen)$ in place of $(\vY,\vX^\trunc)$.

\begin{proof}
We prove the estimate for
$Y^{\RomI}$ versus $X^{\trunc,\RomI}$; the other bounds follow by the same argument. It follows from the definition~\eqref{e:def.Y} that
	\[
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	= \sum_{a\in B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))}
	\frac{X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a)}{|B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))|}
	-\sum_{a\in B(q_d,a(q_d))}
	\frac{X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)}{|B(q_d,a(q_d))|}\,.
	\]
Marginally, $a(q_d)$ is a uniformly random index from $[M]$. Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$, the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is sampled uniformly at random from  $B=B(q_d,a(q_d))$, the bucket at time $q_d$ that contains $a(q_d)$. 
It follows from the definitions of the buckets (see~\eqref{e:bucket}) that
	\begin{align*}
	\max\bigg\{ \Big|X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a)
	-X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: a\in B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg\} &\le \eta\,,\\
	\max\bigg\{ \Big|X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)
	-X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: a\in B(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg\} &\le \eta\,,
	\end{align*}
where the second bound uses that
$a(q_{d+1})$ and $a(q_d)$ are in the same bucket $B$ at time $q_d$.
Since $\vY(q_d)$ is obtained by averaging $\vX^\trunc(q_d,a)$ over $a\in B$, we immediately obtain
	\[
	\max\bigg\{
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_d))\Big|,
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	\bigg\} \le\eta\,.
	\]
Likewise, since $\vY(q_{d+1})$ is obtained by averaging 
$\vX^\trunc(q_{d+1},a')$ over $a'\in B'=B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))$, we have
	\beq
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_{d+1})
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))\Big| \le\eta\,.
	\eeq
Combining these gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.092066+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19a7768850f54ede9f386b639aa4b492e4365b28ea25b77b59e106103bc8b088","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 49 (Two-spine continuation bound) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Under the assumptions \ref{hyp_A1}, \ref{hyp_A2} and \ref{hyp_A3}, choose
    \(0<\alpha<\rho\) and 
let $w$ be a vertex at depth $r\in\{0,\dots,h-1\}$, and write
\[
m:=h-r, \qquad \ell:=L_r(w):=ar-S_r(w)\ge0.
\]
Thus, if two depth-$h$ descendants have MRCA (most recent common ancestor) equal to $w$, then each continuation from $w$
to generation $h$ has length $m$, including the split step from generation $r$ to generation $r+1$.
\medskip

For $j\in\{0,\dots,m\}$, define the translated continuation barrier event
\[
E_{m,\ell}:=
\left\{
Y^{\mathrm{cont}}_j\le \ell,\ \forall\,0\le j\le m,\ 
-\omega_n-1+\ell\le Y^{\mathrm{cont}}_m\le -\omega_n+\ell
\right\},
\]
where
\[
Y^{\mathrm{cont}}_j:=\sum_{i=1}^j (X_i-a),\qquad Y^{\mathrm{cont}}_0:=0,
\]
and $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ denotes the descendant increment process under the spine law $\Q_t$
along a continuation issued from $w$, with the first increment corresponding to the split step
from generation $r$ to generation $r+1$.
Let
\[
q_m(\ell):=\Q_t(E_{m,\ell}\cap \mathcal G^{\mathrm{cont}}_{n,\alpha}),
\]
where \(\mathcal G^{\mathrm{cont}}_{n,\alpha}\) denotes the event that the starting mass
\(K(w)\) and all masses subsequently encountered along the continuation are at
least \(n^\alpha\).
\medskip

Then there exists a constant $C<\infty$ such that the following holds for all large $n$, uniformly
for those values of $\ell=L_r(w)$ with $\ell+\omega_n=o(\sqrt m)$ (in the application to Lemma~\ref{lem:critical_barrier_second_moment}, this estimate will only be used in the regime \(m\ge (\omega_n)^3\), so that \(\omega_n=o(\sqrt m)\) holds uniformly there):

\smallskip

\noindent{\rm (i)} One-spine continuation bound:
\begin{equation}
q_m(\ell)\le C\,\frac{(1+\ell)(1+\omega_n)}{m^{3/2}}.

\end{equation}

\smallskip

\noindent{\rm (ii)} Two-spine product bound:
let $\mathcal G_r(w)$ be the $\sigma$-field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_r$ together with the full offspring
configuration of $w$. Conditionally on $\mathcal G_r(w)$, consider two descendant spines
issued from two \emph{distinct} children of $w$, each evolved below its initial child according to the tilted spine law $\Q_t$ in the corresponding subtree. Let $E^{(1)}_{m,\ell}$ and $E^{(2)}_{m,\ell}$
be the two corresponding continuation events. Then
\begin{equation}
\Q_t\otimes \Q_t\left(
E^{(1)}_{m,\ell}\cap \mathcal G^{(1),\mathrm{cont}}_{n,\alpha},
\ 
E^{(2)}_{m,\ell}\cap \mathcal G^{(2),\mathrm{cont}}_{n,\alpha}
\ \middle|\ \mathcal G_r(w)
\right)
\le
C\,\frac{(1+\ell)^2(1+\omega_n)^2}{m^3}.

\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform product measure on the discrete cube {-1,1}^n","f real-valued and square integrable on the cube","C is a universal constant, in particular independent of n and of f"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19af561bcf040b56cc9b3aa80d52d5dd62e1e00c1b7ecb97b574cbacb19b5603","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform product measure and let Delta_i f (x) = ( f(x) - f(x^{(i)}) ) / 2, where x^{(i)} flips coordinate i. Then there is a UNIVERSAL constant C with Var(f) <= C sum_{i=1}^n || Delta_i f ||_2^2 / ( 1 + log( || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1 ) ), with the convention that a term is 0 when Delta_i f = 0. The unimproved bound Var(f) <= sum_i ||Delta_i f||_2^2 is the Efron-Stein inequality on the cube; Talagrand's refinement gains a LOGARITHMIC factor for every coordinate whose influence is spread out, that is whose L2 and L1 norms are far apart, and gains nothing for a coordinate whose discrete derivative is essentially an indicator. This is precisely the inequality Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm apply to first-passage percolation with two-valued weights to obtain Var <= C n / log n, and the reason their theorem carries a two-point weight hypothesis is that the L1-L2 comparison must be run on that specific cube structure. The p-biased and Gaussian analogues exist with modified constants; the Gaussian version replaces the log ratio by an entropy term (Falik-Samorodnitsky). [Talagrand (1994), 'On Russo's approximate zero-one law', Ann. Probab. 22; used in Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:42.390155+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_19d9449dc78aa329fcf2251f05e754255cf30da00d462112942cc381e8941049","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Liouville's theorem: every bounded entire function is constant. Precisely, if f is holomorphic on all of C and there is a constant M with |f(z)| <= M for every z in C, then f is constant. Equivalently, a nonconstant entire function has unbounded image. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.677970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19e29ec65281e3be4c301313c3e3d5d95eddc744d80736e159b8c52dc99436bd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 20 (It\^o-defect characterization and algebraic rigidity) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] The product \eqref{eq:intrinsic-Ito-product} makes
$\Gito_{\mathfrak I,1}(H)$ a two-step Banach Lie group with inverse
$(x,a,q)^{-1}=(-x,-a,-q)$ and central extension
\[
 0\longrightarrow E_A(H)\oplus E_Q(H)
 \longrightarrow\Gito_{\mathfrak I,1}(H)
 \longrightarrow H\longrightarrow0.
\]
Let $\mathcal T^2_{\mathfrak I}(H)$ be the step-two tensor group with product
$(x,U)\cdot(y,V)=(x+y,U+V+x\otimes y)$ and define
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak G^{I}_{\mathfrak I,1}(H)
 :=\bigl\{(x,U,q)\in\mathcal T^2_{\mathfrak I}(H)\times E_Q(H):
 U+U^*=x^{\otimes2}-q\bigr\},
\end{equation}
with the product induced from $\mathcal T^2_{\mathfrak I}(H)\times E_Q(H)$.
Then $\mathfrak G^{I}_{\mathfrak I,1}(H)$ is a closed subgroup and
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_H^I(x,a,q)
 :=\left(x,\frac12x^{\otimes2}+a-\frac12q,q\right)
\end{equation}
is a homeomorphic group isomorphism
$\Gito_{\mathfrak I,1}(H)\to\mathfrak G^{I}_{\mathfrak I,1}(H)$ with
inverse
\[
 (x,U,q)\longmapsto(x,\Anti U,q).
\]
In these coordinates the geometric and covariance readouts are
\begin{align}
 \Theta_H^S(x,a,q)
 &:=\left(x,\frac12x^{\otimes2}+a\right),
 \\
 \Theta_H^I(x,a,q)
 &:=\left(x,\frac12x^{\otimes2}+a-\frac12q\right),
 \\
 \Theta_H^Q(x,a,q)&:=q,
 
\end{align}
and all three maps are continuous homomorphic readouts;
$(\Theta_H^S,\Theta_H^Q)$ is injective.

Moreover, this product is rigid within central-coordinate degree-two
extensions.  Suppose a continuous product on the same underlying space has
the form
\[
 (x,a,q)\star'(y,b,r)
 =\bigl(x+y,a+b+\beta_A(x,y),q+r+\beta_Q(x,y)\bigr),
\]
where $\beta_A$ and $\beta_Q$ are continuous, and assume that the covariance
projection is a homomorphism and that the map in
\eqref{eq:intrinsic-Ito-readout} is a homomorphism into
$\mathcal T^2_{\mathfrak I}(H)$.  Then necessarily
\[
 \beta_Q(x,y)=0,\qquad
 \beta_A(x,y)=\Anti(x\otimes y),
\]
so $\star'=\star$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the uniform product measure on {-1,1}^n","1 <= p <= q < infinity and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","the constant is independent of n"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19e3e9af2b5ddcfa431ba08524a9369ff10ac214b8a1b8391f61eaf614565d0c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform measure, with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_{S subset [n]} fhat(S) chi_S where chi_S(x) = prod_{i in S} x_i. For 0 <= rho <= 1 define the noise operator T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} fhat(S) chi_S. Then for all 1 <= p <= q < infinity, || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_p whenever rho <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). Two standard specialisations: taking p = 2 gives || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for rho = 1/sqrt(q-1); and for f of DEGREE at most d, meaning fhat(S) = 0 whenever |S| > d, one gets || f ||_q <= (q-1)^{d/2} || f ||_2 for every q >= 2, and by duality || f ||_2 <= (q-1)^{d/2} ||f||_{q'} for the conjugate exponent. The degree-d moment comparison is the workhorse: it says low-degree functions on the cube have all L^q norms comparable to their L^2 norm with a constant depending only on the degree and q, not on n, which is exactly the dimension-free input that KKL and Talagrand's variance inequality consume. The measure must be the UNIFORM (or a fixed p-biased, with a different constant) product measure - the theorem is about product measures on the cube. [Bonami (1970), Beckner (1975); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.477127+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a08a9765247444c3f8115b38cc7c9189f198de07c6779afff3a63a73b4e7b89","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:directed-path-propagator of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Fix $u \in \mathcal{V}^m$.  For layer indices $i > j$
and spatial endpoints $r, r' \in \mathbb{Z}$, a
\emph{threshold-constrained directed path} from
$(j, r')$ to $(i, r)$ is a pair of sequences
\[
j = \ell_0 < \ell_1 < \cdots < \ell_k = i,
\qquad
\xi_0 = r', \xi_1, \dotsc, \xi_{k-1},
\xi_k = r,
\]
with $k \ge 1$ steps and internal vertices constrained
by the thresholds:
$\xi_s \le a_{\ell_s}(u)$ for each
$s \in \{1, \dotsc, k{-}1\}$. The
\emph{weight} of such a path $\gamma$ is
\[
w(\gamma) \vcentcolon= \prod_{s=0}^{k-1}
\bigl(-Q_{\ell_s, \ell_{s+1}}
(\xi_s, \xi_{s+1})\bigr).
\]
The \emph{directed-path propagator} is the strictly
lower-triangular family
$B_u \colon \mathbb{Z}^m \times \mathbb{Z}^m \to \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{R}^m)$ with
entries for $i > j$
\begin{align}
[B_u]_{ij}(r, r') &\vcentcolon=
\sum_{\gamma \colon (j, r') \to (i, r)} w(\gamma) \nonumber \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{i-j}
\sum_{j = \ell_0 < \ell_1 < \cdots < \ell_k = i}
\sum_{\substack{\xi_1 \le a_{\ell_1}(u) \\ \vdots \\
\xi_{k-1} \le a_{\ell_{k-1}}(u)}}
(-1)^k \prod_{s=0}^{k-1}
Q_{\ell_s, \ell_{s+1}}
(\xi_s, \xi_{s+1}), 
\end{align}
with $\xi_0 = r'$ and $\xi_k = r$, and with
$[B_u]_{ij} = 0$ for $i \le j$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.238475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a1df96ab25808e8b8cbba267660c7092e59c45a6080cdb999937a03152a1543","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:hausdorff-dimension of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] {Falconer2014}}]

Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) and let \(s \ge 0\).
For any \(\delta > 0\), we define
\[
\mathcal H^s_\delta(E)
=
\inf
\left\{
\sum_{i\in I} (\diam U_i)^s
:
E \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} U_i,
\ 0<\diam(U_i) \le \delta
\text{ for every } i\in I
\right\},
\]
where the infimum is taken over all finite or countable, possibly empty, index
sets \(I\) and all families \((U_i)_{i\in I}\) of subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
The \(s\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure of \(E\) is
\[
\mathcal H^s(E)
=
\lim_{\delta\to0}
\mathcal H^s_\delta(E).
\]
The Hausdorff dimension of \(E\) is
\[
\dim_H(E)
=
\inf\{s\ge0:\mathcal H^s(E)=0\}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:57:28.221733+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a2666e4f2c84e1de45f9737ad5e2755867484ec035e31a896c857ceaf721ac5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2607.17662, 'On the Strong Law of Large Numbers under Sublinear Expectations'] (Independence) Let $\boldsymbol{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_m)$, $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$, and $\boldsymbol{Y} = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ be two random vectors on $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mathbb{E})$. $\boldsymbol{Y}$ is \textit{independent of} $\boldsymbol{X}$ if for each function $\varphi \in C_{l,\mathrm{Lip}}(\mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n)$,
		\[
		\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\boldsymbol{X}, \boldsymbol{Y})] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{Y})] \big|_{\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{X}}\bigr]
		\]
		provided that $\bar{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}) := \mathbb{E}[|\varphi(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{Y})|] < \infty$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\mathbb{E}[|\bar{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{X})|] < \infty$. A sequence $\{X_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is called a \textit{sequence of independent random variables} if $X_{n+1}$ is independent of $(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$ for each $n \geq 1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348620+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a27b956426503b87ec558efaf3bfc71186bae08b1d75e69f13c3410c878df19","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 163 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $0<q_1<q_2<\dots<q_m<1$. For small enough $\delta,\epsilon>0$ there exists $c>0$ such that for $N$ sufficiently large and $K=e^{cN}$, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the following holds for any $(L,\epsilon)$-good $(p,\sigma,b,w)$: 
 there exist points $(\by_w :w\in [K]^m)$, taking values in $\Sigma_N(\iota)$ (or $S_N(\iota)$) such that
  \beq
  \bbW_2\Big(
  \mu^{\sym}_{\bG}(\by_w),
  \mu^{\sym}(p,\sigma,b,w)
  \Big) \le\epsilon\eeq
for all $w\in [K]^m$, and
  \beq
  \lt|\frac{( \by_w,\by_{w'})}{N}-q_{w\wedge w'}\rt|
  \leq \epsilon\eeq
for all $w,w'\in [K]^m$. In fact, we can take $\by_w=\cA_{\chaos}(\bz_w)$ where $(\bz_w:w\in [K]^m)$ is an ensemble of gaussians that are suitably correlated with $\bz\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 

\begin{proof}
Choose $\epsilon\ll q_1$ small. We will take $c$ small in order to union bound over $e^{O(cN)}$ exponentially unlikely events in the proof. Let $\cA_{\chaos}$ be as defined in 
Proposition~\ref{ppn:chaotic-amp-still-works}, taking inputs $\bz=(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. Let $\chi$ be the correlation function associated to $\cA_{\chaos}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:chaotic-iamp-is-chaotic}, we have
  \[p_i\equiv \chi^{-1}(q_i)
  \ge 1-\epsilon\]
for all $1\leq i\leq m$. Let $T$ denote the $K$-ary tree of depth $m$, and identify the leaves with $[K]^m$. Generate a jointly gaussian ensemble
$(\bz_w: w\in [K]^m)$ such that $\bz_{1^m}=\bz=(\bG,\bg^\aux)$, and such that the correlation between $\bz_u$ and $\bz_v$ is $p_{|u\wedge v|+1}$ for any $u,v\in [K]^m$. Let $\by_w\equiv \cA_{\chaos}(\bz_w)$ for $w\in[K]^m$. 
By taking $\eta$ small enough in the 
definition of $\cA_{\chaos}$, and 
applying
Proposition~\ref{ppn:chaotic-amp-still-works} together with a union bound over $w\in[K]^m$, we obtain
that with probability at least $1- e^{-10cN}$, we have 
  \begin{equation}
  
  \bbW_2\Big(
  \mu^{\sym}_{\bG_w}(\by_w),
  \mu^{\sym}(p,\sigma,b,w)
  \Big)\leq \epsilon
  \end{equation}
for all $w\in[K]^m$. Another union bound gives that with probability at least 
 $1-e^{-10cN}$, we have
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \max\bigg\{
  \frac{\|\by_w\|}{N^{1/2}}
  : w\in[K]^m\bigg\}
  &\le 2\,,\\
  \max\bigg\{
  \frac{\|\bG_w-\bG_{w'}\|_{\op}}{M^{1/2} + N^{1/2}}
  : w,w'\in[K]^m
  \bigg\}
  &\leq 10\epsilon^{1/2}\,.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
On the event that the above conditions hold, we have deterministically
  \[
  \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\sym}_{\bG_w}(\by_w),\mu^{\sym}_{\bG}(\by_w)\Big)
  \leq 
  \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\bG_w}(\by_w),\mu^{\sym}_{\bG}(\by_w)\Big)
  \leq 
  \frac{\|(\bG_w-\bG)\by_w\|}{
    (MN)^{1/2}}
  \leq 
  O(\epsilon^{1/2}).
  \]
Combining with \eqref{eq:outputs-good-for-perturbed-disorder} and adjusting $\epsilon$ gives \eqref{eq:all-outputs-good}. Next we note that
  \[
  \bbE\bigg[\frac{( \by_w,\by_{w'})}{N}\bigg]
  =
  \chi(p_{w\wedge w'})=q_{w\wedge w'}\,,
  \]
so \eqref{eq:overlaps-ultrametric} follows from concentration of measure (again taking a union bound with $c$ small enough).  
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is a bounded open subset of R^n, n >= 2","A is measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic (no continuity assumed)","f is in L^1(Omega); the data may also be a bounded Radon measure with the same conclusions","the approximating data f_m are bounded, converge to f in L^1, and have L^1 norms bounded by ||f||_{L^1}","q is strictly less than n/(n-1)","conclusions are for the approximating sequence and its limit, not for an arbitrary distributional solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396034+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, equations with measure or L^1 data","id":"claim_1a2ed3a0477ecc6b19ac15853dd25ba30feec9956659f5a93173e31f2bcfe10f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with n >= 2, and let A be measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic on Omega (alpha|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi, |A(x)| <= Lambda, alpha > 0). Let u_m in H^1_0(Omega) solve -div(A grad u_m) = f_m weakly. Then: (i) for every q with 1 <= q < n/(n-1) the sequence (u_m) is bounded in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) by a constant depending only on n, q, alpha, |Omega| and ||f||_{L^1}; (ii) up to a subsequence u_m converges strongly in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) and almost everywhere, together with its gradients, to a function u in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) which is a distributional solution: integral_Omega A grad u . grad phi = integral_Omega f phi for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega); (iii) the limit satisfies the Marcinkiewicz (weak-Lebesgue) bounds u in M^(n/(n-2)) for n >= 3 and |grad u| in M^(n/(n-1)), with norms controlled by ||f||_{L^1}. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:25:41.599861+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a345d3cfedc5050d1c7f2a4991d859693d44a659300616ed92cda6892bd4d23","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:killing of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let \(G\) be a weighted graph.
The following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item[\textup{(i)}]
    \(G\) satisfies \hyperref[def:SC-infinity]{\textup{{(SC\textsubscript{$\infty$})}}}{}.

    \item[\textup{(ii)}]
    For every \(T>0\), every \(u_0\in\ell^\infty(X)\) and every $\phi \in \mathcal{I}$, the~(eq:GPME of the paper) with initial datum $u_0$ has a unique bounded pointwise solution on
    \([0,T]\times X\).

    \item[\textup{(iii)}]
    There exist \(T_0>0\), \(u_0\in\ell^\infty(X)\) and $\phi \in \mathcal{I}$
    such that the~(eq:GPME of the paper) with initial datum $u_0$
    has at most one bounded pointwise solution
    on \([0,T_0]\times X\).

    \item[\textup{(iv)}]
    There exist \(T_0>0\) and $\phi \in \mathcal{I}$
    such that $u=0$ is the only bounded
    pointwise solution to the (eq:GPME of the paper) on \([0,T_0]\times X\) with initial
    datum \(u_0=0\).

    \item[\textup{(v)}]
    There exist \(T_0>0\) and $\phi \in \mathcal{I}$
    such that the following global bounded comparison principle
    holds: If \(u,v \colon [0,T_0]\times X\to\mathbb R\) are bounded functions such
    that
    \[
        u(\cdot,x),v(\cdot,x)
        \in C([0,T_0])\cap C^1((0,T_0))
        \qquad\text{for every }x\in X
    \]
    and
    \[
        (\partial_t+\Delta\Phi)u
        \leq
        (\partial_t+\Delta\Phi)v
        \qquad\text{on }(0,T_0)\times X
    \]
    with
    \[
        u(0,\cdot)\leq v(0,\cdot),
    \]
    then
    \[
        u\leq v
        \qquad\text{on }[0,T_0]\times X.
    \]

    \item[\textup{(vi)}]
    For every $u_0\in\ell^\infty(X)$ and every $\phi\in\mathcal I$, the~(eq:GPME of the paper) has a unique global bounded pointwise solution.
\end{enumerate}

If one of the preceding conditions holds, then the comparison principle
in \textup{(v)} holds for every \(T>0\).

If $G$ is not stochastically complete at infinity, then, for every $u_0\in\ell^\infty(X)$ and every $\phi\in\mathcal I$, there are infinitely many global bounded pointwise solutions whose restrictions to every $[0,T]\times X$, $T>0$, are pairwise distinct. For $u_0=0$, an infinite family can be chosen of one sign: nonnegative when $\phi$ is nonconstant on $[0,\infty)$, and nonpositive otherwise.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:20:55.464708+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a3e5dd43fe4a07dd901bf5353303b3fcbdb5efccbdbaf806cc9c33d6162a3ae","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi of arXiv:2411.07158, 'Markov chains on trees: almost lower and upper directed cases'] Let $T$ be a finite or infinite tree (see (fig:tree-clup of the paper)).
  \begin{itemize}
\item[{\tiny $\blacksquare$ \normalsize }]  A transition matrix ${\sf U}=\begin{pmatrix} {\sf U}_{u,v}\end{pmatrix}_{u,v\in T}$ is said to be \underbar{almost upper-directed\xspace{}}, ``{\sf AUD}\xspace'' for short, if 
\[\forall u,v \in T, \quad{\sf U}_{u,v}>0 \Rightarrow (v \in \{ p(u)\}\cup T_u)\]
that is, if either $v$  is the parent $p(u)$ of $u$  or a descendant of $u$.
Since $u\in T_u$, ${\sf U}_{u,u}$ is allowed to be positive. 
\item[{\tiny $\blacksquare$ \normalsize }] 
 A transition matrix ${\sf D}=\begin{pmatrix} {\sf D}_{u,v}\end{pmatrix}_{u,v\in T}$ is said to be \underbar{almost lower-directed\xspace{}}, ``{\sf ALD}\xspace'' for short, if 
 \[\forall u,v \in T, \quad {\sf D}_{u,v}>0 \Rightarrow ( v \in c_T(u)\cup \cro{\varnothing,u})\]
 that is if either $v$  is a child of $u$ or one of its ancestor.
Since $u\in\cro{\varnothing,u}$, ${\sf D}_{u,u}>0$ is also allowed.
\item[{\tiny $\blacksquare$ \normalsize }]   A transition matrix ${\sf M}=\begin{pmatrix} {\sf M}_{u,v}\end{pmatrix}_{u,v\in T}$ is said to be the transition matrix of a \underbar{random walk} on $T$, if $\;{\sf M}_{u,v}>0$ implies $v\in\{u,p(u)\}\cup c_T(u)$ (it is simultaneously almost upper-directed\xspace and {\sf ALD}\xspace).\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:19:06.748036+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a3ee89d0fc406be30363f34f6fb8f5b9a62fd07ef89ce456489108b97b3197a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:finite-block-weighted-growth-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let 
\(
(A_0,A_1)
\)
be a pair of almost surely finite nonnegative random variables, and define the possibly extended-valued function 
\(
\kappa:[0,1]\to[0,\infty]
\)
by
\[
\kappa(\theta)
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf 1_{\{A_0>0\}}+\mathbf 1_{\{A_1>0\}}\right],
& \theta=0,\\[8pt]
\displaystyle
\mathbb{E}\left[A_0^\theta+A_1^\theta\right],
& 0<\theta\le1.
\end{cases}
\]
Assume that 
\[
\inf_{0\le\theta\le1}\kappa(\theta)>1.
\]

Let 
\(
\mathcal T=\bigcup_{n\ge0}\{0,1\}^n
\)
be the full binary tree, with root \(\varnothing\). Let
\[
\bigl\{(A_0(v),A_1(v)):v\in\mathcal T\bigr\}
\]
be an i.i.d. family of copies of 
\(
(A_0,A_1)
\).
For 
\(
u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\in\{0,1\}^n
\),
write 
\(
u|_{j-1}=(u_1,\ldots,u_{j-1})
\),
with 
\(
u|_0=\varnothing
\),
and define
\[
A_u
=
\prod_{j=1}^{n}A_{u_j}(u|_{j-1}),
\qquad
A_\varnothing=1.
\]
Then there exist 
\(
N\ge1
\), 
\(
\tau>0
\),
and 
\(
\beta>1
\)
such that 
\[
\beta\tau>1 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{E}\#\{u\in\{0,1\}^N:A_u\ge\tau\}>\beta.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.692788+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_1a4a29cb16bd40a583415157e3d38616","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2.5 (Conditional exponential family (finite symmetric truncation)) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Gr'] Fix $n\\in\\mathbb{N}$ and latent positions $U=(U_{1},\\dots,U_{n})\\in(0,1)^{n}$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:58:38.147848+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1a623f60311ff6f395ec2f67115e52cde7f065279a3c6c63e27ce8eb397ff9e7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:stochastic_domination of arXiv:2606.24465, 'History estimation in random recursive trees:\\Pointwise approach via iterated Jordan cent'] Let $n\in\mathbb{N}, u \in \mathcal{U}$, and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then, for all $k\ge 3\log_2(1/\alpha)$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$
    \[
    \mathbb{P}\left(\big|\{i\in\mathbb{N} : \mathrm{Fr}_n\left((u,i)\right) \ge \alpha \mathrm{Fr}_n(u)\}\big|\,>\, k \, \mid \, \mathrm{Fr}_n(u) =\ell\right)\ \le \ 0.95^k.
    \]
    \begin{proof} 
        We analyze the splitting as in (equation eq:uniform-splitting of the paper).
        We track for each child of $u$ if its fringe-tree size exceeds slightly less than its expectation: let
        \[
        Y_j=\mathbbm{1}{\{X_j\ge R_j/2\}}, \qquad Y^{(k)}=\sum_{j=1}^k Y_j.
        \]
        Observe that $\mathbb{P}(Y_j=1 \mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{j-1})\ge 1/2$ as $X_j$ is uniform on $\{1,\ldots, R_j\}$. Moreover, each time $Y_j=1$, the remaining mass halves, i.e.,  $R_{j+1}\le R_j/2$. Hence, after $m$ halvings the remaining mass is at most $R_12^{-m}$. In particular, if the number of halvings among the first $k$ children exceeds $\log_2(1/\alpha)$, then the remaining mass before child $k+1$ is less than $\alpha \mathrm{Fr}_n(u)$, and it is impossible to have a $(k+1)$-st child of size at least $\alpha \mathrm{Fr}_n(u)$, i.e., $R_{k+1} < \alpha \mathrm{Fr}_n(u)$.
        So, if there are at least $k+1$ children of $u$ with fringe-tree size at least $\alpha \mathrm{Fr}_n(u)$, we must have that $Y^{(k)}\le \log_2(1/\alpha)$. Since $Y^{(k)}$ stochastically dominates a binomial random variable with $p=1/2$, we find for $k\ge 3\log_2(1/\alpha)$,
        \begin{multline*}
        \mathbb{P}\left(\big|\{i\in\mathbb{N} : \mathrm{Fr}_n\left((u,i)\right) \ge \alpha \mathrm{Fr}_n(u)\}\big|>k\, \mid \, \mathrm{Fr}_n(u) =\ell \right) \le \mathbb{P}\big(Y^{(k)}\le \log_2(1/\alpha)\big)
        \\
        \le \mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{Bin}(k, 1/2)\le k/3\right)\le\exp\left(-k\Lambda_{1/2}(\tfrac{1}{3})\right)\le 0.95^k,
        \end{multline*}
        where $\Lambda_{1/2}$ is the large deviations rate function of a Bernoulli(1/2)-distribution, see (equation eq:large-dev of the paper). 
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:01:25.577218+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1aa7a7e06b5c031b362007e710ef613272c7d6b16e5370bd685de121626bc5e3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:V-decomposition-relative-v of arXiv:2605.16086, 'Loop pruning and downward deviations for maximum local time of discrete-time simple random'] Let $W\in \mathbf{K}(\#E)^{\mathcal U}$ and $v\in V^{\partial}(W)$, and write
$v=(v_1,\ldots,v_\ell)$.
For two addresses $x,y\in\mathcal U$, write $x\wedge y$ for their longest common prefix
(their youngest common ancestor in the Ulam--Harris tree).

Define
\[
V_{\mathrm{exp}}^{v,W}
=
\big\{u\in V(W):\ u\prec_{\mathrm{lex}} v\big\}.
\]
Define the \(\ell\)-th younger-sibling set by
\[
\widehat{\mathcal D}_{\ell}^{v,W}
:=
\{u\in V(W): \mathrm{par}(v)\prec_{\mathrm{anc}}u,\ v\preceq_{\mathrm{lex}} u\},
\quad
\mathcal D_{\ell}^{v,W}:=\widehat{\mathcal D}_{\ell}^{v,W}\cup\{\mathrm{par}(v)\}.
\]
Namely, $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{par}}^{v,W}$ is the subtree generated by descendants of $v$ together with those of its younger siblings, with ``root'' \(\mathrm{par}(v)\); \(\widehat{\mathcal D}_{\mathrm{par}}^{v,W}\) is the same subtree with the root removed.

For each $1\le q\le \ell-1$, define the $q$-th younger-sibling set
\[
\mathcal Y_q^{v,W}
:=
\big\{u\in V(W):\ |u|=q,\ |u\wedge v|=q-1,\ v\prec_{\mathrm{lex}}u\big\}.
\]
For $u\in\bigcup_{q=1}^{\ell-1} \mathcal Y_q^{v,W}$, define its descendant block
\[
\mathcal D_u^W:=\{x\in V(W):\ u\preceq_{\mathrm{anc}} x\}.
\]

Then
\[
V(W)
=
V_{\mathrm{exp}}^{v,W}
\ \sqcup
\widehat{\mathcal D}_{\mathrm{par}}^{v,W}
\ \sqcup
\bigsqcup_{q=1}^{\ell-1}\ \bigsqcup_{u\in\mathcal Y_q^{v,W}} \mathcal D_u^W.
\]
The decomposition is illustrated in Figure~(fig:V-decomposition-relative-v of the paper). In particular, these sets form a partition of $V(W)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A in C4(R,R^{q x q})","0<mI<=H<=MI globally","sup norm A prime<=D; sup norm H^(j)<=B_j, j=1..4","iid z independent of past, z equal in law to -z, EzzT=I, E|z|6 finite","sigma>=0; eta in (0,min(1,1/M)]","u0 deterministic; v0=0","F bounded C3 with bounded derivatives"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:48:21.750439+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_1acc06ed77c5a3544de7b5d174203e8bbf687cbf55975a914b5375320d1a09ac","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft. Status: proof (unaudited), claim w730-T355-C002 version 2; not independently checked. The scalar tangential coordinate is u in R; v is in R^q. Let A:R -> R^{q x q}
be C^4, q>=1 an integer, H=A^T A, and assume, globally,

    0 < m I <= H(u) <= M I,
    ||A'(u)|| <= D,  ||H^(j)(u)|| <= B_j, j=1,2,3,4.

Matrix norms are operator norms. Constants m,M,D,B_j are finite and independent
of eta. Let sigma>=0. The iid label noises z_k have a centrally symmetric law,
E z_k z_k^T=I, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity; put mu_4=E|z_k|^4. No almost-sure noise bound is assumed. In particular E z_k=0. Set
eta_0=min(1,1/M), 0<eta<=eta_0. Start from deterministic (u_0,0).
Consider full-vector label-noise SGD for residual A(u)v and loss
L(u,v)=|A(u)v|^2/2:

    d_k=u_{k+1}-u_k
       =-eta v_k^T H'(u_k)v_k/2 -eta sigma z_k^T A'(u_k)v_k,
    v_{k+1}=(I-eta H(u_k))v_k-eta sigma A(u_k)^T z_k.

On v=0 its noise covariance is sigma^2 Hess L. The limiting ODE is

    U'=b(U),  b(u)=-sigma^2 tr H'(u)/4,  U(0)=u_0.

This is the known limiting flow of Li-Wang-Arora, Corollary 5.2, arXiv
2110.06914v4, printed pp.8-9 and 33. Their Theorem 4.6 supplies convergence,
not the explicit error estimate below. The hardest quantitative step here
is averaging with a coefficient that depends on u and shares the same noise
as the normal update. Section 4 computes that correlation rather than
discarding it as a martingale.

## 1. Constants and conclusion

Let F:R^{1+q}->R be bounded C^3, with bounded derivatives. Write
f(u)=F(u,0), F_j=sup |f^(j)|, j=1,2,3, and
F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||. The displayed bound uses only these seminorms.
Define

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2 + sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4 + 15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        + sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2.

For j=0,1,2,3 put beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4. For T>=0 set

    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                     +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2.

Define

    S0=B_1/(2m),
    S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2,
    C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2,
    Ct=Gtu S0/2.

Finally let

    Qg=G2 J2/2 + Gtu sqrt(J2) + Gtt/2,
    Qc=C0 M^2 c2
       +C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
       +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M) D c2
       +2 C2 Jcv + Ct c2,
    C(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2 + T(Qg+Qc).

Then, simultaneously for all integers 0<=k<=T/eta^2,

    |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C(T) eta.       (1)

The exponent is a=1. The finite constant is explicit in the hypotheses and
the stated observable seminorms. H and H' need not commute. This includes
every finite normal dimension q, and arbitrary smooth rotating output
frames A satisfying the bounds. The tangential dimension remains one.
It permits unbounded symmetric noise, including Gaussian labels. Fixed
off-manifold initialization is not addressed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.306474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1ad16902501eae9ea42da05476ccf44aaa0c773bf2c0262f9815a6452eaa8630","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem: Lemma on entropy of arXiv:2607.20097, 'Phase transition for the asymptotic entropy of branching random walks on groups'] Let $\mu,\nu,\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots,\mu_n$ be probability measures on $G$, where $n\in\mathbb{N}$. The following statements hold\textcolor{blue}{:} 
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
    \item Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n\geq 0$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\cdots+\lambda_n=1$. Then it holds
    $$
    \sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k H(\mu_k)\leq H\Big(\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\mu_k\Big)\leq \sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k H(\mu_k) + \log n.
    $$
    \item Let $c\in(0,1)$. If for all $x\in\mathbb{N}$ we have $\mu(x)\leq c$, then $H(\mu)\geq -\log c$.
    \item  Let $c\in (0,1)$. If for all $x\in\textsf{supp}(\mu)$ we have $\mu(x)\geq c$, then $ H(\mu)\leq -\log c.$
    \item Let $0\leq c<1<C\leq \infty$, and $c\nu\leq \mu \leq C\nu$ pointwise. Then it holds
    $$
    cH(\nu)-\log C\leq H(\mu) \leq CH(\nu)-\log c.
    $$
\end{enumerate}
\begin{proof}
We start with $(i)$. The first inequality is due to the concavity of $x\mapsto -x\log x$. For the second inequality we have 
\begin{align*}
H\Big(\sum_{k=1}^n &\lambda_k\mu_k\Big)  = -\sum_{x\in G}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\mu_k(x)\Big)\log\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j\mu_j(x)\Big)
=-\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\sum_{x\in G}\mu_k(x)\log\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j\mu_j(x)\Big)\\
&\leq -\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\sum_{x\in G}\mu_k(x)\log(\lambda_k\mu_k(x))
= \sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_kH(\mu_k) - \sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\log\lambda_k
\leq \sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k H(\mu_k) + \log n.
\end{align*}
Above we have used again the concavity of $-x\log x$ to conclude that $-\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\log\lambda_k\leq\log n$. Since  $-\log$ is decreasing, $(ii)$ and $(iii)$ follow directly. The last claim $(iv)$ is again a simple calculation. For the first inequality we have
\begin{align*}
H(\mu)=-\sum_{x\in G}\mu(x)\log\mu(x) \geq -\sum_{x\in G}\mu(x) \log(C\nu(x)) \geq -\log C + \sum_{x\in G}c\nu(x)(-\log\nu(x)).
\end{align*}
 The second inequality works exactly the same way, by switching the roles of $c$ and $C$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.441547+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1ad3e11fcf1a534b4a0bea93886abc8c9d9a7f3110ce39a1c7d21980402469d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] The Rook's Walk with dimension $d\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$ and board length $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ is transitive.
  \begin{proof}
  Fix $x,y\in \Omega$ and let $d = (y-x \bmod n+1)$. Define, $\xi_{(x,y)}: \Omega \to \Omega$ as,
  \[v \overset{\xi_{(x,y)}}{\longmapsto} v + d,\quad  \quad \forall v\in \Omega\]
  Now, notice that,
  \begin{align*}
   \xi_{(x,y)}(x) &= x + d\\
   &= (x\bmod n+1) + (y-x \bmod n+1)\\
   &= (y\bmod n+1)\\
   &= y
  \end{align*}
  Therefore, $\xi_{(x,y)}$ satisfies our first condition. Now, fix $z,w \in \Omega$. Notice that the transition probability $P(z,w)$ is dependent only on the Hamming distance between $z$ and $w$ (Recall that $||z-w||_0$ is the Hamming distance). Further we have,
  \[||\xi_{(x,y)}(z) - \xi_{(x,y)}(w)||_0 = ||(z+d)-(w+d)||_0= ||z-w||_0\]
  That is, Hamming distance is invariant under $\xi_{(x,y)}$ and, by extension, \[P(z,w) = P(\xi_{(x,y)}(z), \xi_{(x,y)}(w))\]
  Therefore, the Rook's Walk is transitive.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:50:44.873443+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1ae1878dc7709322c8b0ed1ef5ded63fb44165bae9cebddb3caa4e9f79ceb016","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 38 (Schatten-stable map) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] For $1\le r\le\infty$, define
\begin{align}

 \kappa_r(\Phi):=
 \sup_{A,B}
 \norm{\Phi^{B,A}}_{
   \Sch_r(A\otimes\cC,B\otimes\cE)\to
   \Sch_r(A\otimes\cC',B\otimes\cE')},
\end{align}
where the supremum is over finite-dimensional $A,B$.  The norm in
\eqref{eq:schatten-stable-constant} is the norm of the actual restriction of
the entrywise map to the indicated Schatten class.  It is defined to be
$+\infty$ if that restriction does not take values in the target Schatten
class or is not bounded.
Changing orthonormal bases in $A$ or $B$ conjugates the rectangular
amplification by unitaries on its source and target, so the displayed norm is
coordinate-independent.
If $\kappa_r(\Phi)<\infty$, call $\Phi$ $r$-Schatten-stable.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.709012+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1aef8b559b793276c6604bc9ec988b845a0e81d63866643ff264d6d2131b5ea6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (Hyperbolic random graph) of arXiv:2609.01143, 'The voter model on the hyperbolic graph'] Fix $\alpha\in(1/2,1)$ and $\nu>0$, and put $R:=2\log(n/\nu)$.  Let $\mathcal P_n$ be a Poisson point process on the hyperbolic disk $B_O(R)$ with intensity measure
\[
\lambda_n( \de r, \de\theta ) := \frac{n}{2\pi} \frac{\alpha\sinh(\alpha r)}{\cosh(\alpha R)-1} \mathbbm{1}_{\{0\leq r<R\}}\,\de r \de \theta, \qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
\]

The hyperbolic random graph $G_{\alpha,\nu}(n)$ has vertex set $\mathcal P_n$, and two points are adjacent if and only if their hyperbolic distance is less than $R$.  Thus
\[
N_n:=|V(G_{\alpha,\nu}(n))|\sim{\rm Pois}(n).
\]

Throughout, $n$ denotes the mean vertex count rather than the realised value $N_n$.  This is the model of \cite[Section~2.3]{MR4816414}, with the density parameter encoded through $R$.","status":"unverified"}

Let $\mu > -\frac12$ and ${\boldsymbol{\kappa}} \in {\mathbb R}^{d_2-1}$ with ${\kappa}_i > -1$,

for the weight function 
$$
{\bm W}_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma \times{\mathbb R}_+}({\bm x},{\bm y},\bm z) = {\bm W}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma}({\bm x},{\bm y}){\bm W}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}^{L}(\bm z)
$$ 
on the product domain $({\mathbb B}^{d_1}\rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}) \times{\mathbb R}_+^{d_3}$ satisfy 
$$
   {\mathfrak D}_{\mu,{\bm k}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes\Sigma, ({\bm x},{\bm y})} u  + {\mathfrak D}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}^{L, \bm z} u = -  n u,
    \quad \forall u \in L^2\big(({\mathbb B}^{d_1}\rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}) \times{\mathbb R}_+^{d_3}, {\bm W}_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma \times{\mathbb R}_+}\big).
$$
Moreover, orthogonal polynomials for the weight function 
$$
{\bm W}_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma \times{\mathbb R}}({\bm x},{\bm y},\bm z) = {\bm W}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma}({\bm x},{\bm y}){\bm W}^H (\bm z)
$$
on the product domain $({\mathbb B}^{d_1}\rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}) \times{\mathbb R}^{d_3}$ satisfy 
$$
  2 {\mathfrak D}_{\mu,{\bm k}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes\Sigma, ({\bm x},{\bm y})} u  + {\mathfrak D}^{H, \bm z} u = - 2 n u,
    \quad \forall u \in L^2\big(({\mathbb B}^{d_1}\rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}) \times{\mathbb R}^{d_3}, {\bm W}_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma \times{\mathbb R}}\big).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

expressed in the normalisation \eqref{eq:central-dual-normalisation} and

{"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","(A): u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω), Ω contained in a slab of finite width d (no boundary regularity needed)","(B): Ω bounded, connected, Lipschitz boundary (or convex), u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492434+00:00","domain":"Sobolev inequalities, elliptic PDE, coercivity","id":"claim_1b864127f2bba872e9317da0f8bb92499ed6de1b5bd8779daf961da7ad1cb410","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(A) Poincaré–Friedrichs inequality (zero boundary values). Suppose Ω is bounded in one direction: Ω ⊂ {x : a < x_1 < a + d} for some a and some finite d (in particular any bounded Ω, with d = diam Ω). Then for every u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω)
   ||u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∂_1 u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}.
For p = 2 the sharp constant for a slab of width d is d/π: ||u||_{L^2} ≤ (d/π)||∇u||_{L^2} for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω). NO regularity of ∂Ω is required and Ω need not be connected. Consequently ||∇u||_{L^p} is a norm on W^{1,p}_0(Ω) equivalent to the full W^{1,p} norm, the Dirichlet form ∫|∇u|^2 is coercive on H^1_0(Ω), and for bounded Ω the best constant C_P in ||u||_2 ≤ C_P||∇u||_2 satisfies 1/C_P^2 = λ_1(Ω), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of −Δ.

(B) Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality (mean-zero functions). Suppose Ω is bounded, connected, and has Lipschitz boundary (or is bounded, connected and convex; more generally a bounded connected W^{1,p}-extension domain). Then there is C = C(Ω, p) with
   ||u − u_Ω||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ C ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}  for all u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω),  u_Ω = (1/|Ω|) ∫_Ω u dx.
For convex Ω and p = 2 the sharp constant is diam(Ω)/π (Payne–Weinberger). Consequently u ↦ ||∇u||_{L^p} + |∫_Ω u| is a norm on W^{1,p}(Ω) equivalent to the W^{1,p} norm, and the Neumann problem is coercive on the mean-zero subspace.

Where it fails. (A) fails without zero boundary values: constants lie in W^{1,p}(Ω) with zero gradient. (A) fails on any domain containing balls of arbitrarily large radius (R^n, half-spaces, exterior domains): dilating one test function shows no constant works. (B) fails for disconnected Ω (a function equal to different constants on two components). (B) fails on some bounded connected domains with bad boundary (rooms-and-passages domains, sufficiently sharp outward cusps), where functions that are ≈0 in one part and ≈1 in another can have arbitrarily small gradient energy; Lipschitz boundary rules this out. In (B) the constant depends on Ω and blows up as the domain degenerates (e.g. a thin neck).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.492485+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1b8ae0b0d01f5875dc9e13129cde43e6b3f4417ad1801ca336cfcf80d54c8c25","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Entropy, relative entropy, and mutual information) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] All entropies in this paper are differential entropies with respect to the
Lebesgue measure on the affine span of the relevant polytope or cone.  If
\(p\) is a probability density, we write
\[
\ent(p):=-\int p(x)\log p(x)\,dx.
\]
If \(X\) has density \(p_X\), we also write \(\ent(X)=\ent(p_X)\).  For two
random variables \(X,Y\) with joint density \(p_{X,Y}\) and conditional
density \(p_{X\mid Y=y}\), the conditional entropy is
\[
\ent(X\mid Y)
:=
\mathbb E\bigl[\ent(p_{X\mid Y})\bigr]
=
-\int p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log p_{X\mid Y=y}(x)\,dx\,dy,
\]
whenever the conditional densities exist and the integral is well-defined.  For two
probability densities \(q,p\) on the same space, the relative entropy is
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)
:=
\int q(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\,dx,
\]
with the usual convention that it is \(+\infty\) unless \(q\) is absolutely
continuous with respect to \(p\).  For random variables \(X,Y\), their mutual
information is
\[
I(X;Y):=
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(X,Y)\|
\operatorname{Law}(X)\otimes\operatorname{Law}(Y)\bigr).
\]
When the relevant conditional densities exist, this is equivalently
\[
I(X;Y)=\ent(X)-\ent(X\mid Y).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:37:20.370783+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1bb3b41e03db29b9e63e40545e546673c90e74f9f6e21c15fd9e0f866d4cefac","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Free measure of arXiv:2411.13465, 'Height-offset variables and pinning at infinity for gradient Gibbs measures on trees'] \mbox{}\\
Let $Q: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow (0,\infty)$ be any positive symmetric transfer operator of gradient type such that $\sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}}j^2 Q(j) < \infty$.
Then the following holds true for the corresponding free state $\nu$ on the Cayley tree of order $d \geq 2$.
 \begin{itemize}
	\item[a)]\textbf{Existence.}\hypertarget{res: existence free}{} Let $(H_r)_{r \in \mathbb{N}}$ be as in Definition (def: SphericalAverage of the paper). Then $H:=\lim_{r \rightarrow \infty}H_r$ is a height-offset variable for $\nu$ in the sense of Definition (def: HeightOffset of the paper), where the limit holds almost surely and in $\mathcal{L}^2$ with respect to the same measure $\nu  \circ \left(\sigma^{\rho,0} \right)^{-1}$. In particular, the measure $\mu^H$ associated with $H$ and $\nu$ via Theorem (thm: DLR of the paper) is a proper Gibbs measure on the space of height configurations.
 \item[b1)]\textbf{Regularity of density of HOV.}\hypertarget{res: regularity density free}{} The corresponding distribution of $H^{\rho,0}$ obtained from Definition (def: SphericalAverage of the paper) under $\nu$ has an infinitely often differentiable Lebesgue-density $f_{H^{\rho,0}}$.\\
 Moreover, $f_{H^{\rho,0}}$ is strictly positive on $\mathbb{R}$.
 \item[b2)]\textbf{Localization of single-site marginal of pinned measure.}\hypertarget{res: localization free}{} Assume furthermore on the interaction $Q$ that there is some $R>0$ such that the moment generating function for a single gradient variable, $t \mapsto \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\exp(tj)\frac{Q(j)}{\Vert Q \Vert_1}$ is finite for $t \in (-R,+R)$. \\
 Then, for every $A < (d+1)R$ there exists a $B(A) \in (0,\infty)$ such that the single-site marginal at the root satisfies the following exponential concentration:
 \[\mu^H(\vert \sigma_\rho \vert \geq s) \leq B(A)\exp(-As), \quad \text{for every } s \in \mathbb{N}.\]
  \item[c1)]\textbf{Peculiarity 1.}\hypertarget{res: peculiarity 1 free}{} The lifted measure Gibbs $\mu^H$ is necessarily not invariant under the translations of the tree.
 \item[c2)]\textbf{Peculiarity 2.}\hypertarget{res: peculiarity 2 free}{} The measure $\mu^H$ is not a tree-indexed Markov chain and in particular not extreme in the set of all Gibbs measures for the specification associated with $Q$ via (equation eq: GibbsSpecification of the paper).
 \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.811260+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1bb72ffa7caff8362a6f223872cf6b636938cbd5955b4ad718b7f6932e3202e8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:partition of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] For the positive integers $ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_+ $ and the invertible elements $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_m \in \kappa^\times $,
 	we define: 
 	
 	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
 	\item 
 	For $ \alpha, \beta \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $ 
 	we say that 
 	$ (\ell_\alpha, \lambda_\alpha) $ and $ (\ell_\beta, \lambda_\beta) $ 
 	are {\em compatible}
 	if 
 	$ \alpha = \beta $ or if the following conditions hold:
 	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
 		\item
 		$ \ell_\alpha = 2 k_\alpha - 1 $ and $\ell_\beta = 2 k_\beta - 1  $ are both odd, 
 		for $ k_\alpha, k_\beta \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_+ $
 		and
 		
 		\item
 		$ \lambda_\alpha (-1)^{k_\alpha} = \lambda_\beta (-1)^{k_\beta}  $. 
 	\end{enumerate}
 
	\item 
	For $ \alpha \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $,
	we define 
	\[
		I_\alpha := 
		\{
			\beta \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \}
			\mid 
			 (\ell_\alpha, \lambda_\alpha) 
			\mbox{ and }
			(\ell_\beta, \lambda_\beta) 
			\mbox{ are compatible} 
			\,
		\}

	\]
	and $ \sigma(I_\alpha) := \inf\{ \beta \in I_\alpha \}  $.
	Note that $ I_{\sigma(I_\alpha)} = I_\alpha $ if $ I_\alpha \neq \emptyset $.
 	
 	\item
 	Define $ \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_s \in \{1, \ldots, m \} $ 
 	via:
 		for all $ \alpha \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $ with $ |I_{\alpha}| \geq 2 $ there is a unique $ \alpha_i $ with 
 		$ \alpha_i = \sigma(I_\alpha) $.
 	Moreover, we set $ I_0 := \{ 1, \ldots, m \} \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^s I_{\alpha_i} $. 
 	Hence, this defines a partition of the index set into disjoint subsets:
 	\[
	 	\{ 1 , \ldots , m \}  = I_0 \cup I_{\alpha_1} \cup \cdots \cup I_{\alpha_s}
	 	\ .
 	\]
 \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:22:39.767282+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1bbd37487e5221260495b596ec5210b82ea08f4ab1f0786f1e390cd5b1de688f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:ext3 of arXiv:2508.21658, 'Infinite-dimensional stochastic differential equations for Coulomb random point fields'] {r-simon}, [simon]}]  
\thetag{i} 
Let $ \{ (\E ^n, \mathscr{D}^n) \}_{n\in\N } $ be an increasing sequence of non-negative symmetric closed bilinear forms on $\Lnu $. 
Let $ (\E ^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}^{\infty} )$ be the symmetric bilinear form defined by 
\begin{align}	\notag &
\E ^{\infty } (f,f) = \limi{n} \E ^n (f,f) , 
\quad 
\mathscr{D}^{\infty} =
 \{ f \in \bigcap_{n \in\N } \mathscr{D}^n \, ;\, \limi{n} \E ^n (f,f) < \infty \} 
.\end{align}
It holds that $ (\E ^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}^{\infty} )$ is a closed symmetric bilinear form on $ \Lnu $. 
$ \{ (\E ^n, \mathscr{D}^n) \}_{n\in\N } $ converges to $ (\E ^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}^{\infty} )$ in the strong resolvent sense on $ \Lnu $. 

\noindent \thetag{ii} 
Let $ \{ (\E ^n, \mathscr{D}^n) \}_{n\in\N } $ be a decreasing sequence of non-negative symmetric closed bilinear forms on $\Lnu $. 
Let $ (\E ^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}^{\infty} )$ be the symmetric bilinear form defined by

\quad 
\mathscr{D}^{\infty} = \bigcup_{n \in\N } \mathscr{D}^n 
.\end{align}
It holds that 
$ \{ (\E ^n, \mathscr{D}^n) \}_{n\in\N } $ converges to $ (\E _{\mathrm{max}}^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}_{\mathrm{max}}^{\infty} )$ in the strong resolvent sense on $ \Lnu $.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.588420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1bbdc0671006af81fc37c9885d0816b787449a4a45694ffba824f88710fd9496","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm RT of arXiv:2603.15323, '\Large \bf Small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums'] Suppose that a map $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ satisfies the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) with
\[
\lim_{z\to-\infty}f(z)=0,
\]
and 
\[
|\phi(z)|\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}|z|}, \quad z\in {\mathbb R},
\]
for some constants $c_1,c_2>0$. Then, the solution of the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) is given by
\[
f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}L^{n}\phi(z)=\phi(z)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i_1,\cdots, i_n} 
c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_n}L_{\gamma_{i_1}}\cdots L_{\gamma_{i_{n}}}\phi(z),
\]

$$ 
If $\{\gamma_{j}\}$ is arithmetic with span $\gamma$, then
$$
f(z)=\frac{\gamma}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(z-k\gamma) +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\[
 T_\delta^G(f\circ q)=(T_\delta^Hf)\circ q.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.590254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c10fe6b4003997db129ff47f14d2f95ef1ffc18f1857fb25ac7eadd1b3625ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:existence of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Under Assumption~(ass:params of the paper), the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Well-definedness.}
  For each $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
  $f_n(t,\cdot;H,\alpha) \in L^\alpha(\mathbb{R})$,
  so $X^{(n)}_H(t)$ is a well-defined S$\alpha$S random variable.

\item \textbf{Finite-dimensional distributions.}
  For any $m \in \mathbb{N}^*$, $t_1,\ldots,t_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  and $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$:
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
  \exp\!\Bigl(i\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)\Bigr)
  \right]
  = \exp\!\left(
  -\int_\mathbb{R}\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j f_n(t_j,u)\Bigr|^\alpha\,du
  \right).
  \end{equation}

\item \textbf{S$\alpha$S property.}
  For any $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  the linear combination $\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)$
  is S$\alpha$S. In particular, $(X^{(n)}_H(t_1),\ldots,X^{(n)}_H(t_m))$
  is a jointly S$\alpha$S random vector.

\item \textbf{Scale.}
  $\bigl\|X^{(n)}_H(t)\bigr\|_\alpha^\alpha
  = \int_\mathbb{R}|f_n(t,u)|^\alpha\,du < \infty$.

\item \textbf{Higher-order increment stationarity.}
  For $H$ constant ($H(t) \equiv H \in (n-1,n)$), the
  $n$-th order increment process
  \begin{equation}
  
  \Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)
  := \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}X^{(n)}_H(t+kh),
  \quad h \in \mathbb{R},
  \end{equation}
  is stationary in $t$. For functional $H(\cdot)$, the distribution
  of $\Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)$ depends on $t$ only through the
  values $H(t), H(t+h), \ldots, H(t+nh)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation with the ghost-field magnetisation M(p,h)","Russo's formula and the pivotal decomposition (Simon-Lieb type inequality)","Conclusions are one-sided mean-field bounds and sharpness, never continuity at p_c"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c135835662116d8bd927dc5acd650b6de0faa870e088f5dd7fd1ab1414511d1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Integrating them gives: (i) sharpness of the phase transition, i.e. the susceptibility chi(p) is finite for every p < p_c, hence exponential decay of connectivities below p_c; (ii) the mean-field bounds M(p_c,h) >= c h^{1/2} (delta >= 2) and theta(p) >= c (p - p_c) for p > p_c (beta <= 1). {"assumptions":["complex (or real) terms; the ratio test needs a_n != 0 eventually","limsup and liminf are taken in [0, infinity]; when the limits exist the tests read with the plain limit"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479169+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_1c217f746d95c3909891090744a766ac7bb7f0c720afa221f92c52b6b464afc1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let sum a_n be a series of complex numbers. ROOT TEST (Cauchy): put L = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges (the terms do not tend to 0); if L = 1 the test is inconclusive. RATIO TEST (d'Alembert): suppose a_n != 0 for large n. If limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1 the series converges absolutely; if liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| > 1 (in particular if |a_{n+1}/a_n| >= 1 for all large n) it diverges; otherwise the test is inconclusive. Comparison: for every sequence, liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| <= liminf |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|, so whenever the ratio test decides, the root test decides the same way, and the root test is strictly stronger: for a_n = (1/2)^n for n even and (1/3)^n for n odd, the ratios oscillate between (2/3)^n -> 0 and (3/2)^{n} -> infinity so the ratio test says nothing, while |a_n|^{1/n} takes the values 1/2 and 1/3, limsup 1/2 < 1, and the series converges. Both tests are inconclusive for sum 1/n (divergent) and sum 1/n^2 (convergent), which have L = 1; the radius of convergence of a power series sum c_n z^n is 1 / limsup |c_n|^{1/n} (Cauchy-Hadamard), the root test in its most used form.","status":"unverified"}

E_2 & := \frac{2}{(k!)^2} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \mathbbm{1}\{S_{\mathbf{x}}\cap S_{\mathbf{z}}\neq\varnothing\} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}})] \mathbb{E}[g(\mathbf{z},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x}) \\
E_3 & := \frac{2}{(k!)^2} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \mathbbm{1}\{S_{\mathbf{x}}\cap S_{\mathbf{z}}\neq\varnothing\} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) g(\mathbf{z},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x}) \\
E_4 & := \frac{2}{k!} \sum_{\varnothing \subsetneq I \subsetneq \{1,\hdots,k\}} \frac{1}{(k-|I|)!} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^{k-|I|}} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) g((\mathbf{x}_I,\mathbf{z}),\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^{k-|I|}(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x})
\end{align*}
with $(\mathbf{x}_I,\mathbf{z}):=(x_{i_1},\hdots,x_{i_m},z_1,\hdots,z_{k-m})$ for $I=\{i_1,\hdots,i_m\}$.
Then,
$$
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KR}}(\xi,\zeta) \leq \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathbf{L},\mathbf{M}) + E_2 + E_3 + E_4.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:50:26.915607+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c62cebf0f9bd1d73352e684fa4cad4b50ce25300db0c722dccbfe59326164c5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:int1 of arXiv:2505.09604, 'Exceptional force, uncountably many solutions in the KPZ fixed point'] On a single event of full probability, the following holds for all $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$:  
    \begin{enumerate} [label=(\roman*), font=\normalfont]
        \item (Interfaces have directions)    For every and $(x_0,s)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ the interfaces $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}$ and $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}$ are $-\xi$-directed continuous functions,   i.e.\
        \begin{equation} 
            \lim_{t\rightarrow \infty}\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,{\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(t)/t=-\xi, \qquad {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}\in\{-,+\}.
        \end{equation}
        Furthermore, if $\tau \in \mathcal{T}^{\xi,-} \cup \mathcal{T}^{\xi,+}$, then  we also have
        \begin{equation} 
        \lim_{t \to -\infty} \frac{\tau(t)}{t} = -\xi.
        \end{equation}
        \item (Interfaces  live on the set of branching points $\mathfrak B_{\xi}$) For all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists $s < t$, $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and ${\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{-,+\}$ such that  $x = \tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi, {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(t)$ if and only if $x \in \mathfrak B_{t,\xi}$.
        \item  (Interfaces are ordered) For $s\in\mathbb{R}$, if $x_0<y_0$, then
        \[
            \tau^{\xi,-}_{(x_0,s)}(r)\leq \tau^{\xi,-}_{(y_0,s)}(r), \qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau^{\xi,+}_{(x_0,s)}(r)\leq \tau^{\xi,+}_{(y_0,s)}(r), \quad \forall r>s.
        \]
        \item (Interfaces through common intervals $\mathfrak{I}^{s,\xi}$ coalesce)  If $\xi \in \Xi$, then for any $s\in \mathbb{R}$ and  $\alpha\in \mathcal{I}^{s,\xi}$, if $x_0,y_0 \in \mathfrak{I}_\alpha^{s,\xi}$, then there exists $t > s$ such that
        \[
        \tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(r) = \tau_{(y_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(r),\quad\text{and}\quad \tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(r) = \tau_{(y_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(r),\quad\text{for all }r \ge t
        \]
        Additionally, in this case, there exists an infinite sequence $\{t_n\}$ with $t_n \to \infty$ such that 
        \[
        \tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(t_n) = \tau_{(y_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(t_n)\quad \text{for all }n \in \mathbb{N}.
        \]
        \item (Interfaces through different intervals $\mathfrak{I}^{s,\xi}$ are disjoint).
        If $\xi \in \Xi$ and $x_0 < y_0$, where $x_0 \in \mathfrak{I}_\alpha^{s,\xi}$ and $y_0 \in \mathfrak{I}_\beta^{s,\xi}$ for $\alpha \neq \beta$, then for all $t > s$,
        \[
        \tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(t) \le \tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(t) < \tau_{(y_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(t) \le \tau_{(y_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(t).
        \]
        In particular, combined with the previous item, the set of all leftmost $\xi$-mixed Busemann interfaces and the set of all rightmost $\xi$-mixed Busemann interfaces are forests,  and for each $(x_0,s) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, there is a unique $\tau^- \in \mathcal{T}^{\xi,-}$ such that $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}$ coalesces with $\tau^-$ and a unique $\tau^+ \in \mathcal{T}^{\xi,+}$ such that $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}$ coalesces with $\tau^+$.  
        \item  (Interfaces form interior bubbles)  If $\xi \in \Xi$, there exist infinitely many points $(x_0,s)\in\mathfrak S_{\xi}^L$ (and also infinitely many points in $\mathfrak S_\xi^R$) such that the following holds:  there exist $t_2 > t_1 > s$ and $\delta > 0$ so that
        \begin{enumerate}  [label=(\alph*), font=\normalfont]
        \item $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(r)=\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(r)$ for $r \in [t_1-\delta,t_1]$,
        \item $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(r)=\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(r)$ for $r \in [t_2,t_2 + \delta]$, and
        \item $\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,-}(r)<\tau_{(x_0,s)}^{\xi,+}(r)$,  for all $r\in(t_1,t_2)$.
        \end{enumerate} 
        See Figure (fig:bubbles of the paper) for an illustration. 
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Denote by
\[
\mathcal I_Y:=\{f\in C^\infty(M)\,:\, f|_Y=0\}
\]
the ideal of smooth functions vanishing on $Y$.
A vector field $\rho_Y$ on $M$ is called an \emph{Euler vector field of $Y$} if
\[
\rho_Y f - f \in \mathcal I_Y^2
\qquad\text{for every } f\in\mathcal I_Y,
\]
where $\mathcal{I}_Y^2$ denotes the ideal of smooth functions vanishing at order $2$ along $Y$.
Equivalently, $\rho_Y$ acts as the radial vector field in the normal directions to $Y$, modulo terms vanishing to second order along $Y$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.340897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c9194834ab364c38725ed23d16cf895c3c8524a1c378ff60b21159d274b41ab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Def weighted projective stack and curve of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Consider the $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$-weighted action of $\mathbb{G}_m$ on $n$-dimension affine space $\mathbb{A}^n$, i.e., \[t \cdot (x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (t^{a_1}x_1, \ldots, t^{a_n}x_n)\] where each $a_i > 0.$ 
Then, the {\em weighted projective stack} $\mathcal{P}(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ is given by the stack quotient
\[
\mathcal{P}(a_1, \ldots, a_n) := [(\mathbb{A}^n \setminus 0)/\mathbb{G}_m].
\]
When $n = 2$, we refer to the weighted projective stack $\mathcal{P}(a,b)$ as a {\em weighted projective curve}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.491110+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c9d4f2caa21547e08697f23ef7b4b62e76f0d996c1a36e87301b399297073ac","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.04012, 'Hölder regularity for backward stochastic Volterra integral equations and applications to '] Suppose that $(\Psi, G)$ satisfy the assumptions in Theorem \ref{thm:well-posedness-BSVIE} with $p=2$, and let $(Y,Z)$ be the unique solution to \eqref{eq:bsvie-intro}. Let $(\Psi^\pi,G^\pi)$ satisfy the assumptions in Theorem \ref{theorem:energy-estimates} with $p=2$, with Lipschitz constant $[G^\pi]_L$ independent of $\pi$, and denote by $(Y^\pi,Z^\pi)$ the solution of the BSDE system \eqref{def:BSDE-app-BSVIE}.

Define the approximation errors
\begin{gather*}
    \varepsilon_{\Psi}^\pi
    \coloneqq
    \mathbb E\left[
    \int_0^T
    |\Psi(t)-\Psi^\pi(t)|^2\,dt
    \right], \quad \varepsilon_{G}^\pi
    \coloneqq
    \mathbb E\left[
    \int_0^T
    \left(
    \int_t^T
    \left|
    G(t,s,Y(s),Z(t,s))
    -
    G^\pi(t,s,Y(s),Z(t,s))
    \right|\,ds
    \right)^2
    dt \right].
\end{gather*}
Then there exists a constant $C>0$, independent of $\pi$, such that
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb E\Bigg[
    \int_0^T |Y(t)-Y^\pi(\tau(t),t)|^2\,dt
    +
    \int_0^T\int_t^T
    |Z(t,s)-Z^\pi(\tau(t),s)|^2\,ds\,dt 
    \Bigg]
    \leq
    C\big(\varepsilon_{\Psi}^\pi+\varepsilon_{G}^\pi\big). 
\end{align*}
In particular, if
$\varepsilon_{\Psi}^\pi+\varepsilon_{G}^\pi\to0$ as $|\pi|\to0$, then
\[
    (Y^\pi(\tau(\cdot),\cdot),Z^\pi(\tau(\cdot),\cdot))
    \longrightarrow
    (Y,Z) \quad \text{in $\mathcal H^2(0,T)\times\mathcal H_\Delta^2(0,T)$.}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.463554+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1cdd2ad95d601cfb896d911acbb500734e35904a1f8d83e5f15451e31f6585e0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (A law-weighted Brownian error with sublinear spatial growth) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, $0<\lambda<1$, $\kappa\ne0$, and let $0<\theta<\alpha/2$. Put
\[
  \phi_\theta(x):=(1+x^2)^{\theta/2},\qquad x\in\R,
\]
and let $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)=\wt b(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  a(t,x)\equiv\kappa,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=\kappa+r(t)\phi_\theta(x),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=\wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then the stable coefficient is bounded, bounded away from zero, and H\"older while failing to be Lipschitz at the origin. The perturbed Brownian coefficient is spatially Lipschitz. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions},
\[
  B=0,
  \qquad
  A^2=\int_0^T |r(t)|^2\,\E \phi_\theta(X_t)^2\dd t,
  \qquad
  S=0.
\]
Moreover, $A<\infty$ and
\[
  A^2\le C_{\theta,T}\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^2,
\]
where $C_{\theta,T}$ depends on the baseline moment $\sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t|^{2\theta}$, which is finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:baseline-moments}. Consequently, for every $R>0$ there exists $C_R>0$ such that, whenever $\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}\le R$, $x_0=\wt x_0$, and $A<1$ (for instance, for sufficiently small $\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}$),
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
  \le C_R\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:38:17.799906+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1cee1b276826ef32077698f1aa38b2e64ede4e3e93bc93776ff91e134e36dcb2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem Nkq>1 of arXiv:2509.24452, 'A family of non-uniform distributions on the set of parking functions generated by random '] Consider $N^{(n)}_k$ as in (equation Nk of the paper)  under the measure $\mathcal{P}_n^{(q)}$ with $q>1$.

\noindent i. For $k$ fixed, $N^{(n)}_k$ converges in distribution  to the distribution of
$\sum_{j=k}^\infty Z_{j;k}$, where $\{Z_{j;k}\}_{j=k}^\infty$ are independent random variables and $Z_{j;k}$ has the Bernoulli distribution with parameter $\frac{(q-1)q^{k-1}}{q^j-1}$.
The distribution is supported on $\mathbb{Z}^+$;
\

\noindent ii. For $\{k_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfying $\lim_{n\to\infty} k_n=\infty$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}(n-k_n)=\infty$, $N^{(n)}_{k_n}$ converges in distribution to the distribution of

\

\noindent iii. For $k$ fixed, $N^{(n)}_{n-k}$ converges in distribution to the distribution of $\sum_{i=0}^k Y_i$. The distribution is supported on $\{0,1,\cdots, k+1\}$.
\

\noindent iv. $\sum_{i=0}^\infty Y_i\stackrel{\text{dist}}{=}\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^kY_i\stackrel{\text{dist}}{=}\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{j=k}^\infty Z_{j;k}$.

$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}N^{(n)}_{n-k}\stackrel{\text{dist}}{=}\lim_{k\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}N^{(n)}_k=\sum_{i=0}^\infty Y_i.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:32:11.126945+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1ceec89efac2526de93c14abd3e471b6954aefd5dc785b3149268472e941320a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:det_lemma of arXiv:2510.06891, 'Multivariate CLT for L\\'evy processes: convergence rates without moment assumptions'] Let $\\bm{M}(t)$ be a $d \\times d$ positive definite matrix (i.e. with strictly positive eigenvalues), such that $\\bm{M}(t) \\to \\bm{I}_d$ as $t\\to\\infty$.
