{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.186288+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1cf379941a5ef22c6122c15ef110b3d0748eb7832f969476963f0730decaf4ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 of arXiv:2606.30364, 'Distributional comparison for non-commutative infinitely divisible probability measures'] Let $(\Ac,\varphi)$ be a non-commutative probability space. A family $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$  of subalgebras of $\mathcal{A}$ is said to be   
	\begin{enumerate}
		
		\item[(\textbf{B})] \emph{Boolean independent} if for any alternating product $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ of elements of  $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$ we have
		
		\[\varphi(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n)=\varphi(a_1)\varphi(a_2)\cdots \varphi(a_n) \ .\] 
		
		\item[(\textbf{F})] \emph{free independent} if for any alternating product $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ of elements of  $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$  we have 
		
		\begin{align*}
\varphi(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n) = 0
\end{align*}
		
		whenever $\varphi(a_k) = 0$ for $k=1,2,\ldots,n$. 
		
		
		\item[(\textbf{T})] \emph{tensor independent} if for any (not necessarily alternating) product $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ of elements of  $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i \in I}$ we have 
		
		\[
		\varphi(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n) \ \ = \prod_{B \in \ker[{\bm i}]} \varphi \left( \OrdAsProduct{a}{k}{B} \right) 
		\]
		where $\overset{\longrightarrow}{\prod}_{k \in B} a_k := a_{k_1} a_{k_2} \cdots a_{k_r}$
		
	provided $B = \{k_1 < k_2 < \cdots < k_r \} \subset [m] := \{1,2,\ldots,m\} $ and $\ker[{\bm i}]$ with ${\bm i}=(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)$ denotes the set of all non-empty sets of the form $ \{k \in [m] : i_k = i\}$ with $i \in I$. 
		
		Essentially, the set $\ker[{\bm i}]$ is the partition of $[m]$ that keeps track of all variables that belong to the same algebra.  
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.060710+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d14d0b7e9076743e4b8eb70c925c6f8a70259997b39f59d9cc901a99a3944d0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [LDP for type fractions along a random path]}

Under the joint law of the Galton--Watson tree $\mathcal{T}_\infty$ and the random exploration path, the family of random variables $\{\Upsilon_j\}_{j\in\N_4}$ satisfies the LDP in the Polish space $(0,\infty) \times \mathcal{S}_2$ with rate $j$ and with good rate function $J$ given by
\[
J(x,s) = \inf_{\nu \in \Phi(x,s)} I(\nu), \qquad x \in (0,\infty),\, s \in \mathcal{S}_2.
\]
Here,
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$I\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is the good rate function given by
\[
I(\nu) =
\begin{cases}
H\left(\nu\,\middle\|\, \pi_{1,2}\nu \otimes \zeta^{\otimes 2}\right), & \text{if } \pi_{1,2}\nu=\pi_{2,3}\nu,\\[1ex]
\infty, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
where $H(\cdot\, \|\, \cdot)$ denotes relative entropy and $\pi_{1,2}$, $\pi_{2,3}$ denote the projection onto the first two, respectively, the last two of the three coordinates.
\item
The constraint on $\nu$ is to the subset of $\mathcal{P}(E)$ given by
\[
\Phi(x,s) = \big\{\nu \in \mathcal{P}(E)\colon\,\|G(\nu)\|_1 = x,\,G(\nu)/\|G(\nu)\|_1 = s\big\},
\qquad x \in (0,\infty),\,s \in \mathcal{S}_2,
\]
where $G = (G^\chi)_{\chi \in S}$ with $G^\chi\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is given by
\[
G^\chi(\nu) = \int_{E} h^\chi\,\mathrm{d}\nu
\]
with $h^\chi\colon\,E \to \N_0$ given by
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^{-}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\, c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\, c^\prime>0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{0}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= c-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\,c^\prime=0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{+}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}} + \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.345794+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d2d4fee932c393b7117486d626b7edaa2637bc30325b72dfc7cb52e97eea9ba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:realization of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $U \in C^{0}(0,1)$. The following are equivalent.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\roman*), leftmargin=*]
			\item $U = U_{f}$ for some $f \in \mathcal{D}_{+}^{2}$.
			\item The Hill equation $\psi'' + \tfrac12 U\psi = 0$ has a positive
			solution on $(0,1)$.
			\item The Hill equation is disconjugate on $(0,1)$; equivalently,
			\begin{equation*}
				\int_{0}^{1}(\chi')^{2}\,dz
				\;\ge\; \tfrac12\int_{0}^{1}U\chi^{2}\,dz
				\qquad\text{for all } \chi \in C_{c}^{\infty}(0,1).
			\end{equation*}
		\end{enumerate}
		When these hold, every positive solution $\psi$ and base point
		$z_{0} \in (0,1)$ determine a law by
		\begin{equation}
			Q(z) = \int_{z_{0}}^{z}\frac{ds}{\psi(s)^{2}},
			\qquad
			F = Q^{-1},
			\qquad
			f = \psi^{2}\circ F
			\quad\text{on } J := Q\big((0,1)\big),
			
		\end{equation}
		and this $f$ has unit total mass automatically; conversely, every law
		with potential $U$ arises in this way. We call
		$\mathcal{C} := \{U : \textup{(iii) holds}\}$ the \emph{probability
			cone}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.555108+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d8a66eeaab015ec20716be8da0e452974bc163857548f3d6faecbc07a7ab75d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2604.02312, 'A weak transport approach to the Schrödinger--Bass bridge'] For $x \in \Rd$ and $\eta \in \cP_2(\Rd)$, define
    \begin{equation}
        C_{\rm stat}^\beta(x,\eta)
        := 
        \sup_{y \in \Rd}
        \left\{-q_\beta(x-y) + 
        \inf_{\rho \in \cP_2(\Rd)} 
        \bigl\{H(\rho \,|\, \gamma_y)+ W_\beta(\rho,\eta)\bigr\}
        \right\}.
    \end{equation}
    Then the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
        \item
        For every $(x,\eta) \in \Rd \times \cP_2(\Rd)$, $C_{\rm SB}^\beta(x,\eta) = C_{\rm stat}^\beta(x,\eta)$.
        In particular, $C_{\rm SB}^\beta$ is a continuous standard weak transport cost and admits a $2$-growth bound.
        Moreover, for every $x \in \Rd$, the map $\eta \mapsto C_{\rm SB}^\beta(x,\eta)$ is strictly convex.
        
        
        \item
        Let $(x,\eta) \in \Rd \times \cP_2(\Rd)$, and let $f^\circ \in L^1(\eta)$ attain \eqref{eq:SB.dual} for the pair ${(\delta_x,\eta)}$. Then,
        \[
            C_{\rm SB}^\beta(x,\eta) = \int f^\circ\,\rmd\eta - q_\beta\Box(-\Tcal^\beta_1[f^\circ])(x).
        \]
        Moreover, set $g_1 := \exp\bigl(-q_\beta \Box(-f^\circ)\bigr)$ and $g_t := g_1 * \gamma_{0;1-t}$.
        Then the infimum in \eqref{eq:SB.cost.dynamic} defining $C_{\rm SB}^\beta(x,\eta)$ is attained by $X^\circ = (X^\circ_t)_{t \in [0,1]}$ satisfying
        \begin{align*}
            \rmd X^\circ_t
            &= \nabla \log g_t(Y^\circ_t) \,\rmd t + \bigl(I_d + \tfrac{1}{\beta}\nabla^2 \log g_t(Y^\circ_t) \bigr) \, \rmd B_t, 
            \quad X^\circ_0 = x,
            \\
            \rmd Y^\circ_t &= \nabla \log g_t(Y^\circ_t) \,\rmd t + \rmd B_t,
            \quad Y^\circ_0 = x - \tfrac{1}{\beta}\bigl(\nabla q_\beta \Box(-\Tcal^\beta_1[f^\circ])\bigr)(x).
        \end{align*}
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-11-02T23:06:16.395782+00:00","domain":"dynamical systems","id":"claim_1d935f08a980ccb3970b38e8e040329a1218f9d5da5957ad912737706c91e750","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Partition quadratic stochastic operators converge to the empty body (2026). An F-quadratic stochastic operator acts on the simplex over types {0, 1, ..., m}, where 0 is the empty body: parents of the same sex, or a pair containing 0, produce 0; Rozikov and Zhamilov proved that every such operator has the unique fixed point e_0 and that every trajectory converges to it exponentially fast. Problem 10 of Ganikhodzhaev, Mukhamedov and Rozikov, Quadratic stochastic operators and processes: results and open problems (arXiv:0902.4207), asks whether the same holds when the two sexes are replaced by the blocks E_1, ..., E_q of an arbitrary partition of {1, ..., m}, with same-block pairs producing the empty body. The answer is yes: with y = 1 - x_0, every such operator V satisfies y(V(x)) <= (1 - 1/q) y(x)^2, so e_0 is the unique fixed point and y(V^n(x)) <= c^{-1} (c y(x))^{2^n} with c = 1 - 1/q, and the inequality is an equality at every step along some trajectories for each q. Without the rule that pairs containing 0 produce 0 the statement fails: (x_0, x_1) -> (x_0^2 + x_1^2, 2 x_0 x_1) has a second, attracting fixed point (1/2, 1/2). Exact rational checks and a Lean 4 file accompany the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/partition-qso-empty-body (commit f3a2991ab8c5). Not refereed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.711106+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d9418e5804a11ff3106efad766ed89cbfd57ff9e6078eb7b52d01da2e30a58f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $L \supseteq \textbf{FIK}$ and $\Gamma, \Delta \subseteq \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$.
  \begin{itemize}
    \item We let $\Box \Gamma \coloneq \set{ \Box \varphi; \varphi \in \Gamma }$ and $\Diamond \Gamma \coloneq \set{ \Diamond \varphi; \varphi \in \Gamma }$.\\
          We also let $\Box^{-1} \Gamma \coloneq \set{ \varphi; \Box \varphi \in \Gamma }$ and $\Diamond^{-1} \Gamma \coloneq \set{ \varphi; \Diamond \varphi \in \Gamma }$.
    \item A tuple $(\Gamma, \Delta)$ is said to be a \emph{theory}.
    \item A theory $(\Gamma, \Delta)$ is said to be \emph{maximal} if $\Gamma \cup \Delta = \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$.
    \item A theory $(\Gamma, \Delta)$ is said to be \emph{$L$-consistent} if $L \nvdash \bigwedge \Gamma_0 \to \bigvee \Delta_0$ for any finite $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$ and any finite $\Delta_0 \subseteq \Delta$.
          We note that $\bigwedge \emptyset = \top$ and $\bigvee \emptyset = \bot$.
    \item A theory $(\Gamma, \Delta)$ is said to be \emph{$L$-final} if it is $L$-consistent and
          $(\Gamma \cup \Pi, \Delta \setminus \Pi)$ is not $L$-consistent for any nonempty $\Pi \subseteq \Delta$.
  \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.656989+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d9d7fb453e64435b2f938a0b5b791f570b0656d93935e2a6342d6c8c0fef86d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (Fixed-time moment formula) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] For $k\ge1$, $t_1,\dots,t_k>0$ and $\phi_1,\dots,\phi_k\in\Cc$,

=\gamma^{\,k-1}\sum_{T\in\T_k}
\int
\prod_{\{a,b\}\in E(T)} p_{\,s_b-s_a}\bigl(y_b-y_a\bigr)
\prod_{v\in V_{\mathrm{int}}(T)} ds_v\,dy_v\,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:51:11.644675+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1da3485c41182e8bee8eed1488da910e2376dc24f66537972f0e413591382cf5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 31 of arXiv:2605.31471, 'Convergence Rates of Continuous-Time Random Walks to Time-Fractional Diffusions with Unbou'] Let $\alpha,\beta\in\R$ and $k\in\N_0$.
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item If $u\in\cC^k_{\alpha,\infty}(\cX)$ and
            $v\in\cC^k_{\beta,\infty}(\cX)$, then
            $uv\in\cC^k_{\alpha+\beta,\infty}(\cX)$ and
            \[
                \|uv\|_{\alpha+\beta,k}
                \le C_{\alpha,\beta,k}\|u\|_{\alpha,k}\|v\|_{\beta,k}.
            \]
            The same estimate holds for contractions of tensor-valued
            functions.
            \item Let
            \[
                \eta_h(x)=h b(x)+\sqrt h\sum_{\ell=1}^d\sigma_\ell(x)\xi_\ell
            \]
            and let Assumptions~\ref{asm:weighted-regular} and
            \ref{asm:rw-bounded} hold.  Then, for $0<h\le h_0$ and
            $0\le\theta\le1$,
            \[
                C^{-1}w_\gamma(x)\le
                w_\gamma(x+\theta\eta_h(x))
                \le Cw_\gamma(x),
                \qquad \gamma\in\R,
            \]
            and, for $1\le j\le k+4$,
            \[
                \|\DD^j\eta_h(x)\|
                \le C\sqrt h\,w_{1-j}(x).
            \]
            Moreover, if $\varphi_h^\theta(x):=x+\theta\eta_h(x)$, then
            \[
                \|\DD\varphi_h^\theta(x)\|\le C,
                \qquad
                \|\DD^j\varphi_h^\theta(x)\|
                \le C\sqrt h\,w_{1-j}(x),
                \quad j\ge2.
            \]
            \item If $g\in\cC^k_{\alpha,\infty}(\cX)$, then
            $x\mapsto \E g(x+\eta_h(x))$ belongs to
            $\cC^k_{\alpha,\infty}(\cX)$.
        \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1dc5a679e2211368b630985d58800be61bf289fc83995d52c07c31a39ab91041","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 57 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\star$ as in \eqref{e:star.options} and $\mu \in \sM^\star(\alpha,q_0)$, we have
        \[\|\mu\|_{L^2}^2 \le
    \frac{10}{\alpha}
    +6 + O(\epsilon)\,.\]
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}. Let us write
$X(1)= X(q_*)+\textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}$ where (a) denotes the drift term and (b) denotes the martingale term.
We have $\bbE[X(q_*)^2] \le \epsilon$ under either of the initialization conditions \ref{it:6.1} or \ref{it:6.2}. Next, using the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1
    p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt\bigg)^2
    \bigg]
    \le \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 p'(t)\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 (b_t)^2 \,dt
        \bigg)\bigg]
    \le
    \int_{q_*}^1 \E[(b_t)^2] \,dt\\
    &\le \int_{q_*}^1 \Cost(t)\,dt
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 \budget(t;\alpha)\,dt + \epsilon
    \le \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha} + \epsilon\,,
    \end{align*}
where the last two inequalities hold under any of the budget conditions
\ref{it:4.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, or \ref{it:4.3}
combined with either condition
\ref{it:2.1} or \ref{it:2.2}. Lastly, we have from \eqref{e:loc.mg.L2.bounded} that 
    \[
    \E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 s(t)^2
    \E[(\sigma_t)^2] \,dt
    \le 2\bigg\{ \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha}
        + \epsilon + 1\bigg\}\,.\]
Combining the above bounds gives altogether
    \[
    \E[X(1)^2]
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \E[X(q_*)^2]
    +\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    +\E[\textup{(b)}^2]\bigg\}
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \frac{3(1+\epsilon)}{\alpha}
    +2 + 4\epsilon\bigg\}\,,
    \]
proving the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.975450+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1dcd21646f5f1688cbe5de5658143fcc519a4c1fbf340bebbc33313f3de407bf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 43 (Sharp depth-only no-go and determinant blindness) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Fix $r\ge1$.  For every nonzero compact operator $K$ on a separable
Hilbert space $H$, there is a block-lower-triangular operator model of a
nonzero depth-$r$ primitive word whose only nonzero endpoint block is
unitarily equivalent to $K$.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 s_j(W_r)=s_j(K),\qquad j\ge1.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently primitive depth alone forces no Schatten membership, decay
law, regular variation, Mellin order, or Fredholm growth.

More explicitly, on
$\mathcal H=H_0\oplus\cdots\oplus H_r$, with $H_j\cong H$, choose
adjacent compact blocks $X_j:H_{j-1}\to H_j$ and set
$W_1=X_1$, $W_j=[X_j,W_{j-1}]$.  Then $W_r$ has only its $(r,0)$ block and
realizes the free normal word
\[
 \operatorname{ad}_{\mathsf q_r}\operatorname{ad}_{\mathsf q_{r-1}}
 \cdots\operatorname{ad}_{\mathsf q_2}(\mathsf q_1)
 \in\mathfrak L_r(Q^\sharp).
\]
Moreover $W_r^2=0$.  If $K\in\mathcal S_1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \det(I+zW_r)=1,
 \qquad
 \frac12\log\det(I+z^2W_r^*W_r)
 =\frac12\log\det(I+z^2K^*K).
 
\end{equation}
More generally, if
$D=\operatorname{diag}(D_0,\ldots,D_r)$ and $R_\triangle$ are trace
class, with $R_\triangle$ strictly block triangular, then
\begin{equation}
 \det(I+z(D+R_\triangle))
 =\prod_{j=0}^r\det(I+zD_j).
 
\end{equation}
Thus an ordinary Fredholm determinant can erase an entire strictly
triangular ancestry layer, while hermitized and labelled responses retain it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.474645+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e202035132140ea4bc4f7953ae24f53864051500bde104688dcc6d4af941e2f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:hypercube_entropy}
Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d) \in_R \{\pm1\}^d$ with every $X_i$ asymmetric. 
Let $Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_d) \in \Sym(X)$. 
Then, $H(Y) \ge \frac{1}{d} H(X)$, with equality if and only if the following conditions are all satisfied: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item There exists an index $i \in [d]$ such that both $f_{Y_i} = f_{-X_i}$ and $H(Y) = H(Y_i)$,
\item $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_1-\frac{1}{2}} = \dots = \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_d-\frac{1}{2}}$, 
\item the random variables $X_i$ are mutually independent. 
\end{enumerate}
\begin{proof}
Let $j \in \arg\max_{i \in [d]} H(X_i) = \arg\min_{i \in [d]} \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_i-\frac{1}{2}}$. 
Note that $Y_j$ is an independent symmetrizer of $X_j$ by (lem:Rd_projection_works of the paper). 
Thus we may apply (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) to $X_j$ and $Y_j$. 
Then, 
\begin{align}
H(Y) &\ge H(Y_j) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_a}\\
&\ge H(X_j) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_2}\\

&\ge \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d H(X_i) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_3}\\
&\ge \frac{1}{d} H(X) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_4}
\end{align}
where we used the entropy chain rule in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper)), 
(thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_2 of the paper)), 
and the entropy chain rule and the fact that conditioning reduces entropy in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)). 

Equality is attained in $H(Y) \ge \frac{1}{d} H(X)$ if and only if it is attained in each of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper)-

(ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)). 
The equality condition of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)) is $H(X) = \sum_{i=1}^d H(X_i) $
which is in turn equivalent to mutual independence of the $X_i$ (see e.g. [PW25:book]). 
The equality condition of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_3 of the paper)) is exactly (ii). 
Now consider the conditions

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $f_{Y_j} = f_{-X_j}$,
\item[(b)] $H(Y) = H(Y_j)$.
\end{itemize}
Equality is attained in (equation ineq:hypercube_entropy_2 of the paper) exactly when $H(X_j) = H(Y_j)$, which, in light of (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper), is equivalent to (a). 
Equality is attained in (equation ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper) exactly when (b) is true. 

We claim that (a-b,ii-iii) is equivalent to (i-iii). 
Clearly (a-b) implies (i); we need only show the converse. 
If (i-iii) is fulfilled, then
$$ H(X_j) = H(X_i) = H(Y_i) = H(Y) \ge H(Y_j) \ge H(X_j) $$
where we have used (in order), condition (ii), condition (i), condition (i) again, the entropy chain rule, and (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper). 
Thus, the last two inequalities are equalities, which forces (b) and also forces $H(Y_j) = H(X_j)$. 
The equality condition of (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) (applied to $X_j$ and $Y_j$) then implies (a). 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.735260+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e20a41f161c047e1ee6957c74016e7eae6081e68a687fb3c35fd9ebacfb7ea9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 (Borders and prefix--suffix lengths) of arXiv:2601.16580, 'Coin flipping and waiting times paradoxes \\ Why fair coins are exceptional'] Let \(T\) be a finite string of length \(L\). A \emph{border} of \(T\) is a substring that is both a prefix and a suffix of \(T\). We refer to the lengths \(\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}\) of these borders as the \emph{prefix--suffix lengths} of \(T\); formally, these are the lengths \(\ell\) such that:
\[
T[1..\ell] \;=\; T[L-\ell+1..L].
\]
We write \(\mathcal{B}(T)\) for the set of all such \(\ell\). (Some authors reserve “proper border’’ for \(\ell<L\); in this paper we \emph{include} \(\ell=L\).) The \emph{border polynomial} is
\[
H_T(y)\;:=\;\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{B}(T)} y^\ell .
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω ⊂ R^n open","F continuous on Ω × R × R^n","u continuous on Ω"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415708+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_1e25d63418d6f4a5169a94db2c01063496e715960b47674a81764905279ec8b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 in Ω if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local maximum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity supersolution if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local minimum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. For the evolution equation u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T) apply the definition in the variables (x,t), with test functions φ(x,t) of class C^1 and F((x,t), r, (p,s)) = s + H(x,p); so at a local maximum of u - φ one requires φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≤ 0, and at a local minimum φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≥ 0. Equivalent variants giving the same class: C^1 test functions may be replaced by C^2 or C^∞ ones, local extrema by strict local extrema, and one may normalize φ(x0) = u(x0). The definition is NOT invariant under F ↦ -F: in general the viscosity solutions of F = 0 and of -F = 0 differ. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.525412+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e3a8c564371a739b5605e21da8c93aaa306bbb3450e32eec605d555e69ae575","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 24 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let \(s_0\geq0\), let \(d\in\C\) satisfy \(\left|d\right|\leq s_0\), and
let \((\mathbf{Y}_N)_{N\geq1}\) be any coupling such that, for each \(N\),
\(\mathbf{Y}_N\) is a centred elliptic Gaussian \(N\times N\) matrix with
mixed covariance \(s_0/N\) and holomorphic covariance \(d/N\), in the sense
of \eqref{EqGeneralMatrixCovariance}.  Write
\(d=|d|\mathrm{e}^{2\mathrm{i}\theta}\), taking \(\theta=0\) when
\(d=0\).  Let \((\mathscr{A},\varphi)\) be a tracial
\(*\)-probability space containing a free centred semicircular pair
\(\mathsf{s}_1,\mathsf{s}_2\) of variance one, and define
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{y}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}
       \left(\alpha\mathsf{s}_1+\mathrm{i}\beta\mathsf{s}_2\right),
 \qquad
 \alpha=\sqrt{\frac{s_0+\left|d\right|}{2}},
 \qquad
 \beta=\sqrt{\frac{s_0-\left|d\right|}{2}}.
\end{equation}
Then, simultaneously for every noncommutative polynomial \(R\) in two
indeterminates,
\[
 \tr_N R(\mathbf{Y}_N,\mathbf{Y}_N^*)
 \longrightarrow
 \varphi\!\left(R(\mathsf{y},\mathsf{y}^*)\right)
 \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]
In particular, \(\mathbf{Y}_N\) converges almost surely in
\(*\)-distribution to \(\mathsf{y}\).  Consequently, if
\((b_N)\) is deterministic and \(b_N\to b\in\C\), then
\(b_N\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Y}_N\) converges almost surely in
\(*\)-distribution to \(b\mathbf{1}+\mathsf{y}\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite group Gamma","Q Gamma-equivariant with 0 < Q < I","Holley's inequality in its product-measure form"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T09:49:00.189655+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e3f205f561f7c54656563b1c8fea5afca86c07c42b7412bde1de30d0bb243cb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT (revision 2), no independent review. Let Gamma be a finite group and Q a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction on l^2(Gamma) with 0 < Q < I, and P_Q the determinantal measure with kernel Q. Let HM(Q) be the harmonic mean of the eigenvalues of Q. Then P_Q stochastically dominates the product Bernoulli measure of density HM(Q), and P_Q is dominated by the product measure of density 1 - HM(I - Q). Precise chain: the minimal conditional ODDS of presence is s_min = 1/(J^{-1})_ee = HM/(1 - HM) with J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}, and the minimal conditional PROBABILITY is s_min/(1 + s_min) = 1/(Q^{-1})_ee = HM(Q) (revision 2 states the odds and the probability separately, after a reviewer noted the two had been conflated in a side note). This is weaker than Lyons's Conjecture 5.7 (geometric mean / Fuglede-Kadison determinant), which numerical monotone-coupling linear programs on Z/nZ, n <= 6, satisfy exactly, with FK + 0.01 failing on a tested instance; those LP results are floating-point evidence, not certificates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e595d1ddd4d31f5d20f20448b8cd74340f097f418011ebff2ea7ceb8a77b1af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the scale walk S_k as an exact random walk with identically distributed increments, as if the field were an exact branching random walk, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the comparison of S_k with a random walk (scale-dependent variances, the bounded error terms (iii)) must be explicitly controlled, while the Gibbs-Markov pieces themselves are exactly independent; skipping this control is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each K_eps is Lebesgue integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262329+00:00","domain":"real and harmonic analysis","id":"claim_1e5d0188dd28e245626b909ca5c58042ec03419fa53232852fb9172b6eb55d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A family $(K_\\varepsilon)_{\\varepsilon>0}$ in $L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ (or a sequence $K_N$ with $N\\to\\infty$; the same definition works on $\\mathbb T$) is an approximate identity if (i) $\\int K_\\varepsilon=1$ for every $\\varepsilon$; (ii) $\\sup_\\varepsilon\\|K_\\varepsilon\\|_1<\\infty$; (iii) for every $\\delta>0$, $\\int_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\,dx\\to0$ as $\\varepsilon\\to0$. If $K\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\int K=1$, the dilates $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ form an approximate identity. Standard examples: the Gauss-Weierstrass (heat) kernel $\\varepsilon^{-d}e^{-\\pi|x|^2/\\varepsilon^2}$, the Poisson kernel of the half-space, the Fejer kernel $F_N$ and the Poisson kernel $P_r(x)=\\sum_n r^{|n|}e^{2\\pi i n x}$ ($r\\uparrow1$) on $\\mathbb T$. Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$ satisfies (i) but not (ii), since $\\|D_N\\|_1\\to\\infty$; this is the root of the divergence phenomena for Fourier series. Some texts add the stronger condition $\\sup_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\to0$, which is the convenient hypothesis for convergence at a point of continuity of a merely integrable $f$ (the tail is then controlled by $\\|f\\|_1$). Almost-everywhere convergence at Lebesgue points needs more than either condition: the usual hypothesis is the dilation structure $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ together with an integrable radially nonincreasing majorant of $|K|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:12:09.000066+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e64101b65634dcc3a302f194654f506fed2de18c5553aa24bece5ed40a61c5f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:second-var of arXiv:2608.21805, 'Logarithmic derivatives of variational and singular stochastic partial differential equati'] Under Assumptions~(ass:LR of the paper), (ass:diff2 of the paper), and~(ass:SC of the paper), the \emph{Malliavin--second variation} $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)$ (for $0 \leq s \leq t \leq T$ and $r \in [0, t]$) is the linear map $H \to L^2(\Omega; L_2(U, H))$, $v \mapsto \mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v$, defined fibrewise in both arguments: for each $v \in H$ and each noise direction $a \in U$, the $H$-valued directional fibre
\[
  \mathcal{Z}^{a}(t,s;r)v \;:=\; \bigl[\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v\bigr]a \;\in\; H
\]
is the unique variational solution of the $H$-valued linearised stochastic evolution equation obtained by applying both sides of
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  \mathrm{d}\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r) &+ \mathcal{A}'_u(t, X(t))\,\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
  &= -\mathcal{A}''_{uu}(t, X(t))\bigl(\mathcal{D}_r X(t),\,Y(t,s)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
  &\quad + \mathcal{B}'_u(t, X(t))\bigl(\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}W(t)
    + \mathcal{B}''_{uu}(t, X(t))\bigl(\mathcal{D}_r X(t),\,Y(t,s)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}W(t),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
to $v$ and to the direction $a$ (so that $\mathcal{D}_r X$ is read as $\mathcal{D}_r X(\cdot)\,a = Y(\cdot, r)\bigl(\mathcal{B}(r, X(r))a\bigr) \in V$ throughout), with initial condition
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{Z}(\max(s, r),\,s;\,r)\,v \;=\;
  \begin{cases}
    0, & r < s,\\
    \mathcal{B}'_u(r, X(r))\bigl(Y(r,s)v\bigr) \;\in\; L_2(U, H), & s < r \leq t,\\
    \mathcal{B}'_u(s, X(s))\,v, & r = s \ \text{in Regime A},\\
    0, & r = s \ \text{in Regime B},
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
read directionally as $\mathcal{Z}^{a}(\max(s,r), s; r)v = \bigl[\mathcal{B}'_u(r, X(r))(Y(r,s)v)\bigr]a \in H$ in the second branch, which is defined for every $r$ in Regime~A and, in Regime~B, for almost every $r > s$, namely wherever $Y(r,s)v \in V$. The value at $r = s$ is Lebesgue-negligible in the $r$-integrals where $\mathcal{Z}$ occurs and no statement below depends on it. The equation is posed at the initial time $\max(s,r)$, so that $\mathcal{Z}(\cdot,s;r)v$ is evolved on $[\max(s,r), T]$.

The right-hand side of~(equation eq:second-var of the paper) is well-defined because, by~(SC3),
\[
  \mathcal{D}_r X(t) = Y(t,r)\mathcal{B}(r,X(r)) \in L_2(U, V) \quad \text{for a.e.\ } t:
\]
one has $[\mathcal{D}_r X(t)](f) \in V$ for each $f \in U$, and the bilinear actions
\[
  \mathcal{A}''_{uu}(\mathcal{D}_r X, Y(t,s)) \in V^*, \qquad \mathcal{B}''_{uu}(\mathcal{D}_r X, Y(t,s)) \in L_2(U, H)
\]
are pointwise defined by~(D3)--(D4), using the $V$-valued character of $Y(t,s)v \in V$ for a.e.\ $t$.

The relation $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r) = \mathcal{D}_r Y(t,s)$, directionally $\mathcal{Z}^a(t,s;r)v = \mathcal{D}^a_r[Y(t,s)v]$ for every $a \in U$, is established in Lemma~(lemma:DtYts of the paper); well-posedness at the doubly-fibrewise level, together with the reconstruction of the $L_2(U,H)$-valued object $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v$ from its directions, is Theorem~(thm:Z-wellposed of the paper). Every composition of $\mathcal{Z}$ with a Hilbert--Schmidt argument in the sequel is read directionally in the Malliavin slot: for $\Theta \in L_2(U, H)$, $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\Theta$ denotes the map $(a, u) \mapsto \mathcal{Z}^{a}(t,s;r)(\Theta u)$, an element of $L_2(U, L_2(U,H))$ whenever the corresponding double column sum is finite. As with $Y(t,r)$, the shorthand ``$\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r) \in L(H)$'' refers only to the fibrewise action; almost-sure operator-norm membership is strictly stronger and not provided by the abstract framework.","status":"unverified"}

\[

 \qquad
 \mathcal N_B(R)\sim C_Be^{p_BR}R^{r_B-1}\ell_B(R).
\]
If \(p_A>p_B\), then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal N_{A\otimes B}(R)
 \sim C_A\zeta_B(p_A)e^{p_AR}R^{r_A-1}\ell_A(R).
 
\end{equation}
The symmetric formula holds when \(p_B>p_A\).  If
\(p_A=p_B=p\), then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal N_{A\otimes B}(R)
 \sim p\,\mathrm B(r_A,r_B)C_AC_B
 e^{pR}R^{r_A+r_B-1}\ell_A(R)\ell_B(R),
 
\end{equation}
where
\(\mathrm B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)\).
Consequently the power exponent with larger value dominates, while equal
power exponents resonate and their Mellin orders add.

In the pure logarithmic case, if \(p,r,\rho,a,b>0\) and
\[
 s_N(A)\sim aN^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(r-1)/p},\qquad
 s_N(B)\sim bN^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(\rho-1)/p},
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 s_N(A\otimes B)
 \sim ab\left(
 \frac{\Gamma(r)\Gamma(\rho)}{\Gamma(r+\rho)}
 \right)^{1/p}
 N^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(r+\rho-1)/p}.
 
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(s_N(A_j)\sim a_jN^{-1/p}\), then
\begin{equation}
 s_N(A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_k)
 \sim\frac{a_1\cdots a_k}{\Gamma(k)^{1/p}}
 N^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(k-1)/p}.
 
\end{equation}
Finally, for any \(p,r,\rho>0\), existence of the coefficients on the

\begin{align}
 \mathscr R_p^{(r+\rho)}(A\otimes B)
 &=\mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A)\mathscr R_p^{(\rho)}(B),
 \\
 \mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A\otimes C)
 &=\mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A)\operatorname{Tr}|C|^p,
 \qquad 0\ne C\in\mathcal S_p,
 \\
 \mathscr R_p^{(r)}(cA)

\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the entries a_i are real and nonnegative","in the weighted form the weights are nonnegative and sum to exactly 1","the geometric mean is the nonnegative real root of the product","the convention 0^0 = 1 is used for zero weights"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090495+00:00","domain":"real analysis, classical inequalities","id":"claim_1f1e654f8c410c52b8d725a17d45f62a04496de0ecc32675cb38e67a595827dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For NONNEGATIVE real numbers a_1, ..., a_n, (a_1 + ... + a_n)/n >= (a_1 a_2 ... a_n)^(1/n), with equality if and only if a_1 = ... = a_n. WEIGHTED FORM: if w_1, ..., w_n >= 0 with w_1 + ... + w_n = 1 and a_1, ..., a_n >= 0, then w_1 a_1 + ... + w_n a_n >= a_1^(w_1) ... a_n^(w_n), with the convention 0^0 = 1, and with equality if and only if all a_i with w_i > 0 are equal. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) nonnegativity is essential. With n = 2 and a_1 = a_2 = -1 the arithmetic mean is -1 while the product is 1 and its positive square root is +1, so the inequality as usually read reverses; the theorem is about nonnegative entries, never about arbitrary reals. (ii) With at least one zero entry and n >= 2 the geometric mean is 0 and the inequality is strict unless every entry is 0. (iii) The weights must be nonnegative AND sum to 1; dropping the normalisation makes the statement false, and the correct inhomogeneous relative is Young's inequality ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. (iv) The inequality is homogeneous of degree one, so it can be rescaled but never used to compare means of different orders; that is the power mean inequality, of which AM-GM is the limiting case as the exponent tends to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.266710+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1f1f94b7698f19b8ae1b7ab1f96abe68a6851850eb8625d410c329b1db9f106a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a space $X$ with a sum operation $+$, we can define the convolution of any two probability measures on it by the following formula:

\(\omega\in\mathcal W_N\), and put
\(Y_\omega:=\mathcal B_\pi^\star\omega\) and

Then
\[
  \|Y_\omega\|_{\psi_1}\le K_{\rm sm},
\]
and, for every \(T\ge0\),
\[
  E_{\nu}(Y_\omega-T)_+
  \le2K_{\rm sm}e^{-T/K_{\rm sm}},
  \qquad

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","A is self-adjoint","B is symmetric with D(B) ⊃ D(A)","relative bound a < 1 in ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ on D(A)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770689+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory, Schrodinger operators","id":"claim_1f4ab59f173a44abadbf58bf5376c8c9b2832575e6d08115bf54538bf8f08703","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H and let B be symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A), where 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. If in addition A is bounded below by M, then A + B is bounded below by M − max{b/(1 − a), a|M| + b}. (Wüst's theorem covers the borderline a = 1: if B is symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ ‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖, then A + B is essentially self-adjoint on D(A), though possibly not self-adjoint there.) Standard application (Kato): for n ≤ 3 and V ∈ L²(ℝⁿ) + L^∞(ℝⁿ) real valued, multiplication by V has −Δ-bound 0, so −Δ + V is self-adjoint on H²(ℝⁿ) and essentially self-adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝⁿ); this covers V(x) = −γ/|x| in ℝ³, the hydrogen Hamiltonian.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.831279+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1f6452d7bfac2425ffbcf65327bd3dd9b1fbbd09b924f486e5869945d6c4af60","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:MMi2 of arXiv:2606.24881, 'Queues with Correlated Service Times --- the $M/M_D/c$ Model'] Consider the $M/M_i/2$ queue obtained from the $M/M_D/2$ model by setting
\[
\mu_{12}=0.
\]
Assume the routing rule used throughout this paper: when both servers are
idle, an arrival is assigned to server \(1\) (equivalently, \(p=1\) in the
earlier \(M/M_D/2\) notation). Let
\[
\rho:=\frac{\lambda}{\mu_1+\mu_2},
\qquad \lambda<\mu_1+\mu_2.
\]
Then the stationary probabilities are given by
\begin{align}
\pi_{(1,0)} &= \frac{1+\rho}{1+2\rho}\,\frac{\lambda}{\mu_1}\,\pi_0, \\
\pi_{(0,1)} &= \frac{\rho}{1+2\rho}\,\frac{\lambda}{\mu_2}\,\pi_0, \\
\pi_2 &= \rho\bigl(\pi_{(1,0)}+\pi_{(0,1)}\bigr), \\
\pi_n &= \rho^{\,n-2}\pi_2, \qquad n\ge 2, 
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
\pi_0=
\left[
1+\frac{1+\rho}{1+2\rho}\frac{\lambda}{\mu_1}
+\frac{\rho}{1+2\rho}\frac{\lambda}{\mu_2}
+\frac{1}{1-\rho}\,
\frac{\rho\lambda}{1+2\rho}
\left(\frac{1+\rho}{\mu_1}+\frac{\rho}{\mu_2}\right)
\right]^{-1}.
\end{equation}
In particular, this coincides with Singh~[Singh:1970] for the
two-server heterogeneous independent-service model with \(\beta=1\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.903942+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1f749407390f6042246fa08a838a5b75d57bcc1c6454156066b28fd7ecff97dc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 6 (Normal connection) of arXiv:2609.00922, 'The Morse Index, Nullity and Jacobi Fields of Constant-Curvature 2-Spheres in Complex Proj'] Let \(V\in\Gamma(N_{\phi_{\lambda,n}}S^2)\) have coefficient functions
	\(A_1,A_r^-,A_r^+\) as in
	\eqref{eq:normal-field-complex-coordinates}.  Then \(\nabla^\perp V\) has
	the following coefficient one-forms.
	
	If the central normal summand is present, its coefficient is
	\begin{equation}
		
		(\nabla^\perp V)_1
		=\nabla^0 A_1
		-\frac{b_{\lambda,n}a_{\lambda-2,n}}{\sqrt{D_{n,k}}}\,A_2^-\varphi
		+\frac{a_{\lambda,n}b_{\lambda+2,n}}{\sqrt{D_{n,k}}}\,A_2^+\varphi .
	\end{equation}
	On the lower branch, the first line is the boundary equation at \(2^-\)
	(and contains the central coupling when the central vertex is present); the second
	is the recurrence at the outer vertices:
	\begin{align}
		
		(\nabla^\perp V)_{2^-}
		&=\nabla^0 A_2^-
		+\frac{b_{\lambda,n}a_{\lambda-2,n}}{\sqrt{D_{n,k}}}\,
		A_1\overline\varphi
		-a_{\lambda-4,n}A_3^-\varphi,
		\notag\\
		(\nabla^\perp V)_{r^-}
		&=\nabla^0 A_r^-
		+a_{\lambda-2r+2,n}A_{r-1}^-\overline\varphi
		-a_{\lambda-2r,n}A_{r+1}^-\varphi,
		\qquad 3\le r\le n-k .
	\end{align}
	On the upper branch, the corresponding equations are
	\begin{align}
		
		(\nabla^\perp V)_{2^+}
		&=\nabla^0 A_2^+
		-\frac{a_{\lambda,n}b_{\lambda+2,n}}{\sqrt{D_{n,k}}}\,
		A_1\overline\varphi
		+b_{\lambda+4,n}A_3^+\varphi,
		\notag\\
		(\nabla^\perp V)_{r^+}
		&=\nabla^0 A_r^+
		-b_{\lambda+2r-2,n}A_{r-1}^+\overline\varphi
		+b_{\lambda+2r,n}A_{r+1}^+\varphi,
		\qquad 3\le r\le k .
	\end{align}
	As above, absent vertices and their incident terms are omitted.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:00:15.236155+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1f84239a0554e87a84f720167a05ff33156c8ecab33721353d82827c95e5dcb8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 21 (Smoothed approximation of the initial Dirac mass) of arXiv:2607.19176, 'Exponential Convergence of the Sinkhorn Algorithm for the Schrödinger Bridge with Regime S'] Fix an initial point $(x,i)\in \mathbb R^d\times\mathcal I$ and let
$\varepsilon>0$. We define the smoothed initial distribution
$\mu_0^\varepsilon\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal I)$ by smoothing only
the continuous component and keeping the initial regime fixed. More precisely,
\[
\mu_0^\varepsilon(\mathrm dz,\{k\})
=
\mathbf 1_{\{k=i\}}
(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-d/2}
\exp\left(
-\frac{|z-x|^2}{2\varepsilon}
\right)
\mathrm dz,
\qquad k\in\mathcal I .
\]
Let $(X_t^\varepsilon,I_t^\varepsilon)_{t\ge0}$ be the solution of the same
regime-switching SDE with initial distribution $\mu_0^\varepsilon$, namely
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathrm dX_t^\varepsilon
=
b_{I_t^\varepsilon}\,\mathrm dt
+
\sigma_{I_t^\varepsilon}\,\mathrm dW_t,\\
(X_0^\varepsilon,I_0^\varepsilon)\sim \mu_0^\varepsilon,
\end{cases}
\]
where $(X_0^\varepsilon,I_0^\varepsilon)$ is independent of $W$, and
$I^\varepsilon$ evolves with the same constant transition rates
$(\lambda_{kl})_{k,l\in\mathcal I}$.

For each $k\in\mathcal I$, define the regime-wise marginal measure
\[
\mu_t^{\varepsilon,k}(A)
:=
\mathbb P(X_t^\varepsilon\in A,\ I_t^\varepsilon=k),
\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{app:lem_bound}, for every $t>0$, the measure $\mu_t^{\varepsilon,k}$ admits a
density $p_t^{\varepsilon,k}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure, namely
\[
\mu_t^{\varepsilon,k}(\mathrm dz)
=
p_t^{\varepsilon,k}(z)\,\mathrm dz .
\]
Moreover,
\[
0\le p_t^{\varepsilon,k}(z)
\le
(2\pi\underline a t)^{-d/2},
\qquad t>0,\ z\in\mathbb R^d,\ k\in\mathcal I .
\]
The initial data are given by
\[
p_0^{\varepsilon,k}(z)
=
\mathbf 1_{\{k=i\}}
(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-d/2}
\exp\left(
-\frac{|z-x|^2}{2\varepsilon}
\right),
\qquad k\in\mathcal I .
\]
For $t>0$, the density vector
$p^\varepsilon=(p^{\varepsilon,k})_{k\in\mathcal I}$ satisfies the forward
system
\begin{equation}

\partial_t p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
=
-b_k\cdot\nabla p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
+
\frac{\sigma_k^2}{2}\Delta p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
-
\sum_{l\neq k}\lambda_{kl}p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
+
\sum_{l\neq k}\lambda_{lk}p_t^{\varepsilon,l},
\qquad k\in\mathcal I .
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E contains the empty set and admits countable covers of X, so every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; nonnegativity is essential for the rearrangement of the double sum","the family (A_n) is countable; the sets need not be measurable, disjoint or nested","the conclusion is an inequality only; additivity requires the Caratheodory criterion"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402499+00:00","domain":"measure theory, outer measures","id":"claim_1f8c36eb2db254c54ff701dd08d6243e0a9c40ab1d83ef4c3b9be279b1744140","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let E be a family of subsets of a set X with the empty set in E and with X covered by countably many members of E, let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] satisfy rho(empty set) = 0, and define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k of rho(E_k) : E_k in E, A contained in the union of the E_k } for every subset A of X. Then mu* is an outer measure: mu*(empty set) = 0; A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B); and for EVERY countable family (A_n) of subsets of X, measurable or not, mu*(union of the A_n) <= sum of mu*(A_n). In particular Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is countably subadditive on all subsets of R^n, and finite subadditivity follows by padding the family with empty sets. WHERE THE INEQUALITY CANNOT BE IMPROVED: (a) equality fails in general even for pairwise DISJOINT sets. Let V be a Vitali set in [0,1] (one representative of each coset of the rationals) and let V_q = V + q for q in a countable enumeration of the rationals in [-1,1]. The V_q are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1] and is contained in [-1,2], and by translation invariance all of them have the same Lebesgue outer measure; countable additivity would force that common value to be simultaneously 0 (giving outer measure 0 for [0,1]) and positive (to fill [0,1]), so the outer measure of the disjoint union is strictly less than the sum. Additivity is recovered exactly on the Caratheodory measurable sets. (b) Countable is sharp: the inequality does not extend to uncountable families - [0,1] is the union of its singletons, each of Lebesgue outer measure 0, while the union has outer measure 1. (c) No structure on rho is needed - rho need not be monotone, additive or a premeasure; that is why the construction is so robust, and also why mu* generally does not extend rho (mu*(E) <= rho(E) always, and equality for E in E requires rho to be a premeasure and E to be well behaved).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:31.967012+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1faf6b20925bf437731dd22aff6650d4c1112068b3c333b07f60423099d9161c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.09904, 'Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coeffici'] A path \(\mathbf{Y} : [0, T] \to \CH_{N - 1} = \bigoplus_{n = 0}^{N - 1} \CH_{(n)}\) is a

  \begin{equation}
    R^{Y, f}_{st} = R^f_{st} = \< f, \mathbf{Y}_t\> - \< \mathbf{X}_{st} \curvearrowright f, \mathbf{Y}_s\>
  \end{equation}
  satisfies 
  \[\sup_{s < t \in [0, T]} \frac{|R^f_{st}|}{|t - s|^{(N - |f|)\gamma}} < \infty\] 
  for all \(f \in \CF_{N - 1}\). We denote \(Y_t = \< \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{Y}_t\>\) for the 
  path component of \(\mathbf{Y}\) and furthermore, for \(f \in \CF_{N - 1}\), denote 
  \(\partial^f_X Y_t = \< f, \mathbf{Y}_t\>\). We call \(\partial^f_X Y_t\) the \(f\)-th Gubinelli 
  derivative of \(\mathbf{Y}\) against \(\mathbf{X}\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363466+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb16adade5b99b6afb4fbfd858b71d368ab5f3b8075f27b19a7efee1501cb95","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. In both constructions of the companion memo on Problem 20.2, the subcritical law of its Theorem A (nu < 1) and the critical infinite-variance law of its Theorem B (nu = 1, sigma^2 = infinity), the bulk of the vertices has degree 0 or 1. Hence N_0 = n - N_1 + O(1), and N_bullet inherits the non-Gaussian limit of (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n): a two-point law in the first construction and a mixture of two Gaussians in the second. Assuming those two theorems, fringe-subtree counts are not asymptotically normal in general when nu < 1, nor when nu = 1 with sigma^2 = infinity. The finite-variance critical case is resolved in the literature by Janson (Random Structures Algorithms 48, 2016, Theorem 1.5) and is not included here as own work. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.827360+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb655af0af51c6fd1c94e68562250b7d6520db202e17d88f0a7aea05e01d7a5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 15 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $M$ be a complex manifold  with a contact structure $H \subset TM$. 
\begin{itemize} \item[(i)]
For each $z \in M$, define $\fn_{z, 1} := H_z$ and $\fn_{z, 2} := T_z M/H_z$. Then $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ has a graded Heisenberg algebra structure given by Lie brackets of vector fields. We call it the {\em symbol algebra} of the contact structure $H \subset TM$ at $z \in M$.  Its universal enveloping algebra $U(\fn_z)$ has a grading coming from the grading $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ (this grading is not compatible with the natural filtration of the universal enveloping algebra), which we denote by $$U(\fn_z) \  = \ \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fn_z).$$  As $z$ varies, it defines a vector bundle $U(\fn)$ on $M$ with the fiber $U(\fn)_z = U(\fn_z)$  and a vector subbundle $U_k(\fn)$ for each $k \geq 0$ with the fiber  $U_k(\fn)_z = U_k(\fn_z)$.
\item[(ii)] For each $z \in M$,  define the {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z(\varphi)$ of a local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M, z}$ to be  zero.
The {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z (\xi)$ of a nonzero local vector field $\xi$ is defined to be 1 if it is a local section  of $H$ and 2 otherwise.  A local monomial  differential operator  on $M$ of the form $\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r$ has weighted order $${\rm ord}_z (\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r) \ := \ {\rm ord}_z (\xi_1) + \cdots + {\rm ord}_z(\xi_r).$$ A local differential operator on $M$ is {\em of weighted order $\leq k$} at $z$ if each of its monomial terms has weighted order at most $k$. 
\item[(iii)]
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ has {\em weighted vanishing order $\geq k+1$} at $z \in M$, if $P\varphi$ vanishes at $z$ for any local differential operator $P$ of weighted order $\leq k$. Denote by $\bm^k_z \subset \sO_z$ the ideal of local holomorphic functions with weighted vanishing order $\geq k$ at $z$ and set $ J^k_z := \sO_z / \bm^{k+1}_z.$ The vector bundle $J^k$ on $M$ whose fiber at $z$ is $J^k_z$ is called the {\em bundle of contact $k$-jets}. 
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ naturally determines a local section $j^k(\varphi) \in \sO(J^k)_z$, called the {\em contact $k$-jet} of $\varphi$ at $z$. 
There is a natural surjective homomorphism of vector bundles $ \pi^{k}_{k-1}: J^{k} \to J^{k-1}$ yielding an exact sequence of  vector bundles 
$$0 \to U_{k}(\fn)^* \longrightarrow J^{k} \stackrel{\pi^{k}_{k-1}}{\longrightarrow} J^{k-1} \to 0,$$ where $U_k(\fn)^*$ denotes the dual of the vector bundle $U_k(\fn)$.  \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:32:20.698161+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb8c813ee781cda2d9b4a7d12e0ad773e6c209074d7e527637fc4277ccc107b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 46 of arXiv:2609.00245, 'Higher-order Gaussian bounds for maximally subelliptic boundary value problems'] Let \(\sI\) be an index set, and for \(\iota\in \sI\) let \(W_1^\iota,\ldots, W_{r_\iota}^{\iota}\in \CbinftySpace[U][\Rn]\)
    be smooth vector fields on \(U\). We say that \(W_1^\iota,\ldots, W_{r_{\iota}}^{\iota}\)
    are \emph{H\"ormander vector fields on \(U\), uniformly for \(\iota\in \sI\)} if the following conditions hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \(\sup_{\iota\in \sI} r_\iota<\infty\).
        \item \(\left\{ W_j^\iota : \iota\in \sI, 1\leq j\leq r_\iota \right\}\subseteq \CbinftySpace[U][\Rn]\) is a bounded set.
        \item \(\exists m\in \Zg\) (independent of \(\iota\)) such that if \(X_1^\iota,\ldots, X_{q_\iota}^\iota\)
            is an enumeration of the commutators of \(W_1^\iota,\ldots, W_{r_\iota}^\iota\) up to order \(m\),
            then \(X_1^\iota,\ldots, X_{q_\iota}^\iota\) span the tangent space to \(U\),
            uniformly for \(\iota\in \sI\) (see Definition \ref{Defn::Scaling::UnitScale::SpanTangentSpaceUniformly}).
    \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.751928+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fc20a5681643b475f0f39f7026b6a8536ea7fa315fd2f91358dbeb6b84e3c43","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Fix $c > 0$ and let $Q_t$ be the birth-death process
  with
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $Q_0 \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(c)$;
    \item $n \mapsto n +1$ transitions of rate $c$; and
    \item $n \mapsto n - 1$ transitions of rate $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the first hitting time of $0$,
  \[
    \tau_c \coloneqq \inf\{ t \geqslant 0 \mid Q_t = 0 \},
  \]
  has Laplace transform
  \[
    \E e^{-s\tau_c} = e^{-c}
    \left[1 - c\int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^{s} e^{-cx} \, dx
    \right]^{-1},
    \quad s \geqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $s > 0$. By total expectation,
    \[
      \E e^{-s \tau_c}
      = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty
      \E\left(e^{-s\tau_c} \middle| Q_0 = n\right)
      \PP(Q_0 = n)\\
      = e^{-c} \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}\, \phi_n(s)
    \]
    where $\phi_n(s) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}(e^{-s\tau_c} \mid 
    Q_0 = n)$. So if $\Phi_s$ is defined on $[0, c]$ by
    \begin{equation}
      
      \Phi_s(y) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty
      \phi_n(s) \, \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \quad \text{then} \quad
      \E(e^{-s\tau_c}) = e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c).
    \end{equation}
    Clearly $\phi_0(s) = 1$ and first-step analysis gives
    \[
      (c+n+s) \, \phi_n(s) = 
      n \, \phi_{n-1}(s) + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s),
      \quad n > 0.
    \]
    By taking a weighted sum of this recurrence,
    \[
      \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \left(c + n + s \right)
      \phi_n(s) = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \left[ n \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s)\right].
    \]
    The left-hand side is
    \[
      (c+s) \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_n(s)
      + y \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_n(s)
      =
      (c+s)\left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
    \]
    while the right-hand side is
    \[
      y \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_{n+1}(s)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[ \Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s)\right].
    \]
    We are left with the differential equation
    \[
      (c+s) \left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[\Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s) \right]
    \]
    or equivalently,
    the initial value problem
    \begin{align}
      
      \left(c-y\right) \Phi_s'(y)
      + \left(- c + y - s\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= \overbrace{c \, \phi_1(s) - c - s}^{-K}\\ \notag
      \Phi_s'(y) + \left(-1-\frac{s}{c-y}\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= -\frac{K}{c-y}
    \end{align}
    with condition $\Phi_s(0) = 1$.
    Use the integrating factor $I_s(y) = e^{-y} \, (c-y)^s$ to write
    \begin{align*}
      \left[e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)\right]'
      &= \frac{-K}{c-y} \, e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s\\
      e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)
      - e^{-0} \left(c - 0\right)^s \Phi_s(0) 
      &= \int_0^y \frac{-K}{c-x} \, e^{-x} \left(c - x\right)^s \, dx
      \intertext{for any $y < c$. It's clear from \eqref{eq:Phi} that
      $\Phi_s$ is continuous, so take the $y \uparrow c$ limit:}
      \frac{c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}
      &= K.
    \end{align*}
    Finally, the $y \uparrow c$ limit of \eqref{eq:IVP}
    informs us $-s \, \Phi_s(c) = -K$, thus
    \begin{align*}
      \E e^{-s\tau_c}
      &= e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c)
      = \frac{e^{-c}\, c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \, s \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}\\
      &= \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^s dx}
      = \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^1 c \, e^{-cx} \left(c-c\,x\right)^s dx}\\
      &= e^{-c} \left[1 - c \int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^s e^{-cx}\, dx \right]^{-1}.
      \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)","for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fe4f3b747b727689cb17f579418ee4b2fd98070d9ff3fa9527f2e43df172cf8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite alphabet with distinguished bot, p(bot)=0, n>=1 and |Y|>n+1.","IID samples; uniform two-level generator; exact score-level calibration."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:47:07.141514+00:00","domain":"Probability and statistical learning","id":"claim_1fe7454ed03fbc5eeea1731233890e57bc9fbe461251031ca9ef44c62ace1df2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Y be finite with a distinguished always-true empty fact bot, let n>=1 and |Y|>n+1, and let p be any probability law on Y with p(bot)=0. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:32:58.301708+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fecb0efd49bbb73e769421eed086176c64fbfb0908fd45812ed637cf2688882","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main fluctuations of arXiv:2505.10256, 'Stochastic Oscillators out of equilibrium:\\ scaling limits and correlation estimates'] Let $m>5/2$ be fixed. 
Assume that the sequence of initial measures $\{\mu_N\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ satisfies Assumption (assump:initial_measure of the paper). 
Moreover, assume that bounded measurable functions $v_0:\mathbb T\to\mathbb R$ and $e_0:\mathbb T\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $e_0(u)-v_0(u)^2\ge 0$ for any $u\in\mathbb T$.
Finally, assume that the sequence of initial density fields $\mathcal{V}_0^N$ converges in distribution to an $H^{-m}(\mathbb T)$-valued random variable $\mathcal{V}_0$ as $N\to\infty$.  
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)] 
Let $\mathcal{M}^N_t$ be a mean-zero martingale associated naturally to the volume fluctuation fields $\mathcal V^N_\cdot$ (see (equation eq:dynkin_martingale_definition of the paper) for the definition).  
The sequence $\{\mathcal{M}^N_t: t\in [0,T]\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ is tight in $D([0,T],H^{-m}(\mathbb T))$, so that there exists a subsequence of $N$, which is again denoted by the same letter by abuse of notation, along which the sequence converges to a limit $\{\mathcal{M}_t ; t\in [0,T]\}$ in distribution:
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{N\to\infty} \mathcal{M}^N_\cdot = \mathcal{M}_\cdot 
\end{equation*}
where the limit $\mathcal{M}_\cdot $ is again a mean-zero martingale.
\item [b)]For any $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$, we have that
\begin{equation} 
\lim_{N\to \infty} \mathbb E_N[\langle \mathcal{M}^N(f)\rangle_t]  
= \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb T} 2 \chi(s,u) (\nabla f(u))^2 du ds
\end{equation}
where $\chi(t,u) = e(t,u) - v(t,u)^2$, and $(v,e)$ is the unique weak solution of (equation eq:hdl of the paper) with initial profile $(v_0,e_0)$.  
\item  [c)]
The sequence $\{\mathcal Q^N_m\}_N$ is tight and any of its limit points $\mathcal Q_m$ satisfies the identity 
\begin{equation}

\mathcal{V}_t(f) 
= \mathcal{V}_0(\mathcal T_tf) 
+ \mathcal{M}_t(f)
\end{equation}
for any $f\in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb T)$, where $\mathcal{M}_t$ is a mean-zero  martingale with continuous trajectories and $\mathcal T_t$ is the semigroup generated by the one-dimensional Laplacian $\Delta$. Moreover, $\mathcal V_0$ and $\mathcal M_t$ are uncorrelated in the sense that, for all $f,g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb T)$ and for all $t\in[0,T]$, it holds $E_{\mathcal Q_m}[\mathcal  V_0(g)\mathcal M_t(f)]=0$.
\item [d)] If $\mu_N$ is the invariant measure $\mu_{\rho,\beta}$ for some $\rho\in\mathbb R$ and $\beta>0$, then we can strength our result in the sense that we have the convergence of the sequence $\{\mathcal Q^N_m\}_N$ to the solution of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation
$$
d\mathcal V_t=\Delta \mathcal V_t dt+\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta}} \nabla \dot{\mathcal W_t} 
$$
again provided that $m>5/2$, where $\dot{\mathcal W_t}$ is a one-dimensional space-time white noise. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.686380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20379a5dab6d932dbb7f2d5de4b388201a8eeacc73402556dcd59bdc4ce9d0cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 15 (Resonant skew-Hermitian endpoint identity) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, and choose $m\geq1$ such that
\[
m\omega\in2\pi\Z
\qquad(\omega\in\Lambda).
\]
Let $\Gamma=\gamma^{*m}$ be the $m$-fold concatenation of $\gamma$, naturally parametrised on $[0,mT]$.
Fix $r\geq1$, frequencies $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r\in\Lambda$, and real covectors $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r\in W^*$. No distinctness is assumed: the frequencies and covectors may repeat.
Choose real numbers $\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{j-1}-\sigma_j=\omega_j
\quad(1\leq j\leq r),
\qquad
m\sigma_j\in2\pi\Z
\quad(0\leq j\leq r).
\end{equation}
Set $D=i\diag(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r)$, write $I=I_{r+1}$, and, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\in\R^r$, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_u(a)
 =\ell(a)D
  +\sum_{j=1}^r
   u_j\eta_j(a)(E_{j-1,j}-E_{j,j-1}),
\end{equation}
first as a real-linear map $V\to\uLie(r+1)$. Denote its complex-linear extension by
\[
\rho_{u,\C}:V_{\C}\longrightarrow M_{r+1}(\C).
\]
If $U^u$ is the right development
\[
\dd U_s^u=U_s^u\rho_u(\dd\Gamma_s),
\qquad U_0^u=I,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
U_{mT}^u=I
\qquad(u\in\R^r).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.610180+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2047058969970faf847b7f2324be353be0b235fdd8f019ee565f68c8925fae8c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Monotonicity of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] The Markov chain $Q$ is monotone with respect to the arrival rate, the initial condition, and the departure rate. More precisely:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the arrival rate.} If $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2$, then the chains $Q^{(1)}$ and $Q^{(2)}$ defined by \emph{(2)} with arrival rates $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $Q^{(1)}(0)=Q^{(2)}(0)$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^{(1)} \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^{(2)}.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the initial condition.} If $x \leq y$, then the chains $Q^x$ and $Q^y$ defined by \emph{(2)} with initial conditions $Q^x(0)=x$ and $Q^y(0)=y$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^x \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^y.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the departure rate.} If for all $i \in [1;N]$, $f \leq \mu_i$ (resp. $f \geq \mu_i$), and $Q^f(0)=Q(0)$, then the chain $Q^f$ defined by \emph{(2)} with departure rate $\mu_i = f$ for every $i$ satisfies
    \[
    Q \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^f
    \qquad (\text{resp. } Q^f \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q).
    \]
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.097998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_204a64b197446fee21423591e0771684ec5e77b555e907c6b4ed96647e2e8cfa","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:anchor-taylor-debit of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix $L<\infty$.  Let $r\le L\log(n+2)$,
$0\le\Delta\le r$, and $0\le d\le r+B_0$.  For every physical
translation $a$ in a set of at most $m\le cN$ translations, let
$M(a)\in\{0,\ldots,m\}$ be its remaining gap budget, with distinct
translations giving distinct budgets, and let
\[
 \mathcal X_a^{(M(a))}=\sum_{q=0}^{M(a)}[z^q]\mathcal F_a(z).
\]
Suppose that, for one number $H\ge0$ independent of $a$,
\[
 \sup_{|z|=1}|\mathcal F_a(z)|\le Hn^{-\Delta}
\tag{3.2.10q$_{14}$}
\]
and, when $d\ge1$,
\[
 |[z^q]\mathcal F_a(z)|
 \le H\binom{q+d-1}{d-1}(1-\gamma_n)^q,
 \qquad q\ge0.
\tag{3.2.10q$_{15}$}
\]
For $d=0$ interpret $\mathcal F_a$ as constant.  Then
\[
 \boxed{
 \sum_a|\mathcal X_a^{(M(a))}|
 \le C_LcN Hn^{-\Delta}.}
\tag{3.2.10q$_{16}$}
\]
The conclusion is anchor-averaged: it does not assert a
dimension-free maximal-partial-sum estimate for one prescribed budget.
It remains valid for a final-scalar prescribed-gate contraction, provided
\crefrange{eq:3.2.10q-14}{eq:3.2.10q-15} hold after that contraction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:12.000500+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20617f9b9b46fb63487f619f9bb03437e1dd99ce8449ec0343ceda55e27ed36e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:spatial-scaling of arXiv:2609.02820, 'Sharpness and critical scaling of parking'] Let $d\leq3$, and let $(\eta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ be independent and identically
	distributed, integer-valued and nonconstant, with $\mathbb{E}\eta(0)=0$ and
	$\mathbb{E} e^{\theta|\eta(0)|}<\infty$ for some $\theta>0$. For $R>0$,
	$s\geq0$, and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, let
	\[
		\overline U_R(s,x)\coloneqq
		R^{d/2-2}U_{\lfloor sR^2\rfloor}(\lfloor Rx\rfloor),
		\qquad
		\overline u_R(s,x)\coloneqq
		R^{d/2-2}u_{\lfloor sR^2\rfloor}(\lfloor Rx\rfloor),
	\]
	where the floor is taken coordinatewise. For $R>0$ and
	$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, let
	\[
		\langle\eta_R,\varphi\rangle
		\coloneqq R^{-d/2}\sum_y\eta(y)\varphi(y/R)
	\]
	and
	\[
		\langle\nu_R,\varphi\rangle
		\coloneqq R^{-d/2}\sum_y
		\bigl(A_{\lfloor R^2\rfloor}(y)-H_{\lfloor R^2\rfloor}(y)\bigr)
		\varphi(y/R).
	\]
	Let $\mathcal W$ be a mean-zero spatial white noise with covariance
	\[
		\mathbb{E}\langle\mathcal W,\varphi\rangle\langle\mathcal W,\psi\rangle
		=\Var\eta(0)\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(x)\psi(x)\,dx
		\qquad(\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d))\,.
	\]
	Let $\mathcal U$ be the continuous Brownian optimal-stopping value driven by
	$\mathcal W$, with $\mathcal U(0,\cdot)=0$. Then, jointly,
	\begin{equation}
		(\eta_R,\overline u_R,\overline U_R)
		\Longrightarrow(\mathcal W,\mathcal U,\mathcal U)
	\end{equation}
	as $R\to\infty$, with the first coordinate converging as a random
	distribution and the last two locally uniformly on
	$(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d$.
	Let
	$\mathcal O\coloneqq\{\mathcal U>0\}$ and
	$\mathcal L\coloneqq(2d)^{-1}\Delta$. Then, in
	the sense of distributions on $\mathcal O$,
	\begin{equation}
		\partial_s\mathcal U=\mathcal L\mathcal U+\mathcal W.
	\end{equation}
	For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, jointly with
	(equation eq:space-time-scaling of the paper),
	\begin{equation}
		\langle\nu_R,\varphi\rangle\Longrightarrow
		\langle\mathcal W+\mathcal L\mathcal U(1,\cdot),\varphi\rangle.
	\end{equation}
	Moreover, on $\mathcal O$ the distribution
	$v=\partial_s\mathcal U$ is a smooth function and
	\begin{equation}
		v(s,x)>0\qquad ((s,x)\in\mathcal O).
	\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

If Z is uniform on {-1, 1}^K, then E_Z[f_{J|Z}^(S)] = f^(S), E_Z[f_{J|Z}^(S)^2] = sum over T inside K of f^(S u T)^2, and E_Z ||f_{J|Z}||_2^2 = ||f||_2^2, each norm under the uniform measure of its own cube. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.871767+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_207bdb765cc205e69712a966a37eaf6b75efb9ca522347af69adc7399d52a032","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop sparsestack-fails-osi of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] There is a universal constant $c>0$ with the following property.
Let $\zeta_k\ge2$ be an integer sequence with $\zeta_k\mid k$, set
$b(k):=k/\zeta_k$, and let $r=r(k)$ and $n_k$ satisfy
\[
\rho k\le r(k)\le k
\quad\text{for some fixed }\rho\in(0,1],
\qquad
\frac{n_k}{r(k)}\to\infty.
\]
Set
\[
s_k:=\min\left\{k,\frac{n_k}{k}\right\},
\]
and assume
\[
\zeta_k=O\big(\log s_k\big)^c.
\]
For each such $k$, let $S^{(k)}\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times k}$ be a SparseStack
matrix with row sparsity $\zeta_k$ and block size $b(k)$. Let
$T_k\subseteq[n_k]$ be any deterministic subset with $|T_k|=r(k)$.
Then
\[
s_{\min}\left(((S^{(k)})^\top)_{T_k}\right)=o(1)
\]
with probability $1-o(1)$. In particular, 
the SparseStack with the given parameters
is not $(r(k),1/2)$-OSI. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348858+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_208f7c4d1a65f4167efac3277e11eddaa90b1e153739b4d3e12334ae49c18c70","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 165 ($\by$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\by\equiv \by(q_{d+1})$ as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}, so it is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_{d+1})$, as defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt}.

\begin{proof} Let us abbreviate
	\[

	\equiv \bXi^{d+1}
	\equiv \frac{\bG(q_{d+1})
		-\bG(q_d)}{\sqrt{p_{d+1}-p_d}}\,,

so this is a gaussian independent of $\cG(q_d)$. Then we can express

 $\by$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz in $\bXi$, so the subgaussian claim follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.592384+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2092f4f49ea0d52063ec02bc8e3f7158aa9283d9f4c1bbf8e17c9a7aebe64b24","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Consider $k$ independent Bernoulli populations, each sampled $n$ times, and select the $t$ populations with the largest success counts, breaking ties uniformly. Classical monotonicity reduces the worst case over the preference zone with separation $\\delta$ to the slippage family with levels $p$ and $p+\\delta$, leaving only its absolute location $p\\in[0,1-\\delta]$ undetermined. A Gaussian approximation suggests the symmetric center $p_{\\mathrm c}=(1-\\delta)/2$, and the exact two-population problem is uniquely centered there for every $n\\ge2$. For fixed $k,t$ and $\\delta\\in(0,1)$, we prove that exact eventual centering holds precisely when $k=2t$. When $k\\ne2t$, the least-favorable location $p_{n,k,t}^*$ satisfies \\[ p_{n,k,t}^*-p_{\\mathrm c} =(k-2t)C_\\delta n^{-1/2}e^{-n\\Gamma_\\delta}\\{1+o(1)\\}, \\] where $C_\\delta$ and $\\Gamma_\\delta$ are explicit and positive. In either case, the least-favorable location is eventually unique. The proof writes incorrect selection as a union of pairwise misrankings and applies inclusion--exclusion, yielding a bipartite graph expansion. A single misranking has its exact maximum at the symmetric center and determines the central curvature; two-edge intersections sharing one population determine the central slope through their multiplicity imbalance; all remaining graphs have higher large-deviation rates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space and T: X → X a map","for the orbit-closure characterization, T is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111010+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_20ab9dec4c9cbfd28df1fff4fca5251efcaf20965cb1e82ec6c01020cfd918be","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and T: X → X a map. A set A ⊂ X is (forward) invariant if T(A) ⊆ A. A minimal set is a nonempty closed invariant set M that contains no proper nonempty closed invariant subset. Some authors require T(M) = M (strict invariance); for a continuous T on a compact Hausdorff space a minimal set in the above sense automatically satisfies T(M) = M, since T(M) is then itself nonempty, closed (compact image) and invariant, hence equal to M. Characterization (T continuous): a nonempty closed invariant M is minimal if and only if for every x ∈ M the forward orbit {Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is dense in M. Proof of the equivalence: for x ∈ M the orbit closure cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is nonempty, closed, contained in M, and invariant because continuity gives T(cl O) ⊆ cl T(O) ⊆ cl O; so minimality forces it to equal M; conversely, if every orbit in M is dense and N ⊂ M is nonempty closed invariant, any x ∈ N has its orbit inside N, so M = cl(orbit) ⊆ N. The system (X,T) itself is called minimal if X is a minimal set, i.e. every forward orbit is dense. Examples: a periodic orbit is a minimal set; an irrational rotation of the circle is minimal; the closure of a non-periodic orbit is in general NOT minimal (e.g. the orbit closure of a point of the doubling map whose orbit is dense contains the fixed point 0 as a smaller minimal set). Continuity is used in the orbit-closure characterization; the definition of a minimal set itself does not need it. For flows and group/semigroup actions the same definitions apply with 'orbit' read as the (semi)group orbit.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Examine the branching-process-with-migration proof and where i.i.d. is used. Result: The proof of Theorem 3.10 under (3.10) translates the walk into a branching process with migration whose offspring law at site k is determined by the cookie stack at k; under (IID) the branching process is homogeneous in space and the criterion delta > 1 is the criterion for the branching process to die out... under (SE) the process is a branching process in a stationary ergodic environment (BPRE with migration), whose survival criterion is governed by the Lyapunov exponent of the environment, i.e. by an ergodic average of log-means, not by the mean delta of the drift. So the natural (SE) analogue is NOT 'delta in [-1,1]' with delta = E sum_i (2 omega(0,i) - 1) but a criterion involving the annealed versus quenched growth rate of the associated BPRE; for i.i.d. environments the two coincide because the migration term is affine. I tested this on the simplest non-i.i.d. case: an environment alternating deterministically between two cookie stacks a and b (period 2, hence SE after a random shift): the branching process with migration is then periodic and its two-step transition is again a branching process with migration with delta_2 = delta_a + delta_b; the criterion becomes delta_a + delta_b > 2 for transience, i.e. the average delta > 1, consistent with the naive extension. For genuinely random ergodic environments a similar averaging holds if the migration is additive, which it is (the number of cookies eaten per visit adds). So the expected answer is YES for (SE) with the same delta, and the obstruction to a proof is that the branching-process comparison uses independence between the offspring at different sites when computing the extinction probability of the process with migration; with dependence one needs an ergodic theorem for the total progeny, available via the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer approach only for i.i.d.. Recorded: periodic environments satisfy the naive extension; the general (SE) case reduces to an ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching with migration in stationary environments. Key identity: Periodic two-stack environment: transient iff delta_a + delta_b > 2, i.e. the averaged delta criterion holds. Obstruction: Ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching processes with migration in stationary environments.","status":"unverified"}
