{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.346979+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3083b9a91b3bfb645dd1208a02f4f9ee20f6b1c4e5780669c6f1d7c2726f9b6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $(b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}. 
Fix any vectors $\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}\in\bbR^M$, and let $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ be the centered IAMP specified by Definition~\ref{d:centered.iamp}. 
Then, for $C\equiv C(L,\epsilon,\delta)$, 
there exists a $C$-Lipschitz map $\cA^\dagger$ which agrees
with $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ with probability $1-\exp(-cN)$, and satisfies
	    \[
    \cA(-\bG,-\bg^\aux)
    =
    -\cA(\bG,\bg^\aux)\,.
    \]
In particular, it follows that $\bbE[\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})~|~\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}]=\bzero\in\bbR^N$.
\begin{proof}
    Let $(\hat\by^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxby^{\dagger,k},\hat\bx^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxbx^{\dagger,k})$ be the IAMP iterates corresponding to $(-\bG,- \bg^{\aux})$.
    We claim that for all $0\leq k\leq \ubl$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    (\hat\prxby,\hat\by,\hat\bu,\hat\bw)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (-\prxby,-\by,-\bu,\bw)^{\dagger,k}
      \,\\
    (\hat\prxbx,\hat\bx,\hat\bv,
    \hat\bm,\hat\bsig,\hat\bb)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (\prxbx,\bx,\bv,
    \bm,\bsig,\bb)^{\dagger,k}\,.
    \end{align*}
Indeed, the base case for the first statement above holds easily since
$w$ is even by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} \eqref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, the functions
 $\psi$ and $\prxpsi$ are odd (Lemma~\ref{lem:even-manual-init}), 
the vectors $(\by,\prxby,\hat{\by},\hat{\prxby})^{\dagger,0}$ are defined by \eqref{eq:mean-0-initialization},  and  we defined $\bu^{\dagger,0}=\hat{\bu}^{\dagger,0}=\bzero\in\R^M$.
The remaining statements follow by 
induction, using the formulas \eqref{eq:proxy-y-amp-def}--\eqref{eq:x-amp-def}. 

The above shows the desired symmetry for the mapping $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$, and we must now transfer it to $\cA^\dagger$. This proceeds similarly as in the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}, using the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, except that we now need to ensure that the symmetry requirement is satisfied. 
First, we have by easy induction that $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ is $C$-Lipschitz on a subset $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\subseteq \bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$, similarly to the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}. To be precise, 
    \[\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}
    =\bigg\{
    \begin{array}{c}
    (\bG,\bg^\aux) : 
    \textup{$\bG_\circ$
    satisfies \eqref{eq:Brownian-bridge-condition},
    $\|\bG\|_\textup{op}\le C_0
    (M^{1/2}+N^{1/2})$,}\\
    \textup{$\|\bar\bg^{\ell}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$
    for all $0\le\ell\le\ubl$, and
    $\|\bar\bg^{\init}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$}
    \end{array}
    \bigg\}\,.
    \]
In particular, this choice of $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}$ is origin-symmetric. 
(Again, see e.g.\ the discussion on ``standard optimization algorithms'' in \cite{HuangSellke2021} for the Lipschitz bound on such a domain.)

Thus, let $S=\{\bg_1,\bg_2,\dots\}$ be a countable dense set in $\bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
    For each $\bg_i$, we assume $\tilde\cA^{\dagger}$ has been extended to a $C$-Lipschitz function on $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\equiv \mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\cup \{\bg_1,-\bg_1,\dots,\bg_i,-\bg_i\}$.
    Then by the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, there exists a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\cup \{\bg_{i+1}\}$.
    Since 
  $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}$ is symmetric,  
the unique odd extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i+1}$ is still $C$-Lipschitz. Continuing in this way yields a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $ \mathcal{U}^\dagger\cup S\cup -S$. This set is dense by definition of $S$, so the result follows by continuously extending to all of $\R^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.778420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3094139d6c32ee053ca7cdcf1a48243f534a519ed5d8e61476f08327de9b8c55","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] A \textbf{Navier--Stokes triple} \((\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)\) is called \textbf{admissible} provided the following \textbf{invariant-domain property} holds for each of the two associated Einstein--Navier--Stokes models 
\eqref{eq:pot-production-system} and \eqref{eq:pot-dissipated-system}, as follows. 

Let \(\{\Sigma_t\}_{t_0\leq t<t_1}\) be a spacelike foliation of a compact spacetime slab, and let \((g,\beta,\zeta)\) be a regular solution of the corresponding hyperbolic evolution-constraint system\footnote{A gauge must be chosen to deal with the spacetime metric and formulate a well-posed initial value problem; this is a standard topic, not reviewed here \cite{Choquet-book}.} on \([t_0,t_1)\). Assume that
\be
\zeta(t_0,\Sigma_{t_0})\subset\mathcal K_0
\qquad\text{for some closed fiber subset }\mathcal K_0\Subset\mathscr F.
\ee
Then one has
\be
\zeta(t,\Sigma_t)\subset\mathscr F
\qquad\text{for every }t_0\leq t<t_1.
\ee
Moreover, if the fields admit a continuous limit in the ambient bundles as \(t\uparrow t_1\), while the nonsingular coefficients in the equation for~\(\zeta\) remain bounded, then the terminal relaxing field satisfies
\be
\zeta(t_1,\Sigma_{t_1})\subset\mathscr F,
\ee
rather than merely taking its values in~\(\overline{\mathscr F}\). Equivalently, the constitutive boundary~\(\del\mathscr F\) cannot be the first cause of breakdown of a regular solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:55:37.822334+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_30a1c159d76322869c0f5a96ed54eeb2cdd33a310f11dcbb829485cced88c54b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop cor:explicitcondforXe of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $\Psi$ and $\hat{\Psi}$ be mechanisms, and denote by $\pi$ the L\'evy measure associated with $\Psi$. Assume that $\hat{\Psi} = \hat{\Sigma} - \hat{\Phi}$ with $\hat{\Sigma} \not\equiv 0$. Then the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[1)]
\item Assume $\Hone$ and $\hatHone$. Then the process $X^{\mathrm{m}}$ admits a $[0,\infty]$-valued Feller extension at $\infty$, denoted by $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$, which satisfies (equation def:Xeinftyviamonotonicity of the paper) and the $(0^{+}\cdot \infty, \infty^-\cdot 0)$ Laplace duality relation (equation eq:laplaceduality1 of the paper). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.698481+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_30b5280bf719a7579421520537db05a0d52e3e9c35439e3f9fc07547491c12e3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 20 (Time extension, causality, and restricted operator norms) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $0<T\le T_0$.  There is a bounded linear extension
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak E_{T,T_0}:E_T^{2,\sigma}\longrightarrow E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak R_T\mathfrak E_{T,T_0}=I,
\end{equation}
whose norm is bounded by an absolute constant independently of $T$ and $T_0$.
The analogous assertion holds after translating the interval.

Call an operator $\mathcal A$ on $E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma}$ causal if inputs that
agree on $[0,t]$ have outputs that agree on $[0,t]$, for every $t\le T_0$.
For a causal operator, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal A_{[0,T]}:=\mathfrak R_T\mathcal A\mathfrak E_{T,T_0}.
\end{equation}
This restriction is independent of the chosen bounded extension.  More
generally, if $I=[t_0,t_1]$ and $w\in E_{I,0}^{2,\sigma}$, extend $w$ by zero on
$[0,t_0]$ and by any bounded extension after $t_1$; the restriction of
$\mathcal A$ to $I$ is again independent of the extension after $t_1$.  We
denote this zero-history operator by $\mathcal A_I$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:11.975751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3100f2835a25051436266faf3d1d777072f677dba25cfaa190473f3618c57dd0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:BST of arXiv:2608.19050, 'Online Permutation Embedding: \\ Optimal Stopping and Scaling Laws'] Let $\pi \in \Pi_k$ be a permutation. The binary search tree 
$\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{BST},\pi}$ is constructed by inserting nodes labeled $1,\dots,k$ (containing keys
$\pi(1),\pi(2),\dots,\pi(k)$, respectively) sequentially into an initially empty binary search tree. The first node, labeled 1, is inserted as the root. Each remaining node $i$ is sequentially inserted as follows. Start at the root; descend to the left if the key $\pi(i)$ is smaller 
than the key of the current node, and descend to the right otherwise. Repeat this descent until an empty position is reached, and insert the current node at this empty position. If $\pi$ was drawn uniformly at random from $\Pi_k$, then we further say that $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{BST},\pi}$ is a \textit{random} BST on $[k]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.186720+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31199ef303ea3dc048a12dfd4ffe05c9131d850a43b8c0ee851330f431bc4f9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field, any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:47:07.717860+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_311defe75e47c6347ee11638188d9bdbbd48b3bb50d908a42c86cdbeb3260c0f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (Uniform BMO--Girsanov package) of arXiv:2608.06393, 'Intrinsic Tangential Hadamard Differentiability of Rough-BSDE Solution Maps'] Let \(\{N^\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}\) be continuous martingales on \(I\)
such that
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \|N^\theta\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb P;I)}\leq n_*.
\]
For \(u\leq t\leq v\), set
\[
 L_t^\theta
 :=\exp\left(
  N_t^\theta-N_u^\theta
  -\frac12(\langle N^\theta\rangle_t-
              \langle N^\theta\rangle_u)
 \right),
\]
so that \(L_u^\theta=1\), and define
\(d\mathbb Q^\theta/d\mathbb P=L_v^\theta\) on \(\mathcal F_v\).
There exist exponents \(r_+,r_->1\) and constants
\(C_+,C_-,C_{\mathrm{eq}}<\infty\), depending only on \(n_*\), such that,
uniformly in \(\theta\) and \(\tau\in\mathcal T_I\),
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E_\tau^{\mathbb P}
 \left[\left(\frac{L_v^\theta}{L_\tau^\theta}\right)^{r_+}\right]
 &\leq C_+,
 \\
 \mathbb E_\tau^{\mathbb Q^\theta}
 \left[\left(\frac{L_\tau^\theta}{L_v^\theta}\right)^{r_-}\right]
 &\leq C_-.
 
\end{align}
Moreover, if \(X\) is a continuous \(\mathbb P\)-local martingale and
\[
 \widetilde X^\theta
 :=X-\langle X,N^\theta\rangle,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{eq}}^{-1}\|X\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb P;I)}
 \leq
 \|\widetilde X^\theta\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb Q^\theta;I)}
 \leq
 C_{\mathrm{eq}}\|X\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb P;I)}.
 
\end{equation}
The exponents are selected after the budget \(n_*\) is fixed.  The
proposition does not assert \(r_+=r_-=2\), nor does it prescribe the same
exponent under the two measures. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:25:39.085567+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_314c60f51b3c162d281248f74ddda1383da7af322728a078102cbbd15c592d5f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:flow of arXiv:2606.12143, 'Continuous stochastic flows driven by white noise and their duals'] A \textbf{stochastic flow} driven by $\mathcal W$ is a family of processes 
$$
\mathcal S = \left\{\bigl(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x \ge r\bigr)\right\}_{(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2}
$$
such that, for each $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$, the process $(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x \ge r)$ is the almost sure unique strong solution to~(equation eq:SDE_gener of the paper), and the following properties hold almost surely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(R\arabic*)}, nosep]
    \item $\mathcal S_{r,r}(a) = a$ for all $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$. 
    \item For every $r \le x$, $a \mapsto \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)$ is c\`adl\`ag. 
    \item For any $(a_1,r_1), (a_2,r_2) \in {\mathbb R}^2$ and any $z \ge y \ge \max\{r_1,r_2\}$,
    $$
        \mathcal S_{r_1,y}(a_1) < \mathcal S_{r_2,y}(a_2) 
        \ \Longrightarrow\ 
        \mathcal S_{r_1,z}(a_1) \le \mathcal S_{r_2,z}(a_2).
    $$ 
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{-1.2em}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358403+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_3164e6f087edcf03d0ed5dc5b5362a181abb5563823cfe1cedcf020aa6b01bc9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fitting a per-output affine stack directly in the per-sample relative metric - weighted least squares with case weights $1/\\|y_i\\|^2$, or a per-output simplex fit with the same weights - overfits badly: the weights concentrate the effective sample on the handful of smallest-norm cases and $M + 1$ coefficients fitted to them are unusable out of sample (measured on the EMIT pool, seed 101: 0.1236 against 0.0465 for ordinary least squares on Y1, 0.1591 against 0.1292 on Y2; cross-validation on the weighted fit chooses to discard it entirely). Measured on the same three cells (Y1, Y2, Y4): 0.0451 / 0.1190 / 1.799 against ordinary least squares 0.0465 / 0.1292 / 1.898 (+3.0 / +7.9 / +5.2 percent), matching the cross-validated best heuristic of the pool twice and beating it once; with the residual shrink toward the pooled simplex weights on top (cross-validated amount 0.2-0.4) it is the best estimator on all three cells, +4.1 / +11.7 / +6.7 percent over least squares and +3.4 to +3.9 percent over the pool's best. Two ingredients do the work: the nonlinear shrinkage tames the heavy-tailed spectrum that the small-norm cases create, and the sum-to-one constraint removes the scale and intercept freedom those cases exploit. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:23.369898+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3169129cbe66435587e20b76f86eb07dac3e2b94b97a8bf2946962751914bb5d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 47 of arXiv:2512.07202, 'Hitting Probabilities for Hypoelliptic Differential Equations Driven by Fractional Brownia'] There exists a smooth random variable $\Psi$ such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:43:43.469596+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3174b1f897ac2062c21435034a47b3f3f61a2f619801aa2d6e5f661b4f111f68","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Campanato of arXiv:2509.04155, 'An Approach to Sub-Gaussian Heat Kernel Estimates via Analysis on Metric Spaces'] Let $p \geq 1, \, f \in L^p(X,\mu)$, $R > 0$ and $\delta > 0$.
    Let $M : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be the sharp maximal type function
    \[
        M(x) := \sup_{x \in B(y,r)} r^{-\delta} \vint_{B(y,r)} \abs{f - f_{B(y,r)}}^p \, d\mu
    \]
    where the supremum is taken over all $y \in X$ and $0 < r \leq R$ such that $x \in B(y,r)$.
    Then, there is a constant $C \geq 1$ such that for $\mu$-almost every $x \in X$ the two-point estimate
    \[
        \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \leq C d(x,y)^{\frac{\delta}{p}}(M(x)^{\frac{1}{p}} + M(y)^{\frac{1}{p}})
    \]
    holds for $\mu$-almost every $y \in B(x,R/4)$.
    This result is quantitative in the sense that $C$ depends only on the doubling constant of $\mu$ in (equation eq:muDoubling of the paper), $\delta$ and $p$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:52:17.578262+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3196b475c1ca3b2f971fd0e90364afa15a8b707b9ff96be86dbb5228551298d6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem i:t:GirsanovDK of arXiv:2411.14936, 'Massive Particle Systems,\\Wasserstein Brownian Motions,\\ and the Dean--Kawasaki Equation'] Fix~$\pi\in\msP(\mbfT_\circ)$, and suppose Assumption~(ass:Girsanov of the paper) is satisfied.
Further let~$\phi\in\msD(\widehat\mcE_\pi)^\bullet_{\loc}$ 
be satisfying~(equation eq:t:Girsanov:00 of the paper),~(equation eq:t:Girsanov:000 of the paper), and~(equation eq:PhiTotalPartSpace of the paper).
Finally, let~$(\rho_\bullet,\mbbP)$ be any \emph{time-homogeneous} $\msP^\pa\cap \msP_\phi$-valued $\mcQ_\pi^\phi$-substationary Hunt process adapted to its natural filtration with initial distribution~$P\circ\rho_0^{-1}$ equivalent to~$\mcQ_\pi$. 

Then, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
\item $\rho_\bullet$ is a solution to the martingale problem for~$\big({\widehat\mcL_\pi^\phi,\msD(\widehat\mcL_\pi^\phi)}\big)$, cf.~(equation eq:t:Girsanov:1 of the paper);
\item $\rho_\bullet$ is a solution to the martingale problem for~$(\widehat\mcL^\phi,\hCylP{}{0})$, see~(equation eq:t:Girsanov:1 of the paper);
\item $\rho_\bullet$ is a distributional solution to the shadow martingale problem~(equation eq:d:ShadowMP:0 of the paper) driven by~$\widehat\mcL_\pi^\phi$, that is
\begin{equation*}
\widehat M^{\class{\varphi\otimes f}}_t\eqdef\ (\varphi\otimes f)^\star(\rho_t) - (\varphi\otimes f)^\star(\rho_0) -\int_0^t ({\mcL^\phi}'\rho_s)(\varphi\otimes f)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s
\end{equation*}
is an $\msF_\bullet$-adapted $\mbbP$-martingale for each $\varphi\in\msR_0$ and each~$f\in\msA$.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
As in the proof of Theorem~(t:DK of the paper), (i:t:GirsanovDK:1 of the paper)$\implies$(i:t:GirsanovDK:2 of the paper)$\implies$(i:t:GirsanovDK:3 of the paper) holds by definition.
Since~$\rho_\bullet$ is a $\mcQ_\pi^\phi$-substationary Hunt process, it is identified ---uniquely up to~$\mcQ_\pi^\phi$-equivalence--- by its \emph{Markovian} generator on~$L^2(\mcQ_\pi^\phi)$.
Thus, again in analogy with Theorem~(t:DK of the paper), (i:t:GirsanovDK:2 of the paper)$\implies$(i:t:GirsanovDK:1 of the paper) holds since~$(\widehat\mcL^\phi,\hCylP{}{0})$ is Markov unique on~$L^2(\mcQ_\pi^\phi)$, as a consequence of Theorem~(t:Girsanov of the paper)(i:t:Girsanov:7 of the paper).

Similarly to the proof of~[KonLehvRe19b], the rest of the proof will follow directly from Theorem~(t:DK of the paper), by inverting the Girsanov transform by~$\phi$, as we now show.
Since~$(\rho_\bullet,\mbbP)$ is a Hunt process by assumption, we may consider its Girsanov transform~$\rho_\bullet^{1/\phi}$ by weight~$1/\phi$, which is a Borel right process, see~[Kuw98] or~[Fit97].
Since~$(\rho_\bullet,\mbbP)$ is $\msP^\pa\cap\msP_\phi$-valued (recall that we chose~$\msP_\phi=\msP$),~$\rho_\bullet^{1/\phi}$ is $\msP^\pa$-valued.

Since~$\rho_\bullet$ is identified ---uniquely up to~$\mcQ_\pi^\phi$-equivalence--- by~$(\widehat\mcL^\phi,\hCylP{}{0})$, we may compute the generator of~$\rho_\bullet^{1/\phi}$ on~$u\in\hCylP{}{0}$ as~$\widehat\mcL^{\rho^{1/\phi}} u = \widehat\mcL^{\phi} u + \phi \, \widehat\mcG_\pi(\phi^{-1},u)=\widehat\mcL u$.
Thus, since~$\tparen{\widehat\mcL,\hCylP{}{0}}$ is essentially self-adjoint by Theorem~(t:TransferP of the paper)(i:t:TransferP:1 of the paper), the generator~$\tparen{\widehat\mcL^{\rho^{1/\phi}_\pi},\dom{\widehat\mcL^{\rho^{1/\phi}}_\pi}}$ on~$L^2(\mcQ_\pi)$ is exactly~$\big({\widehat\mcL_\pi,\msD(\widehat\mcL_\pi)}\big)$.

This concludes the proof in light of the analogous assertions in Theorem~(t:DK of the paper) and of Proposition~(p:GirsanovDFSimple of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

A smooth curve gamma: I -> M on an interval I subset R is a geodesic if its velocity field is parallel along itself: nabla_{gamma'(t)} gamma'(t) = 0 for every t in I. Equivalently, in local coordinates x^1,...,x^n a curve gamma(t) = (x^1(t),...,x^n(t)) is a geodesic iff it satisfies the second-order ODE system d^2x^k/dt^2 + sum_{i,j} Gamma^k_{ij}(gamma(t)) (dx^i/dt)(dx^j/dt) = 0 for k=1,...,n, where Gamma^k_{ij} are the Christoffel symbols of g. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.142189+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31bf23c8569447ad87fe2691c4a7ab91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field (e.g. $\\mathbb {C}$), any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator (a scalar multiple of the identity) on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:26:26.764209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_31ea34e18be41e33854145463a4a9a3ae0d4c135b4be38d5c3285271cab34578","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:sc-scalar-HM of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Let $(c_k, \lambda_k)$ be a scalar solution of the
semi-discrete diamond equations
(equation eq:sc-diamond-C of the paper)--(equation eq:sc-diamond-mixed of the paper) and
the fully discrete diamond equations of
Proposition~\textup{(prop:CL-gen-system of the paper)},
and let $F(u) = \det_H(I - zK(u))$ be as in
Corollary~\textup{(cor:sc-Woodbury of the paper)}.
Assume the boundary
conditions\footnote{These boundary conditions are natural in
the probabilistic applications of Chapter~(ch:semi-discrete-model-verifications of the paper).}
$\lim_{\ell \to -\infty} F(T^\ell v) = 1$ and
$\lim_{\ell \to -\infty} \partial_1 F(T^\ell v) = 0$ for all
$v \in \mathcal{V}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}, leftmargin=*]
\item For each pair $i, j \geq 2$, assume
$\alpha_{ij}(u) \neq 0$ and

- \alpha_{ji}(u)F(S_j u)F(TS_i u)
- \bigl(\alpha_{ij}(u) - \alpha_{ji}(u)\bigr)
  F(Tu)F(S_i S_j u) = 0.
\end{equation}

\item For each $j \geq 2$, assume that $c_j(u) \neq 0$,

\begin{equation}
F(Tu)\partial_1 F(S_j u)
- F(S_j u)\partial_1 F(Tu)

For a stationary continuous-time Markov chain with real values, let the chain run at speed c. Leskela (Queueing Systems 100 (2022), 213-215, Problem 3) asked whether some stationary ergodic chain that is not stochastically monotone becomes smaller in the supermodular order of processes as it is speeded up. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161640+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32284a37a5fb577be6830fc324e7c522050893e6ec12cbb41c5a9366e51cc83f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 13 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exists $\epsilon' > 0$ such that 
    \[S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon'] 
    \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
    	\frac\epsilon5, \frac\epsilon3
    	\bigg)\]
for all $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.

\begin{proof}
    We first prove the claim for a fixed $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, where $\epsilon'$ for now is permitted to depend on $(\lambda,\mu)$.
Suppose for contradiction that for all $\epsilon'>0$ we have
    \[ \emptyset\ne
    S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon'] \cap 
	S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;\frac\epsilon5, \frac\epsilon3\bigg)^c 
	\subseteq
    S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon'] \cap 
\overline{S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;\frac\epsilon5, \frac\epsilon{3}\bigg)^c}\,,
    \]
    where $\overline{S}$ denotes the closure of $S$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$. This forms a nested family of nonempty compact sets indexed by $\epsilon' > 0$, so the intersection
    \[
        \bigcap_{\epsilon'>0} \bigg\{
        S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon'] \cap \overline{S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        	\frac\epsilon5, \frac\epsilon{3}\bigg)^c}\bigg\}
        = S_\star(\lambda,\mu) \cap
        	\overline{S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
			\frac\epsilon5, \frac\epsilon{3}\bigg)^c}
    \]
is also nonempty. That is, we can find $\YY\in S_\star(\lambda,\mu)$ with
	\[
	\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)
	+ \frac\epsilon5 \alpha^2\iota^3 (\|\vBBb\|_2)^2
	\ge \frac{\epsilon}{3}\,.
	\]
This contradicts Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.in.S.star.eps}, which implies 
	\[
	\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)
	+ \frac\epsilon5 \alpha^2\iota^3 (\|\vBBb\|_2)^2
	\le \frac{\epsilon}{5}\,.
	\]
This proves that for any fixed $(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda$, the claim holds for some $\epsilon'>0$ that may depend on $(\lambda,\mu)$. 
Next, for any $(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda$, let 
\[\epsilon'(\lambda,\mu)
\equiv \max\bigg\{
\epsilon':

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.030979+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3229415e1b7fb25fd6e65ee00c31af93d78a927ecb8a269942db817520ca6034","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:sibling-reduced-PDE of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Fix \(r\in(0,q)\). For \(\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N\), define \(b_i\) by
		\[
		m_i=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i),
		\qquad 1\le i\le N.
		\]
		Let \(\rho\) be a finite-step probability measure on \([r,q]\), and write
		\[
		\bar x_\rho(t)
		=
		\theta+(1-\theta)\rho([r,t]),
		\qquad r\le t<q.
		\]
		Let \(\phi_\rho\) solve on \([r,q]\)
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				\partial_t\phi_\rho
				+\frac{\xi''(t)}2
				\left(
				\partial_{xx}\phi_\rho
				+\bar x_\rho(t)(\partial_x\phi_\rho)^2
				\right)&=0,\\
				\phi_\rho(q,x)&=\Phi_\zeta(q,x).
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		For
		\[
		Z\sim\mathcal N\left(
		0,\xi'(r)-\frac{\xi'(r)^2}{\xi'(q)}
		\right),
		\]
		define
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\mathcal J_{N,\mathbf{m},q,r}(\rho)

			-\frac1N\sum_i\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)\\
			&+\frac1N\sum_i

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:24:34.422868+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_322c6b7a0bc172a33d5ac4535a0d202800889fd44bdad751b4a36dbd712a25bd","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Signed transport and one-side-fixed composition) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] The following operations preserve affine dependence of network parameters on a
common code vector.
\begin{enumerate}[label={\textup{(\roman*)}}]
 \item A signed scalar $u$ may be transported through any number of hidden
 layers as the nonnegative pair
 $(u_+,u_-)=(\varrho(u),\varrho(-u))$, with the fixed identity update
 $(u_+,u_-)\mapsto(u_+,u_-)$ and recovery $u=u_+-u_-$.
 \item Finitely many networks may be copied or run in parallel.  Their widths
 add.  A $q$-dimensional state is transported coordinatewise by $2q$
 nonnegative channels, so shorter branches can be extended to a common
 depth by fixed signed transport.  If a branch already terminates in a
 nonnegative state or a signed pair, its existing depth gap is filled by fixed
 identity layers.  If only a signed scalar affine readout
 $u=\bmw(\bmxi)^\ts\bmh+b(\bmxi)$ is available, compose that readout with the
 fixed split map $u\mapsto(u,-u)$, whose matrix is $[1,-1]^\ts$, and merge the
 two adjacent affine maps.  The resulting hidden layer produces
 $(\varrho(u),\varrho(-u))$; its two affine
 rows are sign copies of $(\bmw(\bmxi),b(\bmxi))$, so affine code dependence
 is preserved.  This split layer must be included in the interface depth
 ledger.
 \item Two adjacent affine layers with no intervening activation may be
 merged without losing affine code dependence whenever at least one of the
 two layers is fixed.
 \item Repeating an affine slot assignment in copied branches and padding
 unused slots by fixed zeros preserve affine code dependence.  Zero padding
 changes the dense parameter count but not the realized function.
\end{enumerate}
By contrast, merging two code-dependent affine layers need not preserve affine
dependence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.565392+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_325f204f58e8ca23c57f7f099eec30c795391109bf617b227d7b8298f7c6d32b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 (Poisoned first-Cantor class) of arXiv:2608.26516, '2608.26516'] For every \(n\ge1\), let
\[
    X_n=C_n\sqcup P_n,
    \qquad
    P_n=\{p_{n,1},\ldots,p_{n,n}\},
    \qquad
    |C_n|=2n^3+n.
\]
Thus
\[
    |X_n|=2n^3+2n,
    \qquad
    a_n:=n^3+n=\frac{|X_n|}{2}.
\]
Set the final domain to the disjoint union of these blocks, i.e., $\CX^{\mathrm P}:=\bigsqcup_{n\ge1}X_n$.

The label set contains two common labels \(\starlabel\) and \(\dollarlabel\).
For every \(A\subseteq X_n\) with \(|A|=a_n\), introduce a private label
\(\lambda_{n,A}\), and for every \(i\in[n]\), introduce a poison label
\(\rho_{n,i}\).  All private and poison labels are distinct.

For every
\(A\subseteq X_n\) with \(|A|=a_n\), define the Cantor hypothesis
\[
    c_{n,A}(x)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \starlabel, & x\in A,\\
        \lambda_{n,A}, & x\in X_n\setminus A,\\
        \dollarlabel, & x\notin X_n.
    \end{cases}
\]
For every \(i\in[n]\), define the poisoned fallback
\[
    s_{n,i}(x)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \rho_{n,i}, & x=p_{n,i},\\
        \starlabel, & x\in X_n\setminus\{p_{n,i}\},\\
        \dollarlabel, & x\notin X_n.
    \end{cases}
\]
Finally, let \(h_{\dollarlabel}\) denote the all-\(\dollarlabel\) hypothesis.  
The \edefn{poisoned first-Cantor class} is
\[
    \Hpoison
    :=
    \{h_{\dollarlabel}\}
    \cup
    \left\{
        c_{n,A}:
        n\ge1,\ A\subseteq X_n,\ |A|=a_n
    \right\}
    \cup
    \left\{
        s_{n,i}:
        n\ge1,\ i\in[n]
    \right\}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.432691+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32933e83fd7a5f556e24e5932fa396dabba81e079f04c4d0d9ce81b2279700b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:calYzero_representation}
The set $\{ \hat{f}_i^0 \mid i \in \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, \dots \}$ is a basis for ${\rm aff}(\Sym^0)$. 
Moreover, the coefficients in an expansion $f = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0$ with respect to this basis
are given by the formula
$\alpha_i^0 = \frac{2(p f(-2i) - q f(2i))}{p-q}.$

\begin{proof}
Fix $f \in \Sym^0$. 
Note that for all $z \not\in S^0 = 2\mathbb{Z}$ and positive integers $i$, $f(z) = \hat{f}_i^0(z) = 0$. 

Solving the symmetry equation $pf(0) + qf(2) = pf(-2) + qf(0)$ for $f(0)$, we obtain
\(
f(0) = \frac{pf(-2) - qf(2)}{p-q},
\)
so that defining 
\(
\alpha_1^0= 2f(0) 
\)
results in 
\( f(0) 
= \alpha_1^0 \hat{f}_1^0(0) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_k^0 \hat{f}_k^0(0)\). 
Since 
$f(z)=0$ for all other $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} < 2$, this is the unique value of $\alpha_1^0$ satisfying the formula $f(z) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_k^0 \hat{f}_k^0(z)$ when $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} < 2$. 

We proceed by induction on $k$. 

Our inductive hypothesis is that 
\(
\alpha_i^0 = \frac{2(pf(-2i) - qf(2i))}{p-q}
\)
(where $i \in [k]$) is the unique solution to $f(z) = \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(z)$ for $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} < 2k$. 
We compute
\begin{align*}
f(2k) = \sum_{i \ge 1} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(2k) 
&= \alpha_{k}^0 \hat{f}_{k}^0(2k) + \alpha_{k+1}^0\hat{f}_{k+1}^0(2k) \\
&= \left(\frac{2(pf(-2k) - qf(2k))}{p-q}\right)\left(\frac{q}{2}\right) + \alpha_{k+1}^0 \frac{p}{2} 
\shortintertext{thus}
\alpha_{k+1}^0 &= \left(\frac{2}{p}\right)\left(f(2k) - \left(\frac{pqf(-2k) - q^2f(2k)}{p-q}\right)\right) \\
&= \frac{2((p-q+q^2)f(2k) - pqf(-2k))}{p(p-q)} \\

&= \frac{2(pf(2k) -qf(-2k))}{p-q} .
\end{align*}
where we have used the identity $p - q +q^2 
= p^2$. 

Note that the symmetry equation 
\[ pf(2k) +qf(2k+2) = pf(-2k-2)+qf(-2k) \]
may be arranged as 
\[pf(2k) - qf(-2k) = pf(-2(k+1)) - qf(2(k+1)) \]whence the desired formula 
\(
\alpha_{k+1}^0 = \frac{2(pf(-2(k+1)) - qf(2(k+1)))}{p-q} 
\).
A similar argument shows that the same value of $\alpha_{k+1}^0$ is the unique solution to $f(-2k) = \sum_{i\ge1} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(-2k)$. 
Since $f(z) = \hat{f}_i^0(z) = 0$ for all $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} \in (2k,2(k+1))$,

this completes the induction step; 

consequently $f = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0$ everywhere on $\mathbb{R}$. 

Finally, note that 
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 
= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat{f}_i^0(2k) 
= \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(2k) 
= \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} f(2k) = 1. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["l^p norm on R^2","axis direction","d/r -> 0 asymptotics"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T04:06:41.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_32cba36e9ea9ba0c5d9ba247f3e15cf592fb208e4bcf772a85f058485b81ff96","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.300439+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_32db5e05c2234ca8a4c051e226a841c9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the free group $F_{S}$ over a given set $S$ consists of all words that can be built from members of $S$, considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the group axioms (e.g. $st=suu^{-1}t$ but $s\\neq t^{-1}$ for $s,t,u\\in S$). The members of $S$ are called generators of $F_{S}$, and the number of generators is the rank of the free group. An arbitrary group $G$ is called free if it is isomorphic to $F_{S}$ for some subset $S$ of $G$, that is, if there is a subset $S$ of $G$ such that every element of $G$ can be written in exactly one way as a product of finitely many elements of $S$ and their inverses (disregarding trivial variations such as $st=suu^{-1}t$).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.857052+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32e958db18a4be44f23532fc88b129366075f86c021934c666451af981293060","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 (Standard properties of Friedrichs mollifiers,
		see \cite{Li-Liu-Tang-2021-SPA,Taylor-2011-PDEbook3}) of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let $J_n$ be defined by \eqref{Define Jn}. Then the following properties
		hold.
		\begin{enumerate}[label={\bf (\arabic*)},leftmargin=0.79cm]
			\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}
			\item For every $r\in\mathbb R$, $J_n$ is self-adjoint on $H^r$:
			\[
			\langle J_nf,g\rangle_{H^r}
			=
			\langle f,J_ng\rangle_{H^r},
			\quad f,g\in H^r.
			\]
			Moreover, $J_n$ commutes with every Fourier multiplier; in particular,
			it commutes with $\mathcal D^r$, $\partial_x$, and $\mathcal H$ whenever
			the corresponding compositions are defined.
			
			\item For every $r\in\mathbb R$ and $f\in H^r$,
			\[
			\sup_{n\ge1}\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^r;H^r)}\le1,
			\quad
			\lim_{n\to\infty}\|J_nf-f\|_{H^r}=0.
			\]
			In addition,
			\[
			\sup_{n\ge1}
			\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(L^\infty;L^\infty)}<\infty.
			\]
			
			\item For every $a,b\in\mathbb R$ with $a>b$,
			\[
			\|\mathbf I-J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)}
			\lesssim
			n^{-(a-b)},
			\]
			whereas, for $a<b$,
			\[
			\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)}
			\lesssim
			n^{b-a}.
			\]
			Consequently, for each fixed $n\ge1$, $J_n$ is a smoothing operator:
			$J_n\in\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.699820+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32eaa18e15f6b104661ac4d5ddef17f65ed1fffc049b515d257fe3453e40dc0d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 30 (Cutoff tails for the linear and cross-quadratic fields) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $0\le\theta<1/2-\betasum$.  For the difference from the uncut field, let
$p_{a,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}$ and
$q_{\Theta,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}$ be nonnegative majorants of the sum of the
static covariance density and the normalized time-increment density.  For
every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{align}
 p_{a,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)
 &\lesssim
 \one_{\{|\xi|\ge c_0\Lambda\}}
 \langle\xi\rangle^{-2+2\beta_a+2\theta},
 \\
 q_{\Theta,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)
 &\lesssim_{\varepsilon}
 \max\{\langle\xi\rangle,\Lambda\}^{-1+2\betasum+2\theta+\varepsilon}.
 
\end{align}
The corresponding difference of two non-nested admissible cutoffs is bounded
by the sum of the two right-hand sides.  Moreover, for every
\[
 s<-\frac12-\beta_a
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 r<-1-\betasum,
\]
one can choose $\theta,\varepsilon,\delta>0$ so that
\begin{align}
 \sum_{N\in\Dyd}N^{2s+3+\delta}
 \sup_{|\xi|\sim N}p_{a,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)&\longrightarrow0,
 \\
 \sum_{N\in\Dyd}N^{2r+3+\delta}
 \sup_{|\xi|\sim N}q_{\Theta,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)&\longrightarrow0.
 
\end{align}
Both tails decay polynomially along dyadic $\Lambda$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.579659+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32ef89cef6e581c2c2347b6613fe522373bd44679b76541514a68db99ee9a033","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 9 (Pressure; the Jensen gap as a chord--tangent inequality) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Under uniform ellipticity and irreducibility:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:39:18.524866+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32fe9043d4dc639cff84342254afe21aa721acc2041a2ff6fda7ff853c2e7c5a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] For every integer $n\geq4$, there exists a nondegenerate continuum
$K\subset S^n$ with $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}K=1$ such that, with
$M:=S^n\setminus K$, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $M$ is a contractible smooth open manifold that is not simply connected at infinity.

\item There exists a smooth function $\phi:M\to(0,\infty)$ with
$m_0:=\inf_M\phi>0$ such that, for every $t\in(-m_0,\infty)$,
\[
g^{(t)}:=(\phi+t)^{4/(n-2)}g_{st}|_M
\]
is smooth, complete, and locally conformally flat, with
\[
\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}=n(n-1)t(\phi+t)^{-(n+2)/(n-2)}.
\]
Hence $\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}$ is negative, zero, or positive according as
$t<0$, $t=0$, or $t>0$, and
\[
\lim_{t\to0}\int_M|\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}|^{n/2}\,dV_{g^{(t)}}=0.
\]
For $t>0$, the rescaled metric
\[
\bar g^{(t)}
:=t^{-4/(n-2)}g^{(t)}
=\left(1+\frac{\phi}{t}\right)^{4/(n-2)}g_{st}|_M
\]
satisfies
\[
0<\mathrm{Sc}_{\bar g^{(t)}}<n(n-1),
\]
and its scalar curvature decays uniformly to zero at $K$ in the sense
that
\[
 \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
 \sup_{\substack{x\in M\\ d_{g_{st}}(x,K)<\delta}}
 \mathrm{Sc}_{\bar g^{(t)}}(x)=0.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:43:00.033792+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3329edc1a231970e9f1bc1303696aea636d04a4495759bcdad43e2440cb09695","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 (Neumann-boundary compactness and stationarity) of arXiv:2609.00739, '2609.00739'] Let $\Omega\subset\R^2$ be a bounded $C^3$ domain, let $V$ satisfy
Assumption~\ref{assum:potential}, and let
$\eps_j\in(0,1]$ satisfy $\eps_j\downarrow0$.  Let
$u_j:=u_{\eps_j}\in H^1(\Omega;\R^k)$ be weak solutions of
\eqref{eq:intro-system}.  Suppose that
\begin{equation}
\cE_{\eps_j}(u_j;\Omega)\leq M_0
\quad\text{for some }M_0<+\infty.
\end{equation}
Then, after passing to a subsequence, there are a closed countably
$1$-rectifiable set $\Sstar\subset\overline\Omega$, a finite-perimeter
partition $(E_\alpha)_{\alpha=1}^q$ of $\Omega$, Radon measures
$\nustar,\zetastar$, and finite signed Radon measures
$\upmu_{\star,ij}$ on $\overline\Omega$ with the
following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=$(\theenumi)$]
\item The phase fields satisfy
\[
 u_j\to u_0:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^q\upsigma_\alpha\mathbf1_{E_\alpha}
 \quad\text{in }L^1(\Omega),
\]
with
$\sum_{\alpha=1}^q\Per(E_\alpha;\Omega)\leq C(V)M_0$, and the convergence is uniform on
compact subsets of $\overline\Omega\backslash \Sstar$ to a locally constant
map $\bar u_0:\overline\Omega\backslash \Sstar\to\Sigma$ that agrees almost
everywhere in $\Omega\backslash \Sstar$ with
$\sum_{\alpha=1}^q\upsigma_\alpha\mathbf1_{E_\alpha}$.

\item The concentration set satisfies
\[
 \Sstar=\supp\nustar=\supp\zetastar,
 \quad
 \cH^1(\Sstar)\leq C(V,\Omega)M_0.
\]

\item The measures in \eqref{eq:intro-measures} converge weakly star to
$\nustar$, $\zetastar$, and $\upmu_{\star,ij}$, respectively, and
\begin{equation}
 \nustar=e\,\cH^1\llcorner\Sstar,
 \quad
 \zetastar=\Uptheta\,\cH^1\llcorner\Sstar,
 \quad
 \upmu_{\star,ij}=m_{ij}\,\cH^1\llcorner\Sstar.
\end{equation}
There are constants $c_0=c_0(V,\Omega)>0$ and
$C_0,C_1<\infty$, depending only on $V$, $\Omega$, and $M_0$, such that
\begin{equation}
 c_0\leq\Uptheta\leq e\leq C_0\Uptheta\leq C_1,
 \quad
 \abs{m_{ij}}\leq2e
 \quad\text{for }\cH^1\text{-almost every }x\in \Sstar.
\end{equation}

\item At $\cH^1$-almost every point of $\Sstar$, let $(\tau,n)$ denote the
approximate tangent-normal frame of $\Sstar$.  For
$a,b\in\{\tau,n\}$ set $m_{ab}:=a^Tm b$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 2\Uptheta=m_{nn}-m_{\tau\tau},
 \quad
 m_{n\tau}=0,
 \quad
 e=m_{nn}.
\end{equation}

\item The rectifiable varifold $\Vbold(\Sstar,\Uptheta)$ is stationary with
free boundary:
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\Sstar}\diver_{T_x\Sstar}X\,\dd\zetastar(x)=0
\end{equation}
for every $X\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\R^2)$ satisfying
$X\cdot\nOmega=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

\item In the interior, the local straight-segment and constant-density
description of \cite[Theorem 1.3]{Bethuel2025} holds away from an
$\cH^1$-null set.  On a boundary-supported regular arc with no incident
interior branch, $\Uptheta$ has a positive constant representative.  At a
finite-type boundary junction $p$ of $(\Sstar,\zetastar)$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{defn:finite-type-boundary}, each incident punctured branch
carries a positive constant weight $\Uptheta_\ell$, and
\begin{equation}
 P_{T_p\partial\Omega}
 \left(\sum_\ell\Uptheta_\ell\tau_\ell\right)=0.
\end{equation}
In particular, if the decomposition in
Definition~\ref{defn:finite-type-boundary} consists of exactly one
non-boundary half-arc and no boundary-supported or additional branch, then
that half-arc meets $\partial\Omega$ orthogonally.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

## Model and exact candidate

Let N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s<r be integers. There is one unresolved A/S
pair L,R and N-2 fixed known S contexts. S has all K truths; A has an
independent uniform r-subset. The source p chooses contexts uniformly
and then truths uniformly. Actual untagged iid factual samples and an
optional independent partial verifier give known truth unions C_L,C_R
of sizes s and r respectively. Both orientations are still compatible.
If R is A its support is fully known; if L is A it contains C_L but
its r-s residual truths vary over the other K-s candidates.

All generators are allowed. Require source Mis_infinity=0 in EVERY
compatible world, using exact output-probability score bins.
Put F=K-r, G=gcd(r,F), lambda=1/(NK). For j=0,...,G define

 k_j=min(s,r*j/G),
 L_j=K+K*j/G-2*k_j,
 a_j=(j/G)*(F/r)*k_j/L_j.                                (1)

All counts are integers and all L_j>0. The proposed exact conditional
worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V_sat(0)=F*lambda*(1-max_{0<=j<=G}a_j).                  (2)

This is a finite optimization of G+1 explicit rational values, not a
numerical estimate or an unbounded partition search. It includes every
score partition, mixed safe atoms and arbitrary output probabilities.
No optimal positive-budget or global expected frontier is claimed.

## Lower bound for every robustly calibrated generator

Fix g and its exact score partition Pi. Robust zero calibration makes
every p(B)=g(B) invariant across all compatible worlds. Since s<r<K,
swapping two residual L candidates in an A support forces all K-s
uncertified L atoms into a single score bin B*. Let k be the number
of known L truths OUTSIDE B*, so 0<=k<=s. In B* let u be the number
of known R truths, v the number of the F candidates outside C_R,
and w the number of fixed S atoms. Flipping orientation yields

 F*(u+k)=r*v.

Consequently v=F*j/G and u=r*j/G-k for an integer 0<=j<=G, with
k<=r*j/G. The size of B* is

For completeness the divisibility step uses Bezout: r/G and F/G are
coprime; a*(r/G)+b*(F/G)=1. Multiplying by v and using (F/G)|(r/G)*v
gives (F/G)|v, then the displayed parametrization. The brain returned
this standard identity in recall/walk004.txt, full card id

 L=K+K*j/G-2k+w,

and its common calibrated score, computed in the L-A world, is

 q*=lambda*(1-k*F/(r*L)).                               (3)

In any other bin let a be its known-L-truth count, u its known-R-
truth count and v its outside-C_R count. Orientation invariance gives
F*(u-a)=r*v. Its calibrated score is

 q=lambda*(1+a*F/(r*|B|))>=lambda.

Therefore in the actual compatible world R=A (whose support is C_R),
the false mass is at least

 H_R>=v*q*+(F-v)*lambda
    >=F*lambda*[1-(j/G)*(F/r)*k/(K+K*j/G-2k)].            (4)

The second inequality uses w>=0, which can only raise q* in (3).
For fixed j the function k/(K+K*j/G-2k) increases with k on the
feasible positive-denominator range: cross multiplication cancels the
quadratic terms and leaves K*(1+j/G)*(k_2-k_1)>=0. Thus its maximum
is at k=k_j. Formula (4) proves max_world H(g)>=the value (2).
It does not assume arbitrary bins are homogeneous in truth status.

## Attainer for each j

Fix any j and k=k_j. Choose k known L truths for a safe group T;
put all other L atoms in B*. In R put r*j/G-k known truths and
F*j/G outside-C_R atoms into B*. Put k of the remaining known R
truths in T alongside its k known L truths. Put all remaining R atoms
in Z. These choices are possible: k<=s and k<=r*j/G; also j<=G
ensures enough R known truths remain for T.

The groups have these source-invariant counts and scores:

* B*: K+K*j/G-2k atoms, score (3) with w=0;
* T: 2k known true atoms, score (1/r+1/K)/(2N), omitted if k=0;
* Z: r*(G-j)/G known R truths and F*(G-j)/G outside atoms,
  total K*(G-j)/G atoms, score lambda, omitted if j=G;
* fixed S atoms: score lambda.

T has source mass k/(Nr)+k/(NK). Z has source mass (G-j)/(GN)
in either orientation. B* has the remaining pair mass, or its
invariance follows directly from F*(u+k)=r*v. Thus every group has
an invariant p mass and g is its uniform coarsening; equal lambda
scores merge harmlessly. The total is one and g is robustly calibrated
with zero budget in every compatible world.

If L=A its F false atoms all lie in B*, giving H_L=F*q*. If R=A,
H_R=(F*j/G)*q*+F*(1-j/G)*lambda. Since q*<=lambda, H_R>=H_L.
The worst risk is exactly F*lambda*(1-a_j). Maximizing a_j attains
the lower bound, proving (2).

The attaining rule uses only the observed known-truth unions and the
given model parameters: choose j by the explicit optimization, and
choose the displayed subsets of those known unions. It never reads
the hidden orientation or unobserved truth labels. Those labels enter
only the subsequent all-world verification and lower-bound argument.

the earlier smaller-count expression (K-r)*b_s. Thus the saturated
unequal case still has that expression when r and K-r are coprime.
When G>1, additional neutral truth/false bundles may improve it.

a_j for j=1,2,3 are respectively

 1/[6(m+1)], 4/[3(m+4)], 1/(m+2).

The middle value is largest: it beats the last iff m>4 and beats
the first since 24(m+1)>3(m+4). Thus C016's feasible generator is

{"assumptions":["all examples are for Lebesgue measure on [0,1] or R, and counting measure on N"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553628+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_33568bddd455c11696bbce09e0ff678cc9dd457d94aed6dcd3a4a493975ad160","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"There is NO inclusion between L^p and L^q on a general measure space, and the two familiar inclusions run in OPPOSITE directions. (a) Finite measure (mu(X) < infinity), p < q: L^q is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= mu(X)^{1/p - 1/q} ||f||_q; the inclusion is strict, e.g. on [0,1], f(x) = x^{-1/2} is in L^1 but not L^2. (b) Counting measure, p < q: l^p is contained in l^q, with ||a||_q <= ||a||_p - the reverse containment; strictness: a_n = 1/n is in l^2 but not l^1. (c) Lebesgue measure on R^n: NEITHER containment holds. On R, |x|^{-1/2} 1_{{|x|<1}} is in L^1 but not L^2, while (1 + |x|)^{-1} is in L^2 but not L^1 - the first fails by a local singularity, the second by slow decay at infinity. What IS always true is the interpolation statement: for p_0 < p < p_1, L^{p_0} intersect L^{p_1} is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= ||f||_{p_0}^{1-theta} ||f||_{p_1}^{theta}. So a step 'f in L^2 hence f in L^1' is only legitimate after the measure has been declared finite (with the factor mu(X)^{1/2} exhibited), and 'f in L^1 hence f in L^2' only on an atomic space with atoms bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

There is

0,&J_\eps^s\text{ away from the layer or }J_\eps^c,

{"assumptions":["the factors are independent","entries i.i.d. centered Gaussian, variance 1/n","square factors of equal dimension","the largest-singular-value claim needs strong convergence, which is stronger than convergence of the spectral distribution"],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.216158+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_33a8efc37836202fed9468a5983040948a4b1e47488753c7edb06802b1e30ddb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $G_1,\\dots,G_p$ be independent $n \\times n$ matrices with i.i.d. $\\mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$ entries. The limiting singular value distribution of the product $G_p \\cdots G_1$ is the Fuss-Catalan law of order $p$, whose upper edge is $(p+1)^{(p+1)/2}p^{-p/2}$. For $p=1$ this is $2$, recovering the square Gaussian case; for $p=2$ it is $3^{3/2}/2=\\sqrt{27/4}=2.5980\\ldots$; for $p=3$ it is $3.0792\\ldots$. Moreover the largest singular value itself converges to that edge, not merely the bulk. This last point matters and is strictly stronger: convergence of the spectral distribution locates the edge but by itself does not exclude an outlier above it, so a bound that needs no outlier cannot be justified by the Fuss-Catalan law alone.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.016264+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_33aaf30036b4e1a9236d2fc3088932d883aa6aeb4eeb0928bafe8682e6f342c7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 50 (Saturation of the Toeplitz quadratic form) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $b=(b_m)_{m\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be a nonnegative, absolutely summable kernel on $\mathbb Z^d$, with
\[
\|b\|_1 := \sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^d} b_m < \infty.
\]
For any finitely supported vector $\delta=(\delta_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}$, define the quadratic form
\[
Q(\delta) := \sum_{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z^d} \delta_k\,\delta_\ell\, b_{\ell-k}.
\]
Then
\[
\sup_{\delta\neq 0} \frac{Q(\delta)}{\|\delta\|_2^2} = \|b\|_1.
\]
Moreover, this supremum is asymptotically attained by block indicators:
if $\delta^{(L)}_k := \1_{\{k\in\Lambda_L\}}$ with $\Lambda_L := [-L,L]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, then
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty} \frac{Q(\delta^{(L)})}{\|\delta^{(L)}\|_2^2} = \|b\|_1.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Z has i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries with finite fourth moment (orthogonally invariant, e.g. Gaussian, for the sharpest vector statements)","rank(X) = r fixed, its nonzero singular values fixed on the noise scale","m/n -> beta in (0, 1]; the loss is Frobenius"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911379+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_33ac0767a68834a907f3d5ea4c4652965bbd6ad4e44964080117e92a26c8252f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $Y_n = X_n + \\sigma Z_n$ where $Y_n$ is $m \\times n$ with $m/n \\to \\beta \\in (0, 1]$, $Z_n$ has i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment, and $X_n$ has fixed rank $r$ with singular values $\\sigma\\sqrt{n}\\, x_1, \\dots, \\sigma\\sqrt{n}\\, x_r$ (so the $x_k$ are the signal singular values on the scale of the noise, $x_k > 0$ fixed). Write the singular values of $Y_n$ on the same scale, $y_k := s_k(Y_n) / (\\sigma \\sqrt{n})$. THEOREM (Gavish and Donoho, 2017). (i) For each $k \\le r$: if $x_k > \\beta^{1/4}$ then $y_k \\to \\sqrt{(x_k^2 + 1)(x_k^2 + \\beta)} / x_k$, and if $x_k \\le \\beta^{1/4}$ then $y_k \\to 1 + \\sqrt\\beta$ (the bulk edge); every other singular value of $Y_n$ converges to the bulk. (ii) Among all estimators of the form $\\hat X = \\sum_k \\eta(y_k)\\, \\sigma\\sqrt{n}\\; \\hat u_k \\hat v_k^T$ that keep the sample singular vectors and replace each singular value by a function $\\eta$ of it, the one minimizing the asymptotic Frobenius loss $\\lim \\|\\hat X - X_n\\|_F^2 / (\\sigma^2 n)$ is $$\\eta^*(y) = \\frac{1}{y}\\sqrt{(y^2 - \\beta - 1)^2 - 4\\beta} \\quad \\text{for } y \\ge 1 + \\sqrt\\beta, \\qquad \\eta^*(y) = 0 \\quad \\text{for } y < 1 + \\sqrt\\beta.$$ (iii) The asymptotic loss of $\\eta^*$ is strictly smaller than that of hard thresholding at any threshold and of soft thresholding at any threshold whenever some $x_k > \\beta^{1/4}$; on a pure-noise matrix ($r = 0$) $\\eta^*$ returns the zero matrix. The rule selects the rank (the number of $y_k$ above the edge $1 + \\sqrt\\beta$) and the amount of shrinkage of each retained component from the data, without cross-validation; with $\\sigma$ unknown it is combined with the median estimate $\\hat\\sigma = y_{\\mathrm{med}}/\\sqrt{n \\mu_\\beta}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:14:46.480283+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_33c7b7ba5e8497c8644c2f8a006caeb2503c7fa600014694511e3ff18aee9b42","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Consider the hyperoctahedral group $H_N$, which appears as the symmetry group of the $N$-cube, or the symmetry group of the $N$ coordinate axes of $\mathbb R^N$:
$$S_N\subset H_N\subset O_N$$

		second fundamental form $A$, unit normal $\nu$, and mean curvature

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.697689+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_33d3cba0f953ee8bc53f66751429d53425ca35bf149e5caa3cd1994c153c451a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 14 (Admissible spectral cutoffs) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] A family $(\pi_\Lambda)_{\Lambda\ge1}$ is called admissible if
$\pi_\Lambda=m_\Lambda(D)$, where $m_\Lambda\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ is real and
even, and there exist constants $0<c_0<C_0<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
  m_\Lambda(\xi)=1\quad\text{for }|\xi|\le c_0\Lambda,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}m_\Lambda\subset\{|\xi|\le C_0\Lambda\}.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{\Lambda\ge1}\Lambda^{|\alpha|}
  \|\partial^\alpha m_\Lambda\|_{L^\infty}<\infty
  \quad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha,
  \qquad
  m_\Lambda(\xi)\longrightarrow1
  \quad(\xi\in\R^3).
\end{equation}
No radiality, monotonicity, or nesting is imposed.  A fixed-profile family is
given by $m_\Lambda(\xi)=m(\xi/\Lambda)$ for a real even
$m\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ that equals one near the origin.  A dyadic
fixed-profile family is indexed by $\Lambda=2^n$, $n\in\N$.  An \emph{admissible cofinal cutoff sequence} is a sequence
$(\pi_{\Lambda_n})_{n\ge1}$ drawn from an admissible family, with
$\Lambda_n\to\infty$.  Statements for a continuous cutoff parameter are
understood sequentially along every admissible cofinal sequence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.935355+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_33f9b35e85453ac9d7e9c8f68c998c618e25afd4de9adf09b1aabeac2b561e50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:twodir of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Suppose the atoms take exactly two directions. Then the directions are

and $C(q)=\frac12(|m_+|^2+|m_-|^2)$ where $m_\pm$ are the conditional means

\[
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le4}C\le\frac E4,\qquad

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.495384+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_340d9decfe1f007dd6ce9f49d9302740e6338fdd6a9686dda0c41a9c2c01228d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 34 (Finite-dimensional inverse for the negative raw branch) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:double-moment-inverse}
Let \(X,Y,Z,W>0\) satisfy
\begin{equation}\lab{eq:inverse-moment-region}
 X+Y+Z<W<(\sqrt X+\sqrt Y+\sqrt Z)^2.
\end{equation}
There are unique \(S,A,B,D>0\) such that
\begin{align}
 X&=A+\frac{A^2}{S},&
 Y&=B+\frac{B^2}{S},&
 Z&=D+\frac{D^2}{S},\lab{eq:inverse-three-moments}\\
 W&=A+B+D+\frac{(A+B+D)^2}{S}.\lab{eq:inverse-fourth-moment}
\end{align}
Consequently, \(T=-S\) and \(F=-(S+A+B+D)\) give the unique solution
of these moment equations in the raw-parameter branch \(T<0\), \(F<0\).
The scalar equation determining \(S\) has a nonvanishing derivative at its
root.

Moreover, let \(w,w'>0\), let \(u,u'>0\), and suppose
\[
 a^2=w^2+u^2,\qquad b^2=(w')^2+(u')^2,\qquad
 \theta=\frac{u}{w^2}=\frac{u'}{(w')^2}.
\]
If
\begin{align*}
 X_n&=a^2n,&Y_n&=b^2n,\\
 Q_n&=n^{21}+O(n^{20}),\\
 Z_n&=Q_n-2u'n^{11}+O(n^{10}),&
 W_n&=Q_n+2un^{11}+O(n^{10}),
\end{align*}
then \eqref{eq:inverse-moment-region} holds for all sufficiently large \(n\),
and the corresponding solution satisfies
\begin{equation}\lab{eq:inverse-raw-asymptotics}
 S_n=\theta^{-2}n+O(1),\qquad
 A_n=w^2n+O(1),\qquad
 B_n=(w')^2n+O(1).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.971829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_340e082d40e3c67119e2b8e18d01a4edc01332ad451a5e2e17fa94a8e3d2aba1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:sections of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, we define $\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ 
by setting 
\begin{equs}
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\eqdef
\big\{ 
\big(F_{\underline{\tau}}\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] : \underline{\tau} \in \tau\big): \enskip 
\forall \underline{\tau}, \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\;\text{and}\; f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')\,,\; \mathbf{f} F_{\underline{\tau}} =  F_{\underline{\tau}'}
\big\}\,.
\end{equs}
We define $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]\subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ analogously. 

Moreover, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, let $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ be the ``fiber'' map $\big(F_{\underline{\tau}'}\in\mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}'} : \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\big) \mapsto F_{\underline{\tau}}$. 
Observe that $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ has a left inverse given by the ``section'' map $\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$ defined by setting
\[
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]\ni F_{\underline{\tau}}\mapsto\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}F_{\underline{\tau}}\eqdef\Big(\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|}
\sum_{f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')} \text{$\mathbf{f}$} F_{\underline{\tau}} : \underline{\tau}'\in\tau\Big)\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\,.
\] 
We use the same notation for the analogous maps between $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ and $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]$. 

Note that $|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|$ actually does not depend on the choice of $\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}'\in\tau$. In the sequel, we therefore just write $|\mathrm{Aut}(\tau)|\eqdef |\mathrm{Aut}(\underline{\tau})|$ for any $\underline{\tau}\in\tau$.

Finally, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$ we sometimes write $\iota_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ and $\pi_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ to lighten subscripts.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.841905+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_340f155e149dc07ae15cc0fd8ab20ad10eeb6a7fb6aa162572fd2de304523f54","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 2 of arXiv:2609.02173, 'Bounding Selmer Groups of Superelliptic Jacobians via Class Groups'] \begin{enumerate}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d","existence holds in case (a) d=2 with no hypothesis, case (b) F(0) < p_c, case (c) F(0) > p_c with E tau_e < infinity; case (d) F(0) = p_c with d > 2 is OPEN","F continuous is a SUFFICIENT condition for uniqueness","the statement is about FINITE geodesics only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3439799dcf869b96ef8603273809d352afd98579ca6a151dff8f1d66fd0af028","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d with weight law F. EXISTENCE of a finite geodesic between every pair of vertices, almost surely and simultaneously over all pairs, is known in each of the following cases, and the case division matters. (a) d = 2 and F ARBITRARY: Wierman and Reh proved that for any passage time distribution, with probability one there is a geodesic between any two points of Z^2. (b) Any d, with F(0) < p_c(d): existence follows from standard subcritical estimates. (c) Any d, with F(0) > p_c(d) and E[tau_e] < infinity: existence was proved by Zhang. (d) The remaining case F(0) = p_c(d) with d > 2 is STILL UNRESOLVED in general, though existence is known for distributions with F(0) = F(delta) = p_c for some delta > 0 in sufficiently high dimensions. So it is WRONG to say that geodesics need F(0) < p_c; that condition is sufficient and convenient, not necessary, and supercritical zero-weight percolation does not by itself destroy existence. UNIQUENESS is a separate matter: a continuous F is a SUFFICIENT condition for the model to be uniquely geodesic, since two distinct finite paths then have equal passage time with probability zero and there are countably many pairs of paths. With atoms - a two-valued weight law, say - ties are genuine and multiple geodesics occur with positive probability. All of the above is about FINITE geodesics; the existence, direction, uniqueness and coalescence of semi-infinite geodesics is a separate and largely open subject whose known results require differentiability or curvature assumptions on the limit shape. [Wierman and Reh (1978); Kesten, Aspects of First Passage Percolation, (9.23); Zhang; verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.844542+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_343f93727fc15914326f1ba88eeac6b98ee395a33c7c9486b4201a9d20a1a38e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:expectation-taylor of arXiv:2608.23742, 'Second-order fusion asymptotics for $\Sine_\beta$ correlation functions'] Let $d\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and put $D=d\gamma$. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact. Suppose that real random variables $X,Y,M$ satisfy, for some $p,q$,
\begin{equation}
p>\max\{2,D\},\qquad q>\max\{1,D\},\qquad
2q\left(1-\frac1p\right)>1,
\end{equation}
and $X\in L^p$, $Y,M\in L^q$. Suppose, uniformly for $b\in K$ and $1\le j\le d$,
\begin{equation}
U_j(t,b)=tb_jX+\frac{t^2b_j^2}{2}Y+R_j(t,b),
\qquad |R_j(t,b)|\le C_K|t|^3M.

\[

\]
one has, uniformly for $b\in K$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb E F(U(t,b))
&=1+\gamma tA(b)\mathbb E X\\
&\quad+\frac{t^2}{2}\left\{\gamma B(b)\mathbb E Y+
\left[\gamma(\gamma-1)B(b)+\gamma^2(A(b)^2-B(b))\right]\mathbb E X^2\right\}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:53:39.186005+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34485a2662d1f205b9f61a85c08d4cedd08be3cc70ce5a4ec3023715f1808cbf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Independentlemma 2 (Permutation Covariance Bound) of arXiv:2608.27020, 'Representation Measurements Under Function-Preserving Reparameterizations'] Define
\[
  V(S)
  =
  (\tr S)^2-\sum_{j=1}^d S_{jj}^2.
\]
Then, conditionally on \(X\),
\[
  \E_\pi\!\left[
    \left\lVert S^\pi-\diag(S)\right\rVert_\F^2
  \right]
  =
  \frac{V(S)}{n-1}.
\]
Consequently, for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\), with conditional probability at
least \(1-\delta\),
\[
  \left\lVert S^\pi-\diag(S)\right\rVert_\op
  \leq
  \varepsilon_\delta(S)
  :=
  \sqrt{\frac{V(S)}{(n-1)\delta}}.
\]
If \(s_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq s_{(d)}\) are the ordered diagonal entries of
\(S\), then simultaneously for all \(k\),
\[
  \left|\lambda_k(S^\pi)-s_{(k)}\right|
  \leq\varepsilon_\delta(S).
\]
For a real-valued random variable \(Y\), define the upper
\((1-\alpha)\)-quantile by
\[
  Q_{1-\alpha}(Y)=\inf\{y\in\R:\Prob(Y\leq y)\geq1-\alpha\}.
\]
Here \(y\) is a candidate real-valued threshold.
Then the ideal componentwise threshold
\(t_k(X)=Q_{1-\alpha}\{\lambda_k(S^\pi)\}\) satisfies
\[
  t_k(X)\leq s_{(k)}+\varepsilon_\alpha(S).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:33:43.759824+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3472fd236dc83d0eed23eedeeca7a44ca517b29fa69ffa200a45069897a480ef","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn cor:conditional-ldp of arXiv:2609.02682, 'LDP for tensor forms'] (Conditional LDP)

Assume $Q_n$ is a sequence of random symmetric zero-diagonal $v$-tensors.
We say that $ N_n(Q_n,\phi,{{\bf X}})$ satisfies a \emph{conditional LDP} with speed $n$ and a deterministic good rate function $J(\cdot):\mathbb{R} \to [0,\infty]$, if the level sets of $J(\cdot)$ are compact, and for any Borel set $F\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}_{Q_n} \Bigg(
 - \inf_{x \in F^\circ} J(x) - \varepsilon

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.224799+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34734caeb678d53cf2cefe7b4dce8f54bf8c110a25692773c82fd57e216b8bc7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Finite Gaussian orbit reconstruction and stability) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(d,m\geq1\).  For \(P,Q\in\cP_{d,m}\), the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \(Q=P\circ U\) for some \(U\in O(d)\);
\item for every \(r\leq r_*(d,m)\) and every \(\Sigma\in\cS_r\),
\[
  \Law\bigl(P(X_1),\ldots,P(X_r)\bigr)
  =
  \Law\bigl(Q(X_1),\ldots,Q(X_r)\bigr);
\]
\item \(\mathbf J_{d,m}(P)=\mathbf J_{d,m}(Q)\).
\end{enumerate}
Every matrix in \(\cS_r\) is rational and satisfies
\begin{equation}
  \frac12I_r\preceq\Sigma\preceq\frac32I_r,
  \qquad
  |\cS_r|=\binom{D_r+n_r}{n_r}.
  
\end{equation}
All Wick contractions are recovered from \(\mathbf J_{d,m}(P)\) by an
explicit rational finite-difference transform.  In particular the number of
scalar observations is
\begin{equation}
  N_{\mathrm{probe}}(d,m)
  =
  \sum_{r=1}^{r_*(d,m)}
  \binom{\lfloor rm/2\rfloor+r(r+1)/2}{r(r+1)/2}.
  
\end{equation}

Equip \(\cP_{d,m}\) with the invariant tensor norm \(\|\cdot\|_V\), and write
\[
  \delta_{\mathrm{orb}}(P,Q)
  =
  \min_{U\in O(d)}\|Q-P\circ U\|_V.
\]
If
\[
  A_{d,m}
  =
  r_*(d,m)\bigl(6r_*(d,m)-3\bigr)^{2N_{d,m}-1},
\]
then there is \(c_{d,m}>0\) such that
\[
  \|\mathbf J_{d,m}(P)-\mathbf J_{d,m}(Q)\|
  \geq
  c_{d,m}
  \left(
    \frac{\delta_{\mathrm{orb}}(P,Q)}
    {\sqrt2(1+\|P\|_V^2+\|Q\|_V^2)}
  \right)^{A_{d,m}}.
\]
Conversely, on every coefficient ball of radius \(R\), the map
\(\mathbf J_{d,m}\) is Lipschitz with respect to
\(\delta_{\mathrm{orb}}\).  Hence the probe metric and orbit metric are
bi-H\"older on coefficient balls. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.354793+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3476ca2b2d66e332b342e3b77d62e015071a36e4b7a149dab3b5a797c97a4393","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 216 (constraints on $(\bbb,\vvv,\uuu,\rrr,\www)^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For the coefficients defined by \eqref{e:b.plus.coarse}--\eqref{e:w.plus.coarse},
with high probability,
the following hold simultaneously for all $0\leq d\leq d_{\max}-1$:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item 
     
    The ``domain constraint'': for all 
    $B^{\frozen,\coarse} \in \mathcal{C}^\frozen(q_d)$,
    \beq
    \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse}) 
    \ge 
    q_d p'(q_d)
    \frac{\uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse})^2 }
    {\rrr^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse})}
    - \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,.
    \eeq
(If $\uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$ and $\rrr^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$ are both zero, we interpret the ratio on the right-hand side as zero.)
 \item
 
The ``budget constraint'' for the spherical perceptron:
    \beq
    
    \bE_{\bG^N}
    \bigg[ \Cost\Big(
        \bbb^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
            \uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)
        \Big) \bigg]
    \le \frac{1}{\alpha} 
    + \epsilon^\circ
 .
    \eeq
\item 
The ``budget constraint'' for the Ising perceptron:
    \beq
    
    \bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Cost\Big(
        \bbb^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)
        \Big) \bigg]
    \le \frac{\bE_{\bG^N}[
    \www^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)^{1/2}]^2}{\alpha} 
    + \epsilon^\circ\,.
    \eeq
\item  The ``diffusivity'' for the Ising perceptron:
    \[\Big|\bE(\www^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)) -1\Big|
    \le\epsilon^\circ\,.\]
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Assertions
\eqref{it:spherical-budget-constraint-plus-coarse}--\eqref{it:Ising-w-constraint-plus-coarse} follow straightforwardly from Jensen's inequality. For assertion \eqref{it:domain-constraint-plus-coarse}, note 
from \eqref{e:indicator.qd.less.than.qT},
 \eqref{e:def.r}, and \eqref{e:P.plus.hist}
that Proposition~\ref{p:budget-constraints-HIST}\ref{it:domain-constraint-plus-HIST} can be rewritten as
	\[
	\vvv^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen) 
    \ge  q_d p'(q_d) 
    I(B^\frozen)
	\frac{\uuu^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen)^2}
		{\rrr^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen)}
    - \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,,
	\]
where we again interpret a $0/0$ ratio as zero, and
	\[I(B^\frozen)\equiv \ind\bigg\{|B^\frozen \cap[M]| \ge 
		\frac{M}{\BUCKETS^2}
		\bigg\}\,.\]
If $I(B^\frozen)=0$ for all $B^\frozen\in B^{\frozen,\coarse}$,
then the bound \eqref{e:domain.plus.coarse} follows.
Otherwise, consider a discrete probability measure $\pi$, and random variables $v_j,u_j,r_j$ which are zero on a set of indices $Z$, and otherwise satisfy
	\[
	v_j \ge A' \frac{(u_j)^2}{r_j} - a'\]
Assume $\pi_+ \equiv 1-\pi(Z)\in(0,1]$. Then Jensen's inequality gives
	\[
	\frac{\sum_j \pi_j v_j}{\pi_+}
	\ge \frac{1}{\pi_+}
	\sum_{j\notin Z} \pi_j \bigg\{
	A' \frac{(u_j)^2}{r_j} - a'\bigg\}
	\ge A'
	\bigg(\frac{1}{\pi_+}\sum_j \pi_j u_j\bigg)^2\bigg/
	\bigg(
	\frac{1}{\pi_+}\sum_j \pi_j r_j
	\bigg) - a'
	\]
and rearranging gives
	\[
	\sum_j \pi_j v_j
	\ge
	A' \bigg(\sum_j \pi_j u_j\bigg)^2\bigg/
	\bigg(\sum_j \pi_j r_j
	\bigg)
	-a'\pi_+\,.
	\]
If we apply the above inequality with the probability measure $\pi$
over buckets $B^\frozen\in B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ with probabilities 
$\pi(B^\frozen)=|B^\frozen|/|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|$, then we obtain the desired conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment","existence of kappa in (0,2) solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for the environment's local odds ratio rho","transience of the walk, or the appropriate directional condition for the regime under study","technical non-lattice or non-degeneracy conditions on the environment law needed for the stable-law convergence"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.989782+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34a6da748207f4cd112326dff5e5e3f10da84d0a5a8d231a18afecb144c6023f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For one-dimensional nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment in the subballistic or intermediate regime, parametrized by an index kappa solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for rho the local odds ratio of the environment, hitting times of successive integers admit a classical Kesten construction as a branching process with migration: individuals reproduce according to an environment-dependent offspring law with an added immigration/emigration term reflecting the local environment. The Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer theorem shows that for kappa in the relevant range below 2, the hitting time of level n, normalized by n^{1/kappa}, converges to a kappa-stable distribution, via a result on the total population size of the associated branching-with-migration process, which itself has heavy-tailed, stable-scaling behavior. This gives the precise non-Gaussian scaling limits characterizing anomalous, subdiffusive or index-dependent, behavior in one-dimensional random walk in random environment, a phenomenon absent for simple random walk. It does not extend to higher dimensions, since the explicit branching correspondence is a genuinely one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor phenomenon, and it requires the environment to be i.i.d. with a moment condition admitting a solution kappa in the relevant range. Typical failure: Extending the branching-process-with-migration correspondence and its kappa-stable scaling conclusion to multi-dimensional random walk in random environment, or to environments with dependence rather than i.i.d. structure, where no analogous exact combinatorial bijection to a branching process is known; the Kesten construction is a special, essentially exact identity in one dimension that does not generalize by analogy, so claiming kappa-stable scaling outside the one-dimensional i.i.d. setting requires an entirely separate justification. Canonical reference: Kesten, Kozlov and Spitzer, 1975, Compositio Mathematica.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.739477+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34ad0b6f229f363697d39411a6dc1dd9f205630117f36490130de6ce3b0ebccd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\textbf{Regularized geometric Jensen-Shannon divergence between Gaussian measures on Hilbert space}]
		
		Let
		$\mu_i = \Ncal(m_i, C_i) \in \Gauss(\Hcal)$, $i=0,1$. Let $\gamma>0, \gamma \in \R$ be fixed. Let $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$ be fixed. Let $C_{\alpha,\gamma}$, $m_{\alpha,\gamma}$ be as defined in Eqs.\eqref{equation:C-alpha-gamma},
		\eqref{equation:m-alpha-gamma}, respectively.
		The regularized geometric Jensen-Shannon divergence between $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$ is defined to be
		\begin{align}
			&\JS_{G_{\alpha}}^{\gamma}(\mu_0||\mu_1) = 
			\frac{1-\alpha}{2}||C_{\alpha, \gamma}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{\alpha,\gamma})||^2 + \frac{\alpha}{2}||C_{\alpha, \gamma}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{\alpha,\gamma})||^2 
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad +\frac{(1-\alpha)}{2}d^1_{\logdet}[(C_0+\gamma I), C_{\alpha,\gamma}]
			
			
			
			+ \frac{\alpha}{2} d^1_{\logdet}[(C_1+\gamma I), C_{\alpha,\gamma}].
		\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.718634+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34cae7d05f40ab5f2257cb8f4278c2117e6ef4f4496d8e64353f3b697f82b6ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 9 of arXiv:2609.01166, 'Nonparametric inference for density-dependent McKean--Vlasov diffusions'] The rates above can be transferred to the case of finite-time observations, provided that exponential ergodicity holds.

for some \(t_0\geq0\), \(C_{t_0}<\infty\), and \(\rho_\chi>0\), where \(P_t\) and \(\Pi_0\) denote the laws with densities \(p_t\) and \(\pi_0\), respectively. \(

as \(n\to\infty\).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.775897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34dfbe58442731bd1b6183dfdee12b6f2b3292dc0945a7f7bf522ad1af25743a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:gamma-regime-square-expectation-estimate of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Fix parameters $a,\beta$ satisfying $0\leqslant a \leqslant1$ and $0\leqslant\beta<\frac12$, and set
\[
