{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.745645+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42352eb696e723345f53c9e6e74355d5c558605754e55d79a26eaa7fcd004eab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 10 (The configuration process) of arXiv:2605.02499, '2605.02499'] Let $\gs_0\subseteq[N]$ and fix a root-type configuration $S\in\varSigma_{\gs_0}^R$. The \emph{configuration process}, denoted by
$(\Theta_t(S))_{t\geq 0}$, is constructed on the basis of the transitions of $(\As_{[0,t]}(\gs_0))_{t\geq 0}$ as follows.
The process starts at
$\Theta_0(S)= S$. Suppose that at some time the state of the process is the finite collection of cylinders
$\{C^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^r$ for some $r>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item At the times of a coalescence or a relocation event $\coal{\alpha}{\beta}$, every cylinder $C^{(i)}$, $i \in [r]$, performs the transition $$C^{(i)}\mapsto\ocoal{\alpha}{\beta}(C^{(i)}),$$
and the new state of the process is the collection $\{\ocoal{\alpha}{\beta}(C^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^r$.
\item At the times of a deleterious mutation $\timesa$, every cylinder $C^{(i)}$, $i \in [r]$, performs the transition $$C^{(i)}\mapsto\omutr{\alpha}(C^{(i)}),$$
and the new state of the process is the collection$\{ \omutr{\alpha}(C^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^r$. 
\item At the times of a beneficial mutation $\circa$, every cylinder $C^{(i)}$, $i \in [r]$, performs the transition $$C^{(i)}\mapsto \omutb{\alpha}(C^{(i)}),$$
and the new state of the process is the collection $\{\omutb{\alpha}(C^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^r$. 
\item At the times of an FTW event $\ftw{\alpha}{\Bs}$, every cylinder $C^{(i)}$, $i \in [r]$, performs the transition $$C^{(i)}\mapsto\oftw{\alpha}{\Bs}(C^{(i)}),$$
and the new state of the process is the collection $ \bigcup_{i=1 }^r \oftw{\alpha}{\Bs}(C^{(i)})$.
\item At the times of an interactive neutral event $\ine{\alpha}{\beta}{\gamma}$, every cylinder $C^{(i)}$, $i \in [r]$, performs the transition
$$C^{(i)}\mapsto\onint{\alpha}{\beta}{\gamma}(C^{(i)}),$$
and the new state of the process is the collection $\bigcup_{i=1 }^r  \onint{\alpha}{\beta}{\gamma}(C^{(i)})$.
\end{enumerate}
By construction, we have
\begin{equation}
\Ss\big(\As_{[0,t]}(\gs_0), S\big)=\bigcup_{C\in\Theta_t(S)} C.    
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.079769+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4235502eee9a4e05908589f233f495c60ea4970f1f57481b5fe9c9f7821eb580","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2608.27880, 'Precise universal edge asymptotics for planar $\beta=2$ Coulomb gases with radial external'] Under the same assumptions as Theorem \ref{main}, we have the following asymptotic equivalences, classified according to the deviation scale.

(1) Large deviations (fixed displacement). For any fixed $t>t_0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl( \max_{1\le i\le n}\Re \sigma_i \ge t \bigr)
\sim
\frac{\sqrt{\alpha }\, t^2\, t_0 \exp(-nV(t)+nV(t_0))}{2\pi n(t^2-t_0^2) (tV'(t)-2)^{3/2}}
(\frac{t}{t_0})^{2n}.
\]

(2) Critical Gumbel scale and its refined correction.

(a) Pure Gumbel scale (fixed $t>1$):
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl( \max_{1\le i\le n}\Re \sigma_i \ge t_0+\frac{t\sqrt{\gamma_n}}{\sqrt{\alpha n}} \bigr)
\sim
t^{-5/2}(\frac{8\pi^4 (\log n)^5}{\alpha n t_0^2 })^{\frac{t^2-1}{4}}.
\]

(b) Fine correction beyond the Gumbel scale ($1\ll v_n\ll \log n$):
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl( \max_{1\le i\le n}\Re \sigma_i \ge t_0+\frac{\sqrt{\gamma_n}}{\sqrt{\alpha n}}+\frac{v_n}{\sqrt{\alpha n \gamma_n}} \bigr)
\sim
\exp\bigl(-v_n-\frac{v_n^2}{2\gamma_n}\bigr).
\]

(3) Moderate deviations on scale $d_n$. Given $d_n>0$:

\[\aligned
&\quad\mathbb{P}\bigl(\max_{1\le i\le n}\Re\sigma_i \ge t_0 + d_n \bigr)\\
&
\sim
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{t_0}}{4\pi \alpha n d_n^{5/2}}
\exp(-\frac{\alpha  n d_n^2}{2}), & \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{n}} \ll d_n \ll n^{-\frac13},\\[1.2em]
\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{t_0} \exp(-nV(t_0+d_n)+nV(t_0))}{4\pi \alpha n d_n^{5/2}}
(\frac{t_0+ d_n}{t_0})^{2n}, & n^{-\frac13}\lesssim d_n\ll 1.
\end{cases}
\endaligned\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.959154+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4240a05f2ac937ca3b8e24871530fc01f1137b374f00302be45ec317c1ea3d45","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 9 (Poisson-type concentration of roots) of arXiv:2607.13210, 'Punctured Wilson--Evolving Sets and Root Identities for Massive Kirchhoff Forests'] For $U\subset V$, let $\mu_q(U):=\sum_{x\in U}\beta_q(x).$\\
For every family $(s_x)_{x\in U}$ of non-negative numbers, we have:
\begin{equation*}
  \Ee\left[
    \prod_{x\in U}\left(1+s_x\1_{\{x\in\Root\}}\right)
  \right]
  \leq
  \prod_{x\in U}(1+s_x\beta_q(x)).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, for every $\theta\geq0$, it results:
\begin{equation}
  \Ee[e^{\theta N_q(U)}]
  \leq
  \prod_{x\in U}\left(1+\beta_q(x)(e^\theta-1)\right)
  \leq
  \exp\left(\mu_q(U)(e^\theta-1)\right).
\end{equation}
For every $\delta>0$, one finds:
\begin{equation}
  \Pp\left(N_q(U)\geq(1+\delta)\mu_q(U)\right)
  \leq
  \exp\left[-\mu_q(U)
  \bigl((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta\bigr)\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover, one gets:
\begin{equation*}
  \Ee[(N_q(U))_k]
  \leq
  k!\,e_k\bigl((\beta_q(x))_{x\in U}\bigr)
  \leq\mu_q(U)^k.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T15:38:23.784925+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_424daabf6bab4c23b100ce5671977a4d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]\n\nFor every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:01:25.576418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42844e2127eaff14eec2df578472d058508327053c018dff28bcc5d99e2ec4d6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:erase_two_sided of arXiv:2605.16086, 'Loop pruning and downward deviations for maximum local time of discrete-time simple random'] Let \(E\) be a finite set of loops and let \(\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}(-\infty,\infty)\) be a two-sided path. 
Suppose that the set of indices \(i\in\mathbb Z\) for which \((\mathbf{s}_{i-1},\mathbf{s}_i)\) is an \(E\)-cut step is unbounded both above and below.

We say that a step \((\mathbf{s}_{i-1},\mathbf{s}_i)\) is retained in the pruning of \(\mathbf{s}\) by \(E\) if there exist indices \(m_1< i\le m_2\) such that both boundary steps \((\mathbf{s}_{m_1-1},\mathbf{s}_{m_1})\) and \((\mathbf{s}_{m_2-1},\mathbf{s}_{m_2})\) are \(E\)-cut steps, and \((\mathbf{s}_{i-1},\mathbf{s}_i)\) is retained in the finite-window pruning
\[
\mathsf{Prune}\big(\mathbf{s}[m_1,m_2],E\big).
\]
(It is straightforward to check that this notion does not depend on the particular choice of \(m_1,m_2\).)

Collecting all retained steps in chronological order yields a two-sided path (defined up to translation), which we denote by \(\mathsf{Prune}(\mathbf{s},E)\).","status":"unverified"}

Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:55:18.952198+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d674ff5e4aefc9091a3202fb07bce94a88314a20a13a94b9d080df712106c3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Discrete connection on a graph of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] A \emph{discrete connection} on $\mathbb{G}$ is a map
\[
g : \mathbb{E}_+ \cup \mathbb{E}_- \longrightarrow G
\]
such that for every $e \in \mathbb{E}_+$ we have
\[
g(e_+) = g(e_-)^{-1}.
\]
For an edge $e\in \mathbb{E}_+\cup \mathbb{E}_-$, we denote by $i(e)$ and $f(e)$ the vertices such that $e=(i(e),f(e))$. A path in $\mathbb{G}$ is a sequence of edges  $a_1,\dots,a_n$ such that $f(a_k)=i(a_{k+1})$ for all $k=1,\dots,n-1$. If $c = a_1 \cdots a_n$ is a path in $\mathbb{G}$, given as a concatenation of oriented edges $a_i \in \mathbb{E}_+ \cup \mathbb{E}_-$, we define the \emph{holonomy} of $g$ along $c$ by
\[
\mathrm{Hol}(g,c) \coloneqq g(a_1)\cdots g(a_n) \in G.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:23:37.815538+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d869bc98cb9f208052e0350c480289da6e27a0d7ddfbbe9fac30ca8037ffc7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2609.03634, 'Joint Laws of Maximum Drawdown and Maximum Drawup for Spectrally Negative L\'{e}vy Process'] Consider a spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process $X$ with $q$-scale functions $W^{(q)}$ and $Z^{(q)}$. Let $a<0$, $b>0$, $x\in[0,b]$, and $q\geq0$. Then, for $v>0$,
\[
\mathbb E_x\left[e^{-q\tau_a^-};\,M_{\tau_a^-}^{+}\leq v,\ S_{\tau_a^-}\leq b\right]
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
e^{-\left((x-a)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right)},
& 0<v\leq b-x,\\[1.3em]
\displaystyle
e^{-\left((b-a-v)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right)}

\]
In particular,
\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:50:44.862390+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4322a7676f42307da91bd8eb40f8dc519a7107a109f33f24bff35d2cd9fef3b4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 13 (Boundary variance trend for a powered Choquet integral) of arXiv:2607.16502, 'Asymptotic Behavior of Path Functionals for Vector-Valued Gaussian Processes at High Level'] For the process \eqref{eq:nonstationary-model-example} and the functional
\eqref{eq:choquet-excess-example}, the following asymptotics hold as
\(u\to\infty\).  The constants in
\eqref{def:H-choquet-nonstationary-example} and
\eqref{def:P-choquet-nonstationary-example} exist, are finite and positive in
the regimes in which they are used.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item If \(\alpha<\beta\), then
  \begin{equation}
    
    \pk{ C_T^{(\theta)}(u)>L u^{-2\theta/\alpha} }
    \sim
    \mathcal H_{\alpha,c,b}^{\mathrm{Ch},\theta}(L)\,
    \Gamma(1/\beta+1)\,(ab^2)^{-1/\beta}\,
    u^{2/\alpha-2/\beta-1}\,
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-b^2u^2/2}.
  \end{equation}
  \item If \(\alpha=\beta\), then
  \begin{equation}
    
    \pk{ C_T^{(\theta)}(u)>L u^{-2\theta/\beta} }
    \sim
    \mathcal P_{\alpha,a,c,b}^{\mathrm{Ch},\theta}(L)\,
    u^{-1}\,
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-b^2u^2/2}.
  \end{equation}
  \item If \(\alpha>\beta\), then the Gaussian local fluctuation no longer
  appears in the leading constant and
  \begin{equation}
    
    \pk{ C_T^{(\theta)}(u)>L u^{-2\theta/\beta} }
    \sim
    \frac{1}{b}e^{-b\ell_{L,\theta}}\,
    u^{-1}\,
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-b^2u^2/2}.
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Let
\[
  \mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)
  =
  \inf\left\{0<t\le T:
  \Gamma_{[0,t]}^{\mathrm{Ch},\theta}\bigl(u(X-u b)\bigr)>L_u

where \(L_u=L u^{-2\theta/\alpha}\) in the case \(\alpha<\beta\) and

\begin{equation}
  
  \pk{

\end{equation}
If \(\alpha>\beta\), define, for \(S>0\), the unique number
\(y_{S,\theta}>0\) by
\begin{equation}
  
  \int_0^\infty
  \mes\{t\in[0,S]:y_{S,\theta}-ab t^\beta>r\}^\theta\,dr=L .
\end{equation}
Then, for every \(S>0\),
\begin{equation}
  
  \pk{
    u^{2/\beta}\mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)\le S
    \,\middle|\,
    \mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)\le T
  }
  \to
  \exp\{-b(y_{S,\theta}-\ell_{L,\theta})\}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.715852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_432964e9d68a322cbbc9b974a7e15b531a73af7e5e8ccf15a7efc49f9df9a079","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition p:preserve of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] The following operations preserve real stability and (strong/complete) log-concavity.\footnote{(s/c) log-concave is to be read as strongly log-concave or completely log-concave or log-concave, respectively.}
    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=0.1em]
        \item Product: If $p,q$ are real stable (respectively, log-concave) then $p\cdot q$ is real stable (log-concave).
        \item Symmetrization: If $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real stable ((s/c) log-concave), then $p(z_1,z_1,z_3,\ldots, z_n)$ is real-stable ((s/c) log-concave).
        \item 
        Specialization: If $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real stable ((s/c) log-concave), then $p(a,z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real-stable ((s/c) log-concave) for $a\in \mathbb R$ ($a\geqslant 0$).
        \item External field: If $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real stable ((s/c) log-concave), then so is $q(z_1,\ldots, z_n) = p(w_1 z_1,\ldots, w_n z_n)$ for any $w_1,\ldots, w_n\geqslant 0$.
        \item Differentiation: If $p$ is real stable or strongly or completely log-concave, then so is $\partial_{i} p$. 
        \item Homogenization: If $p$ is real stable, then $p^{\mathrm{hom}}(z_1,\ldots, z_{n+1}) = z_{n+1}^{\deg p}p\pa{\fc{z_1}{z_{n+1}},\cdots, \fc{z_n}{z_{n+1}}}$ is real stable. 
        
        \item Polarization ([anari2024trickle], [branden2020lorentzian]): Suppose $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb N_0^n} c_\alpha z^\alpha$ is homogeneous and strongly log-concave with degree at most $\kappa_i$ in $z_i$. Then so is its polarization with degree $\kappa$, $\operatorname{polar}_\kappa(p)$, defined by 
        \[
        \operatorname{polar}_\kappa(p) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb N_0^n} c_\alpha \prodo in \rc{\binom{\kappa_i}{\alpha_i}} e_{\alpha_i}(z_{i1},\ldots, z_{i\kappa_i})
        \]
        as a polynomial in $z_{ij}$, $i\in [n]$, $j\in [\kappa_i]$, where $e_k(y_1,\ldots, y_n) = \sum_{S\in \slice{n}{k}} y^S$ is the $k$th elementary symmetric polynomial.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:25:35.765952+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4331c5d2ae19d69ddef45ca5804523c3d05087cec0278bc478af69fa7301563d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def.balanced of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in (0,1]^n$. A standard extremal sequence $(X_i)$ for $(\alpha_i)$ will be
    called 
    
    \emph{balanced}
    
    if each index $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ 
    can be mapped 
    
    bijectively to
    $j_i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ 
    so that $X_{j_i} \sim - X_i$.

    We call $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in (0,1]^n$ \emph{balanced} if
    a balanced standard extremal sequence exists for $(\alpha_i)$, equivalently, if for each $\alpha \in (0,1]$ either $\alpha^{-1}$ is an odd integer or $|\{i: \alpha_i=\alpha\}|$ is even.     We denote this probability by ${t_{SE}^{bal}}(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:54.999702+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_434e75f1a97b0c35a552126b687d9dabbad8d880bf133cfc1fefe1287a0888af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:extrinsic-persistency of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {bozic_models_1984}}] 
  Let $\mathfrak{F} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset)$ be an f-frame. Then:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item $\mathfrak{F} \in \FrameClass{\Box\text{-p}}$ iff $\Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M}$ is $\Box$-persistent for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.
    \item $\mathfrak{F} \in \FrameClass{\Diamond\text{-p}}$ iff $\Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M}$ is $\Diamond$-persistent for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  \begin{proof}
    (1 $\Rightarrow$) Take any $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ and $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\Box$, then use an induction on the construction of $\varphi$.
    Consider the case when $\varphi = \Box \psi$. Take any $x, x'$ such that $x \leq x'$ and $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \psi$.
    Take any $y'$ such that $x' \sqsubset y'$, then by the $\Box$-p condition, there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \leq y'$.
    Here, $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \psi$ implies $y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$,
    and the induction hypothesis implies $y' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$.
    Therefore, $x' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \psi$.

    (1 $\Leftarrow$)  Suppose that $\mathfrak{F} \notin \FrameClass{\Box\text{-p}}$, then there are $x, x', y'$ such that $x \leq x' \sqsubset y'$ but no $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \leq y'$.
    Take a fresh variable $p^\ast \in \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$, then we construct a countermodel $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ by letting $w \in V(p) \mathrel{\ratio\Leftrightarrow} (p \ne p^\ast \mathrel{\text{or}} \exists v\,(x \sqsubset v \leq w))$.
    Here, each $V(p)$ is upward closed with respect to $\leq$.
    Then, $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box p^\ast$ by $\forall z \sqsupset x\,(z \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast)$, and $x' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box p^\ast$ by $y' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast$.

    (2 $\Rightarrow$) Take any $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ and $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\Diamond$, then use an induction on the construction of $\varphi$.
    Consider the case when $\varphi = \Diamond \psi$. Take any $x, x'$ such that $x \leq x'$ and $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \psi$,
    then there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$.
    Now that $x' \geq x \sqsubset y$, then by the $\Diamond$-p condition, there is $y'$ such that $x' \sqsubset y' \geq y$.
    Here, $y \leq y'$ implies $y' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$ by the induction hypothesis.
    This and $x' \sqsubset y'$ imply $x' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \psi$.

    (2 $\Leftarrow$)  Suppose that $\mathfrak{F} \notin \FrameClass{\Diamond\text{-p}}$, then there are $x, x', y$ such that $x' \geq x \sqsubset y$ but no $y'$ such that $x' \sqsubset y' \geq y$.
    Take a fresh variable $p^\ast \in \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$, then we construct a countermodel $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ by letting $w \in V(p) \mathrel{\ratio\Leftrightarrow} (p \ne p^\ast \mathrel{\text{or}} w \geq y)$.
    Here, each $V(p)$ is upward closed with respect to $\leq$.
    Then, $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond p^\ast$ by $y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast$, and $x' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond p^\ast$ by $\forall z' \sqsupset x'\,(z' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast)$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Equipping the Cantor space with two standard metrics, we show that under both, a typical martingale diverges at a typical point. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.478361+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43624cfb0d0aeb543c3ad7cc9de650d2b3c963cb430da22556eb9c96f8ca470d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:moment-problems of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Building on Definition~(def:moment-constraints of the paper), we assume that $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ 
and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ are measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-algebra 
$\mathcal{F}$. We define the linear optimization problems
\begin{align}

g_\mathrm{fin}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G_\mathrm{fin}(C) \},\\

g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) \}
\end{align}
on the spaces $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ of finitely atomic measures. If $f$ is 
bounded below by a real constant, then we also define
\begin{align}

g(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G(C) \},\\

g_\mathrm{ext}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in \ext G(C) \}.
\end{align}
The optimization problem $g(\mathbf{q})$ in (equation eq:PM of the paper) at a specific point $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ 
is an example of the problem of moments [shapiro01]. This problem is also known 
as the generalized moment problem if $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{B}(X)$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on a Borel 
[lasserre10], closed [henrion-etal20], or compact [klerk-laurent19] set 
$X$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$. Loosely speaking, we refer to each of 
(equation eq:PM-atomic of the paper)--(equation eq:PM-ext of the paper) as a \emph{generalized moment problem}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.643087+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43642bc6c97fa91517e6d43355abe203afdd42e9710168b5c4cb642c6ac2a30a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 20 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(g\) be the right-continuous inverse of the function

where the family

\]
on \(D([0,\infty),\bR^{I_0})\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. rows C^{1/2} z with z having i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries and finite twelfth moment","p/n -> q_0 in (0, infinity)","the population spectral distribution converges to a limit with bounded support","the formula is used inside the bulk; isolated spikes are handled by the BBP correction"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_4371e12019521ab578f7c0a985513fd3b35fa6f43b024c62adc7360470e48a4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E = \\frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = p/n \\to q_0 \\in (0, \\infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \\frac{1}{p}\\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, and $g(z) = \\int (z - x)^{-1} F(dx)$ that of its almost-sure limit $F$, the limiting sample spectral distribution, with $g(\\lambda - i0) := \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} g(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ inside the bulk (the finite-sample $g_E(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ has no useful limit as $\\eta \\downarrow 0$: it diverges at each sample eigenvalue and is real between them). THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, as the weighted measure $\\frac{1}{p}\\sum_k \\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\delta_{\\lambda_k}$, converge almost surely to $\\xi(\\lambda) F(d\\lambda)$ on $(0, \\infty)$, where $$\\xi(\\lambda) = \\frac{\\lambda}{\\big|\\, 1 - q_0 + q_0\\, \\lambda\\, g(\\lambda - i0) \\,\\big|^2};$$ informally $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\approx \\xi(\\lambda_k)$ for sample eigenvalues inside the bulk (the theorem is about the weighted measure, not a limit for each $k$). This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\\xi(\\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\\lambda_k - i\\eta$ with a small $\\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \\sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.696829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43becc0a32d69c9f1d7e52351c81e29884b19599f45ba56ca7e68640d333c371","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition p:EC-equiv of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] {anari2024trickle}}]

    Suppose $\mu$ is a probability measure on $\Omega$ and $P$ is a Markov kernel from $\Omega$ to $\Omega'$. 
    If $\nu\ll \mu$, then 
    \[
\operatorname{KL}(\nu\|\mu) - \operatorname{KL}(\nu P \|\mu P) 
= \mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}_{Y \sim \mu P} \ba{\mathop{{}\boldsymbol{\mathrm{Ent}}}_{X\sim (P_\mu^*)(Y,\cdot)}\ba{\dd{\nu}{\mu}(X)}}.
    \]
    Hence, $P$ satisfies $(1-\rho)$-entropy contraction with respect to $\mu$ iff for all non-negative functions $f$ on $\Omega$,
    \[
\mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}_{Y \sim \mu P} \ba{\mathop{{}\boldsymbol{\mathrm{Ent}}}_{X\sim (P_\mu^*)(Y,\cdot)}[f(X)]}
\geqslant \rho \cdot \mathop{{}\boldsymbol{\mathrm{Ent}}}_\mu[f].
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:43:04.632618+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43dcd6495c9ac91520285f9a66adc2d4d28ab8c68f62ee2cbe9f88deb694373c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2605.17155, '2605.17155'] Let \(B\) be a Banach space and let \(f:\Nzero\to B\).  

\begin{enumerate}
\item A positive integer \(\tau\) is a
\emph{Bohr \(\varepsilon\)-translation number}, or simply an \emph{\(\varepsilon\)-translation number} of \(f\), if
\[
   \sup_{n\ge0}\norm{f(n+\tau)-f(n)}<\varepsilon .
\]
The sequence \(f\) is \emph{(Bohr) almost periodic}, if for every
\(\varepsilon>0\), the set of Bohr \(\varepsilon\)-translation numbers is
relatively dense.

\item The sequence \(f:\Nzero\to B\) is \emph{limit periodic} if
it is a uniform limit of periodic sequences, equivalently if for
every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a periodic sequence \(g:\Nzero\to B\) such
that
\[
   \sup_{n\ge0}\norm{f(n)-g(n)}<\varepsilon .
\]

\item The sequence \(f:\Nzero\to B\) is
\emph{asymptotically almost periodic} if
\[
   f(n)=g(n)+c(n),\qquad n\ge0,
\]
where \(g:\Nzero\to B\) is almost periodic and \(c(n)\to0\) in \(B\).

\item For \(q\ge1\), define the \emph{Weyl \(q\)-seminorm} of a sequence
\(u:\Nzero\to B\) by
\[
   \norm{u}_{W^q}
   :=
   \limsup_{L\to\infty}\sup_{N\ge0}
   \left(\frac1L\sum_{n=N}^{N+L-1}\norm{u(n)}^q\right)^{1/q}.
\]
A positive integer \(\tau\) is a
\emph{Weyl \(q\)-\(\varepsilon\)-translation number} of \(f\) if
\[
   \norm{\,f(\cdot+\tau)-f(\cdot)\,}_{W^q}<\varepsilon .
\]
The sequence \(f\) is \emph{Weyl \(q\)-almost periodic} if, for every
\(\varepsilon>0\), the set of Weyl \(q\)-\(\varepsilon\)-translation numbers is
relatively dense.

\item For \(q\ge1\), define the \emph{Besicovitch \(q\)-seminorm} by
\[
   \norm{u}_{B^q}
   :=
   \limsup_{L\to\infty}
   \left(\frac1L\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}\norm{u(n)}^q\right)^{1/q}.
\]
A positive integer \(\tau\) is a
\emph{Besicovitch \(q\)-\(\varepsilon\)-translation number} of \(f\) if
\[
   \norm{\,f(\cdot+\tau)-f(\cdot)\,}_{B^q}<\varepsilon .
\]
The sequence \(f\) is \emph{Besicovitch \(q\)-almost periodic} if, for every
\(\varepsilon>0\), the set of Besicovitch \(q\)-\(\varepsilon\)-translation
numbers is relatively dense.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.719208+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43f88b09656b274b445cfb9d461f7ab1be075373b26a80784e79d5679ec9f1d3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:ik-nnbox-to-boxnn of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] For every $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$,
  $\textbf{IK} \vdash \neg \neg \Box \varphi \to \Box \neg \neg \varphi$.
  \begin{proof}
    By completeness, it suffices to prove validity in every IK-model.
    Let $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$ be an IK-model,
    and fix $x_0 \in W$ such that $x_0 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Box \varphi$.
    To prove $x_0 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \neg \neg \varphi$,
    fix $x_1, y_0 \in W$ such that $x_0 \leq x_1$ and $x_1 \sqsubset y_0$.
    We show that $y_0 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \varphi$.

    Fix any $y_1 \in W$ such that $y_0 \leq y_1$.
    By FS2 applied to $x_1 \sqsubset y_0$ and $y_0 \leq y_1$,
    there is $x_2 \in W$ such that $x_1 \leq x_2$ and $x_2 \sqsubset y_1$.
    By persistency, $x_2 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Box \varphi$.
    By the $\leq$-reflexivity of $x_2$ and the fact that no world forces $\bot$,
    it follows that
    $x_2 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \Box \varphi$.
    Hence there is $x_3 \in W$ such that $x_2 \leq x_3$ and
    $x_3 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \varphi$.

    By the $\Diamond$-p condition applied to $x_2 \sqsubset y_1$ and $x_2 \leq x_3$,
    there is $y_2 \in W$ such that $x_3 \sqsubset y_2$ and $y_1 \leq y_2$.
    By the $\leq$-reflexivity of $x_3$ and the forcing clause for $\Box$,
    we have $y_2 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$.
    Therefore, $y_1 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \varphi$.
    Since $y_1$ was arbitrary, $y_0 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \varphi$.
    Since $x_1$ and $y_0$ were arbitrary,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:02:28.646940+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43fa0399ee5d9bc4e0fedc8166f9f52788571929a0934fc357214c494b3bde2c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Def 26 of arXiv:2609.01389, 'K-stability and birational rigidity of Fano 3-fold weighted complete intersections'] Let $X$ be a $\mbQ$-Fano variety of dimension $n$.
For a prime divisor $E$ over $X$, we define
\[
S_X (E) \coloneq \frac{1}{(-K_X)^n} \int_0^{\infty} \vol (-f^*K_X - t E) d t,
\]
where $f \colon \tilde{X} \to X$ is a projective birational morphism such that $E$ is a prime divisor on $\tilde{X}$, and
\[
\delta_X (E) \coloneq \frac{A_X (E)}{S_X (E)},
\] 
where $A_X (E)$ is the log discrepancy of $X$ at $E$.
The \textit{global delta invariant} of $X$ is defined as
\[
\delta (X) \coloneq \inf \Set{ \delta_X (E) | \text{$E$ is a prime divisor over $X$}}.
\]
For a closed point $\msp \in X$, the \textit{local delta invariant} of $X$ at $\msp$ is defined as
\[
\delta_{\msp} (X) \coloneq \inf \Set{ \delta_X (E) | \text{$E$ is a prime divisor over $X$ such that $\msp \in C_X (E)$}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:57:07.301416+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_441a897f603a059b42aa79285dc9e441fe3aab7e983c6c57893a61446e90bc87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2606.23896, 'The one-point Schreier Poisson boundary of Thompson's group \(F\)'] Let \((X_n)\) be a Markov chain on a countable state space

\[

\]

and, for \(k\ge 0\),

\[

The trace chain on \(A\) is

\[

\]

with transition kernel

\[

\]

Then restriction gives an isometric order-isomorphism

\[

\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911755+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_44346e151009d85ee2b6ef52041da819cd6f25e04627d15b65a60bf4ba58a87a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"When one ensemble of $M$ members predicts $D$ output coordinates (spectral bands, pixels, reduced coefficients) and a separate affine stack is fitted per output, the $D$ least-squares weight vectors form a matrix $\\hat W \\in \\mathbb{R}^{D \\times (M+1)}$ with $\\hat W = W + Z$: row $d$ of the noise $Z$ has covariance $\\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$, $X_d$ the calibration design of output $d$ and $\\sigma_d^2$ its residual variance, while the true $W$ has low effective rank whenever the optimal weighting varies smoothly across outputs (neighbouring bands weight the same members similarly). The relevant random-matrix ratio is then $\\beta = (M+1)/D$ - not $M/n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ - and the problem is low-rank matrix denoising: after scaling row $d$ by $1/\\sigma_d$ (and, when the designs $X_d$ are nearly common across outputs, right-whitening by $\\bar G^{1/2}\\sqrt{n}$ with $\\bar G$ the average of $X_d^T X_d / n$), the Gavish-Donoho optimal singular-value shrinkage selects the rank as the number of singular values above the Marchenko-Pastur edge $1 + \\sqrt\\beta$ and debiases each retained singular value, with no cross-validation. Shrinking every row toward one global weight vector by a cross-validated scalar - the best heuristic found on the EMIT/OCO-2 pools, beating per-output least squares on 69 of 70 cells by 3.1 percent - is the rank-one special case of this estimator with the direction fixed and the amount tuned by hand. For EMIT ($M = 23$, $D = 285$) $\\beta = 0.084$; for OCO-2 ($M = 18$, $D = 40$) $\\beta = 0.475$, a wide bulk in which only strong structure clears the edge.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:28:34.901789+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_443d204d79e3b31e64417d251c30df7d95d32e0c27cf9c3a50f3e0d20301b299","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def.scvec of arXiv:2412.05698, 'Controlled rough SDEs, pathwise stochastic control and dynamic programming principles'] {FHL21}}]
   Let $\beta, \beta' \in (0,1]$ and $\gamma >1$ be some fixed parameters.
   We call $(f,f')$ {\em stochastic controlled vector field on \( \mathbb{R}^d \)} and write \( (f,f')\in \ensuremath{{\mathbf D}}^{\beta,\beta'}_XL_{p,q}{\mathcal{C}}^\gamma_{b}\)
   if the following conditions are satisfied.

   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
      \item
      The pair
      \[
      (f,f')\colon\Omega \times  [0,T] \to {\mathcal{C}}^\gamma_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{d}; \mathbb{R}^m) \times {\mathcal{C}}^{\gamma-1}_{b} (\mathbb{R}^d ; \mathrm{Lin}(\mathbb{R}^{d_X},\mathbb{R}^m))
      \]
      is  progressively measurable in the strong sense and uniformly $n$-integrable in the sense that
      \begin{align}
         \|(f,f')\|_{\gamma;q}:=\sup_{s\in [0,T]}\||f_s|_{\gamma}\|_q +  \sup_{s\in [0,T]}\||f'_s|_{\gamma-1}\|_q 
      \end{align}
      is finite.

      \item
      Letting
      \begin{align}
         \llbracketZ\rrbracket_{\zeta;p,q}:=\sup_{(s,t)\in \Delta_T:s\neq t}\frac{\Big\|\big\|\sup_{y\in {\mathbb{R}^d}}|Z_{s,t}(y)|\,\big|\,{\mathfrak F}_s \big\|_p\Big\|_q}{(t-s)^\zeta}\,,
      \end{align}
      the quantities
      $\llbracket\delta f\rrbracket_{\beta;p,q}$, $\llbracket\delta f'\rrbracket_{\beta';p,q}$, \( \llbracket\delta Df\rrbracket_{\beta';p,q} \) are finite.

      \item The map $(s,t)\mapsto \mathbb{E}_s R^f_{s,t}=\mathbb{E}_sf_t-f_s-f'_s \delta X_{s,t}$ satisfies 
      
      \[
      \bk{\mathbb{E}_{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}} R^f}_{\beta+\beta';q}
      =\sup_{(s,t)\in \Delta_T:s\neq t}\frac{\|\sup_{y\in {\mathbb{R}^d}}|\mathbb{E}_sR^{f}_{s,t}(y)|\|_q}{(t-s)^{\beta+\beta'}}
      <\infty\,.
      \]
   \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A generates a C_0-semigroup","B is bounded and defined on all of X"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771619+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, perturbation theory","id":"claim_44590f6f567cac894b075cc256edb639f4eb70dd5a268efb5afb31d4a111e31f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A generate a C_0-semigroup (T(t)) on a Banach space X with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt}, and let B ∈ B(X) be bounded and everywhere defined. Then A + B with domain D(A + B) = D(A) generates a C_0-semigroup (S(t)) satisfying ‖S(t)‖ ≤ M e^{(ω + M‖B‖)t}. The perturbed semigroup solves the variation-of-constants equation S(t)x = T(t)x + ∫_0^t T(t − s) B S(s)x ds for all x ∈ X, and is given by the Dyson-Phillips series S(t) = Σ_{n ≥ 0} S_n(t) with S_0(t) = T(t) and S_{n+1}(t)x = ∫_0^t T(t − s)B S_n(s)x ds, converging in operator norm uniformly on compact time intervals. In particular boundedness of the perturbation is enough; no relative-boundedness smallness is needed, and D(A) is unchanged.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:21:56.743224+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_446119dd9198fb6e538fd6b7e1a9b87bd3c0ac767f0d0a9b03cf00f43f2b3884","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi gie of arXiv:2507.20324, 'Non-existence of several random fractals in Brownian motion and Brownian loop soup'] Let $X_{0},X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}$ be independent Brownian motions started uniformly from $\mathcal{C}_0$, and stopped upon reaching $\partial\mathcal{B}(0,e^{r})$. Let $\Gamma$ be a Brownian loop soup with intensity $\mathbf{c}\in (0,1]$ in the plane, and $\Gamma_{r}$ be the collection of loops in $\Gamma$ which are fully contained in $\mathcal{B}(0,e^{r})$. We write $\widetilde{X}_{i}$ for the union of $X_{i}$ and the clusters in $\Gamma_{r}\backslash\Gamma_{0}$ that it intersects. Let $\Pi_{r}$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $X_{1},\ldots,X_{k},\Gamma_{r}\backslash\Gamma_{0}$. Define
\[\widetilde{Z}_{r}:=\mathbb{P}(X_{0}\cap(\cup_{j=1}^{k}\widetilde{X}_{j})=\varnothing|\Pi_{r}).\]
For all $\lambda>0$, let $p(\mathbf{c},k,r,\lambda)=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}_{r}^{\lambda}]$. Then the generalized intersection exponent $\xi_{\mathbf{c}}(k,\lambda)$ is defined by
\[\xi_{\mathbf{c}}(k,\lambda):=-\log\lim_{r\to\infty}(p(\mathbf{c},k,r,\lambda))^{1/r}.\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.501240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_447b097c91911dd606f656732b99fcd4ef5f1356ba2a290440b07e25757d8a35","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:conditional-remainder-cost of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:one-spike}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:33:23.329614+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_447d384f508f4bec36dcdfebd7923a7a2f23961c83560f4311915feff646bb76","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 2 of arXiv:2506.21829, 'Some notes on Lamperti's recurrence of stochastic sequences'] (Lamperti \cite{L}.)
Assume that a nonegative stochastic sequence $X_n$ satisfies \eqref{1}, and assume that for $x\to\infty$, we almost surely have
\begin{eqnarray}
\mu(x)&=&\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n-1},\ldots,X_0\}=\frac{\xi}{2x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right), \\
v(x)&=&\mathsf{E}\{(X_{n+1}-X_n)^2~|~X_n=x,  X_{n-1},\ldots,X_0\}=r^2+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{\epsilon}}\right),\nonumber\\
&&\text{where}\ \xi \ \text{is a positive value}.\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
Then the stochastic sequence is recurrent, if for almost all $x\to\infty$,
\[
\mu(x)\leq \frac{v(x)}{2x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right).
\]
If instead for some $\theta>1$ and  almost all large $x$,
\[
\mu(x)\geq\frac{\theta v(x)}{2x},
\]
then the stochastic sequence is transient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ be 2-cell complexes. Let $\pi : \mathcal{M}^{[1]} \to \mathcal{C}^{[1]}$ a map of their 1-skeletons, such that $\pi(\mathcal{M}^{[0]}) \subset \mathcal{C}^{[0]}$. Suppose $\pi$ is continuous and surjective.

On any common probability space for these arrays, phi_N converges almost surely to alpha/lambda+lambda rho^2/2 when lambda<=lambda_c=sqrt(2alpha)/rho, and to rho sqrt(2alpha) when lambda>=lambda_c. The two expressions agree at lambda_c. Independence is required within each N; no independence across different N is needed. Equivalently, for independent Gaussian patterns xi_mu~N(0,I_N) and a state x_N of norm rho sqrt(N), chosen independently of these patterns, one may take epsilon_(mu,N)=<x_N,xi_mu>/N. The result applies to that fixed state or independently chosen state sequence. It does not assert a uniform limit over pattern-dependent states or along an adaptive retrieval trajectory. This is the classical Gaussian random energy model condensation formula, used as a noise free-energy computation, not a retrieval or basin theorem. Source: Lucibello--Mezard, arXiv:2304.14964v4, equations (4)--(5), PDF p2; variational derivation Appendix A, PDF pp7--9. The exponentially large count may equally be exp(alpha N)-1 with the usual integer rounding, since its logarithmic rate is unchanged.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:55.114065+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_44a609a05205872504a9ba1477b2975b4ef10834d4b7ffc16ce4f86d375cb6ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] (1) $\textbf{IK} \vdash \Diamond \neg \neg \varphi \to \neg \neg \Diamond \varphi$.
  (2) $L \nvdash \Diamond \neg \neg \varphi \to \neg \neg \Diamond \varphi$ for $L \in \set{ \textbf{FIK}, \textbf{KI} }$.
  \begin{proof}
    (1) Take any $\Diamond$-p and FS2 model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$,
    and any $x \in W$ such that $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \neg \neg \varphi$.
    Then there is $y \in W$ such that $x \sqsubset y$ and $y \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \varphi$.
    To show that $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Diamond \varphi$, take any $x' \in W$ such that $x \leq x'$.
    By the $\Diamond$-p condition applied to $y \sqsupset x \leq x'$, there is $u \in W$ such that $x' \sqsubset u$ and $y \leq u$.
    By persistency, $u \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \varphi$, and hence $u \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \varphi$.
    Therefore, there is $u' \in W$ such that $u \leq u'$ and $u' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$.
    By the FS2 condition applied to $x' \sqsubset u \leq u'$, there is $x'' \in W$ such that $x' \leq x''$ and $x'' \sqsubset u'$.
    Thus $x'' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \varphi$, and so $x' \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \Diamond \varphi$.
    Since $x'$ was arbitrary, $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Diamond \varphi$.
    Therefore, $\textbf{IK} \vdash \Diamond \neg \neg \varphi \to \neg \neg \Diamond \varphi$ by completeness.

    (2) Consider the model $\mathfrak{M}_{\textsf{FS2}}$ from Proposition (prop:fik-is-weaker-than-ik of the paper) (2).
    Here, $x \sqsubset y \leq y' \Vdash^{\text{h}} p$ implies $y \Vdash^{\text{h}} \neg \neg p$, so $x \Vdash^{\text{h}} \Diamond \neg \neg p$.
    On the other hand, $y \not \Vdash^{\text{h}} p$ implies $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}} \Diamond p$, so $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}} \neg \neg \Diamond p$.
    By $\mathfrak{M}_{\textsf{FS2}}$ satisfying the $\Diamond$-p and $\Box$-p conditions,
    we have $L \nvdash \Diamond \neg \neg \varphi \to \neg \neg \Diamond \varphi$ for $L \in \set{ \textbf{FIK}, \textbf{KI} }$ by soundness.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the perturbation K is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar","the ambient space is a Banach space (Hilbert space for the adjoint form with conjugated lambda)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573224+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_44c2b247a9f29b24f5479cb03b211daeeab0cd1b96adb5f6a3837b72135ca330","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The alternative 'injective implies surjective' for operators of the form lambda I - K is carried entirely by two hypotheses: K is compact, and lambda is nonzero. (1) Compactness is load-bearing. On l^2 the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is bounded and injective but not surjective, and S = I - K with K = I - S bounded but not compact; its index is -1, not 0. So for a general bounded perturbation of the identity the two alternatives can both fail to be the right dichotomy: the equation x - K x = y can be uniquely solvable for some y and unsolvable for others, with no finite-dimensional solvability condition of equal dimensions on the two sides. What actually powers the alternative is that the index is 0, which compactness guarantees; a Fredholm operator of nonzero index (like S) is a counterexample to the dichotomy but not to Fredholm theory. (2) lambda nonzero is load-bearing. Take K = diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2, which is compact and injective, with dense but proper range (the sequence (1/n) is not in ran K, since it would need preimage (1, 1, 1, ...)). So for lambda = 0, 'injective' does not give 'surjective', the range is not closed, and 0 is in the spectrum of every compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space. (3) In the Hilbert-space version the solvability condition uses the conjugate: lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly when y is orthogonal to ker(conjugate of lambda times I - K*), not to ker(lambda I - K*); forgetting the conjugation is a common slip for complex lambda. (4) The dimension identity dim ker(lambda - K) = dim ker(lambda - K') is an identity of the two kernels, not a claim that the kernels correspond naturally, and it fails for non-compact perturbations (for S, ker S = 0 while ker S' is one-dimensional).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["C a class of measurable sets (or of {0,1}-valued functions); the suprema are assumed measurable (a countable class, or the standard measurability conditions)","i.i.d. sampling from an arbitrary P on X","the constants 4, 8 and 8, 32 are the classical ones; several textbooks state slightly different constants from the same proof"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706632+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_44ca0346ee27a0d7980b7facd63807b8439c3deb8db5ffcd25f0f1d03c270b4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITIONS. For a class C of subsets of X and points x_1, ..., x_n, the number of distinct traces |{ A intersect {x_1, ..., x_n} : A in C }| is at most 2^n; the growth (shatter) function is s(C, n) = max over all n-point sets of this number; the VC dimension d = VC(C) is the largest n with s(C, n) = 2^n (infinite if s(C, n) = 2^n for all n). Sauer-Shelah: if d < infinity then s(C, n) <= sum_{i <= d} binom(n, i) <= (e n / d)^d for n >= d. THEOREM (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971). Let X_1, ..., X_n be i.i.d. from P and P_n the empirical measure. For every eps > 0 and n >= 2 / eps^2, P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 4 s(C, 2n) exp( -n eps^2 / 8 ); a form valid for all n is P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 8 s(C, n) exp( -n eps^2 / 32 ). COROLLARIES. If VC(C) = d < infinity, then sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| -> 0 almost surely for EVERY P (C is a uniform Glivenko-Cantelli class), with E sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| <= C_0 sqrt(d / n) for an absolute constant C_0 (Talagrand's sharpening of the log-free bound); the sample size n = O( (d log(1/eps) + log(1/delta)) / eps^2 ) makes the sup at most eps with probability 1 - delta; and the condition is also necessary: if VC(C) = infinity there is a distribution P for which the sup does not converge to 0 in probability (Vapnik-Chervonenkis; Assouad; Dudley). In learning: for a class of classifiers of VC dimension d, every classifier's true error is within eps of its training error simultaneously once n is of order d / eps^2 (up to logarithms), so empirical risk minimisation is consistent exactly for finite VC dimension (the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, PAC learnability iff finite VC dimension).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda; divergence form","u >= 0 and a local weak solution on the whole cylinder B_{2r} x (t_0 - 4r^2, t_0)","the two cylinders are separated in time, with Q^- earlier than Q^+"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106483+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / Harnack inequalities","id":"claim_44dbfa0199ed26c36b75aa732eeca6cc025e4e1a57803299d2f6b3708baf81ca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $A$ be measurable and uniformly parabolic with constants $\\lambda,\\Lambda$ and let $u\\ge0$ be a local weak solution of $\\partial_tu=\\mathrm{div}(A\\nabla u)$ in $B_{2r}(x_0)\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Set $Q^-=B_r(x_0)\\times(t_0-3r^2,t_0-2r^2)$ and $Q^+=B_r(x_0)\\times(t_0-r^2,t_0)$. Then $\\sup_{Q^-}u\\ \\le\\ C\\,\\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $C=C(n,\\lambda,\\Lambda)$. The time lag is essential and so is the direction: the past cylinder's supremum is controlled by the future cylinder's infimum, never the reverse, and no inequality of this form holds on a single time slice. Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder $B_{2r}\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$ is required. Consequences: interior Holder continuity of solutions, the near-diagonal lower bound for the fundamental solution, and (through chaining) Aronson's Gaussian lower bound; the inequality is equivalent to the conjunction of the volume doubling property and a Poincare inequality in the Grigor'yan-Saloff-Coste characterization on manifolds and graphs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:56.346980+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_44dc923f043aad7cedb71dc65486d9a3fa15fe851c82c95f8c883726bd1eee1a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2603.13798, 'Iterated Graph Systems (I): random walks and diffusion limits'] See Figure~\ref{fig:canonical_xi} and Figure~\ref{fig:two_colour} for examples.

An \emph{Edge Iterated Graph System} is a triple
\[
   \mathscr I=(\Xi^{0},\mathcal R,\mathcal S)
\]
specified as follows.
Let $K\in\mathbb N$ be the number of edge colours.
For every graph $G$ that appears in the construction, let
$
   \mathscr{C} : E(G) \longrightarrow[K]
$
be a colour map.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Initial graph.}
      $\Xi^{0}$ is an edge-coloured finite directed graph.
      If $\Xi^{0}$ is just an edge, we denote its two vertices by $\mathfrak v_+$ and $\mathfrak v_-$.
      In particular, $\Xi_{\iota}^0$ denotes the special case that the initial graph is just one $\iota$-coloured directed edge.
      In this paper, $\iota$ always represents the colour of the initial graph if it only contains one edge or one vertex.

\item \textbf{Rule graphs.}
      $\mathcal{R} = \{ R_i \}_{i=1}^{K}$ is a family of finite directed graphs.
      Each $R_i$ contains two \emph{planting vertices}
      \[
         \beta_i^{+},\beta_i^{-} \in  V(R_i)
         \quad\&\quad
         \beta_i^{+}\neq\beta_i^{-}.
      \]
      Every edge of $R_i$ is coloured by the same map $\mathscr{C}$.

\item \textbf{Substitution operator.}
      For an edge $e=(a,b)\in E(G)$, the operator
      $
         \mathcal S\colon e\longmapsto R_{\mathscr{C}(e)}  \ \big|\
         a\equiv\beta_i^{+},\ b\equiv\beta_i^{-}
      $
      replaces $e$ by a \emph{fresh copy} of the rule graph $R_i$ where \(i=\mathscr C(e)\), identifying
      $
         a\equiv\beta_i^{+}
      $ and
      $
         b\equiv\beta_i^{-}.
      $
      All arcs are substituted \emph{simultaneously in parallel} at each step.
      Vertices are identified only at the planting vertices of their respective copies, and no further identifications are made.

\item \textbf{Iteration.}
      Set $\Xi^{n+1}:=\mathcal S(\Xi^{n})$ for $n\ge 0$; explicitly
      \[
         \Xi^{n+1}
         =
         \bigcup_{e\in E(\Xi^{n})}\mathcal S(e),
      \]
      where the union is taken with the vertex identifications described above.
      The sequence $(\Xi^{n})_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is called the \emph{EIGS substitution networks}.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.836546+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_44e454c4a3fb98f8ef6fdda283afac1db278935752df13ef947d999bcb42659e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corr FRSB of arXiv:2605.05631, 'Wandering Exponents and the Free Energy of the High-Dimensional Elastic Polymer'] Consider the model $B(x)=(1+x)^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma<1$ at some fixed $(\beta,t)$. The Larkin mass $\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ exists and is given by the unique $\mu$ which solves the equation
		\[2\gamma(\gamma+1)\left(1+\frac{2}{\beta \sqrt{\mu t}}\right)^{-\gamma-2}=\sqrt{\mu^3t}.\] 
		For all $\mu\ge \mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ the model is RS, and for all $\mu<\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ the model is FRSB.\\
		
		\noindent Moreover, in the FRSB case, the Parisi pair, $(q_c,\zeta_c)$, in Theorem (theorem:intro:1-d continuum T>0:FRSB of the paper) may be found explicitly. The value for the unique triple $(q_0,q_*,q_c)$ immediately follows from the equations
		\[q_c-q_0=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{c_0}{\mu^{\frac{3}{2(2+\gamma)}}}-1\right),\;\;\; q_0=c_1\mu^{\frac{3(\gamma+1)}{2(2+\gamma)}+3},\;\;\; q_c-q_*=\frac{1}{\beta\sqrt{\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)t}}, \]
		with constants given by $c_0=(\frac{2\gamma(\gamma+1)}{\sqrt{t}})^{1/(\gamma+2)}$ and $c_1=\frac{\gamma t}{c_0^{1+\gamma}}$. The measure $\zeta$ can then be found from its CDF, which is given for $s\in [q_0,q_*)$ by 
		\[\zeta_c([0,s])=\frac{\gamma+2}{3\beta}\left(\frac{4}{t\gamma(\gamma+1)}\right)^{1/3}(1+2q_c-2s)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{3}}, \]
		and otherwise by $\zeta_c([0,s])=0$ if $s\in [0,q_0)$ and $\zeta_c([0,s])=1$ if $s\in [q_*,q_c]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:58:49.164270+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_44eebfa67f00c602e0e7fbbc83a9b119a28016877ee79d496a128f66be871a6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 1 <= p < infinity and let Omega be a bounded connected open subset of R^n with Lipschitz boundary. {"assumptions":["Source-v1 scope note; intended endpoint and normalization conventions remain for independent source review."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:23:54.108206+00:00","domain":"Finite-width neural tangent kernels","id":"claim_44fdfe307f1a5966893681807e04240038b2429085a58bb33bec882bd105df92","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Hanin-Nica, Finite Depth and Width Corrections to the Neural Tangent Kernel, arXiv1909.05989v1, Section2 and Theorem1 (PDFp4), is a source for initialization moments of the diagonal NTK of a fully connected ReLU network. A comparison E[K^2] comparable to (E[K])^2 exp(5 beta) does not by itself establish Var(K)=O(1/n), even if beta tends to zero: the unspecified comparison constants prevent subtracting (E[K])^2 to obtain that rate. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:51:30.076170+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4527e58724eb5ad3a0b5956fdb92b0df82b829e9a4270dbdd40f6f94392f0fab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 21 of arXiv:2606.02036, 'Self-intersection local times for Volterra Gaussian processes in stochastic flows with int'] A family of random maps $\{\phi_{s,t}:\mbR^d\times\Omega\to\mbR^d,\ 0\leqslant s\leqslant t<\infty\}$ is called a stochastic flow of homeomorphisms if for $\prob$-almost all $\omega\in\Omega:$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:53:30.624665+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4531e288970728ee9250e994904e79a270a3c2bb99ef596bdadf36f46fd5b8b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_martingale of arXiv:2505.24043, 'Weak solutions of Navier-Stokes Equation with purely discontinuous L\'evy Noise'] A process  $\mathrm{M}\colon  \Omega  \times [0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ is a martingale with respect to a filtration $\mathbb{H}=(\mathscr{H}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.300964+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45335c4ddd389e0162937528dc826fd5f85d749df3a02030b02af149d2559f9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 (Posterior Gaussian-mixture geometry) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] For \(c\in\{\pm1\}\),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.273086+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_453cdc3caad94d439041d887f802b242","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In information theory, the entropy of a random variable quantifies the average level of uncertainty or information associated with the variable's potential states or possible outcomes. This measures the expected amount of information needed to describe the state of the variable, considering the distribution of probabilities across all potential states. Given a discrete random variable $X$, which may be any member $x$ within the set ${\\mathcal {X}}$ and is distributed according to $p\\colon {\\mathcal {X}}\\to [0,1]$, the entropy is $\\mathrm {H} (X):=-\\sum _{x\\in {\\mathcal {X}}}p(x)\\log p(x),$ where $\\Sigma$ denotes the sum over the variable's possible values. The choice of base for $\\log$, the logarithm, varies for different applications. Base 2 gives the unit of bits (or \"shannons\"), while base e gives \"natural units\" nat, and base 10 gives units of \"dits\", \"bans\", or \"hartleys\". An equivalent definition of entropy is the expected value of the self-information of a variable.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.913525+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_455a60571276a5980c784e8a027162555c51d4cdab57f4504c62040134d03228","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2boxtimesfp of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S$ be an APS and let $\triangle v$ be a one-variable APS term of degree two.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:52:51.764090+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_455a9281b5ff01bd45314dde35272d41e87072fe484f1d128a89790c23f4c5dc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:spectral_duality of arXiv:2605.00657, 'Spectral Duality and Reset-Neutral Distributions\\ in Random Walks with Multi-Site Geometr'] Let $\{z_1,\dots,z_m\}$ be a set of sites. A
\emph{spectral duality} on this set is an involution
$sigma:\{z_1,\dots,z_m\}\to\{z_1,\dots,z_m\}$
(i.e., $sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$) together with positive
coefficients $kappa(z)>0$, independent of $nu$, such that
\begin{equation}
B_nu(z) = kappa(z)\,A_nu(sigma(z))
\qquad \forall\,nu=1,\dots,N,\quad \forall\,z\in\{z_1,\dots,z_m\}.

\end{equation}
A site $z_0$ with $sigma(z_0)=z_0$ is called a
\emph{spectrally neutral site}. A pair $(z,sigma(z))$ with
$sigma(z)\neq z$ is called a \emph{spectral pair}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:45:32.083682+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4560b83bbc36d25a58f6e6707443563bbec829cdeb58179043c418a8bc2e9407","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop exm of arXiv:2411.14236, 'Size of chaos for Gibbs measures\\of mean field interacting diffusions'] Suppose that one of the following assumptions holds true.
\begin{itemize}
\item (Flat semi-convexity \dots)
The interaction kernel writes $W = W_+ - W_-$
with both $W_+$, $W_-$ being continuous and of positive type.

inequality uniformly in $m \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ for some $\rho_0 > 0$.
Moreover, one of the followings holds.
\begin{itemize}
\item (\,\dots\ with bounded force)
The kernels $W$, $W_-$ satisfy
$\lVert \nabla_1W\rVert_{L^\infty} \leqslant M_W < \infty$
and $\lVert \nabla_1W_-\rVert_{L^\infty} \leqslant M_W^-
< \sqrt{\rho_0}/2$.
In this case, we set
\[
\rho = \rho_0\biggl(1 - \frac{2M^-_W}{\sqrt{\rho_0}}\biggr),\qquad
\gamma = 2M_W,\qquad
M = 4M_W^2.
\]
\item (\,\dots\ with Lipschitz force)
The state space $\mathcal X$ is $\mathds R^d$.
The kernels $W_+$, $W_-$ are $\mathcal C^2$ and satisfy
$\lVert \nabla_{1,2}^2W_+\rVert_{L^\infty} \leqslant L_W^+ < \infty$
and $\lVert \nabla_{1,2}^2W_-\rVert_{L^\infty} \leqslant L_W^- < \rho_0/2$.
In this case, we set
\begin{align*}
\rho &= \rho_0\biggl( 1 - \frac{2L^-_W}{\rho_0}\biggr),\\
\gamma &= \frac{64(1+\delta_N)^2(L^+_W+L^-_W)^2}{\lambda_N},\\
M &= 4(L^+_W+L^-_W)^2
\biggl( \frac{\delta_N}{\lambda_NN} + \frac{d}{\rho_0}\biggr),
\end{align*}
where $\lambda_N$, $\delta_N$ are given by
(equation eq:def-lambda-N of the paper), (equation eq:def-delta-N of the paper)
respectively with $\varepsilon$ replaced by $1/2$
and $\Var m_*$ by $d / \rho_0$.
\end{itemize}

\item (Displacement convexity)
The state space $\mathcal X$ is $\mathds R^d$.
The confinement $V$ is $\mathcal C^2$ and satisfies
$\nabla^2V \succcurlyeq \kappa_V$ for $\kappa_V > 0$

Then Theorem~(thm:sharp of the paper) applies with the constants

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:41:54.335723+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_457b5eb39c4db3cab4679f5798bd9f07a010e32c2b53efea62fe75ce09ab5c24","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:2DNSE of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] Assume that $B\in L_2(U,W^{1,2}_{0,\,\operatorname{sol}}({\mathcal O}))$. Assume that for some $\lambda\in (0,1)$,
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le\frac{1}{4}\lambda\nu^3 c_0^2,\]
and
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le(1-\lambda)\nu c_0^2.\]
Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic incompressible 2D Navier-Stokes equations~(equation eq:2DNSE of the paper) with degenerate additive Wiener noise possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with second moments in $V$.

Furthermore, if there exists $\gamma\in (0,\nu c_0^2]$ and $\lambda\in (0,1)$ such that
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le\frac{1}{4}\lambda(\nu^3 c_0^2-\nu^2\gamma),\]
and
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le(1-\lambda)\nu c_0^2,\]
then $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ is exponentially mixing and exponentially ergodic, and we have the following upper bound for the $\varepsilon$-mixing time
\[\tau^x_{\textup{\textsf{mix}}}(\varepsilon)\leq 
\frac{2}{\gamma}\left[\frac{1}{\lambda \nu^2 }\|x\|^{2}_H+\log\left(\|x\|_H+\frac{\|B\|_{L_2(U,H)}}{\sqrt{2\lambda \nu}c_0}\right)+\log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\right].\]","status":"unverified"}

\[
\mu = \sum_{x\in P} \delta_{x},
\]
where $P$ is a finite or countable multiset consisting of elements in ${\mathbb R}$, and
\[
\mu(K) < \infty \quad \text{for every compact set } K \subset {\mathbb R}.
\]
That is, $\mu$ is a purely atomic Radon measure consisting of unit
masses at its atoms, with only finitely many atoms in each bounded region.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.047253+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4591479bf7b6eb5166178b4d1dc1e82f2fff537d01ab77d4524b9d8848d9a231","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Total variation cutoff) of arXiv:2608.15914, 'Absorption cutoff and stationary singularities for rounded Gaussian random dynamical syste'] Let $\mathcal I\subset\R$, and let $r_\ast\in[-\infty,\infty]$ belong to the
  closure of $\mathcal I$ in the extended real line. For each $r\in\mathcal I$, let $P_r$ be a
  Markov kernel on a measurable space $E_r$, let $\pi_r$ be an invariant
  probability measure, and let $x_r\in E_r$. Set
  \begin{equation}
    d_r(t)
    :=
    \norm{P_r^t(x_r,\cdot)-\pi_r}_{\TV},
    \qquad
    t\in\N_0 .
  \end{equation}
  For $u\in\R$, write
  $\lfloor u\rfloor_+:=\max\{0,\lfloor u\rfloor\}$.
  Let $t_r\to\infty$ and $a_r=o(t_r)$ with $a_r>0$. We say that
  $(P_r,x_r,\pi_r)_{r\in\mathcal I}$ has total variation cutoff at time $t_r$
  with window $a_r$ if
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{r\to r_\ast}
    d_r\left(\lfloor t_r-ca_r\rfloor_+\right)
    =
    1,
    \qquad
    \lim_{c\to\infty}\limsup_{r\to r_\ast}
    d_r\left(\lfloor t_r+ca_r\rfloor_+\right)
    =
    0.
  \end{equation}
  A function $F:\R\to[0,1]$ is a cutoff profile on the scale $a_r$ if, for
  every $c\in\R$,
  \begin{equation}
    d_r\left(\lfloor t_r+ca_r\rfloor_+\right)
    \to
    F(c),
    \qquad
    r\to r_\ast,
  \end{equation}
  where $F(c)\to1$ as $c\to-\infty$ and $F(c)\to0$ as $c\to\infty$.

  When no window is specified, cutoff at time $t_r$ means that, for every
  fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$,
  \begin{equation}
    d_r\left(\lfloor(1-\delta)t_r\rfloor_+\right)\to1,
    \qquad
    d_r\left(\lfloor(1+\delta)t_r\rfloor_+\right)\to0,
    \qquad
    r\to r_\ast.
  \end{equation}
  Equivalently, there exists $b_r=o(t_r)$ with $b_r>0$ such that the family
  has cutoff at time $t_r$ with window $b_r$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.948513+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_459e3f5c96453b53e8e613ed62d6b9f098f17a2bdcc1ccf3ce0c4d0ccfac689e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:backoff-cohorts of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and 
a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on non-negative integers. 
Let $X$ be the {backoff process}  
with send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth distribution~$\mathcal{D}$.
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a finite set of cohorts. The $\mathcal{C}$-cohorts of~$X$  are defined as follows.
For every $t\geq 1$, partition the set  $\mathbf{n}^{X}(t)$ of balls born at time $t$ 
by choosing a cohort~$D\in \mathcal{C}$ uniformly at random for each ball,
and letting $\mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t)$ be the balls in~$\mathbf{n}^X(t)$ that choose cohort~$D$.
 The cohorts have no effect on the evolution of the backoff process -- they will be  useful only for accounting in proofs.
For each $t\geq 1$, each $j\geq 0$, and each $D\in \mathcal{C}$, define
\begin{align*}
\newsym{b-j-X-D}{balls in bin~$j$ after step~$t$ in cohort~$D$, Def~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)}{\mathbf{b}_j^{X^D}(t)} &= \mathbf{b}_j^{X}(t) \cap \cup_{t'=1}^{t} \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t'),\\
\newsym{B-j-X-D}{balls in bin~$j$ before sends at~$t$ in cohort~$D$, Def~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)}{\mathbf{B}_j^{X^D}(t)} &= \mathbf{B}_j^{X}(t) \cap \cup_{t'=1}^{t} \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t'),\\
\newsym{s-j-X-D}{sends from bin~$j$ at step~$t$ in cohort~$D$, Def~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)}{\mathbf{s}_j^{X^D}(t)} &= \mathbf{s}_j^{X}(t) \cap \cup_{t'=1}^{t} \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t'),\\
\newsym{e-j-X-D}{escapes from bin~$j$ at step~$t$ in cohort~$D$, Def~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)}{\mathbf{e}_j^{X^D}(t)} &= \mathbf{e}_j^{X}(t) \cap \cup_{t'=1}^{t} \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t').
\end{align*}
The respective sizes of these are $b_j^{X^D}(t)$, $B_j^{X^D}(t)$, 
$s_j^{X^D}(t)$, and $e_j^{X^D}(t)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:58:40.870630+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45b16861f49dd1a9548a7140acef2da40af5998f72dfeb8c23a2bcf1836d2086","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem main_thm_2 of arXiv:2605.10491, 'Zero-couplings of infinite measures with cyclically monotone support and multivariate regu'] Let $P$ and $Q$ in $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be regularly varying probability measures with auxiliary functions $b_1$ and $b_2$, indices $\alpha_1 > 0$ and $\alpha_2 > 0$, and limit measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ in $\mathrm{M}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, respectively. 
    Let $\pi \in \Pi_{\mathrm{cm}}(P,Q)$ with $\operatorname{spt} \pi \subset \partial \psi$ for some closed convex function $\psi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} \cup \left\{\infty\right\}$. 
    
    
    If we further assume that
    
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item $\mu$ vanishes on sets of Hausdorff dimension not larger than $d-1$,
        \item         $
        \forall y \in \operatorname{spt}\nu\setminus \left\{0\right\}:
        \exists x \in \operatorname{spt}\mu:
         \langle{x,y}\rangle>0
        $,
    \end{enumerate}
    then we have the following properties:
    
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item
    $\Gamma_{0,\mathrm{cm}}(\mu,\nu)$ is a singleton with single element $\gamma= ( \operatorname{Id} \times \nabla\bar{\psi})_{\#}\mu$ for some closed convex function $\bar{\psi}$ satisfying $\operatorname{spt} \gamma \subset \partial \bar{\psi}$ and $\bar{\psi}(0) = \inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} \bar{\psi}(x) < \infty$.
    Moreover, $\gamma$ is proper, so that $\gamma = \operatorname{res} \rbr{(\operatorname{Id} \times \nabla\bar{\psi})_{\#}\mu}$ and $\nu = \operatorname{res} \rbr{(\nabla\bar{\psi})_{\#}\mu}$.

    \item
    Writing $V = \operatorname{int} \left(\operatorname{spt} \mu\right)$ and $B(t) = \operatorname{diag}(b_1(t) 1_d, b_2(t) 1_d)$ for $t > 0$, we have, as $t \to \infty$,
    \begin{align}
    
        t \, \operatorname{res}\pi(B(t) \,\cdot\,) &\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\,\scriptsize$\stackrel{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\mbox{\tiny $0$}}}{\longrightarrow}$}\, \gamma 
        &&\text{in $\mathrm{M}_{0}(\reals^d\times\reals^d)$}, \\
    
        (B(t)^{-1} \partial \psi) \llcorner V
        
        &\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\,\scriptsize$\stackrel{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\mbox{\tiny $\mathcal{F}$}}}{\longrightarrow}$}\, \left( \partial\bar{\psi} \right) \llcorner V  
        && \text{in $\mathcal{F}(V\times\mathbb{R}^d)$}.
    \end{align}

    \item
    The measure $\gamma$ is homogeneous in the sense that, writing $E = \operatorname{diag}(\alpha_{1}^{-1} 1_d, \alpha_{2}^{-1} 1_d)$, for all $\lambda > 0$, we have
    \begin{align}
        
        \gamma(\lambda^{-E}\,\cdot\,) &= \lambda \gamma,
        \\
        
        \lambda^E \operatorname{spt} \gamma &= \operatorname{spt} \gamma.
    \end{align}
    

    \item
    The gradient $\nabla\bar{\psi}$ is defined and determined uniquely $\mu$-almost everywhere. We have
	\begin{equation}
		
    	\nabla\bar{\psi}(\lambda x) = \lambda^{\alpha_1/\alpha_2} \,\nabla\bar{\psi}(x), 
        \qquad \lambda > 0,
    \end{equation}
	for $\mu$-almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Moreover, the function $\bar{\psi}$ may be modified such that $\bar{\psi}(0)= 0$; then it is determined uniquely $\mu$--almost everywhere and satisfies
	\begin{equation}
         
    	\bar{\psi}(\lambda x) = \lambda^{\alpha_1/\alpha_2+1} \, \bar{\psi}(x),
    	\qquad \lambda \geqslant 0,
    \end{equation}
	for $\mu$-almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
    
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:40:26.977020+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45d712561bedb63ac4fe8ebf6952cd8d5586ca3380c7ce283812b78ff02e9a76","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defa of arXiv:2604.11412, 'Stability of invariant measures of the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation with vani'] Given 
  $ \mathbf{u}_0 \in H^1({\mathbb R}^2)$,
  $\varepsilon\in [0,1]$, $\delta\in(0,1]$ and 
  $T>0$,
   a  
 continuous     $H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$-valued  $\mathcal{F}_t$-adapted
 process $\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta}$
   is called a solution of (equation 1.3* of the paper) if 
$$
 \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon, \delta}\in 
L^2(\Omega; L^\infty(0,T; H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)))
\cap
L^2(\Omega; L^2(0,T; H^3(\mathbb{R}^2)))
 $$ 
such that for all $t\in [0,T]$,   $\mathrm{P}$-almost 
surely,
\begin{align*}

&\quad-\int_{0}^{t}(1+|\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta}(s)|^{2})\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta}(s)ds
+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\sum_{k= 1}^\infty
\int_{0}^{t}(\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta}(s)\times \mathbf{f}_k)\times \mathbf{f}_kds
+\varepsilon\sum_ {k= 1}^\infty\int_{0}^{t}(\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta}(s)\times \mathbf{f}_k+\mathbf{f}_k)d W_k 
\end{align*}
in   
$H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^2 )$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.869721+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45d93405a9d94e490d24e2e56de77358ecc313387fd4c0b878acd42272f56485","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:double-overlap-partner of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Column $j'$ of a matrix $M$ 
is a \textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{double-overlap partner}} of $j$ if
\begin{equation}

\bigl|\operatorname{supp}M_{\cdot j}
\cap
\operatorname{supp}M_{\cdot j'}\bigr|\ge2.
\end{equation}

For a deterministic sequence of matrices  
\(
M^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n_k}
\)
for $k \in \mathbb{N}$, 
we say that it satisfies
the \textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{local sparse double-overlap condition}} if
there are sets
\[
\mathcal G_k\subseteq[n_k]
\quad \mbox{ and } \quad \varepsilon_k \searrow 0
\]
such that
\[
|\mathcal G_k|=(1-o(1))n_k
\]
and, for every $j\in\mathcal G_k$,
\[
\left|
\left\{
j'\in[n_k]\setminus\{j\}:
\bigl|\operatorname{supp}M^{(k)}_{\cdot j}
\cap
\operatorname{supp}M^{(k)}_{\cdot j'}\bigr|\ge2
\right\}
\right|
\le
\varepsilon_k\,\frac{n_k}k.
\]","status":"unverified"}

\(E\in\mathbb R\). Suppose that
\[
        \mathbf 1_{[E,\infty)}
        \bigl((1-Q_\omega)P_\omega(1-Q_\omega)\bigr)
        =
        0
        \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Then
\[
        \tau\bigl(\mathbf 1_{[E,\infty)}(P_\omega)\bigr)
        \le
        \tau(Q_\omega)
        =
        \mathbb P(o\in W_\omega).
\]

        \le
        2\mathbb P(o\in W_\omega).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["offspring distribution with finite mean m","Z_0 = 1 (otherwise q is raised to the power of the initial population)","the critical conclusion excludes the degenerate case p_1 = 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543433+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45fc062a637215cf5de5e927c5e37e9088fb287a9abe4d2162d6b99b9588a972","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Z_n) be a Galton-Watson branching process with Z_0 = 1 and offspring distribution (p_k)_{k >= 0} having generating function f(s) = sum_k p_k s^k and mean m = sum_k k p_k, assumed finite. Let q = P( Z_n = 0 for some n ) be the extinction probability. Then q is the SMALLEST root in [0,1] of the equation f(s) = s, and: if m < 1 (subcritical) then q = 1; if m = 1 (critical) then q = 1 UNLESS p_1 = 1, in which case the process is deterministic and never dies; if m > 1 (supercritical) then q < 1. The critical case is the one that gets misquoted: a critical branching process dies out almost surely even though E[Z_n] = 1 for every n, so the population is not uniformly integrable and the mean survives while the process does not. Excluding the degenerate p_1 = 1 is necessary. A second standard trap: q < 1 does not mean the process survives with probability 1 - it survives with probability exactly 1 - q, and conditioned on survival Z_n grows geometrically at rate m. [standard; e.g. Athreya and Ney, Branching Processes, Chapter I, or Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 4.3.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H a real or complex Hilbert space; X a normed space for the general remarks"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492120+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, weak topologies","id":"claim_46001c947b4cab76c499d85088d68c6f5587b6afdebff362beafde43fb023003","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a Hilbert space H a sequence (x_n) converges weakly to x, written x_n ⇀ x, if ⟨x_n, y⟩ → ⟨x, y⟩ for every y ∈ H; by the Riesz representation theorem this is convergence against every bounded linear functional. The weak topology on H is the coarsest topology making every functional x ↦ ⟨x, y⟩ continuous. Norm convergence implies weak convergence; the converse fails in infinite dimensions (an orthonormal sequence e_n converges weakly to 0 while ||e_n|| = 1). Weak limits are unique; weakly convergent sequences are norm-bounded (Banach–Steinhaus); the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous (||x|| ≤ liminf ||x_n|| when x_n ⇀ x); norm-closed convex sets are weakly closed (Mazur), and in infinite dimensions the weak closure of the unit sphere is the closed unit ball. If x_n ⇀ x and ||x_n|| → ||x|| then x_n → x in norm (Radon–Riesz property of Hilbert spaces). Bounded operators preserve weak convergence; compact operators turn weak convergence into norm convergence.\n\nIn a general normed space X the weak topology is the coarsest topology making every f ∈ X* continuous, and the weak-* topology on X* is the coarsest making every evaluation f ↦ f(x), x ∈ X, continuous. The weak-* topology on X* is in general coarser than the weak topology of X* (which is induced by X**); the two coincide when X is reflexive. In a Hilbert space, after identifying H* with H, weak and weak-* convergence are the same notion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:28.473262+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_461419348d36a6e265549b461847003ca30c1958508e75c486488c71b15f68cf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 52 (Sum/intersection duality) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let $m\ge1$ and $1\le r\le2$.
The space $\mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\Sigma}$ is Banach, stochastic-leg
permutations act isometrically on it, and symmetrization is a contraction.

the identity in $\mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\Sigma}$; in particular, algebraic
kernels are dense.  The completion of $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{alg}}$ in
\eqref{eq:algebraic-low-cut-norm} is canonically and isometrically
$\mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\Sigma}$, and the analogous symmetric completion is
$\mathfrak W_{m,r}^{\Sigma}$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak T_{m,2}^{\Sigma}=\mathfrak T_{m,2},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak W_{m,2}^{\Sigma}=\mathfrak W_{m,2}
\end{equation}
isometrically.  For $1<r<2$ and $r'=r/(r-1)$, the coefficient pairing
induces the conjugate-linear isometric isomorphism
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak T_{m,r'}\longrightarrow
 (\mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\Sigma})^*,
 \qquad
 L\longmapsto\bigl[K\longmapsto\ip{K}{L}\bigr],
 \qquad
 \norm{K\mapsto\ip{K}{L}}_{(\mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\Sigma})^*}
 =\max_{S\subset[m]}\norm{\Flat_S(L)}_{\Sch_{r'}}.
\end{equation}
Finally, for $1\le r\le2$ the identity on algebraic kernels extends to
contractive inclusions
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\cap}\longrightarrow\mathfrak T_{m,r}^{\Sigma},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak W_{m,r}^{\cap}\longrightarrow\mathfrak W_{m,r}^{\Sigma},
\end{equation}
with norm at most one.","status":"unverified"}
