{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.820998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_589202f03b99b9f1482c8a4024de03ebf8483baf5b41dc2e63ebbc1c538e4c68","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:compression-master of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$, $k\geq2$, and let
$A=(a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_{k-1})$ be an ordered real $k$-set.  If
$r=r_h(A)$, define its successive active-relation degrees by
\[
 p_i(A)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(A)\geq i\},
 \qquad 1\leq i\leq r.
\]
Put $d_A=k-1-r$.  Since $r\leq k-2$, one has $d_A\geq1$.
Then there is an integer set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A^*&=(0=a_0^*<a_1^*<\cdots<a_{k-1}^*),\\
 a_{k-1}^*
 &\leq d_Ah^{d_A-1}\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i(A)
 \leq(k-1-r)h^{k-2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the empty product is one,
such that, simultaneously for every $1\leq j\leq h$ and every
$u,v\in\mathcal U_{j,k}$,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A^*\bigr)
 =\operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus the ordered addition tables are identical in every degree $1\leq j\leq h$;
in particular, $|jA^*|=|jA|$ for $1\leq j\leq h$.

There is a complementary intrinsic statement.  Suppose $k\geq3$ and
\[
 B=(0=b_0<b_1<\cdots<b_{k-1}=d),
 \qquad \gcd(b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1})=1.
\]
For $1\leq i\leq k-2$, define the successive relation degrees
\[
 p_i(B)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(B)\geq i\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=d\leq\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}p_i(B).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $h\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
 \max_{\substack{B\subset\mathbb Z,\ |B|=k\\r_h(B)=k-2}}
       \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=h^{k-2}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-09T16:48:21.412485+00:00","domain":"stochastic processes","id":"claim_58bc2e019d5c41d686fda3087ff61e3e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A filtration on a probability space (Omega, F, P) indexed by a totally ordered set T (typically T = {0,1,2,...} or T = [0, infinity)) is a family (F_t)_{t in T} of sub-sigma-algebras of F such that F_s is a subset of F_t whenever s <= t; F_t represents the information available at time t. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58c2f90a212f274a241ad1ba9cc4d9d7695182d21fe0fbe058f607ce2eb09584","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 95 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $L,\alpha>0$ and let $(\cA_N)^\circ$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Let $\cA_N$ be the perturbation of $(\cA_N)^\circ$ from Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}. By passing to a subsequence $N_j\to\infty$, we assume that $\chi_{\cA_N}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, pointwise and in $L^1$. Denote $q_0\equiv \chi(0)\in[0,1]$. The function $p\equiv\chi^{-1}$ belongs to $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ and is concave, with
\[\frac1{L^2}
\le p'(q) \le L^2\] for all $q\in [q_0,1]$. Suppose $(\mu,\mu^\Ising)$ satisfies 
	\beq
	\bbW_2\big(\mu,\mu(\cA_N)\big)
	+\bbW_2\big(\mu^\Ising,
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_N)\big)
		\le \epsilon_\textup{apx}
		\,.
	\eeq
Then there exist $C(L) > 0$ and $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold. Let $B(t)$ and $W(t)$ be standard Brownian motions and
\begin{align} 
        dX(t)
        &= p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + s(t) \sigma_t\,dB(t)\,,
        \\
        dX^{\Ising}(t)
        &= w_t\,dW(t) 
        \end{align}
on the time interval $q_* \le t \le 1$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.  Then: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t=b(t,X(t))$,
$\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X(t))$,
and $w_t=w(t,Y(t))$ 
for functions $b:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[-C(L),C(L)]$ and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[0,C(L)]$, such that the functions $p'(t)^{1/2} b(t,x), s(t) \sigma(t,x), w(t,x)$, are $C(L)$-Lipschitz in $(t,x)$.
\item 
We have the diffusivity constraint
        \beq
            \max\bigg\{
            \Big|\bbE[w(t,X^\Ising(t))^2]-1
            	\Big|
	:q_* \le t\le 1
\bigg\} \leq  o(1)\,.
\eeq

\item 
    We have the approximate budget constraints
       \beq 
            \int_{q_*}^1
            \bigg\{
            \bbE\bigg[ b(t,X(t))^2+ \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}
            	(\sigma(t,X(t))-1)^2\bigg]
            -
            \frac{(\bbE w(t,X^\Ising(t)) )^2}{\alpha}
            \bigg\}_+
            \de t
            \leq o(1)\,.\eeq

 \item  The initial measures $\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ satisfy $|\bE[X(q_*)^2]|\leq o(1)$ and  $|\bE[X^\Ising(q_*)^2] - q_*|\leq o(1)$.
\item  The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+ o(1)]$ and satisfies $p(q_*) \le o(1)$. 
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
\beq
\begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\mu)
	&\leq 
	O(\epsilon_\textup{apx}) 
	+ o(1)\,,\\ 
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),\mu^{\Ising})
	&\leq  O(\epsilon_\textup{apx})
	+ o(1)\,.
\end{aligned}
\eeq
In all the above assertions, the $o(1)$ denotes an error which can tend to zero as $L^{-\Theta(1)}$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:41:33.836561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58c6c283671fb8da1e7792c6ed7d3a0caeda1eeeaf76b5fa52fe32f6231e4f69","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 (Random clock) of arXiv:2604.11434, 'Maxima of stationary systems of randomly time-changed L\'evy particles'] Given a L\'evy process $(L_t)_{t\ge 0}$ and a bounded function $\alpha:\RR \to (0,\infty)$, we define
\begin{align*}
  A_x(t)
  \ = \
  \int_0^t
  \alpha(L_r+x)
  \,\mathrm{d}r
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  T_x(t)
  \ = \
  \inf\{s\ge 0 \mid A_x(s)> t\}
  \,,\qquad
  t\ge 0 \,, x\in\RR\,.
\end{align*}
  We call $(T_x(t))_{t\ge 0}$ the random clock, $(A_x(t))_{t\ge 0}$ the inverse random clock, and $\alpha$ the mass function.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A noisy weak-PRF family with uniform random input samples; polynomial parameter lengths and n>=lambda.","One shared independent seed,pad,permutation; fresh sample inputs,noise and filler per encoding.","At most polynomially many calls,with a fixed polynomial upper bound Q."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:49:17.343706+00:00","domain":"Pseudorandom codes and sampling couplings","id":"claim_58ed9e6ef15a9c4f1dc1d61d11f40b5735573a1dd8c9b15a2a5fec59e23069ac","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda<=n(lambda)<=poly(lambda), and let m,N and the seed length be polynomially bounded positive integers with N>=(n+1)*m. Choose one uniform seed S, one independent uniform N-bit pad Z, and one independent uniform permutation Pi of N coordinates as the secret key. Each encoder call independently samples m uniform X_j in{0,1}^n, m independent Bernoulli(q) bits E_j, and a fresh uniform filler R of length N-(n+1)*m; it returns Pi applied to(C xor Z), where C concatenates the pairs(X_j,F_S(X_j) xor E_j) and R. For any probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher making at most Q polynomially many adaptive encoder calls, there is a polynomial-time weak-PRF sample-oracle distinguisher making at most M=Q*m calls whose advantage bounds the encoding-oracle advantage up to min(1,binom(M,2)/2^n). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:04:30.613492+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58eea891642796f0dfe5b9cf5720dcbef765363175f6cb411fdd9c6e66dbd2a1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem HSf of arXiv:2411.10586, 'A convergence framework for Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble\\ via pole evolution'] Take any Nevanlinna function $Y:\mathbb{H}\to \mathbb{H}\cup{\mathbb R}$, with Nevanlinna representation

 Y(w)=b+cw+\int \left( \frac{1}{\lambda-w} - \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2} \right)  {\rm d} \mu(\lambda),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:26:02.656719+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58f52c72045d7c076505248d8be68c372a3d2d1b1d9cb5170027ced77933e9a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma ddco of arXiv:2608.30747, 'Compact homogeneous complex manifolds'] For any $G$-invariant Hermitian structure $(J,g)$ as in (equation Jg of the paper) on a C-space $M=G/K$, the only possibly nonzero components of the $4$-form $dd^c\omega$ are given by 
\begin{align*}
dd^c\omega(E_\alpha,E_{-\alpha},E_\beta,E_{-\beta})
=& -2g_\ag(A_\alpha,A_\beta) 
- 2N_{\alpha,\beta}^2(x_{\alpha+\beta}-x_{\alpha}-x_{\beta}) \\
& - 2\epsilon_{\alpha-\beta}N_{\alpha,-\beta}^2(\epsilon_{\alpha-\beta}x_{\alpha-\beta}-x_{\alpha}+x_\beta), \qquad \forall \alpha,\beta\in\Delta_\qg^+, \alpha\ne\beta,

&+ \epsilon_{\alpha+\delta}N_{\alpha,\delta}  N_{\beta,\gamma} (-x_\alpha+x_\beta-x_\gamma+x_\delta+2\epsilon_{\alpha+\delta}x_{\alpha+\delta}).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.917510+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58ffc21014799f6ba9dde03765b16731732113257ed5337a11b7a7e9422e4c49","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $a,b\in(0,+\infty)$, $\eta>0$, $k,d\in\mathbb N$, and $d\ge2$. There exists
a constant $C:=C(a,b,\eta,k,d)>0$ such that, for every
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_k),Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$
satisfying
\[
a\le \operatorname{Var}(X_j)\le b,
\quad
a\le \operatorname{Var}(Y_j)\le b
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and
\[
\det \Sigma^d(X)\ge \eta,
\quad
\det \Sigma^d(Y)\ge \eta,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X,Y)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X,Y)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}.
\]

In particular, if a sequence
$X_n\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$ converges in distribution to an
$\mathbb R^k$-valued random vector $X_\infty$ whose distribution is absolutely
continuous, then the convergence holds in total variation and
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X_n,X_\infty)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X_n,X_\infty)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}
\]
for some constant $C>0$ depending on the sequence and on the limiting
distribution. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.635990+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_592169432c2b95ccc1b27d69f321a5d51b40f31b5ac1c0310c55bc6264920664","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Second-order smooth consistency) of arXiv:2609.00673, '2609.00673'] Let \(\gamma\in C^6(I,\mathbb R^3)\) be a unit-speed space curve.
Assume that, on a compact subinterval \(J\Subset I\),
\[
\kappa(s)\ge \kappa_0>0,\qquad |\tau(s)|\ge\tau_0>0.
\]
Sample it uniformly by
\[
P_i=\gamma(s_i),\qquad s_i=s_0+ih.
\]
For the quotient indexed by $i$, call $C_i=[s_{i-1},s_{i+2}]$ its associated four-point cell. All quotient estimates below are uniform whenever $C_i\subset J$; estimates for the defect $D_i^h$, which involves two consecutive quotients, are uniform whenever $C_i\cup C_{i+1}=[s_{i-1},s_{i+3}]\subset J$.
Let \(\theta_i^h\) and \(\phi_i^h\) be the turning and signed torsion
angles of the chord polygon and set
\[
x_i^h=\tan\frac{\theta_i^h}{2}.
\]
There exists $h_0=h_0(\kappa_0,\tau_0,J)>0$ such that, for $0<h<h_0$ and all cells under consideration,
\[
0<\theta_i^h<\pi,\qquad \phi_i^h\notin\{0,\pi\}.
\]
Hence the sampled polygon lies in the generic Frenet branch and all quotients below are well defined.
With $m_i=s_i+h/2$, the midpoint convention compatible with the chord tangents gives the
asymptotic expansions
\[
x_i^h=\frac h2\kappa(s_i)+O(h^3),
\]
and
\[
\phi_i^h=h\tau\left(s_i+\frac h2\right)+O(h^3).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{x_i^h+x_{i+1}^h\cos\phi_i^h}{\sin\phi_i^h}
=
\frac{\kappa}{\tau}\left(s_i+\frac h2\right)+O(h^2).
\]
If
\[
D_i^h:=
\frac{x_{i+1}^h+x_{i+2}^h\cos\phi_{i+1}^h}{\sin\phi_{i+1}^h}
-
\frac{x_i^h+x_{i+1}^h\cos\phi_i^h}{\sin\phi_i^h},
\]
then, uniformly on such cells,
\[
\boxed{
\frac{D_i^h}{h}
=
\left(\frac{\kappa}{\tau}\right)'(m_i)+O(h)
},
\qquad m_i=s_i+\frac h2.
\]
Thus the finite-step conservation law approaches $(\kappa/\tau)'=0$, equivalently \(\tau/\kappa=\mathrm{constant}\) on intervals where \(\kappa\tau\neq0\). The scalar quotient itself is second-order accurate, whereas its normalized finite difference is first-order accurate. If the underlying smooth curve is a general helix, then
\[
D_i^h=O(h^3).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:56:03.904439+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5923da4d2493474c444bb371850c13e9b84792e417d982b68692dd3bc623e1c1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.20948, '\textsc{Slot decomposition of\\ continuous Box-Ball Systems}'] [The slot diagrams of a positive point configuration]
 \rm  Let $\sN\in\cN_+$. Proceed recursively. Denote $\sN_0 \vcentcolon =\sN$, $\su_0\vcentcolon = 0$, $\sM_0\vcentcolon = \emptyset$, and a function $\sg_0(y) \equiv 0$ for all $y> 0$. 

Recursive step. Suppose that $\sN_{k},\su_{k},\sM_{k}$ are defined.
See Fig.~\ref{Mk}.
 For $k\ge1$ let $\sg_k\vcentcolon =\sg[\sM_k]$,  the right boundary of the slot diagram $\sM_k$, as defined in \eqref{sca7}. Then, use \eqref{sc12} to define
\begin{align}
 (\su_{k+1}, \sM_{k+1})&\vcentcolon = (\su[\sN_{k}], \sM[\sN_{k}]),  \\
 \sN_{k+1} &\vcentcolon = \Bigl\{\bigl(u-\su_{k+1}-\sg_{k+1}(\ell), \ell\bigl):(u, \ell)\in\sN_{k}\setminus\sM_{k+1}\Bigr\}. 
\end{align}
A point $(u,\ell)$ in $\sN_{k}\setminus\sM_{k+1}$ is shifted leftwards to a point in $\sN_{k+1}$ having the same vertical coordinate~$\ell$, and horizontal coordinate $u-\su_{k+1}-\sg_{k+1}(\ell)$. 
Note that given a finite set $\mathcal T(y+\su_{k+1})$ that verifies \eqref{eqRy} for $\sN_{k}$, once we shift it as in \eqref{sc111} we get a finite set $\mathcal T(y)$ that verifies \eqref{eqRy} for $\sN_{k+1}$.
Therefore we inductively get that $\sN_{k}$ is $\mathcal T$-finite.

Iterate the recursive step to obtain a map from $\sN\in \cN_+$ to a sequence of slot diagrams and insertion points 
\begin{align}
  \sN\mapsto  (\su_k[\sN], \sM_k[\sN])_{k\ge 1}.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241560+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_598e07ea2375a52e9d6b6e42cebfe08fec80ff91ff7170cea3f5881c896575e9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 (Canonical solvability of the metric Hodge system) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X:\Real_y^n\to\Real_x^n$ be an orientation-preserving global
bi-Lipschitz map with $d\mu=J dy$.  Fix $1<p<n$ and put
\[
 p^*:=\frac{np}{n-p}.
\]
For every $q\in L^p(\mu)$ there is a unique vector field $F=F^i\eframe_i$ along $X$, whose Cartesian components belong to
$L^{p^*}(\mu;\Rn)$, satisfying \eqref{eq:invdiv} in the conjugated
distributional sense: equivalently, $u:=F\circ X^{-1}$ satisfies
\[
 \partial_{x^i}u^j-\partial_{x^j}u^i=0,
 \qquad
 \partial_{x^i}u^i=q\circ X^{-1}
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_x^n).
\]
The solution is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_{\gmetric}q
 :=\mathcal C_X\nabla\Delta_x^{-1}\mathcal C_X^{-1}q, \qquad \mathcal{C}_Xf=f\circ X,
\end{equation}
and it satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathcal P_{\gmetric}q\|_{L^{p^*}(\mu)}
 \le C_{n,p}\|q\|_{L^p(\mu)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for
\begin{equation}
    r_{\mathrm{HLS}}:=\frac{4n}{n+4},
\end{equation}
one has $1<r_{\mathrm{HLS}}<n$ for every $n\ge2$ and $r_{\mathrm{HLS}}^*=4$; hence
every $q\in L^{r_{\mathrm{HLS}}}(\mu)$ has a unique solution

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:56:25.277057+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5994786ed7673abfd0e9fb218f1d74716f17f0ffba61f7c8ae5301ab9d1c34a0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 2 (\Adam\ optimizer) of arXiv:2606.21433, 'Central limit theorem for\\ the averaged Adam optimizer'] Consider
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item an innovation $ ( X, U ) $,
\item $ \alpha, \beta \in [0,1) $, $ \epsilon \in (0,\infty) $ with $ \alpha < \sqrt \beta $ (the \emph{damping factors}),
\item $ n_0 \in \N_0 $, $ \theta_{ n_0 }, m_{ n_0 } \in \R^d $, $ v_{ n_0 } \in [0,\infty)^d $ (the initialisation), and
\item a decreasing $(0,\infty)$-valued sequence $ ( \gamma_n )_{ n \in \N } $ (\emph{sequence of step-sizes}).
\end{enumerate}

An $\R^{d}$-valued stochastic process  $(\theta_{n})_{n\in\N_0\cap[n_{0},\infty)}$ is called \emph{\Adam\ algorithm with damping parameter $(\alpha,\beta,\epsilon)$ and step-sizes $(\gamma_{n})$ started at time $n_{0}$ in $(\theta_{0},m_{n_{0}},v_{n_{0}})$} if and only if
for every $ n \in \N \cap ( n_0, \infty) $, $ i \in \{ 1, \dots, d \} $ it holds that
\begin{equation}
  \thetai_n = \thetai_{ n - 1 } + \gamma_n \, \sigmai_n \, m^{(i)}_n,
\end{equation}
where for all $ n \in \N \cap ( n_0, \infty) $, $ i \in \{ 1, \dots, d \} $ we have
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item  $m_n=\alpha \,m_{n-1}+(1-\alpha) \,X(\theta_{n-1}, U_n)$,
\item  $v^{(i)}_n= \beta \,v^{(i)}_{n-1} +(1-\beta) \,(X^{(i)}(\theta_{n-1},U_n))^{2}$, and
\item  $\displaystyle \sigma^{(i)}_n= \bigl[ \epsilon + ( v_n^{(i)}/(1-\beta^{n}) )^{ 1 / 2 } \bigr]^{ - 1 } $
\end{enumerate}
and where $ ( U_n )_{ n \in \N \cap( n_0, \infty ) } $ is a family of independent copies of $ U $.
We call the sequence $(t_{n})_{n\in\N_{0}}$ given by
$
  t_n = \sum_{ k = 1 }^n \gamma_k
$
the \emph{training times} of the \Adam\ algorithm.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_59b71972a03cccd34a3b9f19358b0f2ad82bb2b26ccd049a537b06518a32a52b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a positive finite Borel measure mu on R, its STIELTJES TRANSFORM (also Cauchy transform) is m_mu(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu(dx) for z in the open upper half plane C^+. It is analytic on C^+, maps C^+ into C^+ when mu is positive, and satisfies the a priori bound |m_mu(z)| <= mu(R)/Im(z). INVERSION: for a < b continuity points of mu, mu( (a,b) ) = (1/pi) lim_{eta decreasing to 0} integral_a^b Im m_mu(x + i eta) dx, so the transform determines the measure. CONTINUITY: a sequence of probability measures mu_n converges weakly to a probability measure mu if and only if m_{mu_n}(z) -> m_mu(z) for every z in C^+; convergence on any set with an accumulation point in C^+ suffices, by analyticity plus a tightness argument. In random matrix theory the transform of the empirical spectral distribution of a Hermitian matrix H is m_n(z) = (1/n) tr ( H - z I )^{-1}, the normalised trace of the RESOLVENT, which is why resolvent methods and Stieltjes-transform methods are the same method. Sign conventions differ across the literature: some authors define the transform with (z - x)^{-1}, which flips the sign of the whole calculus; the convention must be checked before importing a formula. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Section 2.4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.792181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_59dbe3f3ea68e2662d224e6f76a98dd9fe2a2ee60bee197e1829b68bcacd30f4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] The Bregman divergence of $\psi:Q\to \mathbb R$ is $D_\psi:Q\times Q\to \mathbb R$ defined as 
\[
D_\psi (x,y) = \psi(x) - \psi(y) - \ip{\nabla \psi(y)}{x-y}.
\]
    We say that $F:Q\to \mathbb R$ is $c$-strongly convex with respect to $D_\psi$ if for all $x,y\in Q$,
\[
F(x) \geqslant F(y) + \ip{\nabla F(y)}{x-y} + cD_\psi(x,y).
\]
We say that $F:Q\to \mathbb R$ is $C$-smooth with respect to $D_\psi$ if for all $x,y\in Q$.
\[
F(x) \leqslant F(y) + \ip{\nabla F(y)}{x-y} + CD_\psi(x,y).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.835847+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_59e2ec10a29aad2ce21a11a16f2592e948f2f8a893c3141e52ad31c6bd0897e6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 13 (Posterior thresholds) of arXiv:2607.20373, 'Embedding martingale diffusions as binary posteriors in sequential inference'] Let $0<\alpha<p<\beta<1$ and $\tau_{\alpha,\beta}$ be the first exit time
    \(
        \tau_{\alpha,\beta}
        =\inf\{t\geq 0:P_t\notin(\alpha,\beta)\},
    \)
    where $P$ is the posterior for a binary experiment. Assume $P$ is an autonomous win-martingale with $P_0=p$. Then $\tau_{\alpha,\beta}<\infty$ a.s.~and
    \begin{equation}
        \widetilde{\mathbb P}(P_{\tau_{\alpha,\beta}}=\beta)
        =\frac{p-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{\mathbb P}(P_{\tau_{\alpha,\beta}}=\alpha)
        =\frac{\beta-p}{\beta-\alpha}.
    \end{equation}
    If the decision is $1$ at $\beta$ and $0$ at $\alpha$, then
    \begin{align}
        \widetilde{\mathbb Q}^0(\textnormal{decide }1)
        &=\frac{1-\beta}{1-p}\frac{p-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{\mathbb Q}^1(\textnormal{decide }0)
        =\frac{\alpha}{p}\frac{\beta-p}{\beta-\alpha}.
    
    \end{align}
    The expected decision time under the marginal law is
    \begin{align}
        \widetilde{\mathbb E}[\tau_{\alpha,\beta}]
        =2\bigg[&
        \frac{\beta-p}{\beta-\alpha}
        \int_\alpha^p\frac{y-\alpha}{\sigma^2(y)}\,dy
        +\frac{p-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha}

        \bigg].
    
    \end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.250966+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5a149bb6e7718b3087427678a1beddfcaac907987a267282f2eb84406df0ced5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.23222, 'On global solutions to the semidiscrete stochastic heat equation'] If $\beta$ is sufficiently small, the following statements hold. 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item For all $(x,s), (y,t) \in \Z^d \times \R$, the partition functions $Z_{x,s}^T$ and $Z_S^{y,t}$ converge in $L^2(Q)$ as $T \to \infty$ and $S \to -\infty$, respectively, to the \emph{limiting partition functions} 
$$
	Z_{x,s}^{\infty} := \lim_{T\to \infty} Z_{x,s}^T
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
	Z_{-\infty}^{y,t}  := \lim_{S \to -\infty}  Z_S^{y,t}.
$$
There is $\theta > 0$, independent of $x,y$ and $s,t$, such that 
$$
\lim_{T \to \infty} (T-s)^{\theta} \langle \left(Z_{x,s}^T - Z_{x,s}^{\infty} \right)^2 \rangle = 0 \
\text{and}
\lim_{S \to -\infty} (t-S)^{\theta} \langle \left(Z_S^{y,t} - Z_{-\infty}^{y,t} \right)^2 \rangle = 0. 
$$
\item There is a set $\Omega^{\lim}_+ \in \Fc$ with $Q(\Omega^{\lim}_+) = 1$ and $\theta_t(\Omega^{\lim}_+) = \Omega^{\lim}_+ \ \forall t \in \R$ such that for all $(x,s), (y,t) \in \Z^d \times \R$ and all $\omega \in \Omega^{\lim}_+$, the limiting partition functions $Z_{x,s}^{\infty}(\omega)$ and $Z_{-\infty}^{y,t}(\omega)$ exist as pointwise limits $\lim_{T \to \infty} Z_{x,s}^T(\omega)$ and $\lim_{S \to -\infty} Z_S^{y,t}(\omega)$, respectively, and are positive. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:36:49.878173+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5a1a6580e1cfe0174a113dd4e729bb39463a91a54b870ddc7d9ee3b6e79c5f54","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition cor : sr of arXiv:2609.00105, 'Weighted composition operators and classification of weighted Hardy spaces'] Let $\mathcal{H}_i$ be a weighted Hardy space in $d_i$ variables with generating function  $G_i$ with radius of convergence $r_i^2\in(0,\infty]$, $i=1,2$.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $d_1\ge d_2$, then $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ are isomorphic via an RKHS isomorphism and $d_1=d_2$.
        \item If $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ strongly related, then $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ are isomorphic via an RKHS isomorphism and $d_1=d_2$.
        \item If $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ strongly related, then $G_1$ is entire if and only if $G_2$ is entire.
        \item If $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ strongly related and $r_1<\infty$, then $r_2<\infty$ and $G_1(r_1^2)<\infty$ if and only if $G_2(r_2^2)<\infty$.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

\begin{enumerate}

let $\nu\in\cuP_0(\sa{k}{\C})$.
Define
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) := \int  \bT(\bI + \bS\bT)^{-1} \nu(\de \bT) - \frac1\alpha\bS^{-1},\quad\quad \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}:\C^{k\times k} \to\C^{k\times k}.
\end{equation}

For any $z \in\bbH_+$, there exists a unique 
solution 
$\bS_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z)$
to
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) = z\bI,\quad\quad \bS\in\bbH_+^k := \{\bB\in \C^{k\times k}: \Im(\bB) \succ\bzero\}.
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
    \begin{equation}
        s_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z) := 
         \frac{\alpha}{k} \Tr(\bS_\up{\alpha,\nu}(z))\quad\quad\textrm{for}\quad z\in\bbH_+
    \end{equation}
is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure 
$\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu}\in\cuP(\R)$ such that, almost surely
\begin{equation}
    \hmu_{\bW_k} \Rightarrow \mu_\up{\alpha,\nu} \quad\quad \textrm{almost surely, as} \quad\quad n\to\infty,\;\frac{n}{p} \to\alpha,
\end{equation}
where $\hmu_{\bW_k}$ is the empirical spectral distribution of $\bW_k$ and $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence of probability measures.

Finally, if $\dist(\{\bT_i:i\le n\},\supp(\nu))\to 0$ (with $\dist$ denoting
Hausdorff distance between sets in $(\reals^k,\|\,\cdot\,\|$), then,
almost surely,

\begin{align}
\dist\big(\supp(\hmu_{\bW_k}),\supp (\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu})\big) \to 0\, .
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.238901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5aae15f417c796ccacf0479a7b8204d192fab8a958a4bd33cb7cbe32a81bb366","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:prefix-free-ball-code-dimension of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] Let \(\varphi\) be a prefix-free ball code.
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(r\in\omega\), define
\[
K_\varphi(x;r)
=
\min
\left\{
|p|
:
p\in\dom(\varphi),
x\in \varphi(p),
\ \diam(\varphi(p))\le 2^{-r}
\right\},
\]
with the convention that \(K_\varphi(x;r)=\infty\) if no such \(p\) exists.

\[
\dim_\varphi(x)

\liminf_{r\to\infty}
\frac{K_\varphi(x;r)}{r}.
\]

\[
\dim_\varphi(E)
=
\sup_{x\in E}\dim_\varphi(x).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["conjugate exponents with 1 <= p <= 2","convention e^{-2 pi i x . xi}, for which the constant 1 is available on R^d","on T the transform is the coefficient sequence, with the counting measure on Z"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264720+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_5aeb07b2cba38ad9cc3665ecb9550bf24a5d74fc445f8cf0332b5120f3c59861","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The inequality $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|f\\|_p$, $\\frac1p+\\frac1{p'}=1$, holds for $1\\le p\\le2$ (Riesz-Thorin interpolation between $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ and Plancherel) - and only there. The restriction $p\\le2$ is load-bearing: (i) On $\\mathbb T$, $L^p\\subset L^2$ for $p>2$, so the coefficients are automatically in $\\ell^2$, but no better exponent is available: Carleman's example provides a continuous (hence in every $L^p$) function $f$ on $\\mathbb T$ with $\\sum_n|\\hat f(n)|^q=\\infty$ for every $q<2$. So no bound $\\|\\hat f\\|_{\\ell^{p'}}\\le C\\|f\\|_{L^p}$ with $p'<2$ can hold for any $p>2$. (ii) On $\\mathbb R^d$ and $p>2$, the Fourier transform of an $L^p$ function exists only as a tempered distribution and need not be representable by a locally integrable function, so the left-hand side of the inequality is not even defined in general. (iii) The direction matters too: the dual statement '$\\hat f\\in L^{p'}$ implies $f\\in L^p$' is false in general; what is true is the companion inequality $\\|f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|\\hat f\\|_p$ for $1\\le p\\le2$. (iv) On $\\mathbb R^d$ the constant $1$ is not sharp: Babenko-Beckner give $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\big(p^{1/p}/(p')^{1/p'}\\big)^{d/2}\\|f\\|_p$ for $1<p<2$, attained by Gaussians, whereas on $\\mathbb T$ and $\\mathbb Z$ the constant $1$ is sharp.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.196732+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b039ed3752039b01ea8cf017e5c61df9a7c9d64410c69bf9a9f8837e70a31e3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 2 (Derivative of the propagated functional) of arXiv:2608.03412, 'A McKean--Vlasov semigroup and its application to a martingale representation problem'] Assume {\rm \Cref{assum:main,assum:G}}. Then, for every $0\le t\le s\le T$, the map
\[
m\longmapsto \Gr(s,t,m)=G(\mu^{t,m}_s)
\]
admits a differentiable linear functional derivative. More precisely, for
$m\in\Pc(\R^d)$ and $x\in\R^d$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_x\delta_m\Gr(s,t,m)(x)
&=
\E\Big[
\bigl(J^{t,m}_s\bigr)^\top
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(S^{t,m}_s)
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s, U=x
\Big]
\\
&\quad+
\E\Big[
\bigl(\overline J^{t,m}_s\bigr)^\top
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(\overline S^{t,m}_s)
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s, U=x
\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently, for every $h\in\R^d$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_x\delta_m\Gr(s,t,m)(x)\cdot h
&=
\E\Big[
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(S^{t,m}_s)
\cdot J^{t,m}_s h
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s,\ U=x
\Big]
\\
&\quad+
\E\Big[
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(\overline S^{t,m}_s)
\cdot \overline J^{t,m}_s h
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s,\ U=x
\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]","status":"unverified"}

Let $W>0$ and let $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\\hat f=0$ a.e. outside $[-W,W]$. Then $\\hat f\\in L^1$, so $f$ has a (unique) continuous representative $f(x)=\\int_{-W}^{W}\\hat f(\\xi)e^{2\\pi i x\\xi}d\\xi$, and for that representative $$f(x)=\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f\\!\\left(\\frac{n}{2W}\\right)\\operatorname{sinc}(2Wx-n),\\qquad \\operatorname{sinc}(t)=\\frac{\\sin(\\pi t)}{\\pi t},$$ the series converging in $L^2(\\mathbb R)$ and uniformly on $\\mathbb R$. Moreover $\\sum_n|f(n/2W)|^2=2W\\|f\\|_2^2$, so the samples determine $f$ isometrically. The sampling rate $2W$ (the Nyquist rate) is critical: functions bandlimited to $[-W,W]$ are in general not determined by samples at a slower rate, and the theorem's conclusion uses $f\\in L^2$ - the distributionally bandlimited function $\\sin(2\\pi Wx)$ has all samples $f(n/2W)=0$ without being zero, and it is excluded only because it is not in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.433149+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b2f1a3c50fbcde76c3148afa2540ddcf2e4fe34d40b000444da8a0b2f61fd46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:Bernoulli_calY_representation}
The set $\{\hat{f}_k^r \mid r \in [0,1] \text{ and } k \in I^r \}$ is a basis for ${\rm aff}(\Sym(f))$. 

That is, for $f \in \Sym$, denoting 

$ R_f = \{ r \in [0,1] \mid \supp(f) \cap S^r \ne \emptyset \}, $ we have
\[ f = \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r , \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r = 1 . \]
\begin{proof}
The PMF $f$ is discrete, so its support is at most countable; therefore $R_f$ is at most countable. 
Write $f = \sum_{R_f} f\big\vert_{S^r}$ and for each $r \in R_f$ define $c_r = \sum_{z \in S^r} f(z)$. 
Then for each $r \in R_f$, $f_r = \frac{1}{c_r} f\big\vert_{S^r} \in \Sym$ by (lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers of the paper). 
Now apply the (lem:Bernoulli_calYr_representation of the paper) to each $f_r$ to find constants $\alpha_k^r[f_r]$; it is then obvious that $c_r \alpha_k^r[f_r] = \alpha_k^r[f]$ for all $k$ and $r$. 

Thus we compute 
\[ 
f = \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r f_r 
= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} c_r \alpha_k^r[f_r] \hat{f}_k^r 
= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r 
\]
as needed. 
Finally, 
\begin{align*} 
\sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r 
&= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \bigg( \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} \hat{f}_k^r(z) \bigg) \\
&= \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} \bigg(\sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r(z)\bigg) 
= \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} f(z)
= 1 . \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357189+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b6f7b66106ac510bc178ea79662cbf40119d6a1b20f404e79fcc46b2807147f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\alpha,L > 0$, $\fq \in [1,2]$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$. 
	Then, for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$,
	\begin{align}
		(\E \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu))^2
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\,,\\
	
		(\E \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\})))^2
		&\ge \bbW_2(\mu^\Ising(\cA_N),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))^2 - o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.

\begin{proof}
	Abbreviate $X = \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)$.
	By Jensen's inequality, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq]^{2/\fq} 
		\le \E[X^2] 
		= (\E X)^2 + \E[(X-\E X)^2] \stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}}{=} (\E X)^2 + o_N(1)\,.
	\]
By convexity of $\bbW_\fq(\cdot,\cdot)^\fq$, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq] = \E [\bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)^\fq] \ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^\fq\,.
	\]
	Rearranging yields the first assertion \eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}.
	The second assertion
	\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound.ising} is proved in the same way, replacing $X$ with $J \equiv \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))$ in the above argument and using \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var.ising} from Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} in place of \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376193+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_5b83f139822195103c3c1ab119a904f870e3174a3d3e76e705114a8eea765198","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A metric space is a pair (X, d) where X is a set and d is a function from X x X to the real numbers satisfying, for all x, y, z in X: (i) d(x,y) >= 0, with d(x,y) = 0 if and only if x = y; (ii) symmetry, d(x,y) = d(y,x); (iii) the triangle inequality, d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:55.028141+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b86fa0e9f153039f9ec482831a1e05d394b005dbc1c5709a834803981a5e968","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:diafree-vi-is-veb of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] $\mathcal{V}^i \cap \mathscr{L}_\Box = \mathcal{V}^e_\Box$.
  \begin{proof}
    ($\subseteq$)
    It suffices to show that for any $\Box$-p model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\Box$, and $w \in W$,
    $w \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$ iff $w \Vdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$.
    This can easily be proven by induction on the construction of $\varphi$,
    reusing the proofs of Proposition (prop:int-ext-coincides of the paper) ($\Box \Leftrightarrow$) by replacing persistency with $\Box$-persistency.

    ($\supseteq$) Suppose that there are $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\Box$, $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, and $w \in W$ such that $w \nVdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$.
    We construct a new f-model $\mathfrak{M'} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset', V)$ by letting
    $\mathord{\sqsubset'} = \mathord{\sqsubset} \cup \set{ (x, y'); \exists x'\, (x \leq x' \sqsubset y') }$,
    then $\mathfrak{M'}$ is clearly a $\Box$-p model.
    \begin{claim*}
      $x \Vdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \psi \iff x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M'} \psi$ for every $\psi \in \mathscr{L}_\Box$.
      \begin{subproof}[Proof of claim]
        We use an induction on the construction of $\psi$.
        We shall only prove the case when $\psi = \Box \chi$.

        ($\Rightarrow$)
        Suppose $x \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M'} \Box \chi$, then
        there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset' y \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M'} \chi$.
        Here, $y \nVdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \chi$ by the induction hypothesis.
        Also, $x \sqsubset' y$ implies either $x \leq x \sqsubset y$ or $x \leq x' \sqsubset y$ for some $x'$.
        In any case, $x \nVdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \Box \chi$ holds.

        ($\Leftarrow$)
        Suppose $x \nVdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \Box \chi$, then
        there are $x', y'$ such that $x \leq x' \sqsubset y' \nVdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \chi$.
        Here, $y' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M'} \chi$ by the induction hypothesis.
        Also, $x \leq x' \sqsubset y'$ implies $x \sqsubset' y$ by definition.
        Therefore, $x \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M'} \Box \chi$ holds.
      \end{subproof}
    \end{claim*}
    By the claim, $w \nVdash^i_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$ implies $w \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M'} \varphi$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:09.061920+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5baf01bfb5abdc1615b4c9aa36d03e4af83f46bcc2735dfe6edefe53e5823e91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 9 of arXiv:2606.27078, 'Semimartingale Optimal Transport with Jumps: A General Framework and Equivalent Formulatio'] Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{S}_+^d \times \mathcal{L}$ be measurable. For any $\overline{\mathbb{P}} \in \overline{\mathfrak{P}}_{\Theta}^{t,x,b,c,v}$ and any $\overline{\mathbb{F}}$-stopping time $\overline{\tau}$ taking values in $[t,1]$, the following hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)]\text{(Conditioning property.)} There exists a family of regular conditional probability measures $(\overline{\mathbb{P}}_{\overline{\omega}})_{\overline{\omega}\in\overline{\Omega}}$ of $\overline{\mathbb{P}}$ given $\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{\overline{\tau}}$ such that for $\overline{\mathbb{P}}$-almost every $\overline{\omega} \in \overline{\Omega}$,
\[

:=\overline{\mathbb{P}}_{\overline{\omega}}\bigl(\overline{\omega}\otimes_{\overline{\tau}}\tilde{\omega}\mid\tilde{\omega}\in\cdot\bigr)
\]
belongs to

\item[(2)]\text{(Concatenation property.)} Let $\{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\overline{\omega}}\}_{\overline{\omega}\in\overline{\Omega}}$ be a family of probability measures such that
\[
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\overline{\omega}} \in \overline{\mathfrak{P}}_{\Theta}^{\overline{\tau}(\overline{\omega}), \overline{\omega}_{\overline{\tau}(\overline{\omega})}}

satisfies $\overline{\mathbb{P}} \otimes_{\overline{\tau}} \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \in \overline{\mathfrak{P}}_{\Theta}^{t,x,b,c,v}$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.193766+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bb12fe1ad83e77252ac62dc01a007f8e25cd3f4eab3256370750d44415e2fdb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 24 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0$ and $0\le \rho<1$.
A random vector $(X_1,X_2)$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}_+^2$ is said to follow the
Moran--Downton bivariate exponential distribution if it has joint density
\begin{equation}
f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)
=
\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2}{1-\rho}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda_1 x_1+\lambda_2 x_2}{1-\rho}\right)\,
I_0\!\left(\frac{2\sqrt{\rho\,\lambda_1\lambda_2\,x_1x_2}}{1-\rho}\right),
\qquad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+,
\end{equation}
where $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order $0$,
\[
I_0(z)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{1}{(m!)^2}\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2m}.
\]
Under the rate parametrization used in \eqref{eq:downton-pdf}, the marginals are exponential
with rates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, and $\rho=0$ yields independence.
(Alternative scale parametrizations appear in the literature; see, e.g.,
\cite{downton1970bivariate,hanandeh2013inference}.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on R^n (for a general Radon measure on a locally compact Hausdorff space, density of C_c in L^p, p < infinity, still holds)","1 <= p <= infinity as indicated"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553780+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_5bc45a179230b3bc44038a44275348cd59550ba798a4169de50c05821e9e46a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Standard approximation arguments in L^p silently use p < infinity. On R^n with Lebesgue measure: (1) DENSITY. Continuous compactly supported functions are dense in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but their closure in L^infinity is C_0(R^n) (continuous functions vanishing at infinity), a proper closed subspace; L^infinity(R^n) is not separable, while L^p(R^n) is for p < infinity. (Simple functions are dense in L^p for every p including infinity; simple functions with support of FINITE measure are dense only for p < infinity.) (2) MOLLIFICATION. If phi is an approximate identity then phi_eps * f -> f in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but not in L^infinity: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)} each phi_eps * f is continuous, and any continuous g satisfies ||g - f||_infinity >= 1/2, so the convergence fails; in L^infinity one only gets convergence at points of continuity (and weak-* convergence). (3) TRANSLATION. h -> f(. - h) is continuous from R^n to L^p for p < infinity; in L^infinity it is not: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)}, ||f(. - h) - f||_infinity = 1 for every h not equal to 0. Consequences for proofs: any argument that proves an estimate for nice functions and 'passes to the limit by density', or that uses continuity of translation (Riemann-Lebesgue, convolution identities, Lebesgue differentiation via density), must be carried out in L^p with p < infinity, or re-done by a separate weak-* / pointwise argument at p = infinity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.766694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bd4c1726835221c5d5fda9b83b4589e84df194ca1e1f3f5d18a48455038de18","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.30223, 'Fairness in Multi-class Multi-group Classification Problems via Contextual Coherent Risk M'] A lower semi-continuous functional $\varrho: \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M) \to \Rb\cup\{+\infty\}$ is a systemic coherent risk measure with preference to small outcomes if it satisfies the following properties:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[A1.] \emph{Convexity:} For all $Z, Z' \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$ and $ \alpha \in (0,1)$, the following holds\\
                $ ~ \varrho[\alpha Z + (1-\alpha)Z'] \leq \alpha \varrho[Z] + (1 - \alpha)\varrho[Z']. $
            \item[A2.] \emph{Monotonicity:} For all $Z, Z' \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$, if $Z_i \geq Z'_i$ for all components $i = 1, \dots, M$, $P$-a.s., then $\varrho[Z] \geq \varrho[Z']$.
            \item[A3.] \emph{Positive homogeneity:} For all $Z \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$ and all constants $t > 0$, the relation $\varrho[tX] = t\varrho[X]$ holds.
            \item[A4.] \emph{Translation equivariance:} For all $Z \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$ and for all constants $a \in \Rb$, the following relation holds $\varrho[Z + a\one] = \varrho[Z] + a\varrho[\one].$
        \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:43:45.387694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bd7c5acd4bda33e96d87cae15b1afc3e6d39b68c767eddc3b7dd8179ceda9b5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 of arXiv:2609.04139, 'The conformally invariant metric on CLE$_4$ II:\\ existence of geodesics'] We define a \emph{geodesic CLE$_4$ metric coupling} to be a family of couplings
	\begin{equation*}
	 	D = \left\{\left( \Gamma_U, D_{\Gamma_U}^U \right)\right\}_U
	\end{equation*}
	where $U \subsetneq \BC$ ranges over all simply connected domains and $\Gamma_U$ is a non-nested CLE$_4$ in $U$, such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*), ref=\Roman*]
		\item {\bfseries (Geodesic metric)} $D_{\Gamma_U}^U$ is a.s.\ a metric on $\Gamma_U$ such that the following hold.
			\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=\roman*]
				\item For each $\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma_U$, there exists an admissible path $P$ (which we refer to as a \emph{$D_{\Gamma_U}^U$-geodesic}) connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$ such that $D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL_1, \SCL_2) = \len(P; D_{\Gamma_U}^U)$. The same is true with a deterministic connected arc (resp.\ two deterministic and disjoint connected arcs) of $\partial U$ in place of $\SCL_1$ (resp.\ $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$).
				\item Let $\phi\colon U \to \BD$ be a conformal mapping. For every $\SCL \in \Gamma_U$, the process $(\phi(\SCB_t(\SCL; D^U_{\Gamma_U}){)})_{t\ge 0}$ is c\`adl\`ag for the Hausdorff distance, and the same is true with a deterministic connected arc of $\partial U$ in place of $\SCL$.
				\item For all $t, s\ge 0$, if $\SCB_t(\SCL_1; D^U_{\Gamma_U}) \cap \SCB_s(\SCL_2; D^U_{\Gamma_U}) \neq \emptyset$, then $D^U_{\Gamma_U} (\SCL_1, \SCL_2) \le t+s$. The same is true with a deterministic connected arc (resp.\ two deterministic and disjoint connected arcs) of $\partial U$ in place of $\SCL_1$ (resp.\ $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$).
			\end{enumerate}
			Note that $\len(P; D_{\Gamma_U}^U) \ge D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL_1,\SCL_2)$ for every admissible path $P$ connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$, by the triangle inequality along the chains in the definition of $\len$; a path attaining equality is thus 
			what the term geodesic refers to. 
		\item {\bfseries (Locality)} Let $V \subset U$ be a deterministic simply connected subdomain. Let $I \subset \partial U$ be a deterministic connected arc. Let $\{V_j\}_j$ be the connected components of $V^\star$. Then, conditionally on
				\begin{multline}
					\bigl\{\SCL \in \Gamma_U : \SCL \not\subset V\bigr\}, \quad \bigl\{\SCB_t(\SCL; D_{\Gamma_U}^U) : \SCL \in \Gamma_U, \ \SCL \not\subset V, \ t \in [0, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL, \partial V^\star)]\bigr\}, \\
					\text{and} \quad \bigl\{\SCB_t(I; D_{\Gamma_U}^U) : t \in [0, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(I, \partial V^\star)]\bigr\},
				\end{multline}
			the $(\Gamma_U|_{V_j}, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\bullet, \bullet; V_j))$'s are independent and their conditional laws are those of $(\Gamma_{V_j}, D_{\Gamma_{V_j}}^{V_j})$, respectively. 
		\item {\bfseries (Conformal invariance)} Let $\phi \colon U \to \phi(U)$ be a deterministic conformal mapping. Then,
		\begin{equation*}
			\left(\phi(\Gamma_U), \left( D_{\Gamma_U}^U\left(\phi^{-1}(\SCL_1), \phi^{-1}(\SCL_2) \right) \right)_{\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \phi(\Gamma_U)} \right)
			 \overset{(\mathrm{d})}{=} \left( \Gamma_{\phi(U)}, \left(D_{\Gamma_{\phi(U)}}^{\phi(U)}(\SCL_1, \SCL_2) \right)_{\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma_{\phi(U)}} \right).
		\end{equation*}
		The equality in law is understood as in \Cref{def:weak_axioms}.
		
			
				
				
			
		
		
			
			
		\item {\bfseries (Uniform exploration)} The collection $\{(\SCL, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL, \partial U))\}_{\SCL \in \Gamma_U}$ has the law of a uniform exploration of $\Gamma_U$ (cf.~\cite{CoInCLEExpl}), in the sense of \Cref{def:weak_axioms}.
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the ambient space is R^d with Lebesgue outer measure defined by countable covers by boxes","L is the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable sets and lambda = lambda* restricted to L","R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and lambda is finite on bounded sets - this is what drives regularity","the axiom of choice is used only for the remark that non-measurable sets exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815011+00:00","domain":"measure theory, real analysis","id":"claim_5be137db7963f504ae7ade7e44a43ba8c850915205425ffc83a5dcc77d7cfe50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda* denote Lebesgue outer measure on R^d, defined by lambda*(E) = inf of sum of volumes of countably many open boxes covering E, let L be the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable (Lebesgue measurable) sets, and let lambda = lambda* restricted to L. Then: (1) OUTER REGULARITY, valid for EVERY set E contained in R^d, measurable or not: lambda*(E) = inf { lambda(U) : U open, U contains E }. (2) MEASURABILITY CRITERION: E is in L if and only if for every eps > 0 there is an open U containing E with lambda*(U \\ E) < eps, if and only if there is a G_delta set G containing E with lambda(G \\ E) = 0, if and only if there is an F_sigma set F contained in E with lambda(E \\ F) = 0. (3) INNER REGULARITY by compact sets, valid for every E in L: lambda(E) = sup { lambda(K) : K compact, K contained in E } (both sides may be +infinity). Equivalently, for E in L with lambda(E) < infinity and eps > 0 there is a compact K contained in E with lambda(E \\ K) < eps. Thus lambda is a Radon measure: it is finite on compacta, outer regular and inner regular. (4) COMPLETENESS: if lambda*(N) = 0 then N is in L and lambda(N) = 0, and hence every subset of a null set is measurable with measure zero. Equivalently, (R^d, L, lambda) is the completion of (R^d, Borel, lambda|Borel): L = { B union Z : B Borel, Z a subset of a Borel null set }. SHARP EDGES. (a) The Borel sigma-algebra itself is NOT complete: the Cantor set is Borel and null, it has 2^continuum subsets, all of them Lebesgue null and hence Lebesgue measurable, while there are only continuum many Borel sets; so L is strictly larger than the Borel sigma-algebra, and 'measurable' must never be silently upgraded to 'Borel'. (b) Regularity statements about the MEASURE are for measurable sets. Outer regularity in the form (1) does hold for arbitrary sets because it is the definition of the outer measure, but inner regularity fails badly for non-measurable sets: a Vitali set has inner measure 0 and positive outer measure, so the two approximations do not meet. It is exactly the meeting of the two that measurability expresses. (c) Completeness is what makes 'a.e. defined' harmless: if f = g almost everywhere and f is measurable then g is measurable. That inference is FALSE in the Borel sigma-algebra, and is a frequent silent error. (d) Regularity is not automatic for general Borel measures: on a non-sigma-compact or non-locally-compact space a finite Borel measure need not be inner regular by compact sets. Lebesgue measure is regular because R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and because lambda is finite on boxes. (e) Not every set is measurable: the existence of a non-measurable set uses the axiom of choice, and translation invariance plus countable additivity forbid extending lambda to all subsets of R^d.","status":"unverified"}

\begin{enumerate}[(Z1)]
\item If $e_1,e_2,e_3$ are the three edges forming the boundary of a triangular face and
\[\Theta(e_1)+\Theta(e_2)+\Theta(e_3)>\pi,\]
then for every permutation $\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}$ we have

\[\Theta(e_1)+\Theta(e_2)<\pi.\]

\item If $e_1,e_2,e_3$ are the three edges forming the boundary of a triangular face, then for every permutation $\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}$ we have
\[\cos\Theta(e_i)+\cos\Theta(e_j)\cos\Theta(e_k)\ge 0.\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda, u~v} G(x,u) J_{uv} G(v,y), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:01:39.423634+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bf5cd8a3b8073b000bf586e49d568cc59681217a314e43111c183fd44b73f72","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:max_string of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Assume that $\mu$ is critical and belongs to the domain of attraction of a stable law.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Assume that $\mu_{1}>0$.  Set
$$t_n^* = \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log n + \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log(1-\mu_1).$$

$$\P\bigl(H_{1} ( \mathcal{T}^{n})  \leq \lfloor t_n^* + t\rfloor\bigr) - \exp\bigl(-\mu_1^{t+1 - \{t_n^* + t\}}\bigr)   \quad \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{n \rightarrow \infty} \quad  0$$
\item[(ii)] Let $r\ge2$ be such that $\mu_r>0$, and set
$$
  t_n^{**}=\log_r\log n-

$$
Write $m_n=\lfloor t_n^{**}\rfloor$ and
$\theta_n=\{t_n^{**}\}$, where $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ is the fractional part, and define
$$
  J_n=
  \begin{cases}
    \{m_n-1,m_n\},&\theta_n\le\tfrac12,\\
    \{m_n,m_n+1\},&\theta_n>\tfrac12.
  \end{cases}
$$
Then $
  \P(H_r(\mathcal T^n)\in J_n)\longrightarrow1$.
Moreover, if $\liminf_n\min(\theta_n,1-\theta_n)>0$, then
$\P(H_r(\mathcal T^n)=m_n)\to1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.678434+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5c3942bd72d7c650445c0a7f0f535117f53e452df25a1c1183aaee75dd916652","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2607.25949, 'Block-hierarchical covariance decompositions for finite-block additive functionals'] (Projection onto the marginal subspace).\\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.970423+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5c4af63f01fa043c0fc1620209c3d84310c587020dc89813c7e27378b396d249","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $q\geq2$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.381791+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5c68e6b514684d6e146036428d36a08a1fd20636c38b9ca637fd6e405389756d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:block-shuffle-law of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] A random permutation $\rho\in S_n$ with law $q_B$ is generated as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Sample an offset $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0,1,\dots,B-1\}$.
  \item Work in the rotated coordinates $t'=\phi_{U}^{-1}(t)$ and partition
        $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into consecutive blocks of size $B$
        (except possibly the final block).
  \item On each block, independently sample a uniform random permutation.
        Let $\Pi$ denote the resulting blockwise permutation in the rotated
        coordinates.
  \item Define the final permutation on the original labels by
        \[
          \rho(t)
          \;:=\;
          \phi_{U}\bigl(\Pi(\phi_{U}^{-1}(t))\bigr),
          \qquad t=1,\dots,n.
        \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.693153+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5c7b13f7fba33cd3e84c4bfb37125ee68eb1ca4704cb7e852e1d0bfe5bf9fe27","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 33 (Atomless Stieltjes product measures) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_N$ be finite signed or complex Borel measures on a compact interval $I$, and suppose that each total-variation measure $\abs{\nu_j}$ is atomless.

\[
\abs{\nu_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\nu_N}
=
\abs{\nu_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\abs{\nu_N}.
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:16:46.139236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5c84a93ce032fbe1f581a997a5b63862de131c898d4cf62a7ed28413d1c6e64e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:tilted-gibbs-derivatives of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Let the tilted partition function be
    \[
        Z_{A,\beta, x_0} := \sum_{\sigma \in \{-1,1\}^n} e^{\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i , j}A_{i,j}\sigma_i\sigma_j + \left\langle\sigma,y_t\right\rangle}\,.

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu) is a probability space and T is measure-preserving","the partition is finite or countable and consists of measurable sets","for the two-sided join T must be invertible"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250796+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_5c8ad06c4539071020c4a52ccb50fab1a5b23a0b5f4b9e11e00d40a599f8d3a6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a measure-preserving system on a probability space with $T$ invertible (a measure-preserving automorphism). A finite or countable measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, A_2, \\dots\\}$ of $X$ is a (two-sided) generator if the smallest $\\sigma$-algebra containing all the sets $T^{-n} A_i$, $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$, coincides with $\\mathcal{B}$ up to $\\mu$-null sets; in join notation, $\\bigvee_{n=-\\infty}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi = \\mathcal{B}$ (mod $\\mu$). For a non-invertible $T$ one uses the one-sided join $\\bigvee_{n=0}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi$ and speaks of a one-sided (strong) generator. Why it matters: by the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem, if $\\xi$ is a generator with finite entropy $H_\\mu(\\xi) < \\infty$ then the measure-theoretic entropy of the system equals the entropy relative to $\\xi$, $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; no supremum over partitions is needed. Existence (Krieger): an ergodic automorphism of a Lebesgue probability space with $h_\\mu(T) < \\log k$ has a generator with $k$ atoms; a system with infinite entropy has no finite generator. Sharp edges: a partition may generate for one invariant measure and not another; the join over $n \\geq 0$ alone need not generate for an automorphism (e.g. the time-zero partition of a two-sided shift does not generate one-sidedly); and 'generates' is a statement mod null sets, not about separating every pair of points, although separating points does imply generating (see the Walters entry).","status":"unverified"}

and that the associated conditional law of large numbers error is of
order $\hat\varepsilon_N$.

Under convenient Lipschitz and growth assumptions, if
$X^1,\ldots, X^N$ are i.i.d. (conditionally on the common noise when
present), then there exists a constant $C$, independent of $N$ and of
the discretization parameter $ n,$ such that

\[
\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(X_{s,t}^{n,N}(X),\widehat{X}_{s,t}^{n,N}(X))
\le
C\Big(
\frac1N+\bar\varepsilon_N+\hat\varepsilon_N
\Big).
\]
The same estimate holds for the associated continuous-time flows.
In the central-limit setting, the quantitative
results of Rio and Bonis imply

\[
\bar\varepsilon_N+\hat\varepsilon_N
=
O(N^{-1}),
\]
so that
\[
\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(X_{s,t}^{n,N}(X),\widehat{X}_{s,t}^{n,N}(X))
\le
\frac{C}{N} .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:48:17.118405+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5cb1147c8aa67ab196c57532cee91f3cc261ff327b72d78a1aa0e6562baadaf5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2605.27212, '2605.27212'] Let \(P\) be a coordinate-replacement kernel as in
\eqref{eq:abstract-fibre-decomposition} on \(\mathcal X=S^N\), with invariant
set \(\Omega\), product law \(\mu\), stationary law \(\pi=\mu(\cdot\mid\Omega)\),
and good set \(G\subseteq\Omega\).  Assume \(\pi(G)>0\).  Suppose that the
following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=*]
    \item There is a constant \(A<\infty\) such that, for every nonnegative
    \(F:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) with \(\supp(F)\subseteq G\),
    \[
        \Ent_\mu(F^2)\le A\cE_P^\mu(F,F).
    \]
    \item There are \(t_*\ge0\), an integer \(L\ge1\), and \(\eta\ge0\) such
    that, uniformly in \(x\in\Omega\) and all integers \(s\ge t_*\),
    \[
        \Prob_x(\exists\,u\in\{0,1,\ldots,L\}:X_{s+u}\notin G)\le\eta.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
Set
\begin{equation}
    t_{\mathrm{conf}}=2A\log(e+\log|\Omega|),
\end{equation}
and define
\begin{equation}
    \zeta=\Prob(\operatorname{Poi}(t_{\mathrm{conf}})>L),
    \qquad
    R=e^{-t_{\mathrm{conf}}/A}\log|\Omega|+A\frac{\pi(G^c)}{\pi(G)}.
\end{equation}
Then, for every \(x\in\Omega\) and every integer \(s\ge t_*\),
\begin{equation}
    \left\|\delta_xP^s e^{t_{\mathrm{conf}}(P-I)}-\pi\right\|_{\TV}
    \le 2(\eta+\zeta)+\sqrt{R/2}+\pi(G^c).
\end{equation}
Consequently, if
\begin{equation}
    2(\eta+\zeta)+\sqrt{R/2}+\pi(G^c)
    +\Prob(\operatorname{Poi}(2t_*)<t_*)\le\frac14,
\end{equation}
then the continuous-time chain satisfies
\[
    t_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{cont}}(1/4)\le 2t_*+t_{\mathrm{conf}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["self-similar variable D = eps/3 + (2/3) D' with eps in {0,+1,-1}, weights P(eps=0)=1/2, P(eps=+-1)=1/4 each, D' an independent copy of D","C acting on the space of functions analytic on a disk of radius R>1 for any such R (each of the three branches maps such a disk strictly inside itself since (2/3)R + 1/3 < R)"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.981254+00:00","domain":"probability/Bernoulli convolutions","id":"claim_5cc090e69a1249a99b39654f730fe87b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the composition operator (C phi)(t) = sum_eps p_eps phi(eps/3 + (2/3) t) of the Bernoulli-2/3 self-similar variable D = eps/3 + (2/3) D' (eps in {0, +1, -1} with weights 1/2, 1/4, 1/4): the three branches map every disk of radius R > 1 strictly into itself, since (2/3) R + 1/3 < R, so C is compact on functions analytic there, with eigenvalue 1 on the constants; and its spectrum is exactly {(2/3)^n : n >= 0} union {0}. Proof: every branch has the same derivative 2/3, so C(t^n) = sum_eps p_eps (eps/3 + (2/3) t)^n = (2/3)^n t^n + (terms of lower degree), the leading coefficient being (2/3)^n times sum_eps p_eps = 1; C maps the polynomials of degree at most n into themselves with diagonal (2/3)^k, and on a space of analytic functions in which the monomials form a basis the spectrum is exactly these powers together with 0. In particular the second eigenvalue is exactly 2/3 (an interval-arithmetic estimate near 1/2 is wrong). Numerically, Chebyshev discretisations at 24, 40, 60 and 80 nodes give leading moduli 1, 0.666667, 0.444444, 0.296296, 0.197531, 0.131687, the powers of 2/3 to six figures and stable under refinement. Consequence: an argument for a square-integrable density of the Bernoulli convolution at ratio 2/3 needs a rate strictly below 2/3 with exponential room, and this spectral gap is exactly 2/3, so no argument whose only input is this gap can work - consistent with the equivalence, via a Fejer minorant, of the rate 2/3 exactly with square-integrability. The general lesson: for a self-similar measure whose maps share one contraction ratio, the transfer operator is triangular in the monomial basis and its gap is forced to be that ratio.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.970695+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ce4be691da27769be2ee03e26358ef7f514395397311b53c2845958d59d86bd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 20 (Low degrees, long hooks, and unbounded depth) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Over \(\mathbb C\), with excess-row Schur functors understood to vanish,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.333344+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5cebffbb64d5b1bda122261e55afae0fd9ff228e7522de7b592b418e505d7af0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:motivationnormaltrace of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain with unit outer normal $\nu.$
    We denote by ${\operatorname{tr}}_N$ the normal trace operator
  \begin{align*}
      {\operatorname{tr}}_N&:H^{\operatorname{div}}(\Omega) \to H^{-1/2}(\partial \Omega) = (H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega))',
  \end{align*}    
    which extends the normal component trace operator 
    $$H^1(\Omega)\to H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega), f\mapsto {\operatorname{tr}} (f) \cdot \nu.$$
    The normal trace operator ${\operatorname{tr}}_N$ is well-defined, bounded and surjective, see e.g. Lemma 20.2 in [tartar2007introduction].
 For $f\in C^1(\Omega)^n, \psi \in H^1(\Omega)$,  we note the identity 
 \begin{align} 
    \int_{\partial \Omega}  {\operatorname{tr}}(\psi) f\cdot \nu \;\mathrm{d} \sigma &= \int_\Omega {\operatorname{div}}(f\psi)\;\mathrm{d} x 
    \\&= \int_\Omega f\cdot \nabla \psi + {\operatorname{div}}(f)\psi \;\mathrm{d} x,\nonumber
 \end{align} which extends by density to 
\begin{align}
      \duality{{\operatorname{tr}}_N(f)}{{\operatorname{tr}} (\psi)} &= \int_\Omega f\cdot \nabla \psi + {\operatorname{div}}(f) \psi \;\mathrm{d} x 
  \end{align} for $f\in H^{\operatorname{div}}( \Omega),\psi \in H^{1}( \Omega).$
      Here and in the following, we understand that if $\Omega$ is a one-dimensional domain and $f$ is some function defined on $\partial\Omega$, then $$\int_{\partial\Omega} f\cdot \nu\;\mathrm{d}\sigma = f\left(\sup_{x\in \Omega} x\right)-f\left(\inf_{x\in \Omega} x\right) ~\textnormal{ and }~\int_\Gamma f\cdot \nu \;\mathrm{d}\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} \mathds{1}_\Gamma f\cdot \nu \;\mathrm{d}\sigma. $$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.379007+00:00","domain":"computational complexity","id":"claim_5cf451104b9a1b84418b2f8b52dd40b240808050404e42746fff312bc8777f09","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) is the class of languages with polynomial-time verifiable membership certificates: L is in NP if there exist a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine V (the verifier) such that for every string x, x is in L if and only if there exists a certificate string y with length at most p(length of x) and V accepts the pair (x, y). General T267 remains open.

# C018 v1: finite-width nonlinear transfer of the iid-head construction
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
This is a four-point, label-noise-averaged witness theorem. It does not
claim double descent for one realized label vector or settle general T267.

## 1. Exact model and statement
Use C017's definitions: 0<e<1/4, D=1+e^2+e^4, uniform population on
x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2 t)/sqrt(D), one training observation at each of these
four inputs, and u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The teacher is
 g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2, c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2.
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. For each of the sixteen sign vectors
xi in {-1,1}^4, train a separate network with labels
 y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, sigma_e=2 alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e)).
All sixteen networks share their initial parameters. At width m these are
 f_m(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_(j=1)^m a_j ReLU(w_j.x),
 w_j(0) iid N(0,I_3), a_j(0) iid uniform {-nu,nu}, independent of w_j(0).
Train BOTH layers by simultaneous discrete GD with step gamma=1/2 on
(1/8) sum_i (f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2. Set the derivative at a zero gate to zero.
No pairing, tying or resetting of the readout is imposed.
Define the clean population risk averaged over the sixteen trained networks:
 R_(e,m)(k)= (1/16) sum_xi (1/4) sum_i (f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
Probability below is over initialization only. In particular R is NOT the
risk trajectory of any one of the sixteen networks.

Let lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of C=H/4, where
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z],
and let b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s.
The clock premises proved in C009 are b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), eta_e~e.
Let independent standard normals G_s,G_t define
 a=2nu^2 G_s^2, B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2,
 p=P(kappa^2>4aB).

For every epsilon>0 define E_(e,m)(epsilon) as existence of integers
0<=k0<k1<k2<k3 such that
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),
and k2 maximizes R on the integer interval [k1,k3], with
 | k2 / ((6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e)) - 1 | < epsilon.
Then
 liminf_(e downarrow 0) liminf_(m to infinity) P(E_(e,m)(epsilon)) >= p
 >= max(0,1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2).                       (1)
More precisely, for every zeta>0 there are constants c>0,L<infinity
such that the inner/outer liminf probability of witnesses with each of
the three displayed strict risk gaps >=c alpha_e^2 eta_e and
 |b_s k2-(3/2)log(1/e)|<=L
is at least p-zeta. Negative lower bounds are understood as vacuous.
This proves two descents separated by a rise in the finite-witness sense,
with an interior interval peak. It does not prove unique stationary points
or monotonicity of the intervening integer-time segments.

## 2. What the preceding proofs provide
C017 proves, in its joint Gaussian initialization coupling, locally uniform
convergence of centered risk differences
 [Q_e(t_e(s))-Q_e(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
       -> V(s)-V(0),
where t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s and
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
The derivative converges too, although this proof only transfers values.
On Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0, V has a simple minimum r and a simple maximum v,
with r<v, decreasing before r, increasing on (r,v), decreasing after v.
Their formulas are r=-log((kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a)) and
v=-log((kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a)). The probability a=0 is zero.
C009 Section 3 proves the following finite-horizon fact for the SAME
nonzero iid initialization: for fixed e, bounded labels, and finite integer T,
actual nonlinear predictions at all four inputs, uniformly over k<=T and
all sixteen label patterns, approach frozen deterministic-C predictions
started from the actual initial vector, in probability as m tends to infinity.
That proof controls gates through initial weighted Gaussian bands and keeps
the exact simultaneous-update remainder. Its deterministic residual bounds
can use any finite initial residual bound; replacing its old teacher/labels
by the present bounded labels changes only this bound. Thus its argument
applies verbatim for each fixed e here. The small-e limit is taken AFTER the
width limit; no uniform width estimate in e or T is inferred.
These preceding claims are unaudited dependencies, not independent audits.

## 3. From nonlinear prediction transfer to the correct joint risk limit
For fixed e and T, the initial four-vector converges by the multivariate iid
CLT to C017's Gaussian Z_e (expressed in Walsh coordinates). The empirical
initial tangent kernel converges in probability to the deterministic C.
These facts hold jointly: no independence between the finite-width initial
output and its empirical kernel is needed, since the latter limit is constant.
C009's comparison is already to deterministic C with the same initial output.

Frozen predictions at times 0,...,T are affine continuous functions of the
initial four-vector, with labels fixed. For the finite sixteen-label family,
the corresponding frozen risk array is therefore a continuous function of
this vector. Actual and frozen risk arrays differ by o_P(1). Indeed for
vectors u,v measured in population L2, the exact bound
 | ||u-g||^2-||v-g||^2 | <= ||u-v||(2||v-g||+||u-v||)
applies; the finite frozen array is tight at fixed e,T by its continuous
Gaussian limit, and C009 supplies uniform o_P(1) prediction error. Averaging
a finite sixteen terms preserves this estimate. Slutsky then gives joint
weak convergence of the whole actual risk array to (Q_e(k))_(k=0)^T.
At fixed e, alpha_e^2 eta_e is strictly positive, so the same assertion holds
for risks centered at any fixed time and divided by this scale. There is
no claim that an unscaled o_P(1) error is uniform in e.

## 4. Finite witnesses, rounding, and the open-event argument
Fix a Gaussian realization in {Delta>0,a>0}. Choose small radii h0,h1>0
with r-h0<r<v<v+h1. Because V is strictly decreasing immediately before
r, increasing on (r,v), and decreasing after v, the values at
 r-h0, r, v, v+h1
have the required decrease/rise/decrease gaps. All are strict. On the
closed interval [r,v+h1], V has its unique global maximum at v. For any
sufficiently small d>0, the maximum over the complement of (v-d,v+d)
in that interval is strictly smaller than V(v), by continuity and compactness.

Convergence of centered risk differences locally uniformly in s therefore
preserves the three gaps, as well as the separated interval maximum, for
all sufficiently small e depending on this realization. Round all four
t_e anchor times to nearest integers. Their s coordinates change by at
most b_s/2, which tends to zero. They remain ordered because their fixed
s spacings are positive. The interpolation values at the rounded anchors
converge to the same V values. The same local uniform convergence controls
ALL integer times between the rounded second and fourth anchors. It gives
an interior maximizing grid index, with s coordinate in (v-d,v+d).
It follows pathwise that its s coordinate tends to v: apply this argument
for every rational d>0. Its peak-time leading coefficient is consequently
6pi/nu^2. This rounding step makes no claim about continuous interpolation
of actual nonlinear GD, which is only evaluated at integer times.

For precision in passing probabilities, fix zeta>0. The preceding pathwise
argument and a countable exhaustion allow deterministic c>0,L<infinity
such that, on an event of probability at least p-zeta, the three gaps of
the Gaussian-limit integer curves exceed 2c alpha_e^2 eta_e, all their
anchors lie in |s|<L-1, and an interior interval maximizer lies in |s|<L-1,
for all sufficiently small e in the following probabilistic sense: the
liminf of these event probabilities is at least p-zeta. One explicit
exhaustion bounds all four Gaussian coordinates, bounds a away from zero,
bounds Delta away from zero, bounds r and v, and then restricts each
positive limiting value gap and peak-separation margin away from zero.
These compact events exhaust {Delta>0,a>0}; local uniform convergence and
Fatou give the asserted liminf. Uniform convergence over compact Gaussian
parameters can also be used, but is not required.

For each fixed sufficiently small e, there are only finitely many indices
with |b_s k-(3/2)log(1/e)|<=L. Consider the following event in this FINITE
risk array: there exist k0<k1<j<k3 in this window such that all three
witness gaps at j exceed c alpha_e^2 eta_e, and every index in [k1,k3]
with a peak time outside the desired localization band has risk strictly
less than R(j). This is a finite union of finite intersections of strict
inequalities, hence open. If the excluded set is empty its inequalities
are vacuous. An interval maximizer then lies inside the desired band,
and substituting that maximizer for j preserves the three strict gaps.
The Gaussian arrays just constructed belong to such an open event (with
extra positive margins), taking either the band |s|<L or the relative
peak-time band of (1); for small e the whole fixed s window is inside the
relative band. Enlarge the finite horizon to include the whole window.
The joint weak convergence in Section 3 and the open-set Portmanteau
inequality transfer its probability LOWER bound to the nonlinear arrays.
Take liminf in e, then let zeta decrease to zero, proving (1).
For the refined gap statement retain zeta and c,L from the exhaustion.
Only fixed-e finite arrays are used in each width limit. There is no
exchange of the two limits, no infinite-horizon NTK claim, and no assertion
that finite-width Gaussian mode coefficients are independent.

## 5. Probability bound and scope
C017 gives E(4aB)=8nu^2(1+nu^2) using independence of G_s and G_t.
Markov's inequality bounds P(4aB>=kappa^2) and yields (1). Arbitrarily
large fixed kappa makes the bound approach one; sigma_e still tends to
zero and is <=1 for sufficiently small e. The teacher direction has norm
one. The input distribution is uniform on four shrinking, clustered atoms,
with a stratified training set of size four, not an iid Gaussian sample.
Width tends to infinity first, so this is an iterated-limit lazy-regime
result about actual nonlinear parameter updates, not macroscopic feature
learning. The risk average spans sixteen different GD trajectories.
The unresolved hardest piece for a one-dataset theorem is control of the
realized-noise cross terms on the alpha_e^2 eta_e central gap scale.
General Target 1, fixed-noise regimes, continuous iid-input extensions of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.193935+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5d1ee31e82c101a10ca5dbcc236666bbe2b6db422227f098a9f33cfb76b005fb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 26 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $q_1,q_2\in(0,1)$, $\beta_1,\beta_2>0$, and $\theta\in(0,1]$.
A random vector $X=(X_1,X_2)$ on $\mathbb{N}_0^2$ is said to follow the bivariate discrete Weibull
model (as used in this paper) if its joint survival function is

\begin{equation*}
S(k_1,k_2)
=
\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge k_1,\;X_2\ge k_2)
=
q_1^{k_1^{\beta_1}}\,q_2^{k_2^{\beta_2}}\,\theta^{\,k_1^{\beta_1}k_2^{\beta_2}},
\qquad (k_1,k_2)\in\mathbb{N}_0^2,
\end{equation*}

and the pmf is computed from $S$ via \eqref{eq:pmf-from-survival}.
The marginals satisfy $S(k_1,0)=q_1^{k_1^{\beta_1}}$ and $S(0,k_2)=q_2^{k_2^{\beta_2}}$,
so each component is a (univariate) discrete Weibull distribution in the sense of
Nakagawa--Osaki \cite{nakagawa1975discrete}.
The case $\theta=1$ yields independence (product survival).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.058677+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5d2a01932e237707051bd26d248165e1f5a46518e45c599bcfda662ab88e05f5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2608.15914, 'Absorption cutoff and stationary singularities for rounded Gaussian random dynamical syste'] For every $0\leq\beta<N$, the operator $\Lcal_{A,N,\beta}$ is bounded on

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:31.978017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5d3007c7da3959991387d099cb2cfebc8dd36b5a291a370b77a87c2c75e804b8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 6 (Stability and uniqueness) of arXiv:2606.11369, 'Mean-field limits for stochastic particle systems on dense graphs'] Let $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ and $(\nu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ be two weak solutions of
\eqref{eq:weak_limit} satisfying the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lem:moment_limit}.
For $k\ge0$, write
\[
\mu_t^k(du):=\mu_t(du,\{k\}),\qquad
\nu_t^k(du):=\nu_t(du,\{k\}),
\]
and set
\[
\Delta_t^k:=\mu_t^k-\nu_t^k .
\]
Define
\[
\Theta(t):=\sum_{k\ge0}(1+k)|\Delta_t^k|([0,1]).
\]
Then there exists a constant $C_T>0$ such that
\[
\Theta(t)\le e^{C_Tt}\Theta(0),
\qquad t\in[0,T].
\]
In particular, if $\mu_0=\nu_0$, then $\mu_t=\nu_t$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.","status":"unverified"}
